0.title: Day 0: The calm before the storm
paragraphs: Wow, it's all happening.
For those of you that I did not have the pleasure to catch up with before I left, and fill in on what I'm doing, here's a quick summary.

I'm moving to Germany semi-permanently, and making a bit of a voyage out of getting there. Tomorrow morning, I'll be flying from Sydney up to the Whitsundays in Queensland to get on a boat, where I'll volunteer/work for the next ~six weeks as a crew member as we sail over to Indonesia.
No, I don't know how to sail. No, I've never met the captain before. Yes, it's just the two of us. Should be fun!

I have a week to learn the ropes (heh) before we get to Cairns and begin the crossing over to Indonesia. I'm hoping with some quick training and a little how to sail for dummies Youtube video on the plane ride tomorrow, we'll be right as rain.

Once in Indonesia I'm going to say goodbye to Dave (the captain 🫡) and start my overland crossing to Germany. This will include a few more short boat rides over to Malaysia. Then the rest of the way to Germany.
The current route looks like this:

Indonesia
Malaysia
Thailand
Laos
China
Kyrgyzstan*
Kazakhstan
Azerbaijan**
Georgia
Turkey
Bulgaria***
Serbia***
Hungary***
Austria***
Germany***
* I may pass straight from China into Kazakhstan, depending on whether I want to see Kashgar in China or the Almaty region in Kazakhstan more.
** Azerbaijan has closed its land borders to travelers since COVID. I may bypass them out of spite so I don't have to get in a plane.
*** Route from Turkey to Germany is very flexible, may go further east into Romania depending on what month I get there.

This little mosey over there should take around 5 months, but eh, no biggie if I get there later than I had planned. My 1 year german visa starts in September, so arriving later that that will just mean I don't get to spend as much time in Germany, unless I stay longer on another visa.
It hasn't really hit me that I'm leaving yet, I think that will probably happen on the plane ride tomorrow.
It's late and I have to take my computer apart now, stay tuned for another update tomorrow!

1.title: Day 1: On the water
paragraphs: Today, I have taken the following modes of transport in order:
Car - Train - Plane - Bus - Dingy
I started in my bed in Wollongong this morning and ended up on a boat in the Airlie beach harbour, where I am currently gently rocking as I write this.

Upon arriving at Airlie Beach I met Dave, the owner of the boat, and knew we'd get on when I saw he had a copy of Homo Deus, a book I'd been meaning to read! Also aboard is Kate, the other crew member and a nice woman who helped me shop and get set up in my bunk.

Dave and I jumped in the dinghy and motored out to "Cheshire Cat", Dave's 10 1/2 metre Catamaran that we'll be taking over to Indonesia. He gave me a half hour tour and rundown of the sails(main, jib, and screecher), electronic system(generator, inverter, batteries, and switches), water pumps(salt and fresh), anchor system, outboard motor, and emergency protocol. I've tried my best to retain as much as possible but will need to see much of it in practice before I understand what is going on at all. at least I've retained how to press the man overboard button if they both fall out.
I made a stir fry for us for dinner, over which we had a good chat. Feeling good about today, and looking forward to the journey!

2.title: Day 2: Getting moving
paragraphs: The journey has begun under excellent conditions. This morning we unmoored and motored over to the public jetty to refill our water supply, and then once we were done and clear of the marina we raised our sails.
First we flew directly with the wind with the mainsail and screecher out in opposite directions, then turned to head mostly perpendicular to the wind and flipped the screecher.

It was great fun to feel the boat move with the wind, and I helped Dave all through the process as much as I could. We sailed for about an hour to an inlet on Hook island, and anchored here for the rest of the afternoon. We'd pulled nearby to Flying Colours, the boat of an old friend of Dave's, Darren, who we'll be continuing up to Indonesia with.

I went for a swim, a paddleboard and a brief unsuccessful snorkel, while still managing to fit in a good nap on the deck under the cool shade of the stowed paddleboard. While on the paddleboard I thought I saw a large orange Jellyfish like we have in the Hawkesbury down in Sydney, and if you followed my Perth trip you'll be familiar with the disdain I harbour for jellies. I was pleasantly surprised to see a little head pop up next to the orange blob, revealing it to be the shell of a sea turtle!
In the evening we all jumped in the dinghies and rode over to the beach for a fire, though I cut my foot on some coral on the wade through the low tide.

On the way back to the boat we saw a stingray and innumerable fish panicking and jumping out of the dark water, and Dave even pointed out some bioluminescence in the wake of the dinghy! We're still deciding if we'll stay here tomorrow or start heading north, as there's going to be some bad weather later this week that we won't be able to sail in.

3.title: Day 3: Small travels
paragraphs: It has surprised me that this journey has been far less arduous, and with less actual work involved, than I had suspected before my involvement. This may change in the future when we pass Cairns and aim to cover more ground per day, but today we sailed for just a few hours, and only had to tack once right before we arrived at Gloucester island. That means that the only real work to do is raising and lowering the sails to start the journey which doesn't take more than 10-15 minutes, and on route the autopilot adjusts the steering to stay on the course set on the computer.

The scenery here is incredibly beautiful, and there is a distinct difference between viewing the coast from a terrestrial point of view, versus from on the water. The novelty assuredly plays a large role.

We arrived at the island in the late morning, and so I swam the ~200m to the beach to take a look around. Before I jumped in Kate warned me that the area was a fisherman's paradise with a knowing look, and confirmed that she was worried about sharks when I asked. As much as I know that being attacked by a shark has an infinitesimally slim chance of occurring, that did little to assuage my primal fear as I swam the distance alone over the water with only the sunlight beams penetrating into the hazy blue visible beneath me.

In the evening we all went over to the beach for a small fire, and I spent around half an hour opening a coconut that I had found, that didn't look as rotten as some of the others. I amused the others with my paleolithic antics as I repeatedly bashed the husk between two rocks to loosen it, crouching on the sand near the fire. At one point the tiresome effort had me working up a decent sweat and feeling quite warm, and internally I debated taking my shirt off, but decided that would be a little too far in the caveman direction.

I eventually opened the thing and drank the water out after a few very hesitant sniff tests, and then split it and shared the hard flesh around. There's no sign of me having and resulting stomach issues yet so I think I'm in the clear.

As there hasn't been an abundance of work, I've been reading plenty, and have picked up a book about Flinders, the Australian explorer that Dave had on board. I didn't realise he named so many of the places around my hometown! Port hacking, I'm looking at you.

4.title: Day 4: A stroll on the beach
paragraphs: Last night the swell assaulted us quite heavily, and I found myself waking up repeatedly just due to being rolled around in my bunk so much. Dave had had enough by this morning, and a bit past 6 I jumped out of bed at the sound of the anchor being weighed.

We motored to another beach roughly 20 minutes upwind, and spent the rest of the morning there. Though the swell was similar we swung around to face it better from our anchor that spared us the worst of the side to side action.
We then took the dinghy into the beach and went for a great long walk as far down the coast as we could go, crossing a small stream along the way.

Along the walk we saw a few prickly pear bushes, and Kate mentioned how she'd seen some other travellers eat them! I consider myself an enterprising vegan and thought that was a marvellous idea, Dave was trying to fish, why shouldn't I do some gathering of my own? I found a recipe online that proposed a quite detailed methodology on how to pick them, wearing gloves, and how to burn the glochids (spiky hairs) off. Well, I didn't have gloves on me but I reeeeeeally wanted some, how bad could the spines be if I carefully pull around them? Fucking awful, as I soon found out. The spines aren't just thorns, they're that little fibreglass type of needle that gets everywhere and are extremely irritating to remove. I've been finding them on me all afternoon and may even have to throw away my hat due to using it as my gathering vessel. I sat down for about half an hour with tweezers removing them from my hands, arms, torso and legs, and I'm sure there will be more to remove tomorrow. I'm still feeling them every now and then.
I didn't even get to eat the prickly pears today, but when I do, boy, they better be fucking delicious considering what I've put myself through to acquire them.

The rest of the walk was nice even with the overcast weather and sudden spurt of rain. We had a friendly dog come out of an old weatherboard beach shack and follow us for as long as it could until we crossed a river.

I opened some coconuts I found on the boat and while both mine were bad, the one Dave picked had delicious water inside. We still have one intact that has a live shoot coming out of it, that I spiked my feet on an aloe vera like plant to retrieve from where it was growing. Overall a chill day today but it was good to get out for a bit and get some reading done!

5.title: Day 5: A stroll up the hill.
paragraphs: We didn't move at all today so it was going to be a very slow day where I just read my book. However, the book I have been reading is about Mathew Flinders explorations around Australia, and it had me worked up to go on a bit of an adventure.

We're posted up near this big hill, so I asked Dave if he could drop me over on the shore so I could try and summit it. I had a gander at the maps and it looked about 2km to the summit with 400m elevation gain. Reckoning that that was only the Sydney park hill ~6 times, I didn't think it would take that long.

What I failed to factor in was that the Sydney park hill is paved, and not a complete bush bash. I spent around 3 rough hours in the rain getting up and down this thing, copping scratches and ant bites as I scrambled through the bush. It was reasonably entertaining, but I'm not in a rush to do it again soon.
I hope Flinders would be proud.

6.title: Day 6: Goin' into Bowen
paragraphs: Pretty relaxed day today again. In the morning we sailed for an hour or so up to the beach on the North of Bowen, then walked the hour into town for some food and a little restock. I also finished my book and went for a quick swim. x

7.title: Day 7: Stationary
paragraphs: We had another relaxed day today, and didn't move the boat at all. In the morning we took the tender in for a nice walk around the Bowen headland, and in the afternoon I swam into the beach and back, and did some yoga for the first time on the boat. I might try and make yoga and/or some exercise a habit as the boat can be a bit confining. It's looking like tomorrow will be a good day of sailing, we're going to get moving at 6:30 so I've set an alarm for 6. 😱

8.title: Day 8: The wind in our sails
paragraphs: Wow, what a beautiful day.
Before today, we hadn't moved much recently and as I'm sure you've seen from my recent posts, I was waiting to get some more kilometres under the old belt.
Well, my prayers have been answered as today we started moving at 6:30, meaning I was up at 6 to demolish some weetbix before getting the sails up and underway.

I have already made the mistake of just rolling out of bed when we started sailing, and not being able to eat until lunch. This isn't to say you can't eat while sailing, but with a sloppy food like weetbix and some decent swell, it can be best to avoid it.
So an early start it was, and what a privilege it was to see this day begin.
Greeted by a beautiful sunset and then put in high spirits by my growing ability to actually assist with the sailing sailing setup, we were off to an excellent start.

Then we sailed, sailed, and sailed some more. As I've said previously, once the wind is at a workable angle and the boat is moving smoothly under its clandestine power, it's just a matter of keeping an eye on the horizon and making sure the autopilot is putting away with its jerky wheel movements.

I spent much of today on the "trampolines" at the front of the cat, lying supine on the netting and gazing up at the billowing sales that were shading me from the heat of the sunny day. The crisp blue water was sliding away under me and as we moved further away from shore, it was magical to look out and see just ocean waves surrounding for miles around.
I'm not going to get over this feeling any time soon, and allowing myself to bask in this feeling was a special experience.

I may have been basking in it a little much as at one point Dave had to climb up the front and get my attention with a whistle, letting me know that he was going to have a power nap and that I should keep an eye on things. Now it wasn't exactly the most involved job, given the fact I literally did not touch a single instrument for the 45 mins I sat in the captain's seat, but it was fun feeling trusted enough to do that. At one point Kate called me captain with a cheeky smile which put a grin on my face.
The rest of the time I read 300 pages of a travel book that I am actually very much not enjoying, but given the finite nature of my reading material, by God I'm going to finish this drivel.

The sailing day ended just after 5, 10.5 hours of sailing later, when we pulled into the lee (aha why yes that is a sailing term, it means downwind of, which I know that because I am actually a sailor now have I not mentioned?) of Russel Island, just off of Cape Bowling Green.
I cooked a nice little stir fry after a pretty sunset that bookended the day perfectly.
We're going to have a brief digression.

Surely I can't be the only one that has always had a nagging desire to sit on cars roofs, right? You know how the rare opportunities to sit on a mates SUV while camping are just amazing and special, but you can't always be running around doing that? Well, with a boat you just can, it's strong enough. I'm currently sitting on the fibreglass roof of the cabin, and as an adult, I have free reign to do this as much as I like.

The wind is warm up here and the stars are out in force. I'm using a star map app to peer around the galaxy and just enjoying being alive right now, really savouring that feeling of being lucky enough to be here right now.
The sun has gone down enough now that I'm going to do another round of the sky with my app.
Ciao.

9.title: Day 9: Maggie
paragraphs: Today started at midnight technically, with the worst overnight swell, and therefore boat rocking, that we've had so far. On the bright side, it wasn't actually the worst sleep I've had, as my ability to sleep through swell has improved dramatically over the last week from much rolling around in my bunk.

It was another early start to get on the water, but first I had to help get the crab pots out of the water. Not only do I dislike this for vegan reasons, I also don't like pulling them out of the water because it's quite difficult. I had to hang off the front corner of the boat with the hook that we couldn't get to extend, and attempt to hook up the rope attached to the underside of a small white foam floater.

After going wide with the boat twice, as Dave can't actually see the floater from where he's steering in the back, he started to get frustrated, and became a bit terse with Kate which was pretty awkward for everyone.
We eventually got the poor crabs up and were on our way an hour later, the mood off, a new tear in the trampoline, and the boat reeking of mud and fish.
Is it not just easier to eat some tofu?

We sailed for a few hours and got to Magnetic Island (Maggie, as the locals call it), where I've come to previously on a family holiday. I was keen to get off the boat and have a wander around the island, and talk to some people that I wasn't living with.
Dave dropped me at shore and I pretty much just did a bit of exploration, and took full advantage of how much easier it is to talk to strangers while on holiday. I spoke to:

It was great getting to talk to a few people, and I came back to the boat after the last Germans left. I considered going back to the bar and joining in on the pool comp, but I didn't want Dave to have to pick me up with the dinghy too late, and I'd lost a game with 4 balls still on the table earlier.
When Dave picked me up we went over to the other boat for dinner, and Shane, the crew member on the other boat, decided it was time to engage me in a discussion about veganism.
For reference, this guy is a self identified carnivore, and said he eats 500g of meat for breakfast every day. 🤢

beliefs and reasoning, but he clearly had strong opinions he wouldn't budge on. Apparently a meat based diet is better for the environment! This is empirically complete bullshit by every metric. He did allude to being a vaccine skeptic though so that was actually quite gratifying, and made me feel like there was no longer any onus on me to represent veganism to him, what would be the point?
The captain of that boat, Darren, was actually the original one I was lining up to travel with, so in an alternate universe I am on the same boat as Shane lmfao. Thank fuck that isn't the case.
Overall I had a great day talking to people in town, and am looking forward to the next few days of us being parked up here!

10.title: Day 10: Walking the island
paragraphs: I'm writing this journal the day after for the first time, as I collapsed into bed so tired last night I just could not rouse the strength to pen the events of the day.

In the morning, I met up with Margot the French woman I'd lined up the walk with, and we quickly bumped into Sven, a young Swiss German who was solo travelling. We then all hung out together for the entire rest of the day, which is one of the lovely changes when you're travelling. I wouldn't dare talk to anyone around in Sydney, but when people are on the road it's so easy to make transient friends.

We started the day with the "Forts" walk on Magnetic Island, which takes you past some of the old WW2 bunkers situated on top of the hill. After Pearl Harbour, Townsville was deemed an important military defence point, and the population grew from 30k to 100k with the arrival of Australian and American servicemen!

A koala was kind enough to be napping just above head height right next to the path which was very cute to see, and meant we didn't have to go to the backup koala park nearby to see them in captivity.
We then visited a couple of beaches on the way to the next residential bay, cracking open some coconuts on the first and then swimming at the second.

With no official warning on any of the maps or signs, on the way to the second backy, a handful of big rocks were spray painted with "NUDE BEACH." We hoped this would not be the case but alas some naked old guy was walking up and down the beach constantly. The spray paint signage gave us the impression that some local just reeeeeeally wanted it to be a nude beach and so added that himself, trying to will it into being a beach he could get his kit off at.
When we arrived back in Horseshoe bay, we then had a late lunch and caught the bus back to the start of the walk, having time to fit in another in the opposite direction.

As the sun was getting low and Margot was keen to see the sunset, we rushed back on the bus again to Horseshoe bay. I'll try not to post too many sunsets as I know how brimming the internet already is with them, but this one was gorgeous. The cloud on the left added a light purple glow to an otherwise blue and tangerine palette.
We watched it slowly set while Sven and I played with some floating seeds in the water, seeing how far we could throw and catch them while swimming.
The third boat had also finally caught up to us, and our crews were having a drink at the pub, so I said my goodbyes to Margot and Sven and joined them.
Kate, Dave and I finished off the night by watching Misery on our tv on the boat and I enjoyed it enough to stay awake to the end, immediately collapsing and falling asleep after.

11.title: Day 11: Townsville
paragraphs: Even though I collapsed last night around 10 and slept until 7, I was still a little groggy this morning when we started moving off Magnetic Island to go into Townsville for the day.

That grogginess was quickly dispelled as we started sailing closer into the wind than we had before, facing a large swell to match. Riding the easy trade winds north so far has been nothing compared to the little journey south this morning. The boat was constantly crashing up and down each wave as it clawed its way against the wind.

As we were being rocked about the cabin, we saw the solar panel that had previously sat glued to the roof fly off and dangle for a second by its power cords. I had to quickly grab it and hold it in place, battered by the spray and wind while Dave tied it back in place enough to hold for the journey. During this debacle I also spotted dolphins for the first time this trip! I didn't manage to snap a photo, my hands being occupied holding the panel down, and myself onto the boat.

We eventually made it into the Townsville marina and refilled our water, and all headed into town to sort out various errands. My day was an abject failure, having failed to procure the one item, an iPod, that was the main reason for my journey. I managed to do a few little jobs I needed to sort at the local library which was nice, though.

Townsville wasn't the most beautiful town, but it was nice having a day on solid land and to just have a stroll around a new city. In the evening I jumped on the ferry back to Magnetic Island, where Dave and Kate had already sailed the boat back to earlier in the day, and am now back on Cheshire Cat.

12.title: Day 12: Wandering
paragraphs: Another day wandering around Magnetic Island.

We will be heading off in the next few days, but I'm coming to like being posted up here. We're right on a beautiful beach, there are buses to transport you around the island, and plenty of people to talk to.

In the morning I helped make some repairs to the boat, specifically where there was a small tear in the trampoline at the front I stitched back up and then glued together, which took about an hour so I hope it holds. I then did some washing at a hostel, read my book for a while, went for a swim, and had a nice lunch at a restaurant.

In the afternoon the weather was quite grey so I was making my way back to Horseshoe bay when I saw a woman pulling out a ukulele at a park bench. I went over and struck up conversation, asking how she was going with it, as I'd played a little before. She told me she was part of a beginners group, pulled out a spare she had with her, and we chatted about the learning process. We were joined by another novice and attempted to play a few little songs together. After about an hour I said goodbye and went to get the bus home, but it made my afternoon.

Unfortunately on the dinghy back to the boat my phone got wet and died, so I am going to be harder to contact for a little while. Luckily there is a laptop on the boat that I am writing for now, but these blogs will be without pictures until I can pick up the replacement I ordered to Cairns.

13.title: Day 13: No phone no worries
paragraphs: Wow, look at me go. I've lost my phone and am reconnecting with nature, wandering around the island not knowing the time and saying good morning to people when it's 1pm, waiting yonks for buses because I can't check the schedule, what a life.
(I ordered a new one this morning)

I did have a good day though. I went to Arthur Bay and read for a while, then wandered up the Forts Walk in the other direction, seeing a wallaby and a couple of koalas on the way. One of the koalas was right next to the path, napping in a tree just above head height. It must have been a young one, as it was small and adorably fuzzy. Alas, if only I had some way to capture pictures for sharing later.

I bumped into a couple of German girls and we spent the arvo together, checking out the rock wallabies and playing some Uno at a brewery. I never imagined I'd be able to practice my german this much in Australia, and as much as every German tourist complains about the abundance of other German tourists, I'm glad there are plenty of open ears for me to practice on (and be corrected by.)
We're not going to be leaving tomorrow, so you know what that means. Another day of wandering around Maggie, reading, and swimming. It could be worse.

14.title: Day 14: Last day on Magnetic Island
paragraphs: Over the course of the next week, we're going to be making our way to Cairns. Tomorrow we will be sailing out to the outer reef, a section of the Great Barrier Reef about 50nm off the coast and staying there for a few nights.

I cannot wait to get out there, but even the sailing journey out in the morning will be enjoyable. Staying on the boat out on the reef overnight is an exciting prospect, and it will be interesting to see how much wind and swell we get, but I'll not get too far ahead of myself as I'm sure the next few posts will reveal how they go.

After a few nights on the reef we will be heading into Hinchinbrook Island, where I will get dropped off by the boat, and hike a section of the Thorsborne Trail. I'll be jumping off on one side of the island, hiking alone, and then meeting back up with the boat ~2 days later on the other side. Adventure awaits!

Today I had a final wander around Maggie, saying goodbye to the nice little island that we've been staying on for a better part of a week. I first went to the butterfly forest, where lo and behold, a swarm of butterflies were settling in to overwinter. I then hiked some of the east side of the island that I'd done a previous day, but took it slow and spent a few hours reading and swimming at a couple of nice spots.

In the afternoon I posted some long overdue postcards, and did my food shopping for the next week on the water to cairns. I'm just now realising that I have no gas for my camping stove, or appropriate food for the hike, but we'll cross that bridge when we come to it.

15.title: Day 15: The actual last day on Magnetic Island, I hope
paragraphs: Well, the weather was not in our favour this morning, with a grey sky and gusty wind leading Dave to the decision to postpone our departure another day. Sailing, as it turns out, is as much a game of patience as it is skill, as you're better off avoiding the bad weather altogether than you are having to struggle through it.

I wasn't too worried, as it meant that while I was groggy in the morning I didn't have to immediately start lifting the anchor and the sails, and instead had another relaxed day on land. I'm relishing all this downtime while I can, as I know that once I get to Indonesia the days will be far more full.

As it was grey and I've completed about every walk on the island, I decided to check out some of the hostels. There are two that I know of on the island, and as it turns out you can just walk in and use whatever of their facilities you want. I took a swim at the first and read in a hammock there for a couple of hours, then went to the second where I read for a few more hours and had a vegan burger for lunch (Mmmm, that is a tasty burger!)

On the way back to the boat I swung by a hardware store to see if I could pick up some gas for my stove to heat and cook my food for the coming hike, but alas they only had the butane cylinders. This means I'll not be cooking or eating any warm food for a couple of days, but my stomach will warm it up eventually anyway.
It's looking good to head out to the reef tomorrow, so hopefully tomorrow's update has some movement for you!

16.title: Day 16: The Reef
paragraphs: We did it, we finally left Magnetic Island.

We left early and sailed the ~55km out to John Brewer reef, arriving just before noon. I've been to the reef before but it's still astonishing seeing a light, shallow sandy patch appear out of the otherwise deep ocean. We maneuvered around to the northern side of the reef and dropped the anchor, surprisingly close to the coral nearby.
After a quick lunch I was keen to go for a swim so I chucked on my snorkel and jumped in, following an outer perimeter of shallow coral around on a large circular lap back to the boat.

The fish are absolutely stunning. I must have seen over a hundred different species, parrot fish, some rainbow, some with a tasteful blend of certain colours, a large cod eyeing me cautiously as I swim past, massive shoals of crisp neon teal chromis that only react to me when I almost touch them, butterflyfish and angelfish lower down amongst the coral near fearful gobys that carefully watch me and clownfish that nuzzle their way into their anemone homes as I pass by. Surprisingly, most of the fish seem totally unphased by my presence and are more interested in politicking with each other over their territories, as I witnessed many small chases happen around the sandy bottom.

The coral wasn't as vivid as in the nature documentaries, but the absolute size of some of them were breathtaking. Table coral as wide as I am tall and huge trees of finger coral with their branching white tips reaching up toward the surface. At their bases small mounds of hump coral crowd the ground.
Delicate feather stars reach out from their coral platforms to filter the water with their intricately patterned arms, and blue starfish sparingly litter the seafloor.

There were at least 5 different species of sea cucumber, some more delicate, only slightly thicker than my thumb, and gently rocking in the current, while their massive cousins lined with a thick coating of a thorn like pattern sat like immobile tanks in the sand.

As I followed the edge of the coral around, the sandy wastes outside of it gradually dropped away into the depths, and eventually I was peering over the drop off to a bottom I could barely make out, saturated of colour and light at the bottom of the cliff astride me. I wasn't game to swim over it, and even diving down the cliff a little way to peer in at the vertical structures made my skin crawl slightly.

I had a rest after I got back, and went for another swim just after 4, heading the other direction from the boat a little way over the unsettling sandy plains. I was rewarded with a glimpse of an eel sliding into an unseen crevice, and as I was about to turn back to the boat, I was lucky enough to see a black tip reef shark!

They're not large enough to be a threat to a person, so I was going to try and get a little close to admire it, but clumsily as I thrust toward it my foot went above the surface and slapped against the waters surface, spooking it away with an incredible speed.
I've never stayed out on the ocean proper before, and slept quite well last night. Looking forward to another day of snorkeling and exploring the reef today.

17.title: Day 17: Into the deeps
paragraphs: Yesterday morning, the sky was clear and the sun was shining, so we decided to go for another dive to explore an underwater art exhibition that was installed on the reef.

One of the installations is at a depth of about 6m, concrete humanoid figures sitting on small platforms to anchor them to the ground. At that depth I can dive down to take a look at them, but not spend too much time admiring them before my drive for air becomes overpowering.
The other installation, the 'Coral Greenhouse' was far deeper, sitting at a depth of about 15 metres.
As I don't have a camera, enjoy a photo of the structure that I found online.

It was eerie to swim above, as we could just see the vertical spines and larger metal structure beneath, but couldn't dive down beyond that. It looked like the ribcage of a decomposing ship, or the top spires of a church.

When we arrived back at the boat, we repositioned to another, deeper side of the reef. Here, the wide coral reef pillars reach up just as close to the surface as the earlier area, coming to less than a metre from the surface, but the sandy bottom in between these structures is far deeper. When swimming from one coral outpost to another, the coral cliffs rapidly drop off into darkness below. I'm getting better at being comfortable swimming over these depths, but it's still unsettling. One strategy I have employed is looking at the tiny fish that are swimming around in the open waters and thinking, if those little things can brave it, surely I can too.

I went for a few more dives around the boat here, and saw a massive manta ray cruising over a coral head. It moved so gracefully, and its large slow moving wings belied its incredible pace as it disappeared off into the distance. I encountered it again a minute later when I was admiring a number of fish, and it gave me a shock as I saw a large dark shape in the water moving towards me before it saw me and angled away.
We're going to go for another swim this morning and then move over to another reef, so I'm looking forward to that.

18.title: Day 18: Trunk Reef
paragraphs: I jumped out of bed this morning to the sound of the motor coming on - that's my normal cue to get the anchor up as we're getting on the road. Normally, I'm already up and ready so I was a little surprised that we'd be moving so quick, but I quickly got changed and groggily shambled up to the deck.
Turns out it wasn't the engine starting, but the generator coming on due to it being overcast this morning, oops.

We sailed to a new reef, Trunk Reef, that was about 5 hours away. At one point on the way over I was in my bunk when out of nowhere a roaring sound grew to an incredible decibel all within about 3 seconds. At first I thought something catastrophic was happening to the boat, but as it passed and grew quieter I realised it was a fighter jet flying right over us. I'd seen a few from Magnetic Island, as they are based in Townsville, and apparently they like to fly as low as they can over unsuspecting boats for fun. I only wish I'd been outside to see it fly past.

Once we arrived at the reef I explored around an long edge, but didn't see many new species. I swam against the current for the first half of my swim, meaning on the way back to the boat I could mostly drift with it, making it a leisurely trip.

19.title: Days 19-21: Hinchinbrook Island
paragraphs: 17th - 19th May
I hadn't heard of Hinchinbrook Island before, so when Kate mentioned that we were going passed it and I may be able to jump off for a overnight hike, I did a little research.

It's a beautiful island that lies about halfway between Townsville and Cairns, and it quite large at 393 square kilometres. The main attraction on the island is the Thorsborne Trail, that covers a section of the east coast of the island.

All 7 of us were going to go to Zoe Beach on Saturday at lunch, and so we decided that I would stay on the island afterwards, to be picked up on Monday morning, my birthday, at the north end of the Track. Zoe Beach is about halfway down the full track, so I would only be covering a section of it, and marching against the regular walking direction, as most people complete the walk south to north.

I packed my hiking pack with food that didn't need to be cooked, my camping equipment, and some extra clothes, and we headed in for the island. The first stop was actually 20 minutes in the wrong direction for me, as further down the track at the south end of the beach you can find Zoe Falls, a waterfall that feeds the estuary on the beach.

Although I still had to cover 10.5km, with a time estimate of 6hrs in the other direction after lunch, the trip down to the waterfall was definitely worth it. At the base of the waterfall is a natural swimming hole that I have to say, is the best I've ever seen. I've been to almost every swimming hole in the Blue Mountains so that isn't a title I give lightly, but it was beyond belief. The water was so crystal clear, being fed from the unpolluted peaks of the island, and you could clearly see the bottom of the pool even where it went to 3 or 4 metres in depth. The pool was full of spotted fish, and as I swam under the water I could see them all around when I opened my eyes. The waterfall feeding the far end of the pool made for a great natural massage, and I held myself under it while it slammed onto my back.

I didn't dare dally too long though as I was all to aware of the fact I needed to get to camp before sunset, so I dried off, grabbed my pack, and got walking. The rainforest here is so different to what we have in nsw, so many kinds of trees that I'd never seen, and some with sharp hidden spikes that gave me some good scratches. There were a few river crossings too, with water so pure you can drink it straight from the stream. I was starting to worry about the time, given that the sun was getting low behind the canopy and I had no way to tell the time, and also that it felt like I was heading too far west, when I knew the trail eventually moved to the north east. Both fears turned out to be unfounded as I turned and ascended a large saddle that gave me an overview of the path I'd walked, and emerging from the jungle showed that the sun wasn't even about to go down, it had just felt much later shrouded by the dense canopy.

I made it to the campsite and picked the furthest spot from the large 8 strong family that were already camped there, and jumped in the lagoon behind the beach for a swim. There were multiple crocodile warning signs at the various streams, but I could see that the young kids had already been swimming and figured that if a crocodile was going to eat something, it would be them.

Sunday morning I took it very slow, as I only had 2km to cover to the next campsite. In the morning there were some conspicuous lizard tracks leading from the beach up to the lagoon that I figured was a crock, but given how small the drag marks were it must have been pretty small. I also spied a ray cruising along the bottom of the lagoon, which was surprising that there were freshwater stingrays in such an isolated location. I sat around all day reading my book and relaxing in the lagoon, only leaving in the late afternoon when the temperature had cooled down.

At the next campground I met a nice group of five locals that were doing the walk together and had just started that day. They told me where the freshwater was and invited me to have dinner with them. They were great company and even offered me a birthday present of a pack of dehydrated mushrooms that was very sweet. We played some cards and then turned in pretty early.

This morning I was up before dawn to see the sunrise creep over the water, and I felt very lucky to be there in that moment to witness it. The whole trip on the island was a great breath of forest air, and the mountains rising steeply out of the jungle behind the beach reminded me of Brackenwood, a flash animation that I fondly remember from my childhood that used to transport me to a mysterious verdant forest world. I later found out that the animator was actually from Leura, Sydney, and I think that may be why they resonated with me so much, as I subconsciously recognised the aussie bush in the artwork.

I said goodbye to my new friends, after having a brief but deep chat to one of them about life and community, and summited a final peak behind the campsite. It gave a commanding view of the rivers on the northern side of the island and the sea behind them and to the east, with a sharp wind that ripped over the top of the hill. I'd endeavored to leave early to ensure that I met the 11am pickup time that I'd agreed upon with Dave, but as I got the jetty feeling like I'd left plenty of time, within 2 minutes I could hear the roar of the dinghy engine approaching. It turns out it was only 9:50, so we we're both over an hour early but arrived within 2 minutes of each other.

Back on Cheshire Cat, we sailed north to Dunk Island, just outside of Mission Beach. Arriving here at around 2, we had a relaxed afternoon and I stayed on the boat, as most of the amenities on the island are unfortunately closed. Tomorrow we'll be doing a hike on the island together, and should be aiming to get to Cairns around Friday or this weekend.
Couldn't ask for a better place to spend my birthday, and I'm very grateful to be here.

20.title: Day 22: Kent Island
paragraphs: 20th May

Yesterday started very early, as I was awoken in the early hours of the night by the sound of the engine coming on. I lay there confused for a second thinking that it was the generator coming on before jumping up to see what was going on. We'd drifted around a small coral outcrop and tangled the anchor chain around it, meaning that the boat was restricted in its bobbing with the waves leading to harsher movements in the night.
I had to stand in the pulpit in my undies, shining a torch into the water looking for more coral as we pulled the anchor up and moved to a better location, slightly out from the beach.

After getting back to bed and the rest of the night's sleep, it was an early start to do a walk on Dunk Island where we had anchored. The rest of the crews turned around at the peak of the island, but I decided to do the full loop. It was a rainforested track, that felt dark and cool even in the late morning, with the sounds of scrub fowl and other rustlings moving off in the bush.

The island used to be a resort, but most of the buildings were heavily damaged during a cyclone, so there has been minimal activity there for the past few year. I walked past a few damaged villas with rooves torn open and plants growing on the balconies.

I arrived back on the boat and we sailed on for a few hours to Kent Island, which is the most idyllic location we've been to so far. We were next to a small sand outcrop next to a thick jungle on the small, steep island. The water was clear and the wind was calm on the lee side of the island, with the sun shining down.

In the late afternoon we had a poke around the beach that was covered in shattered white coral on the sand, and ended up assembling an alphabet with all the pieces of coral we could find that looked like each letter. It was a fun evening and we turned in pretty early.

21.title: Day 23: Russel Island
paragraphs: 21st May

It was an early start from Kent Island, leaving the small island sand bars in our wake. I was disappointed to leave the tropical paradise, but could not have been better compensated by our next destination. After a couple of hours sail northward, we pulled into an isolated sand beach, a spot known by Darren who lives out of Cairns not too far away. Behind the beach was a thick, wild jungle, with a small rocky cascade bubbling down into the seawater in the innermost corner of the strand. We jumped in Darren's tender and motored onto the sand a little way to the right of the stream, where there was a clear path through the rocks to the beach.

The beachfront was shadowed by massive trees, reaching out over the water with their thick cover. The branches and trunk were lined with a variety of epiphytes, in addition to staghorns there were other thin ferns and needle line plants hanging from a multitude of patches above us. The staghorn clumps were so large in places that it looked like one would be able to comfortably lie on them, held 20 metres in the air on the verdant cushion.

The shade provided complete cover from the day's heat as we made our way down to the stream, with the water on our right lapping gently against the shore. To our left, the jungle was thick with giant ferns and tangled vines, the humid climate allowing for much denser growth than home in NSW.

The stream looked small from afar, but arriving at its mouth allowed us to see up its length, with a large gap in the trees along its length. The canopies touched at great heights over the water, with massive creeper vines hanging all the way down to the rocky water, some in thick loops that you could sit in. The water was still shallow but wide, and there were some pools deep enough to wallow in. Dave went for a swim but I progressed further up the stream with Darren and Shane. Darren was immensely proud of the spot, he told us how he used to bring his family here when his kids were young, and I was grateful that he shared it with us.

Up the stream I could see a sunlit area where the canopy broke open and we came to a sharp bend in the flow, where the water was flowing down from a steep rock to the right, turning and raising at the same time. The rock was wide enough to hold the trees back on each side, and there were small waterfalls along its length. I clambered up the slippery rock a little way, gripping onto magnificent tree roots that clamped onto the stone and were woven around it tightly.

I would have loved to follow the stream as far up as I could, but I could see that Dave had turned around and Shane was just arriving at the opening, so I made my way back down. At the base of the rock there was a small pool that I dipped myself into, and a waterfall that I held myself under, with enough of an overhang that I could cling to the rock behind it and hide in the watery void.

After Shane and I had a swim, we made our way back down to the boats, where I looked in vain for some more wood to carve, something I'd done with a piece of light balsa wood that I found at Kent island, but had no luck.

We then sailed out to Russel Island, that was only half an hours sail out to sea, but against the wind. It was blowing 20 knots, a considerable force to sail against, and it was a rough ride out there. I slipped on the front of the boat while putting the main sail up, as even minor tasks become much more difficult when the boat is rocking violently and the wind is blowing you off balance. I'll have to be more careful in future when I'm on deck in those conditions.
When we arrived at Russel Island it was later in the afternoon, and we wrapped up the day with the new episode of Alone, before turning in with the island before us to explore in the new day.

22.title: Day 24: Fitzroy Island
paragraphs: 22nd May

The weather was quite overcast in the morning and the water was choppy, so I opted not to join Dave for an early morning snorkel and just for the walk afterwards with Kate. Russel Island is a part of the Frankland Group, with one jungled hillock rising out of the ocean and a projecting sand cay that has built upward from the reef, forested by casuarinas that can tolerate the sandy soil.

Before the walk started, Dave and Darren had chatted to some people that were in at the small camping area - strange, as there was no other boat near us. From their accounts, the group consisted of three, two chinese nationals and a model from Sydney who were filming some online content for one the guys social medias, where he apparently has 20 million followers. They were apparently filming some sort of fake survival video, pretending that they were stranded on the island with no food or supplies. Strange, but it's a real grind out here in the content creator world.

We walked along the eastern coast of the island and hunted down the start of an incredibly decrepit concrete track that ran up to a lighthouse. Pushing our way through the dense bush and up the track we slowly made it up to the peak of the island where the lighthouse stood. It used to be manned but was now fully automated, and as such did not appear to be visited very often. A metal grate begged us not to move it and climb the steel tower, but unfortunately was not very persuasive all by itself on the island, so we moved it aside and climbed the thin structure. I'd actually pushed ahead of the group somewhat on the way up, so was at the top before the others had arrived, and wasn't a massive fan of the rusting joints and thin beams that made up the structure, but I figured that it had survived some serious storms in its time so the chance I made the difference in its survival was slim. It was another story when the other four arrived and began to climb the tower after I'd already come back down, as I could feel it vibrating with everyone's steps, but I didn't let my fears get the better of me and ascended again.

The tower commanded a panoramic view of the Frankland Group, and the mainland off in the distance, with the treetops swaying around underneath us. It's amazing how much different opaque floors make for out feeling of safety in all the large buildings we enter in our lives, as being able to look straight down through the security mesh flooring to the distant ground, and feeling the wind come back up through it was not reassuring.

On the way back down I was shown the remains of an old Land Rover, in the final stages of decomposition. The Iron body had collapsed into the ground and was rotting well away, but the aluminium tray and two of the rubber tyres were holding up reasonably well.

After our walk we passed back by the other group and I got a look at them for the first time. They had some tents set up and a generator humming, with solar panels half out in the sand while one of the guys was squatting behind a camera pointing at the tents. There were some loose foodstuffs in bags near the camping area and a few 12 packs of large water bottles, an interesting sight overall. As we passed by Darren was having a chat to them again, and I asked if there was anywhere I could see the video they made when done, but as it was going on a chinese social media I wouldn't be able to access it, probably RedNote. The girl seemed disappointed too that she wouldn't be able to watch it, but it was a weird situation overall.

We then went for a snorkel, Dave taking the boat further afield whereas I just jumped in from the boat and swam over to the nearest coral. It wasn't as spectacular as the outer reef where I was, with most of the coral bleached and the water quite milky. I didn't stay in for long but when Dave returned to the boat he said the spot he went to was great, much more coral with a few quite large fish.

We then detached from out mooring and made our way to Fitzroy Island, a popular tourist destination just a day trip out of Cairns. It's pretty much just a beach, a resort, a bar and a 'general store' that stored chips, sunscreen, and a few other tourist essentials.

I've been eating very well on the boat, cooking a variety of meals and having a fair amount of fruit, so it was great to get a garlic bread and beer and switch from one to the other until they were both gone.

I spent the afternoon into the evening on the beach while the others were at the bar, and I found that some pieces of coral were quite apt for skipping, so I amused myself skipping them out across the calm water into the bay. A tipsy patron saw me from the bar and started commentating on each and every throw, "ooh that was a good one," "The last one was better than that," and so on, much to my chagrin. He then tried to give me some pointers that I was trying not to react to though my eyelid was twitching, but luckily his mate started bagging him out for it which was pretty funny.

23.title: Day 25: Cairns
paragraphs: 23rd May
The formula had been working quite well for us recently, so we ran it back again today: A morning walk followed by some sailing.

We motored over into Fitzroy Island early in the morning, and made an early start on the one loop track the included the peak of the island. It was a solid climb that was roughly 300m in elevation gain, but a cool wind helped to offset the high humidity of the region. The view of the island put into perspective how much of the island is wild, with only a small section developed and the rest mostly wild. On the way back down the loop includes an old defunct lighthouse, but I didn't stay there long and opted to head straight to the beach.

The weather was still quite overcast so I decided to mend some clothes rather than going for a swim, and while the others went for a snorkel on the north side of the island, I put my sewing kit to work. I enjoy working with my hands and it was very satisfying fixing the tear in my board shorts with a nice neat hand stitch of a complementing colour.

When the others arrived back we jumped on the boats and sailed into Cairns. It was a slow start until we escaped the protection of the island, where the wind picked up and sent us on our way. As we arrived in Cairns we had to refill on fuel and water, and so went into the marina to do so. When were docking against the fuel station, we reversed in too quickly and bashed the rear of the boat against the dock, breaking off some of the fibreglass and even digging into some of the wood below.

Initially, I had been at the rear of the boat where the damage happened, but at the time was at the front of the boat as Kate had told me to go up there and get the bow line, and she instead stood at the back watching us reverse in. It was strange, I could kind of see it happening from the front of the boat, but Kate was standing right there looking down at the rear corner of the boat as we came in hot so I assumed it was under control.

I don't think there was any reason for me to be at the front of the boat, as Dave wasn't intending on throwing that line in, but as Kate's been on the boat longer than I, I defer to her for calls like that.
I feel that if I was at the back of the boat I probably could have prevented it, and it is kind of annoying fielding orders from two people that aren't always on exactly the same page.

Dave was pretty understandably pissed off, and aired his frustration to me afterwards that the dock worker should have attached us onto the cleat earlier so we didn't have to reverse. He wanted to be moving forward adjacent to the dock, be roped on at the centre of the side of the boat, which would have meant the forward momentum would have twisted us into the dock.

Dave also said that the rear fender should have been further back, whereas I'd placed it slightly forward on the next vertical pole, which is the wrong spot. I felt bad that I'd put it in the wrong spot, but I'd only seen it done once before, and Kate had seen them after I'd placed them anyway.
Oh well, a few things had to go wrong for that to happen, and I'm sure we'll all be much more careful next time.
After that debacle, Kate and I jumped off the boat at the marina and went into Cairns to pick up my new phone from the PO, fantastic!

Kate wanted to check out a fruit market after we picked up the parcels, but was having a good browse so we decided to meet up at a restaurant where I wanted to eat after, which I glanced at the location of on her map. Unfortunately the restaurant was closed and I walked past it, so we lost each other in Cairns for an hour or so. It could've turned into an issue as I had no way to contact either her or Dave, but luckily I saw her again at the marina.
Back at the boat, I've got my phone set up and had a chill night in, keen to get back into Cairns tomorrow and pick up a few more things for the journey ahead.

24.title: Day 26: Cairns errands
paragraphs: In the morning we went into town.
At a laundromat I washed all our gown.
I needed a munch,
went to a cafe for lunch,
and came back to lay my head down.

25.title: Day 27: Filling the larder
paragraphs: 25th May
Today was another relaxed day, with a couple of trips into town.

In the morning we traveled in to stock up on food as we haven't had a chance to resupply since Magnetic Island. I filled three large shopping bags with vegetables, tinned beans, and all sorts of foodstuffs that was almost too heavy to carry back to the dinghy. Every 50 metres or so I had to pause and put the bags down, as it felt like a constant heavy deadlift.

Later in the afternoon after taking all the food back to the boat, we met some friends and family of Darren's at the bar in the Hilton, where they were hosting a jazz event. We stayed there for a couple of hours, but then the group was keen to go to a few other bars.

I didn't feel like sitting around drinking with them, so read my book on the Cairns foreshore esplanade. Overall I've been very impressed by Cairns, in sharp contrast to Townsville that I didn't like at all. Cairns' city centre is small and walkable, with an absence of buildings of over 2 storeys. There were also a couple of great markets, Rusty's and the Night Market to wander around, while a mix of tourists and locals filled the area.

I read and wandered around for a few hours until the others were ready to head back to the boat, when I piloted the dinghy back home. We finished up the final episode of Chernobyl (great series!) and tucked in the for the night afterwards.

26.title: Day 28: Out to the reef
paragraphs: 26th of May
We're on the move again!
In the morning, we pulled up the anchor, hoisted the sails, and quickly got underway out to see. We arrived at our destination a few hours later, Vlasoff Reef.

Kate also took some videos of me grabbing the mooring in, which is a permanent fixture to the seafloor with a float that boats can tie on to. The challenge can be grabbing it and tying on before the boat drifts past, but today was quite easy. I find it quite a fun process overall.

It was cleansing getting back in the clear blue ocean water after a few days in the muddy river water in the Cairns anchorage, and I immediately jumped in for a snorkel. The water was so warm to swim through, and even under the boat it was only 4 m deep, where I swam over the sand to the nearest coral.
The snorkeling highlights in this spot were as follows.There were massive giant clams, some about a metre long and almost have that wide, with velvety patterned lips covered in tiny neon eyes.

What I initially thought to be a bit of dead floating plant matter turned out to be a tiny nudibranch swimming in the open water upon closer inspection! It was about the size of my thumb but very thin, and swimming along with its 'wings' undulating in a waveform to propel it forward. It had the most intricate patterning on its back, a golden base colour with gumleaf shaped pink stripes asymmetrically placed along the scape of its hide. I watched it for a good 15 minutes, at one point it landing on the seafloor and curling around a tiny stem of plant before taking off into the current again.

On my way back to the boat I was surrounded in a flash by a innumerable school of fish, there must have been over a thousand in total. They were about 30 cm long each, silver, with slightly pointed noises and a tailed with a gentle gradient into yellow. They came quite close underneath me but any movement I made caused them to flush back in a wave, before turning and slowly creeping forward again.
I have some footage from my work on

27.title: Day 29: Snorkeling
paragraphs: 27th May

We didn't move the boat today, and filled the day with lazy snorkeling around the area. We're moored near a small sand cay, with underwater continents of reef scattered around us, some linking to one another while others stand on their own as islands in the sand.

After snorkeling around for a while, I worked up the courage to start swimming quite far away from the boat to a reef I could see deeper and further out. As I started swimming toward it, I suddenly felt a searing pain across me neck and right shoulder; I had been stung by a jellyfish. As I tried to wipe it away I felt more stings on my left elbow, but I succeeded in removing the invisible assailant that I never saw, and was left with the pain. I made my way back to the boat to apply vinegar that dulled the pain very effectively, and the mosquito-bite looking lumps quickly flattened and dwindled away.
During the time in the day that I wasn't snorkeling, I read more of my book and embroidered the outside of my backpack.

28.title: Day 30: Back to Cairns
paragraphs: 28th May

After two nights out on the reef, it was time to head back into Cairns so Dave could sort some visa forms out for Indonesia with the other skippers. Not to let the reef get away from me so quickly, I jumped in before breakfast for an early morning swim and headed out to the west, a direction I hadn't explored in previously. It also turned out that Kate had an underwater camera that I could use, so I managed to get some footage!

I was quickly rewarded, getting both a shark and a turtle in the one clip, which is also the first time I've seen a turtle while snorkeling on this trip. Unfortunately I can't upload videos here, but will put it on my Instagram instead.

After I'd breakfasted back at the boat we sailed back into Cairns, quite a bumpy ride that gave me a bit of a headache. I spent most of the afternoon at the "lagoon" swimming pool on the esplanade, trying to hide in the shade and not get too sunburned. At one point I was doing some embroidery and a french woman asked me about it, and we got to chatting. When I told her about the sailing trip I was doing, she was pretty impressed by the idea and asked if there was any room for more crew, so she may be joining us until Cooktown if it works out. It would be nice to have someone my own age to chat with, and switch up the group dynamic for a bit.
The state of origin was on in the evening but I wasn't interested in heading into a loud pub for that, so I hung out with Kate for dinner, and she told me a little about her life.

When I went back to wait at the dinghy, I found that the gate to the pier was locked and we had no way in, so I waited at the door for someone to come out. The first guy that exited completely ignored me as I asked to be let in to get to the dingy, shut the door behind him and walked off with no reaction. The second person was more amiable, and let me in with no problems, so I could wait and later let the others back in at the end of the night.

Dave informed us that unfortunately the bowsprit had a large crack in it, which will prevent us from leaving tomorrow. Instead, he will be heading into town to find an aluminium welder, and we may be here another couple of days. Looking at the damage it's amazing that it held on as long as it did, one of the fixtures has a deep crack in the welding going all away around where it is attached to the base pole, and only the internal flaring is holding it in place. Hopefully we can get it fixed tomorrow and get back on the water by Friday, but I'll know more tomorrow.

29.title: Day 31: Goodbye Cairns
paragraphs: 29th of May

The sun was beating down with full force during the peak of the day, and I found myself slowly shuffling my towel backwards as I chased the shade of a tree that diligently slid away to expose me to the heat.

It was another relaxed day in Cairns. Dave had left early to attempt to get the bowsprit welded, and so that morning I had been left in town to my own devices. The lagoon was my main squeeze as I dived laps along it, seeing how far underwater I could swim as practice for snorkeling on the reef. I rotated between swimming, reading, and embroidery in a relatively quick rotation to suit my attention span. It really was the computer > phone > bed rotation of the outside world.

Unfortunately Noemie, the french woman, had got cold feet and decided not to join us to Cooktown. It was just as well, as Dave had said that there wasn't enough room in the boat to clear out the fourth bunk, and I would have been sleeping on the couch.

My main task for the afternoon was to give away two of the books I'd finished reading on the boat. I don't plan on lugging any finished paperbacks with me along my voyage, but they also weren't important enough to mail home, so I had to pass them on somehow. I decided to head to a hostel as most of them had a communal bookshelf, and the first one I tried was more than happy to have me add them to the collection. Instead of letting me palm them off on her, the manager told me that I was welcome to swap and take one too, so I went upstairs and traded them for one that looked good enough (I'm most of the way through this book now, and I'm not enjoying it). There was also interestingly an Andy Griffiths book there, and as it's not the normal place for kids to stay, I assume a backpacker had been engaging with aussie kids books?

By the time I'd dropped the books off and left the hostel, I realised I had a bit of a moral quandary regarding my actions. One of the books I had dropped off, "Yakity Yak: Bombay to Beijing by Bicycle", I had not enjoyed at all. I'll be brief but the author was a bit of a twat, disparaging the locals and acting like a drunk fool at every opportunity. The only thing it did do for me was serve as a timely reminder of the type of traveling I do not want to partake in. I'm not saying I regretted reading it, I know they can't all be winners, but I'd definitely had rather read something else.

Now, seeing as I had not enjoyed the book, and regarded it as quite a poor read overall, should I have not left it at the hostel? Some hapless backpacker is going to pick it up, and probably go through the same arduous read I had to. However, in wanting to spare someone from the book, this would only leave me with one option, to destroy it. I detest waste, so dare I wield the authority to destroy books that I don't like, rather than pass them on? Is my ego big enough to view my literary judgement as an objective mark, and does it outweigh my frugal recycling and reusing mindset? I did not end up returning to steal the book back and dispose of like some kind of paperback assassin, but I do find the idea of spitefully dumping a poor book a fun way to avenge the hours lost to it.

I ventured to another vegan restaurant for a late lunch, before rendezvousing with Dave and Kate at the tender at 3. In a great turn of events, Dave had managed to get the bowsprit completely fixed by an aluminium welder in one outing, due to Darren having contacts in the area.

Just before sunset, Dave and I set about getting it back in place on the front of the boat, which was quite an involved process. I had to stand in the tender, walk it around the side of the boat, and park it just in front of the catamaran, so I could reach up beneath where we needed to put the sprit on. There were a number of small pins to get into place while the metal cords were under tension, which proved a difficult task and had Dave on edge, worried that I would drop something into the water. At one point, I stumbled in the tender while holding a crucial bolt and he flinched more than I did. Come sunset, we had it fixed and tightened back into place. It was a great feeling, that it had been broken in the morning, and now we had the green light to sail on tomorrow.

30.title: Day 32: Low Isles
paragraphs: 30th of May

It was mid afternoon by the time we'd made it to the Low Isles from Cairns, a lengthy sail in the morning straight downwind had led us to the great view we currently beheld. The Low Isles are a pair of very different islands. One is a tiny, treed island populated with some amenities and an old but still operational lighthouse in the classic red and white colouring looking like it had been cut out of a picture book, and the other is far larger, swampy and skirted with mangroves reaching into the earth with fractal roots.

Another site with moorings, I was up the front in the pulpit as we arrived, hook in my hand and rope in my teeth, waiting until we were within my striking range to grab the loop of rope we could tie to. As we approached, Kate and I say a massive stingray on the surface dive down as the boat narrowly passed over it.

Late afternoon rapidly approaching, I jumped on the paddleboard and made my way into the island. It was a dicey ride as the tide was at its lowest, so I had to skirt around the small rocky outcroppings that populated the shore outside the beach. I thought I'd picked a deep channel but before I could react I was standing over a coral field that looked less that a foot deep, making a normally soft tumble into the water a dangerous prospect. The coral came together into a shelf, and the lowest fin started to touch the bottom, forcing me into a slow, painful, dainty walk along the dead coral shelf to the beach, pulling the paddleboard alongside me. Just then I saw movement in the water ahead, and two reef sharks were in water so shallow that their find were cresting out of the water. My splashing sent them quickly on their way, so long for being scary sharks, they are quite skittish creatures.

I walked a lap around the island but didn't see much, and the last tourist group for the day was wrapping up as I wandered around. Not wanting to head back out the shallow, coral ridden way I arrived at the beach, I asked the tour guide where the channel was. He told me to pass around two white markers and a post, but as I passed the post I realised it didn't signify the end of a coral shelf, but the centre of it. Again I was gliding over sharp pillars just beneath the water, and while I was stable on the board I was worried that the fin would catch, jerking the board and tumbling me off into the water. Luckily, it was deep enough for that not to transpire, and I made it back out to deep waters staying dry. It's quite a stunning sight seeing the structures silently pass by in the clear water underneath the boat.

Before turning in for the night, there was quite the show out the back of the boat. A pair of batfish, the beggars of the sea, peered up at the back of the boat with their vacant eyes, having learned that by milling about behind boats they may be rewarded with delicious food scraps. Needless to say it worked on me, and I fed the dopey looking creature the a squishy persimmon that has passed its prime. Later in the night the water was churning with giant trevally, massive fish that arced through the water, splashing the surface from underneath at they passed close beneath it.

31.title: Day 33: Port Douglas
paragraphs: The famed reef at Low Isles that tourists are shipped to throughout the day, is in its final throes of death. Sheets of bleached coral were covered in a dirty green-brown layer of hairy algae, with empty giant clam skeletons littering the desolate bottom. Fish were still populous, though less so than the on the healthy reefs we'd visited previously. It was devastating to see, even more so to Dave that had visited the same reef years ago when it was nowhere near as bad.

In light of this we decided not to stay for the rest of the day, and instead head into Port Douglas instead. It was only a short sail away, being just over an hour, and before we knew it we were pulling into the anchorage.

It was a relaxed afternoon lying in the park reading, a full pub pizza in my stomach, while the foreshore slowly filled with people. It was a veritable backpacker haven, looking more like a festival scene than a far north Queensland town. There were multiple slack lines up, dreadlocked Europeans spinning light sticks and doing other juggling tricks, people knitting and drawing all around. It was extremely cliche but by god, I was going to get a piece of it while I was here.

I considered myself alright at slack lines, being able to cross the small one at the climbing gym comfortably back and forth, but I was wholly unprepared for the 15 m line between high points in two trees. After a couple of twisting falls I was sufficiently humbled and sat back with the group I'd got to talking to.

My newfound embroidery skills were put to good use as I put some flowers on some Argentinian guys hat and some girls bag, while an Italian girl did a drawing in my diary. They were talking about the small backpacker drama in the town, and the girl drawing in my diary apparently couldn't go to some party due to wanting to avoid some other girl there, the high school drama of which truly made me feel old. It was funny overall, and I ended up grabbing a quick beer with the Argentinian guys afterwards.
Back on the boat, we finished up the second half of Scarface, and called it a night.

32.title: Day 34: Hope Island
paragraphs: 1st of June

We arrived at the Sunday markets 20 minutes before they were open, as a quick start was in order today. A hasty browse of the stalls in different stages of setup left me with some breakfast, a donut and a piece of brownie, and a postcard. The reason for our early start was that we had over 40 nm of sailing to cover, a trip that would take over 6 hours, and we didn't want to arrive any later than we had to.

Back on the boat I dolled out a corner of the donut to everyone that wanted any, just me, and we were on our way. The wind was avoiding Port Douglas to the best of its ability, the shielding effect of the headland causing it to fly fast over, leading to a crawl along the waves for the first hour.

Preparing food while under sail is something that's possible but best avoided, and delightfully Kate had bought us all some savoury coconut dishes from the mark,et in the morning. The stall owner drilled into each coconut with a special porcelain drill attachment to shred the flesh inside, and filled it with tomato, avocado, and salad. I don't think I've had coconut in a savoury meal before, barring in milk or cream form of course, so it was novel to try a relatively new food. I probably wouldn't have it again, but it was novel nonetheless.  I again tried to peddle my donut to the others, but they weren't interested, so I had some and figured it would last longer this way anyway.

In the late afternoon we pulled in adjacent to a small picturesque island, mooring near Flying Colours, one of the other boats of our little flotilla that had caught up to us from Cairns. It was quite grey and windy so we opted to postpone exploring the island until the next morning, and had a relaxed evening on the boat. We watched "Priscilla: Queen of the Desert", and I finished off the rest of my donut and brownie, so long for it lasting longer than a day.

33.title: Day 35: Endeavour Reef
paragraphs: 2nd of June
Hope Island turned out to be quite bare when we poked around it in the morning. It had a few overgrown campsites and a toilet, with a shallow rocky reef cupping it ocean side.

A few of the islands I've visited have campsites maintained by the national parks that they are in, and none of them have ever been occupied. It makes me wonder who would really use them, as if you've sailed there the would generally have your own bed on board the ship, as we did.

As the reef was less coral and more rock, not ideal for snorkeling, it was decided that we would sail further out to Endeavour Reef. Navigating out way into the the relative safety of the hollow centre of the reef, I stood on the roof of the boat and called out the coral bombers as I saw them, and we navigated the maze into a shallow seabed. At one point we had to turn around and exit the small dead end we'd entered, and we had to reposition the anchor once as we'd drifted uncomfortably close to a coral outcrop.

It was worth the effort. It was, far and away, the best conditions we've had so far. The pristine, clear water put the healthy reef on full display, with species of clams and fishes I hadn't seen before populating the coral floor. It was a grand spectacle, and I am lucky to have witnessed it.
The night was the calmest we've had so far when staying out on the reef, and I had an almost uninterrupted sleep.

34.title: Day 36: Reef to Reef
paragraphs: 3rd of June

I grabbed the knock-off GroPro as we jumped in the tender, and the three of us were off early in the morning to explore more of the beautiful reef. My focused efforts at videography were thwarted by the shakiness and poor quality of the footage, which as I've looked back over is about 20 minutes of blurry fish swimming away from me, but I had fun capturing it.

I took a nice close shot of a shark back at the boat, as Dave had speared a fish, the scent of which really does draw them in quickly from afar. They are amazingly fast compared to most other fish where the movement in their bodies is very obvious; sharks can accelerate instantly with a subtle flick of their tails.

I'm not a fan of spearfishing, obviously, but the worst part is how bad fish smell when coming out of the water. Aren't they being washed constantly as they swim through the water? Why do they reek so badly with some a pervasive odour?

Before heading back to the catamaran and sailing on, we took a detour to the outer edge of the reef. Here, the white breakers crash onto nothing as the large swells coming in from further out are force against the underwater coral wall. There was a steep drop off from less than a metre down to over 10, with larger fish barely visible swimming further out in the saturated depths. These are the breakers that lookouts would have been keeping watch for on wooden tall ships, and you can only imagine the terror that would have swept through the crew when "Breakers!" was called during a night sail.

A couple of hours later we were at Osterlund reef, and back in the water for another swim. It was nowhere near as clear as the last spot unfortunately, as the water was slightly opaque. We still swam around for a while and I saw a shark and a turtle, which I've come to learn aren't as rare as I would have thought.
At the end of the day I was truly spent from swimming, and it was a welcome return back to the cat to turn in for the evening.

35.title: Day 37: Cooktown
paragraphs: 4th of June

We didn't waste any time this morning at the blurry reef, and sailed straight into Cooktown after breakfast. It was quite choppy and gave me a bit of a headache, a residual bit of seasickness that still affects me.
Cooktown is nestled against the south shore of a bay, hidden from view until the last minute. It's much smaller than Port Douglas, and had one main strip with a scattering of shops.

In the afternoon I explored the small botanic gardens, and in the evening we all went to the bowling club for Kate's birthday. We're going to be here for a few days, so tomorrow I plan on waking up the nearby mount cook.

36.title: Day 38: Starvation
paragraphs: 5th of June
Well not really starvation, but today I didn't wear the shirt that I'd put my debit card in the pocket of last night, and had to subsist on an apple and a pack of Oreos between lunch and dinner.
I pretty much just strolled around some walks in the area today, as my attempt to climb Mt Cook was foiled due to there not being a path from where I was to the start of the walk.

At the end of the day there was a bit of drama, as when I arrived back at the boat there was a knock from the owner of the dock. Apparently we'd only booked for one night, not two, and had to move off to go and anchor. I called Dave down from the pub and we moved the boat. It's kind of annoying because when you're anchored it's a pain getting into shore, you can only get there with use of the tender.
In the evening we watched the final two episodes of Alone, which I would recommend to anyone interested.

37.title: Day 39: Mt Cook
paragraphs: 6th of June
Today was a great day.
