We started the morning by getting our shopping done. I visited the IGA and an independent grocer, and am looking forward to some of the meals I've got lined up. Stir fry has really become a mainstay (mainstay is also a boating term btw), but I now also have ingredients for some curry and mexican!
After bringing all the shopping back to the boat, I defrosted the back of the fridge that had a carrot and spring onion horizontally lodged quite comically in the ice.

I was still determined to get some post in the mail and climb Mt Cook, so I was dropped in town in the early afternoon. The post took a while, and the journey from town to where the walk actually starts was long too.

I was quite waylaid by the fact that the 'road' I was following to get there turned out to not be a road at all. Coming to a bushy dead end where Google maps said the road continues, I found myself bush bashing through the scrub mainly hoping it would thin back out. A local later informed me that this phenomenon was called 'paper roads', roads that exist only on paper.

At one point, I came to an unmarked dead end. To get around it, I would have had to walk a few hundred metres back and then around the block. An aerial view revealed, however, that the road I needed to get to was only 100m away as the crow flies, passing through some dense swampy land wedged between two lots. Needless to say, I stumbled my way through the mucky ground and emerged victorious, in a way.

It was 4pm when I finally arrived at the start of the hike, that was supposedly a 3 hour return journey. It's always a pleasure to explore a biome away from home, and the thick tropical forest was the perfect cool temperature at the time of year and day that I was there.

There were a couple of nice lookouts, but I dared not dwell at them too long, the setting sun a spur in my flank. On the way back down I was accosted by some walker's dog, but he quickly turned out to be as friendly as his owners Heidi and Jason, who offered to give me a lift back into town. We had a great chat on the walk back down and in their car, and they told me how they couldn't wait for their son to finish high school so they could get back on the road and do some travelling!

When they dropped me back at the famed solitary Thai restaurant in town, I was very keen for a feed. As a vegan, Thai places are a safe haven where you can always get a nice tofu dish, but not this one. When I went to order, I was informed there was nothing at all they could do for me, as they used oyster sauce in everything.
Luckily, the pizza van nearby did me a vegan special and even dropped the price for me, I believe out of pity for my vegan condition.
I'm very excited for tomorrow. It's going to be an early start into an 8 hour sail, as we're aiming for Lizard Island a fair way north.

38.title: Day 40: Lizard Island
paragraphs: It was an early start this morning as we had a good distance of ground(water) to cover. At 7am we were back on the dock, refilling our water tanks, as they will need to last us until either Thursday Island or Darwin.

The owner of the dock was there, having a yarn with Dave about the large crayfish boat that had come through yesterday. He was complaining about how they always leave the dock a mess, when he asks them to leave it clean. I was shocked when as he was talking and picking up bits of seaweed and chucking them back into the water, he grabbed a large tangle of fishing line, and plopped it into the water next to his own dock. A bin was less than 10 metres away. Fishermen eh.

On the way out of the harbour we passed AOWN, the third boat travelling with us. floundering in the wind. The furler of their screecher sail had snapped, and the sailing was whipping about in the strong wind. We radioed them to see if they needed assistance, but they were able to get it wrapped and use their other sails alone.
We had a hard time ourselves, the wind picking up quickly as we left the lee of the headland, and I was running up and down the deck, rerouting sheets and reefing the sails. It was a bunch of fun.

For the rest of the sail it was a beautiful sunny day and I spent over an hour sitting up the front on the deck, occasionally being splashed by the waves. The coast up here is absent of houses, and islands dot the ocean.
We arrived at Lizard Island around 3, and jumped in for a snorkel. The reef is a bit bleached in parts, but due to it being a marine sanctuary, the fish here are very unafraid.
In the evening I cooked a spicy curry for us for dinner, and took hours to edit a short highlight video that you can see on my Instagram.

39.title: Day 41: Up the hill
paragraphs: There was much discussion in the morning about heading over to the east side of the island for some kite surfing, but it didn't end up eventuating.

Instead, I spent the morning blowing up the two inflatables on the boat, a pink flamingo and a blue narwhal. The sun was beating down so I took them under the front of the boat, a nice grotto to retreat to where the glowing teal water beneath is illuminated more than the underside of the boat.

Dave then took the tender to another beach for a snorkel, and I held on to a rope and rode the narwhal the whole way around the headland. It was quite difficult as unlike a normal wakeboard, the inflatable was not tethered to the boat, and I had to grip the rope very firmly the entire way. Also unlike a wakeboard, the narwhal was not designed with minimizing drag in mind, exacerbating the previous issue. This was compounded again when we left the relative calm of our bay and passed around the headland, as the swell led to the force not being applied at a constant rate, but in waves. As the tender would crest each wave, the rope would fall slack in my arms, and as it then surfed down the face of the wave, the pull of the rope would be redoubled. It was very fun, and Dave and I were laughing throughout, but my forearms were on fire by the end.
The snorkel was nice, as part of the reef is bleached but the outer drop off is healthy, populated by many fishes.
In the afternoon I finished a stamp design for the boat, that we will need to stamp paperwork for Indonesia.

After a late lunch, it was finally time to climb the hill as the sun's heat was abating. I began the walk after 4, but it was less than an hour each way. After reading my book for a while at the top, I came back down and arrived just in time, the beach growing dark as I walked down it.

Tomorrow we will be sailing out the "cod hole" and I'm unsure of what to expect. Good news is that we will be speeding up and pushing hard for Thursday Island, and then Darwin soon after, so I may be there in a couple of weeks!

40.title: Day 42: The Cod Hole
paragraphs: 9th of June

We arrived on the outer reef, at a place called the "Cod Hole", at about midday. The snorkelling here was different, as we were right on the edge of the reef, where the depth drops away to the ocean deep.

The majority of the reef was under a metre deep on a rocky shelf to our south, but we swam along the edge of this where underwater peninsulas and tables grew out of this into the deeper water. There were a few tunnels that I found where it was possible to swim down to a depth of 4m or so, then through a cave to emerge on the other side of a coral ridge.
There were plenty of fish and a few sharks, and the coral on the outer edge was mostly healthy.
It was a quiet evening, and the sunset gave us a great view to end the day.

41.title: Day 43: Back to Lizard
paragraphs: 10th June
There was no snorkel in the morning today, as we sailed straight back toward the mainland with Lizard island as our destination.

This time, we pulled into the east side of the island, where there is a "lagoon" that is more so a sheltered sandy reef. It's connected to the ocean by multiple wide channels, but mostly protected by the reefs and islets in between them.
The snorkelling there wasn't fantastic, and it seems like most of the shallow reefs have been bleached to some extent.

In the afternoon we sailed back around to the comfy harbour to spend the night, which was only a short half hour affair. The others then went into the resort on the island, which is only open to non guests Tuesday and Saturday, but I opted to stay on the boat. As much as I like all the crews on the boats, I don't really enjoy sitting around at a bar drinking with them, as they're all 20 years my senior.

Tomorrow we're going to be passing far north ahead of bad weather, and will be sailing from the morning until Thursday night uninterrupted! I'm excited for the overnight sail tomorrow, and will let you know how it goes!

42.title: Day 44: Into the night
paragraphs: 11th of June
I'm writing this as I retire to bed on the morning of the 12th.

We've been sailing for almost 24 hours straight at the moment, and it's been generally quite smooth. There was some swell yesterday afternoon, but also a period in the lee of a low isle that was stiller than most anchorages.

I've been up since about 3:30 am, as my night shift ran from 4-7 am. It was a great experience being in charge of keeping an eye on everything, and seeing the dawn slowly break over the horizon as I did so.

When I'm at the helm, I have to keep an eye on the wind speed and angle, to ensure that our sail is not backwinded and marine traffic and markers in the area, making sure I have visuals on them when they're in range too.
Unfortunately I didn't sleep that well before my shift, as my body knew I'd have to be up in the middle of the night, but I'm looking forward to getting a good sleep now!

43.title: Day 45: Restoration Island
paragraphs: 12th June

After falling asleep at about 8 in the morning, I was expecting to wake up to the rolling ocean as we powered on until that afternoon, when we had planned to anchor. I could hear the sounds of the anchor dropping as I woke back up around 10, and came upstairs to see what was going on.

Flying colours, the slowest boat of our little flotilla, had a tired crew of Darren and Shane, and wanted us to pull in so they could catch up and rest. We anchored just off of Restoration Island, and I'm glad we were able to stop at this significant spot.

As we'd motored into the bay, there had been a minor engine issue that Dave wanted some help fixing. He needed me to clear out a small water drainage hole under the engine that had become blocked and could not reach, so I chucked my board shorts on and got ready to jump into the water. At that moment, we were hailed on the radio by the residents of the island, advising us to stay out of the water and off the paddleboards, as they'd sighted their resident 4 m long croc 'Boxhead' two days ago. Needless to say I managed to clear the blockage by reaching down past the motor, without entering the water.

Named restoration island by a relieved William Bligh in 1789, it was the first landing spot they'd arrived at in just about a month, after being banished from their ship by mutineers. If you haven't heard the story in a while, here is a great telling of it that I would highly recommend: https://halfarsedhistory.net/2019/05/12/episode-46-mutiny-on-the-bounty-part-1/.

Today, we were greeted on the island by three residents: Steven and Selena, the caretakers, and Colin, the leaseholder. The caretakers lived there all year round in relative isolation, while Colin spent a few months a year there, coinciding with our visit.

They had an excellent mostly self sufficient system, consisting of a great veggie patch and a large house, fitted with modern amenities. Gracious hosts, to my surprise they loaded us with papayas and some vegetables, which I thought would be more valuable to them than us.

We stayed in the harbour that night, with plans to continue on north tomorrow. The forecast for Friday had looked too strong to sail in but has since eased off, so hopefully we will be able to make up some of the ground we lost by quitting earlier today.

44.title: Day 46: Margaret Bay
paragraphs: 13th June

We were quickly underway in the morning, making full use of the unforeseen good weather, that has held out longer than it was forecast. It was easy sailing, and by the early afternoon we'd come 40 of the 50 or so nm that we had to cover.

The one stop we made was at Haggerstone Island Resort, where a friend of Darren's works as a host and manager. It is an extremely remote luxury eco lodge experience, where guests can fly in to stay in open plan villas on a beautiful private island for a family getaway.

Taken for a quick private tour of the island while the guests were in the bay on one of the custom boats, we were shown the impressive main house and some of the water and food logistics that go into running such an endeavour.

Oh to be to able to purchase an island in the 80s, and own a veritable licence to print money. The rich clientele pay up to 13.5k a night for use of the island, a price that has almost doubled since 2020.
Private islands about in Queensland, tropical paradises that you will never visit due to your poor lineage.
After the tour of the island, we sailed the last hour to pull into Margaret bay, where we may shelter for a few days to wait out the strong, gusty winds.

As we rounded the corner to enter the bay, Dave told me to go to the pulpit to watch for reefs and guide the boat, something I do often. We were cutting the corner slightly, and though far from shore, there is a sandbar that extends the point a couple of hundred metres underwater into the passage.

I could see a colour change in the water ahead, but couldn't make out what it was or how deep it would be, as normally the slight lightening of the water is sand deeper at the bottom. As we approached I called out to steer to starboard, as I could see the bottom was closer than I thought. As we swerved around to the right, we still ended up passing over the sandbar that was a perpendicular line in our path. I clenched as Dave was calling out the depth chart, "3 metres... 2.5 metres... 2 metres...," and we ended up passing over a sandy bottom at 1.7m depth. Given we have a 1m clearance requirement, it was much closer than we would have liked.

It's humid up here and I'm lamenting the fact that I can't jump in the water due to crocodiles in the area. Unlike the analogous fear of sharks I had further south, this one is actually quite reasonable, and I will be regrettably be foregoing swimming at any sort of estuary or shoreline.

45.title: Day 47: Waiting
paragraphs: The weather has been too gusty to leave today, so we've remained at Margaret Bay.

There isn't much here bar the wild muddy beach and tropical bushland behind it, so we spent the majority of the day on the boat, taking care of chores and getting things in order. My job of the day was to restitch some of the netting at the front that has been torn.

In the afternoon we took the tender into the beach, as there was a 'Blue Track' trail, with a few comments on an anchorage forum app saying it continues to the other side of the headland but is quite overgrown. The track gets its name from the decorations of blue flotsam that mark it the entire way. Looking like a long thin bowerbird nest, among the markers I saw plastic tubs, helmets, flippers, toothbrushes, fenders, shoes, thongs, rope, cones, and netting.

The fact that it was all rubbish was not greatly to my liking but visually it was interesting, and we discussed on the walk if one person was very devoted and had placed it all, or if every visitor to this anchorage places something new. The diversity seemed too high to consist of purely washed up trash, especially the toothbrushes, so I suspect people bring thing specifically for this spot.

To me the two most interesting sights both involved ant's nests. Cones had been placed on a few vertical mud termite nests in the past, and the termites had continued to build upward. One of the cones was perforated, and the termites had built straight up through it, whereas the solid cones caused them to divert and build around them in the pursuit of elevation.

The other was a clear plastic bottle that had been placed over a broken tree branch. Green ants were living inside of it, allowing for a clear view inside their nest that is normally blocked by the opaque leaves they used. The green ants were a constant annoyance on the walk, and somehow kept finding their way onto me as I pushed through the bush. At one point, I was pulling them out of my short beard I've been growing, as they grabbed on and tried to bite me as much as possible.
The walk took a few hours but apart from that the day was quite empty. There was talk of leaving tomorrow early (4:30 am!), but this has been nixed and now the talk is of the day after.

46.title: Day 48: Idle
paragraphs: 15th of June
Chill day today, didn't get up to much. The weather was grey and rainy throughout the day, so we didn't even go to shore.
I've actually caved and am writing a bit of code on Kate's laptop, it's a lot more fun to do now that I'm not at the computer every day for work.

In the evening we went over to Darren's boat, and they had a large fish skeleton from one of the fish that they'd caught. They strung it over the back of the boat in the water, and within half an hour there were multiple reef sharks splashing in the water and biting onto it.

Eventually, right as we were leaving and I was walking down towards our tender, I saw a massive nurse shark in the water. It was huge, but very slow and considered, moving with gentle movements in contrast to the flighty reef sharks.
Shane even touched it, and after I saw it not react to him I followed suit, reaching down and touching its back as it grubbed around the side of the boat.
Back on our boat for an early night, Dave said we'd be moving at 7 tomorrow which suits me. Keen to see the northern tip of Aus soon enough!

47.title: Day 49: Jardine River
paragraphs: An early start into a rough sea wasn't the best awakening this morning, and I felt a bit seasick as we plowed up and down the swell on our way north.

It rained hard a few times today, something that we've been lucky enough to avoid for most of this trip, but not today. The rain, swell, and travel made for a pretty mediocre day, confined to the rocking cabin until the late afternoon.
The coastline up here is pristine, as we're almost at the northernmost point of Australia and are due to arrive tomorrow.
Around the middle of the day I was trying to sleep and I heard Kate exclaim as she was cleaning up the cabin. Behind the large wine box was a small tree snake!!

We have absolutely no idea how it got aboard, as we've not anchored that close to the forest, and the other crews confirmed that they didn't pull some weird prank and hide it there. Our best guess is that it came aboard with some of our gear somehow, maybe in a box or something like that. I've now transferred it to a bigger box, and will release it next time we go ashore.

Dave also started cursing in the late arvo due to the autopilot failing. As you know, the autopilot is a lifesaver, and protects us from the toil of sitting at the helm manually adjusting the wheel constantly.

Once we anchored we took apart the entire wheel, and Dave concluded that it was the gearbox that is broken. We unfortunately don't have a replacement so this could seriously spell trouble. We're going to investigate tomorrow where we can pick one up asap, but we may be crossing the entire Gulf of Carpentaria with no autopilot. This will lead to much less sitting around the cabin, and constant shifts for each of us at the wheel. Not keen.

48.title: Day 50: The Tip of Australia.
paragraphs: 17th of June.

The fact that today was meant to be a 'calm' day according to the forecast held no weight as we shoved our way through the over 20 knot wind and 1.5 m swells. The lack of autopilot made it even worse, as I had to sit behind the wheel for a while, making constant adjustments to fend off the efforts of the waves to turn us away from our destination.

We were aiming for Thursday Island, a town three thousand strong that lies in the Torres Straight off the northern tip of mainland Australia, just off Cape York. It was one of the rainiest days we've had so far, with intermittent showers pelting down on the unprotected helm of the boat. Thank the heavens that it's so warm up here even at this time of year.

The swell was at its worst as we approached the passage between Albany Island (where Stone Beach is on the map above) and the mainland, but as soon as we passed into the lee of the island it died off.
The passage was beautiful, with rainforested beaches on either side of us, only marred by the dreary weather above.

Finally reaching a major turning point of this trip, we arrived at the northernmost point of the Australian continent. After anchoring at the beach behind the point of interest, we prepared to jump in the tender for the short rainy walk. I grabbed the snake box, spying some jungle behind the beach that would be a perfect release spot for our unwanted hitchhiker.
As we arrived on the shore I thought I should take a peek into the box, just to confirm the snake was still in there. It wasn't.

Somewhere on the boat as I write this, the snake is curled up hidden well enough to avoid the deep search that I undertook on our arrival back at the boat. It must have squeezed out the top in the night, and used the dark hours to crawl off to god knows where. I hope it doesn't find my warmth in the night as a comfortable basking spot.
Back to the walk, it was only a short distance to a small metal plaque that declared the spot as the northern tip, the sign riddled with bullet holes as a testament to the culture of FNQ.
We didn't stay long, and sailed the remaining distance to Thursday Island in the mid afternoon, arriving at the small anchorage at around 4.

The anchorage is closer to Horn Island than it is to Thursday, a distance too great to cover comfortably in the tender. Early tomorrow we plan on getting the ferry service over, and I'll spend the day making a personal assessment of the town for your reading pleasure.

49.title: Day 51: Disaster Strikes
paragraphs: 18th of June

Our sheltered anchorage was almost 3 km away from Thursday Island, a distance too great to ride in our small dinghy. Taking the whole catamaran over won out against the other option of the ferry, so by mid morning we were under motor for the short trip over to the rock.

The boat had been experiencing a strong "weather helm" effect in recent days, where the asymmetrical force of the wind on the sail turns the boat toward the winds origin. Dave was struggling with it, as I had also felt yesterday when bringing the boat through the rougher seas. We even put one of the daggerboards down in an effort to increase drag on the offending side, but it only learned the effect.

Suddenly, Dave goes "Hey would you be able to just look down and check both the rudders are there?" From where I was I could lean down and see the port anchor in the water, so I walked around and looked to where the starboard anchor should have been. Gone. I convey this to Dave and we stare at each other in silence for about 10 seconds, a bad sign as normally Dave curses to himself when things go wrong, but this was too much for him to even do that.
Apparently he's had it righted before, and the subsequent weaknesses had caused it to twist off in the swell we've been having.

We anchored at Thursday Island and had a bit of a chat about the issue. I don't need to state that rudders are very crucial pieces of equipment, and unfortunately there didn't seem to be any facilities on the island that could deal with a problem like this.

On the island, I had a frustrating morning. Hanging over my head was the cloud of consideration that this may be the end of my journey on the boat; this journey has already taken longer than I thought and I would not be waiting around for weeks to have a new rudder sent from afar.

I also walked up the steep hill to a ghost cafe that existed only in cyberspace, and was very disappointed by the take away shack lunch I settled for. The cultural centre was the best part of the day, with fantastic Torres Straight artwork and culture on display.
Overall, I wasn't impressed by the titan of Thursday Island, though it is in a beautiful location.
We reconvened at the pub, and it was thankfully decided that we would just limp to Darwin on one rudder to sort the issue there. I'm unsure of where Darwin will steer our journey.

Dave and I went into town again to fill the jerry cans up, but the bowser we arrived at had been permanently closed. Luckily a kind local offered to drive us across the town and back to the actual servo, which was unfortunately out of unleaded. The local was great, and I love seeing that small town camaraderie between strangers that is unknown in Sydney.
In the evening we brought the catamaran the long way back around to our sheltered anchorage near Horn Island, and I stood in the pulpit steering us around reefs.
We're going to be staying for a little bit as the weather doesn't look ideal, but hopefully it's not too long.

50.title: Day 52 : Horn Island
paragraphs: 19th of June
I thought I'd have the day off today to relax, but it was up at breakfast to start ticking off the chores.
Up first was moving the lone rudder from port to starboard, a task that had me jumping in the water 5 minutes after jumping out of bed as I yanked it from one keel and fiddled it into another.
Next was filling the jerry cans, and luckily on the island near the dock we found an automated pre-pay bowser.
We then took the drogue(a kind of light sea anchor to increase drag) for a joyride in the tender, and confirmed that it would suit us.

The skippers have decided we will hit the water tomorrow! The weather isn't ideal, but it's not getting any better so we're just going to send it. We'll be sailing straight to the Gove Peninsula from here, going through the night tomorrow and Saturday nights to arrive hopefully Sunday day.

Kate is worried about the journey, given that we're down an autopilot and a rudder, but I'd say I'm apprehensive at most. It'll be an interesting experience, and the fact we have 2 other boats with us acts as a reassuring safety net.

In the arvo I went for a shop to top up the larder, and the other crews came over for an hour or so at sunset. Excited to see what tomorrow holds, and tick off a few podcast episodes as I man the helm for hours!

51.title: Day 53: Long Beach
paragraphs: 20th of June

Unfortunately, we've been delayed in our departure across the gulf due to strong winds. Dave's sage advice is that every time he's seen a strong wind warning and decided to push ahead, he's regretted it later and so I'm more than happy to wait it out given the issues we've had with the boat.

Instead, we sailed the short distance over to Friday Island in the morning, and trialed the new drogue, a light sea anchor that increases resistance when dangled off the boat. This will help is balance the weather-helming, and drag caused by a single anchor as we cross the gulf. It was a fun challenge to figure out the best way to anchor the drogue off the back of the boat, given the requirements of the task: We wanted to be able to shift it from one side to the other, winch it in without occupying the same wind as a sail, and have it at a low enough angle to work well in the water. Kate and I had fun trying out a few solutions, and have come up with one that works quite well.

After a short beach walk on Friday Island, the swell prompted us to search for calmer waters. Dave had his eye on Long beach to the southwest, and so we motored our way there. It was a stressful journey, as rather than taking a wide berth around the sandy, shallow waters, Dave took us on a route through the sandbanks. As I'm the one standing at the front of the boat directing, it was my job to make sure we didn't run aground, but with water that was frequently under 3m in depth, it was quite the challenge.
Kate and I weren't pleased with the choice of route, and both would have much rather gone wide around the shallows, and felt like we were risking our one rudder for no good reason.

When we finally arrived at Long Beach to our great relief, we were greeted by a lovely spot. There's some buildings behind the treeline, but no signs of life. The water is also calm and much more protected from the wind chop, so if we're going to be waiting out the wind for a few days I'm glad to be doing it here.
Also, there's still no sign of the snake. Maybe it's slipped away in the night, but Kate's sure it's still lurking somewhere on board.

52.title: Day 54: They see me strolling
paragraphs: 21st of June.

We stayed the whole day anchored at Long Beach today, and so I used the opportunity to go for a walk around the area. I followed the shoreline to the north and crumbled up a dense rocky hill, coming down the other side into a secluded rock beach.

At the south end of the beach there was a shady cave that I sat in for a while, before following the shoreline further around to the next beach and taking the path from there directly back to Long Beach.
In the evening we had a fire on the beach, joined by some locals in the area.
We'll be leaving tomorrow morning to start this double overnight passage, so I've had an early night to rest for the following night shifts.

53.title: Day 55: The Gulf
paragraphs: 22nd of June.
What a rough day. I have to say, I was very excited to experience an ocean passage at the start of the day, but by 1 am that had all melted away into discomfort.

The primary contribution to this is that I never seem to feel 'fine' in rough seas. Maybe I'll always get just a touch seasick, but as the boat jumps around I'm always very slightly nauseous with a very mild headache. While they aren't bad alone, putting up with them for a day hasn't been the most fun experience.

The other is the manual helming. It's a constant effort. While Dave is fantastic, and somehow machines his way through at the wheel for more than half the day, Kate did about one hour yesterday. Now, I'm not wanting to air out all my grievances here, but it's surprising considering the amount of advice she had for me when I was learning how to steer.

I was at the wheel for about 5 hours yesterday day, then another 5 from after 8 pm until 1. The day shifts passed relatively uneventfully, as I've become quite good at steering by the clouds and wind indicator, and I listened to a bunch of podcasts as I did it. The weather was also calmer than forecast which was a welcome boon.

Night was a different story, however, as the cloud cover meant I couldn't steer by the stars, and was steering instead via the compass. It's just a number display, showing your angle to true north, which isn't as intuitive as the wind direction, or better yet just looking at land.

At 10 Dave asked me if I wanted relief, and if I wanted to get back up at 1 to do the 1am to 4am shift. I said I'd rather either power on until 1 and sleep until 7, or do the 4-7 shift, so I could get a 6 hour block of sleep in there somewhere. We decided I'd stay on until 1.

The wind and swell picked up, gusting to 25 knots, and I only got more tired as the night went on. By midnight, I was wrecked and the strong winds meant I couldn't use the light of the other boat, but had to steer using the compass.

I kept confusing myself into steering the wrong way, as the rapid responses required in those conditions meant I had to quickly throw the wheel back and forth in answer. Occasionally we'd start to go quickly in one direction and I'd throw the wheel in the wrong direction, exacerbating the problem quickly. The boat can also quickly gain twisting momentum, meaning that if you start to spin, it can be hard to counteract.

At one point I fully lost control of the boat. I reacted slowly to a strong gust and swell that came in, which spun us just enough for the wind to get on the wrong side of the sail, and suddenly gybe the main over, with the boom swinging violently above my head. We'd spun over 90 degrees downwind, and we're now heading in the wrong direction. I called out to Dave and he turned the engine on, and turned the boat a further 270 degrees to put us back on course, which tacked the boom gently back into position.

He then wanted to make sure I had it under control, and was watching over my shoulder as I tried to keep us on course. The experience had my hands shaking, and I was simultaneously panicked and exhausted. I kept screwing up the direction and he was trying to get me to react earlier to direction changes. There's no point trying to teach someone something new after midnight in the state I was in, and it was an unpleasant experience.

He went back to bed at ~12:15 and I somehow made it through to 1am. I was watching the degree reading like a hawk the whole time, in a panicky state whenever the gusts would start to spin the boat. Let me remind you we only have one rudder, exacerbating this whole situation. This was the complete opposite of the relaxed day sailing I'd been doing earlier, and it required all the attention I could muster to keep us on track.

The worst part is that the compass display also shows the clock, so rather than being able to glance at it occasionally when I'm steering via the horizon, and seeing that another 15 minutes has quickly passed, I had to agonisingly watch every minute tick past. It was one of the longest 45 minutes of my life.
Finally, he re-emerged at 1 and relieved me, and I collapsed into bed. Despite how tired I was, it took me a while to get to sleep due to how wired I was.
The day sailing had been nice, however, and I watched some dolphins play in front of the boat and a bird land right behind us. The boat seems to be a magnet for life when you're this far from shore.

54.title: Day 56: The Crossing
paragraphs: 23rd of June
Another full day of sailing. I started feeling better after getting up and moving around, and most of the day was pleasant.

I crawled out of bed to offer to relieve Dave, as he'd been up late with me, done the 1 am - 4 am shift, and was back on the wheel. He declined, and I honestly don't know how he powers through. I don't think he's had more than 2 hours of uninterrupted sleep as of my writing this at 8pm on day 2, and seems no worse for wear. I'm impressed and thankful.

I jumped on the wheel from 9:45 - 12, then from 4-6:30. In the morning shift I listened to some podcasts and practiced my muscle memory of steering via the compass dial so I don't confuse myself again tonight, and in the evening I listened to some girly pop and sang along to the beautiful sunset. I was vibing hard and in a great mood.

I had to go up on deck an hour ago in the dark to put another reef in the main sail, quite the experience. I insisted on wearing the life jacket and Dave showed me how to attach it to the safety line as I walked up the side of the boat. Falling into the ocean at night and having to float there indefinitely in the darkness is literally my second worst nightmare after a fox getting the chickens. Luckily it went off without a hitch and I'm back in bed, where I can almost pretend I'm in a structure. 😍🏢

It had to come at some point, and I'm on the dreaded 1am - 4am tonight. At least I have some warning, so I'm heading to bed now to hopefully get a few hours sleep before I'm roused, but I'm worried I'll have trouble sleeping due to being anxious about tonight. The wind seems to have picked up again tonight, and it's even swinging around with Dave at the helm. He doesn't complain almost ever, which makes one of us, but even he let out a "what I wouldn't give for an autopilot" half an hour ago. Me too brother, me too.

55.title: Day 57: Land Ahoy
paragraphs: So last night went a little differently to how I had envisioned it. It was taking me ages to get to sleep, but just as I was drifting off at 10pm in preparation for my 1am alarm, Dave woke me up. He said it was time to start me shift, as I was doing 10pm-1am. I was confused, as we'd said I was doing the 1am-4am earlier, but he said I was always on the 10pm one.
There have been a few small communication issues on board but I was more than happy with this one, as it meant that I could get the shift done, get into bed at 1, and sleep until 7.

The shift was far calmer than last time, and I found steering much more forgiving. I was nervous at first, as I really didn't want to repeat the spin out of last night. Once is fine, but god two would just be too much. As the compass dialed incremented quickly up and down I slowly fell into the beat of counteracting the turns, but was still wary that a quick reversal into a sharp turn may have me pulling on the wheel the wrong way.

I'd planned on calling some friends to chat the shift away with, but I thought that that would make me more likely to lapse in concentration, so I listened to some podcasts instead. Finally, minute by minute, 1am crawled around and Dace finally roused from the couch to take over. I collapsed into bed happily, knowing that it was the last night of the passage.

I woke up to one of the best sounds and feelings ever. I could hear the anchor going down and the boat was no longer rocking; we were in the calm safety of a bay. I wondered how we had arrived so quickly, but closed my eyes and slept for another hour.

It turns out that we'd had great winds from 1-7, and the progress had been very fast, bringing us to the Gove Peninsula earlier than anticipated. We were in a small beautiful bay, with white beaches around. The others went to shore in the afternoon, but I decided to stay on the boat as it was indigenous land that we didn't have the required permission to visit.

I did a little research on the 'Hole in the Wall' passage crossing that we would be passing through tomorrow, and quickly dipped in the water to wash off the last couple of days, but I dared not stay in long as there had been croc sightings in the area.

We wanted to make it to the crossing just after the tide started to ebb tomorrow at 9am, which was a couple of hours sail away. As it would be an early morning to make that window, I went for an early night and had no problems getting to sleep quickly.

56.title: Day 58: The hole in the wall
paragraphs: By 7am we were on the water and pushing to make it to the passage by the turn of the tide. The hole in the wall is a thin straight between two islands that the tide rushes through, and we had to ensure that we didn't enter it too late. The ideal time is just after the tide has started to ebb, as this ensures the water is flowing in the right direction but not yet at full speed.

We made it with 10 minutes to spare and shortly entered the flowing passage. With only our engine on we were doing 10 knots in the strong current, and I imagine that halfway between the tides it would be an even wilder ride.
It was great fun, and shortly after we pulled into another beautiful sheltered bay for the night.

57.title: Day 59: Refuge Bay
paragraphs: 26th of June

Not too much to report today, we sailed for a few hours in the morning down to another bay, which was a bumpy ride. The winds briefly hit 30 knots while I was at the helm, the highest I've personally seen, and the wind chop was rocking the boat as we were sailing upwind.

The bay is pretty, and the beautiful red earth is visible on the shore, a definite confirmation that we are in the NT. I didn't go ashore again as it's indigenous land, but it's a nice spot to be in. Tomorrow we're in for another day of sailing, and hopefully a few more days after that we'll be in Darwin.

58.title: Day 60: A short drama
paragraphs: 27th June

Day 60! 2 months on the water, and enough time for me to truly get a feel for what day to day sailing is like. We're aiming to get to Darwin on Tuesday, and this is a goal that Dave is pushing for, as he wants to get the repairs underway before he briefly flies to Brisbane for work.

Aiming for another early start, we'd pulled up the anchor and were starting to motor out of out bay when the engine started to make a sharp scratchy noise, so Dave cut it. A few more restarts and the noise persisted whenever revved, as Dave got more and more agitated, starting to swear.

It got worse and the noise louder, and the engine was having trouble revving at all, and Dave pretty much lost it. He got so worked up he just let out a couple of primal screams into the morning air, I think the first one was fuck but the second was just a pained roar.

Not the best way to handle something going wrong, but I'm sympathetic as we've been through a lot already, and a ruined engine would be extremely expensive and massively jeopardise the trip. He is quite good at keeping his anger to himself though, and it was only when Kate was coming at him with too many questions about it right as he was processing it, which I could sense, that he let out a "please, Kate." I thought that was pretty amusing.

It turned out all the oil had leaked out, and we quickly saw that the lower plug from the oil chamber on the engine was missing. The convoy came to help, and within about half an hour we'd fashioned a new working plug and refilled using Darren's oil donation. I was very glad we managed to fix it, as I'm not sure what a broken engine would have meant. Anchoring straight from sail is a difficult manoeuvre, but I guess it would have been either that or multiple overnight sails straight to Darwin.

In the afternoon we pulled into the bay of an indigenous settlement, the first building I've seen since Friday Island. When we saw a boat launch shortly after our arrival, we thought they might be coming to tell us we weren't allowed to anchor there and to leave, but they were just going fishing. It would have been nice to check out the township but unfortunately you also can't land here without permission.
I'm starting to run pretty low on food, so I'm looking forward to making some strong progress to Darwin over the next few days.
It might be a few days of Dahl for me :)

59.title: Day 61: Leaving the pack
paragraphs: 28th June

We covered double the distance of the other two boats today, leaving them in our wake as we pressed on for Darwin. I'm glad to be making some quick progress and looking forward to seeing my cousin Angus who lives there currently, but am also aware that I may have to wait there.

If I end up jumping ship and joining Darren's boat, I'd have to wait for him to catch up to Darwin, and then also however long he wanted to stay there too. I'm keen to check Darwin out, but I don't think I want to stay more than a week.

The sailing today was uneventful, though there was some decent swell coming in on our port. Some big slow waves picked us up during my shift as they came in from our rear port. It's amazing how close the boat can feel to catching its bow in the base of a wave and tipping when we start to surf down a wave at an awkward angle, even though it's an extremely rare occurrence.

We're anchored off of a small island, and as we were pulling in Kate spotted some movement in the water, about 50m away. We could see the wings from some big rays splashing above the water, and were wondering if they were either eating, mating, trapped in a net, or being eaten themselves. We investigated in the tender and found a couple of rays swimming free in the shallows, so didn't come back with any definite answers.
Another early start tomorrow, and the journey will continue.

60.title: Day 62: Inching closer
paragraphs: 29th of June
Bog standard day of sailing today, made about 60ks, and have 200 to go until Darwin. Seeing as we can't really get that done in two days and arrive on Tuesday, we're now aiming for Wednesday instead.

Today was a lot of work, I did about 4 hours of manually helming, and it feels like we put various sails up and down constantly throughout the day to react to the changing winds. I didn't think this would happen at this point in the trip, but my hands are the sorest they've been! Pulling on ropes as hard as I can really does a number on my finger skin, and I've now got a few knobbly callouses on my wiry programming fingers 🤓☝️

The wind was playing around with the boat at various points today too, making helming no small task. Dave actually lost control of the boat and gybed during his shift which was a surprise, I think because he was looking at his phone lol.

In the tense moments after as we righted the boat and tried to free the fishing line 😢 from the rudder, Dave and Kate had a go at each other. I think they used to be better friends but it doesn't even feel like they like each other anymore and can be quite tense sometimes. There's definitely some communication issues going on there. Personally, I try to play both sides so I always come out on top. I am looking forward to a change of dynamic in Darwin though, and I think Kate may be planning to bail too.

We ended up at a gorgeous bay against a sandy foreshore populated with gums! It's amazing to see such large trees so close to the water and I'm surprised they can survive the sandy saline conditions. The sand has also darkened, and it's clear we're on the edge of Arnhem land rather than the white sandy beaches of the east coast.

I'm getting pretty hungry at this point too, as I don't have that much food left. It was Dahl again today, and while I'm going to skip Dahl for my last mexican tomorrow, I think that will be my last non-dahl meal bar my Weetabix. I'm also down to my last soy milk carton for that and so had to resist the urge to chug from the carton when I was looking for something to snack on. Hamish, you're the only one that would understand my pain. I think I'll treat myself to a Bonsoy when I get back to civilization. 😋

61.title: Day 63: A varied day
paragraphs: 30th of June
We had about the calmest and the roughest seas in the same day today, and I was lucky enough to be at the helm for both.

The roughest was earlier in the day when we passed cape Cockburn, where big swells were dampening my efforts to keep the boat under control. One massive wave in particular picked us up with it and held us racing down its face, getting over 16 knots as we did! I know I've gone out about the boat feeling like it's going to pitch pole before, but my god my stomach dropped when this one came through. The large swells were due to shallower waters of the Cape, where towing 30m cliffs watched over the straight.

In the afternoon we turned up into a smaller channel, and were sheltered from the wind for the rest of the day. It was the calmest sailing we've done so far, and we were travelling at 7 or 8 knots throughout perfectly calm waters, with the wheel needing only the slightest hint of occasional adjustment.

Tucking in behind a small head, I manned the helm while Dave dropped the anchor and fueled the sails, a novel exchange of our usual roles. The water was calm and the sunset pretty, a great spot to rest after a long day of sailing.

62.title: Day 64: Cut Short
paragraphs: 1st of July
We had a big deciding moment today, whether we would make it across the Van Diemen Gulf on the way to Darwin.
There's nowhere we could stop across the large gulf, and so leaving early we aimed to make it there with time to cross it before dusk.
Unfortunately this didn't pan out, and while the day started strong with a strong 10 knot pace, this had petered out by the mid morning leaving us at half that speed.

Arriving at the beginning of the gulf in the early afternoon, the wind wasn't in our favour so we pulled into a bay right at the headland of the protruding national park, ready to leave in the morning. On our way into the boat we were hailed by a large border force ship, an increasingly large presence in this area.

After another Dahl in the evening from my dwindling supply of lentils, we all had an early night. The plan hadn't changed in terms of arriving in Darwin tomorrow, so we would be leaving at 2 am! I tucked in and hoped I wouldn't have to do too much helming before the dawn broke.

63.title: Day 65: Darwin!
paragraphs: 2nd of July
Just after 2am, I awoke to the sound of the engine coming on. Having not set an alarm, I was extra groggy and stumbled upstairs to see if my help was needed, which luckily it wasn't.
Dave had kindly pulled the anchor up and raised the sails himself, rather than wake me, which I very much appreciated, and we were already motoring out of the bay.

There was a powerful wind blowing and we just had the jib and the main with 2 reefs out as we met the swell of the bay. For most of the pre dawn we pounded against every wave, and even when I slumped back into bed sleep was an elusive target as I lurched around in my bed.

Eventually I did fall asleep somehow, and woke up to join the others after 7. The swell had subsided somewhat and when I took my shift at the helm it wasn't as bad as it had been a few hours ago. A few shift changes later and I was again at the helm in the early afternoon, but it was now an entirely different situation.
The primary reason we'd had to leave so early to make Darwin was that the wind was forecasted to die in the afternoon, which it duly proceeded to do.

At one point I saw the wind speed reading drop below 3 knots, the slowest I've seen so far, and we were crawling through the open gulf at a snails pace. Surprisingly, the boat is actually quite difficult to control at these slow speeds, as the rudder's responsiveness is directly correlated to the boat speed. Less speed means less water travelling across the rudder, and means input responses are lethargic and weak.
The afternoon wore on and we approached the Vernon Islands just north of Darwin, but as slowly as anything.

Dave lowered the motor and powered us on, as we couldn't afford to lose any more daylight to these little doldrums. Motoring the last hour or so into Darwin, the skyline of the finish line grew up around us. We anchored in Fannie bay close to town, and I packed my bags to depart the boat. It was a big change packing my bunk up after over two months of living in it, but I'm looking forward to the change.
I'll be staying with my cousin's Angus in Darwin for the next week, while I figure out if I'm sailing or flying out of here when that time is up.
We jumped in the tender that was laden with my worldly belonging and cruised in for a final time under the most beautiful purple crimson sunset.
I'll be seeing them again tomorrow to assist with dropping the rudder at the shipwright, so it wasn't a final goodbye but it was the end of our journey together.

Angus picked me and we ate at an Indian restaurant. The chaat was the most delicious thing I'd eaten in a while. Back at his place there is a spare room for me 😍🙏, and we played a couple of Crokinole games, a fun Canadian wooden chip sliding pool-esque game.
It's very nice to be here and I'm really looking forward to the next week.

64.title: Day 66: About Town
paragraphs: 3rd of July
It's great to finally be in town.

In the morning, Angus kindly offered to pick Dave up with the broken rudder and take him to the marina, and collect the important packages of the autopilot gearbox and boat stamp. I assumed these things wouldn't take more than an hour.

I was very wrong, and we drove between the bay where the boat is parked, the marina, the post office, the electronics repair store, lunch, back to the electronics repair store, and back to the bay, stopping for a good 15 minutes at each place as Dave finished his errands. It was nice to tick everything off though and see the repairs underway, the gearbox picked up, and the stamp I ordered actually turn out well with much more detail than I was expecting.
Congee for lunch was the highlight, and I'm stoked that Angus is here to conduct a royal tour of all the best vegan places in Darwin.

After we'd dropped Dave back off, we went to a gigantic board game store and picked up a few new titles, and then to the "Oriental Emporium", an Asian grocer where I was able to purchase my long awaited fill of snack food.
We then lost at about 7 games of Hanabi over the course of the evening, taking a break to go to the biweekly markets and get some nice Indian food there.
I had a chat with all parties involved about the timeline today, and made some decisions about the next steps. Here is the relevant information.

The current plan is thus: I will wait until next Friday, and if the rudder and boat is fixed before them and good to go, I will leave with Dave and head to Indonesia. If next Friday comes around and the rudder is not ready, and isn't looking like it will be ready that day, I will leave on the hike with Angus and co. In that scenario it should most likely be ready on my return and we will leave.

There is a small danger that the rudder is ready just after I leave on the hike, and Dave doesn't want to wait for me for 5 days and just goes. I'd be perfectly OK with him doing that, I wasn't going to wait for him originally.

I'll try to get an update from the shipwright early next week, and that should provide some more info, but I'm quite happy with this plan. I'd love to do a beautiful NT hike, and am lucky to have access to tickets that are notoriously hard to acquire, but would also be content leaving within the week for Indonesia.

Either way, it looks like I'll be staying on with Dave. This is great, as I know him and the boat, and it's good for him too as Kate will be leaving us. As new as I am to sailing it is much easier with two people, so I think this will sway him toward waiting around for me if he's on the fence.
Excited for the next week of Darwin, and keen to fill the days!

65.title: Day 67: A Feast
paragraphs: 4th of July 🇺🇸🇺🇸🇺🇸

It was a nice relaxed day today, with an afternoon shop being the first excursion outside of the day. I picked up some more things that I'd missed and it was nice to fill up on hummus and crackers when I got home.

We were shopping with a purpose, as Angus had organised to have dinner with some of his friends at their place. Angus cooked up some eggplant and spicy cauliflower for the occasion, and I assisted with the black pepper tofu. Angus' friends live in a gorgeous apartment with a broad view over the city and bay, and we took our offerings there to enjoy the evening. I tell you, it was so, so good just having a group conversation with new people, and they were both very interesting.
We came home at almost 11, and have tentatively organised some wakeboarding and go-karting for the weekend, which should be fun.

There was also much chat about the Jatbula trek, the hike that I am tentatively joining. It sounds so, so good and I'm going to try to see what I can do to make that happen. If I can't, it's not the end of the world, but a week with Angus, James, and Kate would just be so much fun, and who knows when I'll be back in the NT.

66.title: Day 68: Markets
paragraphs: 5th of July
Calm day in Darwin today.

In the morning Angus and I went to the Laksa market to meet a friend of his. Laksa seems to be very popular in Darwin which surprises me as it's always so hot here. The laksa was great though, even if the chilli and heat had me sweating.

His friend had recently done the Jatbula hike, so we talked about the logistics of that, what to take and what to leave. I'm very invested in going now, so I'm looking forward to getting an update from the shipwright about the repairs timeline, which will be a deciding factor in whether I can or not.
Next to the markets was a small art exhibition at the Northern Centre for Contemporary Art. My favourite piece was the shrimp Jesus.

Outside the market I saw a friendly looking border collie that I asked the owner if I could pet. She said yes and then paused, and said "We've met each other before?" I looked at her and recognised her from somewhere, and thought it was perhaps from the frisbee community.

She got there first and said "Hinchinbrook?" and then I realised too. This was one of the group members that I met on the Hinchinbrook hike, on the night before my birthday on the 18th of May! From an island off of Townsville to Darwin, what are the chances! I also think she may have told me that she had an Insta for her dog on the hike, and here I was giving him a pat!

In the late afternoon Angus was getting into some study so I went for a walk into town. It was bustling on the foreshore, with families all around in the dusk light. The piers were also lit up, and I walked out to the end of Stoked Hill Wharf to the food court there.

Darwin was full of life and I like how centralised it was. I think bigger cities like Sydney can lose that in their sprawl, whereas I was quite impressed by the large populated pedestrian areas in Darwins foreshore.
Coming back home Angus, Kabir, (another doctor and Angus' housemate) and I played the new board game I bought, Citadels, and ended up getting into bed pretty late.

67.title: Day 69: Berry Springs
paragraphs: 6th of July

In the mid morning our tentative go-karting plans were quashed by the unfortunate irregular closure of the venue just for today. The plans were pivoted to be a visit to the waterhole Berry Springs instead, a natural swimming hole that lies half an hour out of town.
On the way in, we stopped at some markets for some fantastic bahn mi, friend banana, sweet tofu, peanut dumplings, and sticky rice.

When we arrived at the carpark and started walking down to where Angus' friends were sitting I had a slight feeling that I'd been there before, somewhat recognising the grassy decline, but thought it must have been somewhere else. After saying hello we went down for a swim, and there I realised that I had actually been here before, on the family trip to Darwin many years ago. I'm not sure exactly what year it was, but it must have been around 2010.

The moment of recognition was triggered by the concrete steps down to the start of the waterhole, and the larger, deeper, round lagoon that I was unsettled by on my last visit. The water was crystal clear and uncannily warm, full of people with the pool noodles sold at the store to assist in floating in the fresh water.

Azure kingfishers dived around the air, plucking from the population of dragonflies that hovered above the water. We dried off and chatted for a couple of hours, playing some codenames and monopoly deal before driving back to the house.

On the drive we passed right by a controlled burn off, and firehawks were circling the plume of smoke like flies around a carcass. They wait for prey to be flushed by fires, and are even known to spread wildfires by carrying burning sticks farther afield, to drop them an seed new instances of the burn.

For dinner we walked back to the same pier I'd visited last night, and had some tacos while completing the weekend quiz. Back home, we played another game of Citadels, this time with Dayna, Kabir's partner, too, which shook up the meta.
I turned in afterwards, and I'm hoping to head into town tomorrow to send some postcards and prepare for either the hike or continuing boat journey.

68.title: Day 70: Darwin Tunnels
paragraphs: 7th of July
I spent the afternoon in town again after a slow morning at home. The highlight of the trip in was a tour of the Darwin Tunnels, relics of WW2.
When Darwin's above ground oil tanks were blown to pieces by the Japanese bombings, work began on oil storage tunnels beneath the hills on the foreshore.
They were plagued by leakage issues and not used for long unfortunately, blowing out the budget and the construction of the later tunnels was called off.
The conditions which the builders worked under sounded intense, in high heat and with poor ventilation.
In the evening Angus had a friend around for dinner, and the five of us shared some curries and a Dahl, before playing a board game until later in the night.

69.title: Day 71: Litchfield
paragraphs: After a bite to eat at a cafe we made a late start down to Litchfield National Park, a highlight of the Darwin surrounds.

An hour and a half of driving later we fortuitously found a park in the packed carpark, and made our way down to a large, crowded swimming hole. The water was cool and clear, and fish nibbled at my feet when I stood still on the rocks.

We scrambled up some of the rocky sides, seeing which parts of the outer walls we could get a footing on. Another short walk later and we ended up a smaller cascade, with a few rounded baths underneath little waterfalls.

As I jumped down towards the biggest my sunglasses flew off into the intake of a larger torrent, but I managed to dive beneath it and recover them. It was very reminiscent of when I miraculously recovered my sunglasses from a stream in Kosciusko in the same circumstances. I will not learn anything from these events.
We didn't stay long but had a great time in Litchfield, and while I'm not certain I believe some of the places I had been to before on my last trip to Darwin.
I've also got confirmation that I am indeed going on the hike, which is great news.

Unfortunately Dave's repairs are going to take longer than he thought, but Darren will wait for me to return next Wednesday. We'll then get on the way to Indonesia next Thursday. Shane had decided to head home due to concerns about corruption in Indonesia, which works well as I'm now much more in demand on Darren's boat.

I've been thinking more about the upcoming trip, and how this small intermission is not what most of the travelling will be like. It's been nice to hang out in Darwin, and flit around with friends on Angus, but I need to devote more mental real estate to the voyage ahead. I'm treating the hike with my treasured friends as a final goodbye treat to my Australian life, and hopefully the socialisation will last me through the solo nights to come.

70.title: Day 72: Botanical Gardens
paragraphs: 9th of July
A suburban day today opened with a yuppie café breakfast with some of Angus' friends.

Surprisingly, one of his friends was also moving to Germany, leaving this coming Tuesday, and also heading to Hamburg! It was nice to chat about such a shared upcoming experience, and our game plans for integrating and making lives over there. Her partner has acted as a forward scout and has already been over there for a year, which would be a great asset. I'll get in touch with them once I arrive, and it'll be great to have at least one person in the city I've met before.

I then had a solo walk around the botanical gardens, and sat by the fountain writing some postcards and chatting with some friends on the phone. In the afternoon I posted them and then spent the sunset by the beach.
In the morning we'll be packing our bags and driving down to Katherine, where we have accommodation for Friday night and an early start to the walk on Saturday.

71.title: Day 73: Katherine
paragraphs: 10th of July
The Jatbula starts tomorrow at 8 am near Katherine, so we had to get the drive from Darwin down there today.
Angus and I spent the morning slowly packing, as with all the shopping done yesterday there wasn't much to take care of. I think I've over packed on food, but I'd rather do that than be low.

We left after 2 and sped down the 130 kmh limit roads to the south. At one point the road split into two one way roads, but I didn't notice as I was reading at the time. Angus then overtook a truck around a corner, using the other lane that was heading the same direction. I thought we were in the incoming lane and that he was rolling the dice with our lives before I realised.

As we turned off to meet Kate and James at the end of the highway, there were small fires burning along the sides of the road. No one was present for the burn offs so they looked dangerous as they licked at the edge of the road.

When we arrived at the end of the hike to leave one car for us to pick up next Wednesday, I ducked down behind the dash. We hadn't told Kate and James I was coming, so I jumped out and surprised them with a hug. I hadn't seen them since they gave me a lift on my Sydney to Perth hitchhiking trip, and they had just finished a three month locum stint in Alice Springs the day before.
On the way out they told us they'd seen the cause of the fires, two vehicles driving along, one spraying petrol and the other igniting it as they went.
An hour later we were checked into our hotel at Katherine, and made some final preparations for the hike, including some last minute gear exclusions.
I'll be out of reception for the next 5 days, but should post again next Wednesday.

72.title: Days 74 - 79 Jatbula
paragraphs: 11th - 16th July
Jatbula is a stunning glimpse into the beauty of the NT, and I'd highly recommend it to anyone interested in an easy to moderate difficulty hike in Au.
On the hike was me, my cousin Angus, and James and Kate, two friends of ours from Sydney, where James lived with us for a year.

As I mentioned before, James and Kate had been passing through Adelaide in February this year at exactly the same time as I was hitchhiking to Perth. It was fortuitous timing, and they gave me a lift from Adelaide to Lincoln Gap on the Eyre peninsula, which was the last time I'd seen them before this trip.

The park service only lets 15 people begin the hike each day. In addition to the four of us there were two solo hikers: Kim and John, a sociable group of 5 in their 30s, and a reserved group of 3: a couple and a dad. They would stay at the same campground as us each night for all nights until the last, where only John had also opted to extend the hike and bisect the last day like us.

We arrived at the visitors centre at 8 am on Friday, and were briefed and across the river by 9, ready to begin the hike. After taking some group photos at the start sign and saying our hellos to the other groups, we were on our way.
I won't write a full play by play of the hike but instead give an overview. It was pretty easy hiking, the distances of the 6 days being 8 - 11 - 10 - 17 - 11 - 5 Kms.
The scenery on the walks was pretty. The primary colours were the light red rocks and earth, and the pale green of the foliage that would deepen as we approached the waterways at each campground.

There were a few spectacular views over the countryside, with some torrential waterfalls amongst the undulating ochre hills, but most of the beauty was of a smaller scale as we walked through the sparse gums.

The real undisputed highlights were the campgrounds, where we would spend most of our time after wrapping up the short hikes around noon each day. Every single campsite was pitched next to an unbelievably gorgeous section of river, with cool clear waters cascading down slippery pools and meandering through rocky crevices. There were multiple swimming sites at each, and the relief of getting our packs off and jumping in to escape the heat of the day did not lessen one iota from the first day to the last.

When we weren't in the water we were hanging around eating or chatting, talking to the other groups or puzzling away at a cryptic crossword. Kim, a nurse in her thirties, became a good friend and walked with us for some sections, and would hang out with us at our camps.

Each evening we'd cook our dinners together and have a relatively early night, as we'd try to rise and walk before the heat of the day became too oppressive, a deadline we missed on a couple of occasions.

We had a few minor gear malfunctions but spirits were high throughout the whole trip. The short days meant no one felt too buggered by the end of each one, and we had enough time to recuperate for the next. We would mostly chat, tell stories, or sing as we walked, with Angus and I once even broke into a short sting of rap narrations of our situations.

I'd bought a hammock for the trip, a highly recommended item for the  Jatbula, that proved to be my most prized possession. Not only a comfy place to sit, I ended up sleeping in it every night! I didn't bother to set my tent up after the first night as a backup, and I plan on continuing this into south east Asia as much as possible. I think it will prove invaluable when the greenery is too thick to provide ample space to pitch a tent.

During the hike I also read "Why warriors lie down and die" by Richard Trudgen, a book that dives into the social and health problems faced by the Yolnu people of east Arnhem land. It's an enlightening read, and anyone interested in understanding how we can better help indigenous populations, and how even well meaning programs can wreak social devastation, should check it out.

On Wednesday we finished up the last half day of the hike, and after a slow morning with many swimming opportunities, we stumbled into the carpark at the north of the hike where we'd left Angus' car. After necking a bottle of raspberry Fanta and slurping down an ice block from the kiosk, we crammed into the hatchback and dropped James and Kate off at their car at the start of the hike.

On our drive back up to Darwin we picked up two hitchhikers, an American and a Frenchman, who'd made their way up from the southern coast. We shared stories and dropped them in the Darwin CBD before heading home, where Kabir had cooked a huge curry. A guest was over for dinner so the 5 of us played a game of Spirit Island(!!!) and I held myself to three servings of dinner, an ice cream, a mango pancake, and a few mochi, submitting to an order from my body to counterbalance the calorie deficit I think I'd been eating at.

I didn't manage to see the game through as I was exhausted, and left it to Angus to handle the last few turns of our spirit in the winning game, and collapsed onto my camping mat in the spare room pass out.

73.title: Day 80: Final Preparation
paragraphs: Thursday the 17th of July.
When I arrived back in reception yesterday the first thing I did was confirm with Darren that our trip was still a go with the planned departure for today.

He'd decided to leave tomorrow morning instead of today, which suited me fine, so we said I'd jump on the boat tonight to be ready to go early in the morning. I had a few things that I wanted to get done on my last day in Australia, so I thought I'd get to it.

Angus and I grabbed a late vegan breakfast after a sleep in and I slowly got to ticking off my chores. I wasn't as quick off the mark as I should have been and in the arvo I was stressing, rushing to finish Dayna's book I had to leave behind, write and post postcards, go shopping for myself for the voyage and to cook some thank you lunches for my hosts, all before James and Kate arrived in Darwin for a group dinner. Angus and I also polished off some of the final cryptic clues in amongst it, and I had a necessary afternoon snooze.

I managed to get it all over the line just in time before we patronised a Greek restaurant with an unbelievable vegan menu for dinner, but it ended up running late and I decided to stay one final night in Darwin and join the boat in the morning l. Dayna and Kabir just can't get rid of me. 😎
I said my final goodbyes to Angus, James, and Kate as they went to bed, as Dayna would be dropping me at the sailing club early in the morning before any of them would be up. 😢

I won't see them for an indefinite period, but I'm stoked we were able to spend this time together over the last week. There is a tiny chance that James and Kate will go to Georgia instead of Korea later this year, and an even tinier chance that I will be there at the same time as I make my way to Europe. If that lined up, it would be the third time our adventures lined up this year, which would be incredible.
My great thanks to Dayna and Kabir for graciously allowing me to stay in their house for well over a week!

Angus, thanks so, so much for making my visit to Darwin what it was, it was such a pleasure to see you and hang out again. Not sure when I'll see you next but I look forward to it. We'll always have Paris.

74.title: Day 81: Goodbye, Australia
paragraphs: Friday 18th July
The awaited day has finally arrived.
I slept poorly last night due to the fear of my early alarm; Once I know the alarm is coming in the next few hours my body worries over the awakening which makes it very difficult for me to sleep.

Well rested or not 7 am came and I was shortly out the door with Dayna, to be dropped off at the Sailing Club. Darren was waiting on the shore and I heaved my weighty pack and groceries into the tender as we said our hellos after my two weeks of traipsing around.

We stopped by Cheshire Cat on the way out and had a brief chat with Dave. He should be good to go next week and has another traveller lined up to work with him. The new crewmember asked if he could bring his motorbike on board so they're going to attempt to hoist it onto the boat using the boom as a crane. I'm interested to hear how it goes.
On Flying Colours Darre gave me a quick tour and showed me my room. Yes room. I have a full cabin with a toilet and sink, and the bed is even wider than the last.
The boat is well provisioned and tidy, and I'm looking forward to sailing on it for the passage.

We didn't stay idle as we had to refuel and meet with the Border Force for departure. After wrangling the fuel hose line and almost pulling the boat into another as I moved it up the dock, we were ready to welcome the agents on board.

They were friendly but serious, and  after asking us a few questions sniffed around the boat looking into every hidden storage alcove, which required a bit of work. Dave says they've never been that thorough before and joked that it was because of me. Who knows with how the beard is coming along
Once they'd completed their check we were essentially banished from the kingdom. No more stops in Australia allowed.

I realised after the fact that when I'd jumped onto the boat from the dock after throwing the ropes back, that that was the last time I'd set foot on Australian soil for a while future. If all goes according to plan I would come back next Christmas for a visit.

There is approximately zero wind with change at the moment, so as of my writing this at 11pm we have been motoring for the last 12 hours. Hopefully it'll pick up during the night and we can get some mileage out of the sails, otherwise it'll be closer to a week on the water.

I also think I may have messed up. As there are only two of us on the boat, we are doing 2 x 3 hour shifts each between 6 pm and 6 am. Darren kindly let me pick and as I like seeing the sunrise I chose 9-12 & 3-6. In hindsight I think this was a mistake as I didn't manage to get any sleep before 9, and will have to be back up at 3 for the morning shift. The sunrise better put on a show for me.

My complaints are dwarfed by the relief of not having to manually helm, though. This doesn't even feel like sailing, and I just scrolled for an hour while occasionally glancing up at the horizon and instruments.
The sunset over the water was nice to see again, and I'm excited to be on the next leg of my journey.

75.title: Day 82: Motoring
paragraphs: Saturday 19th July
Well, I didn't get to see the sunrise this morning as it turns out it's after 6am, so the foundations that my shift selection logic was based on have proved to be useless.
I had a great chat with an overseas friend of mine for about an hour from 3:15 which was great for staying awake, and I might see if I can line someone else up tonight.
Once Darren got up to relieve me I slept for almost 5 hours until 10:45.
The wind has hardly blown above 5 knots in the last day, so we've had to have the motor on pretty much the whole day to make any progress.
It's nice to be back out on the water, but crawling along at 4-5 knots means it might take us an extra day or so to get there.

This boat is the slowest of the 3 but by a small margin, meaning that when we were sailing together it would often arrive half an hour after the other two. I'm quite unconcerned if we end up taking another day to get there; I have plenty of food and books to keep me content. Darren, on the other hand, is constantly comparing our speed with AOWN, the fastest of the 3 boats and the one that is sailing over to Indonesia with us.
Darren's easy to get along with and we're having a good time.
I've opted to do the other night shift tonight, so 6-9 and 12-3 will be my responsibility.

76.title: Day 83: Halfway mark
paragraphs: Sunday 20th July

It's 1:50am in the morning as I'm sitting here writing this. I had volunteered for the 6-9pm and 12-3am shifts tonight, but somehow didn't set an alarm for midnight after going to bed at 9 and have only just woken back up. Darren didn't wake me up when I didn't rise which was nice of him, but I feel bad and would rather he have done so.

Last night when I came upstairs at midnight he told me I could just head back to bed, as we had the engines on and there was barely a need for anyone to even be awake. I accepted his offer and he periodically rose to briefly check the surroundings. I think he was doing the same tonight, as he's been asleep on the couch since I awoke. I'll let him know next time he rises that I have the next few hours under control.

We've also officially passed the halfway mark between Darwin and Kupang today, and as of this point have only 155 nm to go. The main indicator that we've left Australian waters is the number of fishing boats, and out on the horizon I can currently count 6 different sets of light around us as we bob between them through the darkness.

Today was quite a slow day, mostly filled with reading, writing some important Indonesian phrases, and some calls to friends back home. We're due to arrive either late Tuesday day or Wednesday morning depending on our speed, and I'm excited to finally arrive. Tomorrow I'm going to make some Indonesian flashcards and commit some hitchhiking terminology to memory.

77.title: Day 84: A real page turner
paragraphs: Monday 21st July

I repented for my missed alarm last night by staying up for my allotted 3 hours starting from when I did get out of bed before 2. Back in bed at 5, I surprisingly only managed to sleep until 8 or so, though I knew I needed more.

We had barely enough wind to justify sailing, so we trawled along at about 4 knots for most of the day, barely sailing. I read the second half of Catch 22, a great way to spend a slow ocean day on a book I greatly enjoyed. I learned a few new words like odious, obsequious, and pugnacious, that I will try to shoehorn into my next few journal entries but hope I won't be able to.

It's now just past midnight and I'm up for my second shift. I just heard some Indonesian chatter on the radio and have crossed my fingers that it wasn't relevant to us, but at least the tone did sound reasonably relaxed.

We'll probably arrive at land tomorrow in the afternoon, but will have to sail or motor another 30 nm or so to get to Kupang up a channel between two islands. I'm hoping my visa on arrival goes smoothly, and mulling over whether I should buy an exit ticket on the ferry to Malaysia as they require, or try to explain that I don't have a fixed schedule so I don't have to waste the money on a ticket I'd probably miss anyway.
If all goes very smoothly I could be staying in Kupang tomorrow night, but I may have to stay another night on the boat in anticipation of the immigration appointment.

I think Darren is being essentially extorted by the agent he used, who has asked for more money at the last minute for an additional boat fee to make some problem go away. I've tried to remove myself from the situation as much as possible; I'm an item on Darren's crew list and nothing more.

78.title: Day 85: Indonesia
paragraphs: Tuesday 22nd July

I was on the phone with some friends on my first shift last night when I saw the glow on the horizon.
