On the second shift, we'd come close enough to see lights on a distant hillside, their terrestrial nature revealed by their height above the dark horizon. When I woke back up in the morning we were only a few kilometres from Timor, and began to make our way up the channel to the east to Kupang by the mid morning.

I'm finally, at long last, ultimately in Indonesia. I sat on the deck as we passed by the first slices of Indonesian life on the shore. A large group of people sat on a barge presumably shucking for pearls. Cars and scooters snaked behind a sharp contrast of strange resorts and ramshackle hovels that alternated down the shoreline.
We were hailed on the radio by immigration, and had to raise a yellow flag indicating that we hadn't been cleared yet as we pulled into the bay of Kupang.

As we moored rubbish bobbed around the boat and the stench of fish drying on the decks on some nearby fishing boats was overpowering as we passed downwind of them. Oh yeah, I'm back in Southeast Asia, baby.
I was wondering what would happen with my visa and essentially how I'd go about getting one, as I'd arrived hoping to procure the 30 day visa on arrival from whichever authority I could.

On the radio immigration called for a pickup and Darren went into the shore to chat to them and his agent. Shortly after, I see the tender packed with 6 people zooming back out to the boat, Darren and 5 immigration officers. The main officer was very friendly, and he and the three women were clearly very excited to be on board, while the other younger guy was slightly more reserved. They asked for photos around the boat, with us and walked around inside with their cameras out like tourists. I did not get the impression that these photos were for official record keeping, but rather that they would end up on Facebook.

The officer asked me if I'd filled out some form with a barcode for him to scan, that I hadn't, and if both of us could present important yellow documents with our immunisation histories, which we couldn't. I was told to download some Indonesian arrival app on my phone and sign up, but wasn't receiving the verification emails so one of the women hotspot me from her phone. I was regretting not sorting out the visa before arriving. I'd finally managed to get halfway through that process but could verify my Australian number so was blocked there, and also couldn't get into mygov to show my immunisation history. Things were going poorly.
Suddenly, they declared that they were happy with the check and that we should all get a photo lowering the flag together like old friends, so up to the deck we went to take a few happy snaps.

Next thing I knew they were content and leaving, with no word or indication about it I had to do anything more. No visa, but no worries, one more group photo and off they all went. Darren got one good use out of his custom boat stamp, a great design of his boat and ID number that his daughter had made and he had ordered a self inking stamp of on the single form they needed filling.

Darren then talked to his agent that said I may have to apply for a visa online that could take a whole week, during which I'd be stuck on the boat. I was questioning my decisions when I heard that. He said he could help if we came into shore, so we semi illegally met him and some buddies sitting under a tree behind the beach to discuss. In a semi power play "Matthew" the agent, a sly looking middle aged hustler with a gravely deep voice had us wait next to him while he finished a 15 minute conversation with his mates. Whenever I even glanced past him absorbing the new sights on Indonesia he would tell me that he wouldn't be long.

Eventually he said he could go and submit the application today, Andi could either give him the money to go and do it or go with him. I was wary after how much money he'd asked Darren for, but he only wanted 50 aud, or 500,000 IDR.
The exchange rate is conveniently slightly better than 1:10000.

I knew that was the fee for a tourist visa and so I wasn't being extorted, but asked to go with him anyway for something to do. He explained I was welcome to but that the office was on the other side of town or something, but I could come to the immigration office to pay the fee myself. I popped on the back of his scooter, helmet on, and we scooted into town.

It feels so good being here finally. The smell that permeates the streets, that gestalt of an odour combined from a million different scents that makes me feel like Grenouille as I pick it apart, reminds me so much of Thailand. I actually had a very intense moment of deja vu in Sydney a couple of years ago when I caught a whiff of it on the air and I was instantly transported years back to my earlier travels to southeast Asia. I look forward to inhaling all it's variants as I travel North, over borders and through climates.

When we arrived at the ATM outside the office, I was thankfully able to confirm my travel card works and that I have access to money. In the office we went back and forth between a couple of rooms to pay for my visa, but I just had a receipt and nothing in my passport. I asked him what I owed him for his help, but he explained it was included in his fee he had charged Darren, that he hadn't received any of yet. He then whisked me back to the beach where Darren's and my passports were kindly confiscated by him with promises that he would be able to get our visas finalised that day.

In a legal dark-grey area, we returned to the boat to await a customs inspection, somehow different from the previous gang. In a sitcom-esque situation, while Darren was picking up these officials from the beach, I managed to break his stamp. I wanted to stamp in my physical diary entry of the day, but on the first press, pushed down too hard and clicked the slider out of position. Try as I might, I couldn't get it working again as they approached the boat in the tender, brimming with forms for the stamping.

One false start later when they'd forgotten our documents and had to return to their office to get them, and two more thickly uniformed officers were on the boat to search around. They diligently checked the engine serial numbers and then started indoors, one of them asking me to show him one bathroom and my bedroom, while Darren escorted the other. In the doorway to the bedroom he asked me if I could take a photo of him, so I obliged and he took one standing next to the bed, one comically looking under the closest corner of the mattress, and one with a thumbs up. We were then done, not just with the photos but the entire inspection.

I was deeply ashamed of breaking the stamp and lamely suggested that we could half press it, and press the paper into the concave semi sheathed stamp and kind of get some ink on the paper. I demonstrated with some scrap and managed to get maybe a quarter of the picture on the page but no numbers or text. Darren rightly thought my shit idea was shit, but the agents were happy enough with it! I proceeded to stamp 5 forms by holding the stamp in one hand as open as I could get it, and pressing the signature that needed stamping into it with the other, scrunching the paper as I did so. It looked hilariously terrible as I marred each crisp form with creases and a smudged bit of ink, but the agents had the final word, and that word was okay. My only regret is that I didn't take a photo of my handiwork.

Once they had gone we only were waiting about half an hour until Matthew called informing us that our passports were ready. Darren went into shore, ran out of fuel, and returned victorious with our shiny visas. Ladies and gentlemen, I am legally in the country. Once again, my poor organisational skills are rewarded with a last minute victory that will only further encourage me to take a similarly lackadaisical approach to visas and the trip more broadly in future.

I was very keen to get into town and start exploring, but it was almost 5 at this point. I shared a beer with Darren instead to celebrate our arrival. Tomorrow morning I'll be heading in early with my packed bag and a twinkle in my eye, and I just can't wait.
Oh, I also fixed the stamp shortly after the officers left.

79.title: Day 86: A stranger in a strange land
paragraphs: Wednesday 23rd July
I'm absolutely buggered, and hope I can make it through writing this before falling asleep.

Darren was up early so I followed suit, and had finished breakfast and packing by 7:30. After briefly trying in vain to get Darren onto a new phone plan, I asked to be dropped in at shore. We swung by Tony and Ivy on the way there and said our goodbyes, and once we were on the shore I shook Darren's hand and that was that. They'll all be journeying at a much slower rate west so I doubt I'll catch them again.
I was almost giddy as I laced up my boots, the whole day and broader trip lying before me unknown, waiting to reveal the forms that they would take.

My first priority was the ferry terminal. I had heard that the ferry to Ende only leaves once a week, and didn't want to miss it if it was that morning. It was about an 80 minute walk there so I set off in the already warm humid day, breaking a strong sweat as I climbed the hilly interior of the island to get there.

When I was most of the way there a small local bus pulled up and beckoned me in. I jumped in with a few other locals riding too, but when they got out the driver absolutely blasted the music in the back, and I had to ask them to turn it down. I'm not talking loud, it was like I was next to the speaker at a concert, and I'm so surprised they weren't uncomfortable with it at that level. They dropped me right at the ferry terminal, diverting from their original route. We didn't name a price before I got there and they asked for 5 bucks. I tried to haggle them down as I felt that they'd only done a 2 minute detour, and I'd seen one of the locals pay a minute fraction of that cost just minutes before. I coughed up, with other drivers leaning into the car to watch as I did so.

I found out from the ferry terminal that the Ende ferry wouldn't be running until Friday, but that a ferry to Aemere would be going tomorrow morning at 10. Aemere is further west than Ende, but that works fine for me as it's in the direction I'm headed, so I agreed to come back tomorrow to make the departure.

Now I had the day to kill and some things to tick off, so I went to find a ride back to Kupang proper. I was immediately mobbed by the locals that had been watching me since I jumped out of the bus. The cheapest they'd quote me was $10, so I asked the ferry guard if that was a good price, which I didn't feel it was. He said it was fair as it was a 25 minute drive back to town, so I paid and jumped in, as the locals laughed around me.

Reflecting on this throughout the day, he was absolutely right and I was being too stingy with the first two lifts. I came in too guarded when really I should just happily pay the tourist tax wherever I go. Unless they're taking the absolute piss with their quoted price, it's cheap anyway.

Some other local jumped in the car with us as we drove to Kupang and they both tried to ask where I was staying, hoping they could be involved in organising my hotel. Despite repeatedly telling them I would book it myself later, I realised we had driven straight through Kupang and were heading to the far side of town. I asked where we were going and the driver informed me that he had a friend that spoke good English that I was going to meet. I informed him I didn't want to meet his friend and had him turn the car around and take me back into town. When we got there, he insisted I take his number to call him in the morning when I needed a ride back to the ferry. I didn't save it.

The first order of business was to get a wall charger I could use to charge my phone, so I bought one of those and a cheap Powerbank to replace my broken one. I then went to a phone repair shop and asked if they could attempt to fix my broken Powerbank, the battery of which was fine but the usb charging ports were salt water damaged. What followed was probably the highlight of the day. Two young workers and I pried apart the glued Powerbank with great difficulty and much broken plastic, and they took out the usb ports and soldered new ones in. We had a laugh doing it as I told them it didn't matter if it didn't work. It bloody worked and I have my ultralight Powerbank back that I forked out for back home. I compensated them and went to get stir fried noodles at a nearby restaurant.

Another pickup was a small notebook which I'm now using to store my Indonesian vocab. It's less cumbersome than whipping my diary out and I've started to fill it out nicely. Language adds so much to the experience of a country, and throughout the day locals have smiled and talked to me in Indonesian when I try my best with my basic greetings. This is my current repertoire, and I have to say I've got most of it down pat already. I will continue to fill it out as I require new phrases.

I booked accommodation with RedDoorz, a hotel booking app that seems to be used widely here, and wandered across town to get there for the 2pm check in. I'm not really sure how I spent so much time between getting off the boat in the morning and then, but the walks, lunch, and the repair were all quite long slow processes.

Once I was checked in I dumped my heavy pack and did some research about what I should see with my one day here. There was a waterfall about an hour away that looked great so I asked reception to help me rent a scooter, which they were able to do. It took another half an hour for the scooter guy to arrive, but I was able to pick the colour from a photo he sent. I chose red, as they're the fastest.

It was 3:30 by the time I started my 70 minute journey to the waterfall, which ended up taking over an hour and a half with refuels both for the bike and myself. Traffic isn't fast here, and I was careful not to be reckless. I'm not even sure if my health insurance covers scooter related shenanigans, but when in Rome...

It is great fun being back behind the handlebars, they're easy to ride and while the traffic seems chaotic, the slow speeds mean everything is easy to react to and flow with. I tried to stay under 70 for Mum.

Getting out of town wasn't the greatest, as the towns are pretty thick and dirty, but the countryside is absolutely wonderful. Suddenly the ramshackle buildings gave way to rice paddies shining in the setting sun, and goats, dogs, chickens, and cows started to meander around the sides of the road.

As I climbed up the hills it only got prettier, climaxing with a stunning view over a shaded valley, with families working and young children playing in the clear irrigation stream. Everyone that noticed me would smile and wave, and I'd call out selamat sore in greeting back to them. It was truly idyllic, and the setting sun only added to the wonder.

After many stops to check the map, and one turn around when I'd gone too far, I arrived at the walk to the waterfall. The stream feeds the well engineered irrigation system that feeds the teal blue water into the terraces of rice, and I rode past it as I approached on the bike. Heralding my arrivals were a few young children that tried their best to educate me about where to park my bike in their family gravel lot, and I obediently did whe I understood. The excitable young boy chased me down the path after I'd embarked, but I'd diverted off to follow the stream and didn't respond when I could hear him yelling on the main path.
The sun was already setting by the time I started the walk so I settled for one of the first pools I saw, snapped a few pictures, and turned back the path.

Back at the bike I paid my parking fee and gave some extra money to hi each of the children. Their family was nearby and came over to talk, and they told me I should come back tomorrow, which I regrettably couldn't. The drive back was dark and difficult, with bugs getting in my eyes as I descended the windy mountain roads by the front light. If I'd had the time I would have taken a longer, more scenic route, but I'm glad I didn't as the windy section I had chosen was more than enough.

After I was back at the hotel I went out for dinner, through the traditional market to a restaurant. In the back streets everyone stared at me, but once I'd hit them with the old reliable selamat malam, they smiled back and responded Malam, the standard response. Even the little kids respond Malam almost instinctively during their gawking, which is adorable.

At the restaurant I was able to get my hands on some gado gado, a delicious peanut vegetable dish that I can see becoming quite the mainstay of my diet. During my meal I was circled by a toddler that kept running toward me, intercepted by his parents at the last second to the amusement of us all in the restaurant. I also treated myself to a dessert, and confirmed that it was on a soy milk base. Right as they'd finished making it they stuffed some condensed milk in it that I can't have, so I explained and asked for another. I still paid for the first and gave it to a kid nearby, and we all had a laugh as I stretched my Indonesian as far as it could go. Turns out I need to learn "what is your name?" In addition to "My name is", as I was stumped by what they were asking me, lol.
On the way back to the hotel I was swarmed by a group of boys, screaming at me a mixture of hello, money, Ronaldo, and Mbappe. I just repeated "no" and they left me alone.
This day has been a blessing. Kupang isn't very touristy; I didn't see another tourist all day. It's allowed me to do as the locals do a lot more, and I look forward to continuing this way.

This entry has taken over an hour to write, and I'm not sure if I'm going to be able to keep up with this much detail, unless I make a converted effort to end my days earlier to make time. It's almost 11 here and I plan to be up at 6:30! I hope you're enjoying it.
- Pat xoxo

80.title: Day 87: Off with the ferries
paragraphs: Thursday 24th July
Bam. 6:30 alarm, out of the hotel by 7:10 and on the way to Bolok. Bolok was where my 10am ferry to Aemere departed from, but also had a cave lake nearby that I wanted to check out in time.

I knew I could have jumped in a taxi for ten bucks and been there in a jiffy, but I don't want to do that all the time. I didn't want to hitchhike either as I strongly dislike city hitchhiking, but I'll write more about where I'm at in terms of hitchhiking later on if I have time.

I walked down the road back into kupang and jumped in a public bus, jumping out 5 minutes later in town. When I say bus, they're actually small trucks with an open side door behind the passenger seat with seating in the back for 6-8 people. I then walked to the outskirts of kupang on the road to Bolok, and jumped in another bus shortly. They said they could take me to Bolok but when all the other passengers had already left by Tenau, the larger town on the way, I knew it wasn't their usual route. This had already happened to me yesterday with the other bus suddenly commandeered by me unknowingly so they could ask for more money, and it is annoying.

Their plans were foiled, however, by a police checkpoint. A group of people were peering down the road at it from behind a corner. The bus halted and the driver just wandered off, so I put the money under the wiper and walked easily through the stoppage.

I had an eye out for another lift as it was almost 8 and I was on the clock, but there were unsurprisingly no unregistered buses past the checkpoint, go figure. A biker picked me up and took me straight to the cave, and declined money when I offered to pay. Even when I'm not hitchhiking, hitchhiking will find me I guess. Thank you biker.
A few workers were upgrading the stony path to the caves and told me on the way to be careful, while another group asked if I had a guide, but didn't stop me when I said no.

The narrow stony entrance to the cave belied the gaping interior, and I picked my way down to the clear water in the bottom past the slippery rocks. It was very dark in the cave, and I had to use my head torch to find footing on the way down. I was alone next to the still water, rimmed with white crystalline rocks that were smooth to the touch. Bats squeaked from crannies in the ceiling, and small white yabbies poked around in the water.

It was already warm and I'd come with swimming in mind, so I stripped off and lowered myself in. The water was tepid and I tried not to think about that cave worm monster from Deltora Quest. One section behind the platform dropped away under the clear water further than I could do into the teal dimness, which I let well alone.

I heard voices and the workers had come to check on me, so I donned my gear and departed for the dock. I enjoy walking down the slightly more rural streets, as all sorts of animals and situations populate the path.

I was greeted by my friends from yesterday at the terminal who had bad news for me: the ferry was cancelled. There was a ferry to Ende going at 2, but tickets for these ferries are sold out weeks in advance. Enter the perks of being a foreigner that I'm grateful for but also very aware of the privilege granted by. They called someone who worked for the ferry company and was corrupt enough to get me a staff ticket at an inflated price, $30. I accepted without hesitation.
Please take me back Ende, I know I ditched you yesterday to go to Aemere but I'm begging on my hands and knees 🥹🙏😥

After a delicious jackfruit curry for breakfast I got a ride to the barber and trimmed down my beard. I was enjoying it but it was getting a little too mommies-basement, so I had it neatened up. +10 GBP.

Down at the ferry I waited worriedly for my spook, well aware that if this guy didn't rock up I'd be booking a ticket maybe a week away, and heading back into Kupang for the meantime. Luckily he did and I was ushered through security and given a dodgy ticket, along with another local chap in my situation. We were guided into a certain spot in the ticket line and our guy tsked a guard to get hit attention and subtlety indicated us. We made it through and onto the ferry safely, heading up to the deck as we don't actually have beds.

I now completely understand how deadly these ferries can be. I've pictured Sydney ferries when I hear about accidents, but these things are massive and have levels of bowls that are multiple stories from the nearest exit. Combined with the heat and smell, I'm glad to be outside on the deck.

Once we were guided to a corner of the balcony passage, our guy told us to say "Di Pam satu" if asked for our tickets, and took them back off us. We think Pam is someone that was saying we already gave them to, or that's the secret password and they know to let us off.

I sat against the wall trying to get comfortable for a while with my friend, but spied a few good beams above our corner. To the amusement of all around I strung my hammock up between them, careful not to intrude too much on the spaces of those around me. It's a perfect set up and I gently sway back and forth with the invisible rocking of the boat. I read for a while then went for a wander around to check the boat out.

While in the hammock I was reminded of the secret phrase as the officers made their way along, catching me sitting in the hammock like a dork. I uttered the phrase and he just said ok and moved on.m, while everybody else was sitting their tickets. I didn't know I was capable of such high stakes intrigue.

At dinner they were checking the tickets but I was able to just show my ticketless passport for some reason, and I had rice and veggies after giving my fish away. During and after dinner I sat with my fellow illegal and two other young guys, and they helped me further fill out my Indonesian phrasebook. It was a real highlight and we shared contact details and recommendations for the area, and they asked if I would come back to live in Indonesia.

I've set my friend up on my camping mat beneath me in the hammock, and were going to get some sleep before our 4 am! Arrival in Ende. I'll probably just start hitchhiking west in the morning as I want to get to the west side of Flores, the island, in only a day or two. I hope I get woken up early enough to tear down my hammock and roll up my sleeping mat before disembarking.
I've had a winner of a day and made my best Indonesian friends so far. This is what it's all about.

81.title: Day 88: Hitchhiking in Indonesia
paragraphs: Friday 25th July
I was packing up my hammock at 4 this morning, in anticipation of disembarking at Ende. The night slowly turned predawn, and the silhouettes of the mountainous Flores island peaks were illuminated.

When my new friends and I walked into Ende we said our goodbyes, and I was invited to start with Bruno's family on the island. They went their separate ways and I made my way through the throng of taxi drivers to the backstreets on the way to town. There I fell into stride with an older lady and introduced myself, using the little Indonesian I have in my book. She spoke no English.

She asked where I was going and I said to get food, so she insisted I come with her as she knew where I could find it. At least that's what I gathered she meant by her gesticulations. As we walked through town she was laughing like a schoolgirl as people started and smiled at us, and I said hello to all of them. It was a lot of fun.

Arriving at a small restaurant run by I presume her family, I had one course of rice, noodles, steamed vegetables and a corn fritter, and followed it up with another. I had only had a small meal on the boat. This veritable feast cost me approximately $2.

The family came from out back to meet me and take some photos. A mother with quite reasonable English handed me her young son for a photo, who immediately burst into tears in my hands, and only quietened when safely back in her arms.

I picked up some water from the supermarket and made my way to the edge of town. A few taxi evasions later, and I thought I'd try Hitchhiking to a pretty looking beach 40 minutes away down the road I was heading on. I was almost instantly picked up by some workers and jumped in the back of their van with one of them, screaming around the windy corners of the seaside villages.

I rapped on the cabin when we were at my intended destination, blue rock beach. While there was some rubbish around, the opaque light blue water made for a nice morning dip. Soon enough I was back on the road in the cabin of a vegetable truck with a middle aged couple, who I chatted with about my trip. Even though it was only 10, I felt myself starting to fall asleep and at one point my head nodded back in the cabin due to my short nights sleep.

They took me for an hour to the junction where they were turning off and I found a new spot to continue from. While waiting I was found and mobbed by a group of young boys. They asked me all sorts of questions, some I gathered were inappropriate in Indonesian as one boy would laugh and hit the others. They were nice overall but at one point were trying to figure out where the boundaries were, translating "poor thing" on their phones to show me. I kind of just laughed at it and they were also apologetic about being loud, and were helping me with Indonesian phrases by the end. It didn't help the hitchhiking though, especially when two men joined the group that I also talked to, but I was rescued by a truck that graciously yoinked me from the crowd. They took me another hour up the road, blasting Eminem most of the way.

I felt like I was the star of the popemobile in the remote villages along the road, as the truck attracted enough attention itself, and the eyes would instantly snap to me accompanied by yells and waves. I laughed out loud when one boy we passed reacted to seeing me with a full body flinch when his eyes moved from the truck to my side window.

When I was out of the truck at a junction I considered heading up a side track, but realised it would be hard to find a lift there and back around the loop I wanted to do. As I wanted to make some distance on my first proper day I opted to push on forward. If I manage to get some Kms covered and at least one activity in each day, I'll be happy.

A fun family took me to the turn off the Aemere, and from there I found an almost 3 hour lift to Ruteng, where I am tonight. I was originally going to stop at Aemere, but as they were headed further along my route I thought I may as well. This means I travelled roughly 6 hours of driving distance across the island today, which is great for hitchhiking, and only have 4 hours to go tomorrow.

In Rutang I was mobbed and followed by a few boys asking for money and chattering about footballers, and decided to stay at a hostel. I met a swiss guy who I had dinner with, and we plan to hang out in the morning.

I'm satisfied that the hitchhiking went well today after not doing much in Kupang, and I enjoyed meeting the people I did. I don't want to stiff the local economy by not paying taxi drivers and hitchhiking, as I'm actually not doing it for financial reasons at all. I've decided that I can offer to pay for petrol money at the end of a trip, and if my ride accepts give them a fair amount. That way I get the two sided relationships with locals that I'm looking for that aren't purely financial, while also not being a cheapskate in a poorer country.

Also, I'm aware some of the locals look slightly stunned in these photos, but don't worry I'm not surprising them with the camera. I always ask, except in the situation where they've just whipped their camera out and taken a photo of me. It's fair game at that point. The old lady this morning pulled out her phone while I was halfway through eating and started taking happy snaps 😂 I think she has a photo of me with noodles hanging out of my mouth on her end.

82.title: Day 89: From high to low
paragraphs: Saturday 26th July
I began the day at Ruteng, at 1188m elevation.
After Remo, my new swiss friend from the hostel, and I had breakfast, I jumped on the back of his bike to begin the half hour journey to the hobbit cave.

Flores is home to the site where in 2003 bones from the "homo floresiensis", or "hobbit" were discovered. Small humanoids around 1.1 metres in height, the homo floresiensis lived on Flores for over a million years, going extinct about 50000 years ago, probably due to the arrival of modern humans.

The ride down to the cave site was about half an hour, and as we exited town we followed along a ridge line, with valleys dropping out to either side. It was densely populated with houses and people, and children leaned out for high fives as we passed.

Upon arrival you are not allowed to proceed directly to the cave, all visitors have to go through a cultural induction where we wore traditional dress and are treated to some coffee and light food. It was a nice experience, but the cynic in me marked how straight after we all passed around an object and said how thankful we were, the mandatory donation box came out.

We were then taken for a tour of the larger, non-hobbit cave, that I really enjoyed. It was one large stunning cavernous space, with light filtering down to the darkness. Our guide told us it was a sacred place that their ancestors dwelled in, and some of the rocks really looked like faces at first glance. He also said it had to do with male and female rituals, as from within the cave the entrances looked like symbols for men and women. I'll let you guess which is which.

We could then go to the Hobbit Cave, passing through a little museum on the way. It was amazing to think we were standing right next to the excavation pit of such an important discovery that had made it onto the front cover of Nature and that beneath our feet there were almost certainly more bones waiting to be found.

We then rode back up the hills to the hostel, and I checked out. Remo offered to bring me to the spider rice fields to the west of town, which was perfect as it was where I needed to be to begin hitchhiking, and would allow me to see the famous viewpoint. It was a short 15 minute ride and upon arriving at the base of the lookout we were swarmed by children telling us to park the bike in their respective lots. As we made our way up to the viewpoint 3 of the kids followed us and tried their best to communicate with us and tell us about the view. Our more complicated questions about where the water was sourced from were not understood.

Back down at the entrance we were invited to sit and enjoy some of their traditional food. A mix of fruit, salt, spice, onion, and chili was mashed in a wooden stump with a concave section in the top using a wooden pole. Essentially a mortar and pestle on a larger scale. The mash was quite spicy and left a slightly numb feeling on my tongue, but wasn't bad at all.

We then said goodbye and I made my way down the road to the outside of the village, declining a few taxis and saying good morning to a few people as I went. As I came to the end of the village a truck was parked and two guys were fiddling with the load in the back. I asked where they were headed and fortuitously they were going all the way to labuan Badjo; it was the only lift I needed for the whole day.  It was a long ride down from the mountains and we stopped just once. I ate some snacks I'd bought earlier from a street vendor.

I arrived in Labuan Badjo around 4, and went for a stroll into town and back after checking into my cheap hotel. It was the worst one I've stayed in, with some stains on the sheets and a small crusty bathroom. I could hear whispers of malcontent signalling from my stomach but thought it was probably just the sweets I had from the street food vendor, so decided to go for another walk into town rather than spend it alone in my room. I also had to decide what I wanted to see in Labuan Badjo and how long I wanted to stay.

I wasn't feeling Labuan Badjo, as it's much more touristy which brings all the other annoyances that come with that. The curious stares and smiles I'd had over the last few days were one thing, being honked at and hassled to get a taxi or rent a bike was another. Greeters from all the restaurants and diving companies call out to you as you walk past, and I was already looking forward to getting back out into the countryside.

As I made my way to a small bar I could feel my stomach complain slightly louder, but thought I could just lock in and overcome it. It's taken all my will to stop myself from listening to my ego tell me that I don't need to worry about the water quality here due to being built different.

At the bar I met a nice German couple with their kid, who I had a great chat with, and they flattered my German skills. I didn't eat but had a couple of beers, which seemed to settle my gut a bit. It wasn't to last though, and try as I might to push through I was forced to excuse myself and start heading back to the hotel.

As soon as I began the 20 minute walk I realised I had left it far too late. I was beginning to sweat and my body was urgently telling me I needed to get to a bathroom. It was. A pure test of will as I made my way back along the street, trying to keep my mind as blank as possible as I put one foot in front of the other. I would periodically check my phone to see just how little I had travelled since the last check. When I was nearing the hotel it was 6 minutes away, 5 minutes later I checked: 4 minutes away. I think I looked incredibly ill to all that passed me, I was dripping with sweat even though the night was cool, and I wasn't sure if i would make it in the last quarter. My death march came to an end as I rounded the corner to my hotel, and charging past the reception without a smile I made it to my room.

I was violently, violently ill and had one of the worst nights I'd had in recent memory. After my initial bout I thought I was done, but a cramping stomach repeatedly drew me back to the bathroom for the next few hours. When I had nothing left to give I was lying pathetically on the cool tiles of the shower floor. Being sick is one thing, being sick alone in a foreign country in a cheap hotel with no hot water or company to tell you it's going to be alright is another. I was feeling incredibly sorry for myself and only finally managed to get to sleep around 2:30 am.
Oh well, on the bright side such a rock bottom experience means it's only uphill from here, right?

83.title: Day 90: Convalescence
paragraphs: Sunday 27th July
I tried to sleep in for as long as possible after my nightmare of a night but had to get up to figure out what my plans were for the next few days.

I didn't really want to stay too long in Labuan Badjo, but I really wanted to see the Komodo dragons on the nearby islands. Stumbling around town for over an hour in my sweaty, tired state I consulted ferry timetables, tour guides, private charters, and hotel availabilities to formulate a plan. I'll spare you the boring details but it boiled down to two main options.

Option 1:  Forget the Komodo dragons and spend the afternoon at a nearby beach/cave, and get the overnight ferry to the next island that departed at 9pm. It would be a 7 hour journey in a seat in a ferry the locals took. The ticket cost $2.

Option 2: Book a hotel for tonight and spend the afternoon doing whatever, then do a full day touristy island tour tomorrow. We'd see not only the dragons but a few nice viewpoints and get some snorkelling in too. Unfortunately there was no night ferry the following night, so I'd have to stay another night in Labuan Badjo and get the 10am ferry the following day, that would get me to the island in the late afternoon.

Option 2 essentially would put me two whole days behind option 1, and I was close to writing off the dragons and hitting the road. In the end I picked the slower option 2, as I was wisely advised by dad that the overnight ferry in my current state would probably not be what I needed. While option one would have eco

That decided, I booked a homestay and rented a motorbike, exhausted and needing some more rest. It was on the outskirts of town and when I pulled in I was greeted by a friendly family, including a sweet black cat. It was a nice place. She asked me when I had booked and I said just 10 minutes ago, so she showed me to my room where I collapsed on the bed, gathering the will to take a shower before having an afternoon nap.
I then received a WhatsApp message from the host, the woman's husband.

Fucking great. He gets to the property and I am kicked out of the room, back into the heat. Apparently he'd forgotten to delist the room that was being renovated. He gives me a recommendation for another property that I can't find and is 2/10 starts, so I give up on that and am back to square one.

For some reason booking.com won't accept my functional cards so I find a property with availability and head there, praying to god I can just check in and lie down. After what felt like an eternity at reception I get checked in and have a shower and rest. I was in bed on my phone from about 2-5pm, not what I came here to do but sometimes you just gotta have a little phone time as a treat.
I thought I should go and see the sunset nearby, so I jumped on the bike and rode 20 minutes to a viewing spot. It was worth it as the sun set over the distant archipelago.

Starting to feel my appetite return, as I hadn't eaten in over a day, I made my way to a local restaurant. I almost gave in and went to a pizza joint lol, and while I resisted this night I think maybe tomorrow night the sirens call of the cheap vegan pizzas will draw me in.

At dinner I got chatting with another solo backpacker, from France. She'd spent a year in Australia previously and this was her second time in Indonesia, spending 3 weeks here. It was nice having someone to chat with, and my spirits were recovering even though I couldn't finish my meagre portion of delicious tempe due to my low appetite. I also messaged Remo, asking if he'd been sick also but he hadn't. Maybe he's the one that was built different after all.

After dinner it was straight back to the hotel and into bed. It was a dorm and a Canadian/Indonesian teenager was staying who I had a little chat with, before getting to sleep. I have to be up before 6 for pickup for the island tour tomorrow.

84.title: Day 91: Komodo National Park
paragraphs: Monday 28th July
Up before 6 for a 6:30 hotel pickup, before I knew it I was crammed onto a boat with a bunch of other tourists and heading out to the first destination of the day, a vista.
It was an hour's journey there, but even though it felt like we'd left early, it was very packed when we arrived.

The view at the top was nice but akin to images I'd seen from the Everest summit. A file of tourists were made to wait by local guides as we pushed our way to the top of the hill. Accompanying the throngs of us tourists like a remora were the local hawkers with Komodo t-shirts, and for some reason a few tame deer that food was available for purchase for. I guess the food would be the reason.
We then stopped at a beach for a quick swim before continuing on to the Komodo dragons themselves, the only reason for my joining of the trip.

It was absolutely worth it, and we were in for a treat seeing a female, baby, and adult male Komodo Dragon. The male was absolutely massive, and really made one feel like they were in the presence of a dinosaur.
We were then hearded through the gift shops, asked for tips by the island guides, taken to a few snorkeling spots, brought back and asked for tips by our guides.

I've sped through the rest of the day in this entry as I didn't really enjoy much of it apart from the dragons. I was still pretty tired after being sick, and these sorts of tours just aren't for me. The constant crowds and tourist mill really isn't something I want to be a part of.

There was a nice German couple on the boat however, and I was offered to be put in touch with a friend in Hamburg in the lab work space which could be an interesting development when I arrive! I may finally put that science degree to temporary use.
Once back in Labuan Badjo I succumbed and went for dinner at the Goodfellas themed pizza joint. It was actually great and I wish that I had been hungry enough to try another of their offerings.

85.title: Day 92: Ocean's Hungry Grasp
paragraphs: Tuesday 29th July
A full day of travel always leaves me feeling accomplished.

I was on the 10am ferry to the next Island, Sumbawa, finally breaking from the unintentional 3 nights I'd spent in Labuan Badjo. The bowels of the ferry were all flaking paint and rusted metal, but emerging into the open upper deck I was pleasantly surprised by a sight that could have been a Marrickville brewery.

Pastel chairs sat in files, surrounded by small trees planted in large iron barrels, providing shade from the intensifying sun. A covered seating area had full shade, while the rest was mostly mottled. It wasn't perfect, but it was far nicer than downstairs and I found a corner to make myself comfortable.

There were other tourists on board and I started chatting with a German and a Swiss, again using my German for maybe the fourth time this week, lol. We later played some card games with a Frenchman, and mostly just whiled away the time as the boat passed around the distant islands.

The head in the peak of the afternoon was still quite intense, and we napped in the small portions of full shade as best we could on the hot metal deck. I found that lying in one spot was best, as my body would actually slowly comfortably cool the metal beneath me, the opposite of warming up a bench.
We arrived at Sape, Sumbawa, after 5pm, but there was no accommodation I could see online in Sape so I jumped into the bus to the bigger nearby town, Bima, with the others.

Bima would be on my way anyway and I figured it would be good to get an hour or so done today, as it would give me a good headstart tomorrow. One twisting mountainous route later and I was dropped conveniently close to my booked hotel. Unfortunately my shitty Indonesian toothpaste tube had no proper locking mechanism and had decided to spill its load inside my bag, giving me a nice little chore to do after a long day of travel.
A quick outing for some nasi goreng later and I was tucking into bed. I hoped to make it all the way across Sumbawa tomorrow, most likely just spending two nights on the island as I press on West.

86.title: Day 93: Zoom Zoom Zoom
paragraphs: Wednesday 30th July
I absolutely flew like the wind today.

My first lift came before I had even asked, a lovely local man who went out of his way to take me much further than he was going to get me to a turn off I was headed to. He told me about his kids in uni and school as we puttered along on his bike.

Sumbawa is a beautiful island. The mountains aren't quite as in your face as Flores, but the road dances along the waterfront, one minute running adjacent to the still surface, slinking back into the trees the next.

I thought a difficult but achievable goal could be to cross the island. It was a big ask, with over 7 hours of straight driving between Bima, my starting point, and Poto Tano, the western ferry departure point. Google Maps driving time estimates have become my go to yardstick, as they factor in road speeds very well. I've found that getting 6 hours of "driving" done constitutes a full day of hitchhiking, due to time walking, waiting for lifts, etc.

I didn't have to wait too long for any of my lifts and rode in stone trucks and private cars. Funnily enough I must have been looking my best today as I was complimented "very handsome" by a few ladies, that was flattering. One said, and I quote "Mister, you handsome, your nose is very out." 😂

My last lift was also extremely kind, and took me over an hour past his destination to drop me at the port. He was a military intelligence officer and we had a great chat using the translator. We passed by his family home that he had impressively built and was gorgeous, and by the end of the trip he was telling me to come back and stay with his family next time I'm on the island. I told him to let me know if he or a family member was in Sydney too. When he jumped out to grab some food for us from a shop I was worried I'd have to gently reject some meat, but he'd bought a huge bag of warm cooked corncobs! They were delicious and I polished off a few, taking one for the road when I left.

Arriving at the port just after sunset, I was already happy with the progress I'd made today. While I hadn't managed to fit in any sightseeing, I was stoked to have covered some good ground, met some lovely people, and be told I had a big schnoz. I decided to push on and jump on the next ferry, taking me to the next Island, Lombok, and leaving Sumbawa with a record of only one night spent.

The ferry between the islands took about 2 hours, and I arrived at 9pm, on a new island with no hotel booked. Many of the hotels aren't available on booking websites, so I hitched a short bike ride into town and went to the first one that had come up on my maps.

It was dangerous leaving it this late, as even the hotel staff may be home in bed, and I couldn't find anyone at the seemingly empty venue. As I started walking to another hotel 20 minutes back the direction I had come from, I thought I'd first try my luck and asked a shopkeep if he could help. It turns out he could, using the tried and tested classic strategy of going into the hotel and banging on the lit up door and calling out. This has saved me multiple times when I've encountered empty shops; the locals are far more game to holler and get the attention of their neighbours than I am.
For the measly price of $9 I had a bed to collapse into, and it was just in time as I fell promptly asleep.

87.title: Day 94: Mount Rinjani?
paragraphs: Thursday 31st July
Biiiiig one.
If there was one thing to see on Lombok, it's mount Rinjani. Or so I had gathered.

Sitting on the northern side of the round island, it's an active volcano that is currently calm enough to be summited, and offers beautiful views of its crater and the surrounding island. I could definitely make time for it.
It was only an hour's drive away from my hotel, but had a campground quite a reasonable 13ks and 1500+m of elevation gain up from the mountain town Sembalun.

My plan was to get to the base as early as possible, hike up to the crater rim campground I could see on my map, and hike back down tomorrow to head to Bali, the next Island. I saw that the actual summit had been closed recently, but was currently open.

It did not play out so, as a later start at 8:30 was quickly piled on by the lack of traffic heading up to the mountain, and I found getting a lift the hardest so far on the trip. I also managed to get lost without realising it, as my map's GPS was snapping to the location of the track, when I'd gone wrong. Fortunately, two young locals were able to see that my GPS was wrong and get me back on the road.

I was swarmed by children a few times, and finally when some hound teenagers were asking about what I was doing, I flagged down a family's truck and jumped in the back with the women and children, while the two men were in the cab. It's always nice hitching a lift while others are asking about what I do, and they bid me a happy farewell as I waved from the back of the truck as we sped off.

The four were great company for the long ride, and the kids were full of energy. Monkeys lurked on the sides of the roads as we climbed from the fields up into the dense, moist jungle, and would run out and eerily chase after the truck in the lane when we drove past them. The boy would point at them and say Monkey!, Monkey!, periodically switch his pointing to be at his little sister.

I don't like monkeys, they're too intelligent and their eyes hold yours as malice flickers and forms in their humanoid brains. If they had all the power I'm sure they'd ruin the world just like us, unlike kind animals like cows or dogs that would build a utopia.

While sitting in the back of Utes I try to position myself with my back to the cab with my backpack sitting between me and the metal bars that would otherwise brain me if we came to a sudden stop. It's hard not to think about safety when you suddenly don't have it, and while helmetless on the back of bikes I similarly try to drill to protect my head if we lose traction.

Despite my dire imaginings we arrived safely in the relative paradise of Sembalun. A picturesque mountain village ringed by peaks scratching the sky, I said bye to the family and started immediately on the walk. It was 12, as the hitching and eating had taken a lot longer than I thought. I estimated the hike at 6 hours, so truly had no time to spare if I wanted to make camp before sundown.

I had over four litres of water in my heavy pack but was quickly doubting I had enough as I climbed out of town. The amount of sweat I was losing was dehydrating me so quickly, and I realised I had to start regulating my drinking almost from the start of the walk. Ascending out of the town revealed a beautiful panorama that spanned from the opposite peaks down to the sea miles below when the clouds cleared, and the sparse cover and low bushes provided this view constantly.

My gps gave up as soon as l'd started the hike, so ensuring I was correctly following the track was another struggle. After 2 hours I'd made it over halfway as the crow flies, but under a fifth of the way up elevation wise. My pack was too heavy and I realised I was in for it over the close of the day, and may have to get the head torch or continue into the night. At the first of the lookout points I allowed myself a good chug of water, wassailing to my legs. I also carved up and enjoyed a tasty treat that I'd twice spotted from a passenger seat but not been able to buy, and had finally acquired two of this morning, dragon fruit!

On I pressed, figuring I could take another short break at the next stop point, but didn't have that much time to spare. When I arrived, I saw that it was built up and populated, with what turned out to be a drinks vendor that I helped myself to three of, instantly solving my water issue.

While I was enjoying my brief break, I also had some news broken to me by a local. I was not allowed to continue and higher as I didn't have a ticket, and even if I had a ticket the hike would be closed tomorrow, no exceptions for me coming back down first thing in the morning. It took a while to figure out the situation, with him putting his boss on the phone twice, but there was no continuing.

After further research I think you can't actually go up without having a guide, which was all news to me. While trying to climb mountains along my path is fun, I need to do a bit more research next time. They're also very on edge at the moment as a few people have been injured on the walk recently, and they didn't want that repeated.

I took it pretty well, as it also meant my legs wouldn't have to carry my ill planned pack up the literal mountain. I'll have to come back next time. Down was quicker than up and before I knew it I was pushing into the outskirts of town, as the sun lowered in the sky.

I toyed with the idea of camping in the jungle as I haven't actually called in Indonesia yet, but spotting some monkeys nearby nixed that idea. The idea of hitching the remaining hour down to the beach was also tempting, but I didn't want to leave booking a hotel until after dark again, in an even less populous area.

As I was deciding I came across a campground/hotel that looked fine. There was only one person here, the one employee looking after the property who showed me to my room and kindly offered me some coffee. He then asked if he could come and chat as I cooled off outside my room, and explained that he was bored as there were no guests at the moment.

His name was Hans, and he was 22 and from Bali, but here for his uncle, who owned the property. He asked if I wanted to go climb the nearby hill that overlooked the town, as he wanted me to enjoy Sembalun even though I hadn't been able to summit the mountain. It was a fantastic spot that he took us to on his motorbike, and it was very kind of him to offer to take me. It was 6pm, and the cacophonous prayer music from the 6 mosques I could see reached the top of the hill. As one would drop in between lines another would start, and was quite the atmosphere in the golden sun.

On the way back he bought us some food and water, and we had a nice chat at the table at the hotel using the translator. I asked him about his life and he said he was mostly bored, as his friends and family were in the main town and Bali, which he doesn't get the time off to visit.

He asked about my family and mentioned his mum was sick back in Bali, and when I asked if he could get the time off to visit her more often he said it was a money issue more than time. I asked him how much it costs to get to Bali and he said $50, which sounds about right with the bus and ferry fares required.

I've been spending less than I thought so I just went and got the money from my room and gave it to him. It took much persuading and he wanted to pay me back when he could, so I insisted he take it as a gift. He was extremely thankful, which is hard as I was in a position of being sooooo nice in his eyes when it really just isn't that much money to an Australian adult. He insisted on going and buying ingredients for a tempe nasi goreng dinner to cook for us, which was very kind. He even said he'd give me a massage in the morning, which would have felt very weird and I declined. There was really no good way to react to his thankfulness, as trying to explain it wasn't that much money to me would have been rude, but him lauding me for something that wasn't as much of a cost to me as he perceived it to be was awkward too.
The dinner was delicious but suuuuuper spicy, and he has insisted on making breakfast too.
I'm looking forward to tomorrow, and maybe I can even make it to Bali if I'm lucky, but either way the day will be off to an auspicious start: breakfast with a friend.

88.title: Day 95: Momentum
paragraphs: Friday 1st August

Breakfast was made by my new homie Hans, and afterwards we said our goodbyes at 8 as I walked off into the warm morning sun. I'd ideally like to start leaving an hour earlier, as there's no time to be wasted when there's road to cover.

The day started very slowly, and I didn't get my first lift until a quarter to nine, which was a short one. What I thought would be a quick journey down to the main road that skirted the island around to the north took a couple of hours, and had me doubting how much progress I would be able to make.

It picked up when I arrived in Bayan on the north coast of Lombok, and I was whisked away instantly in a pickup, crammed in the cab between a tour guide and tour driver. The driver was a talker and he asked about what I was doing. He also gave me the vital information that I could actually get a ferry to Bali from port Bangsal in the northwest of the island, and didn't have to hitchhike multiple hours to the other port in the southwest.
He even called a friend of his who worked there, confirmed that I could make the midday ferry, and put me in contact. Hero.

One other quick lift later and I was at the port, on the phone to the contact who directed me like a remote control car toward him through the crowd of ticket sellers. With a discounted ticket in my hand I fraternised with an Austrian and a German as we waited for the delayed ferry. There are more cats on Lombok and they're very cute.

The ferry was a bumpy ride and I made it to Bali at around 3. Bali is a different beast again and the ferry was absolutely mobbed by taxi drives upon arrival jostling for position like preschoolers around a football. Once I'd made my way out of the downtown I had a late lunch and considered my options. I was already happy with the day's progress as I'd made it to Bali, but decided I could push on further.

Arriving in Padangbai in the east, I realised I could miss the busy south of Bali entirely by heading northeast, to the loop around and follow the northern coast. This adds an hour of travel time but I think it will be worth it, as I abhor he is of hitchhiking though Ubud in the south.

The lifts came quickly even here, and I was dropped right at my hotel by my final lift. When I jumped in his car he opened by saying he would take me to his destination but nowhere else, but after our conversation flowed well he insisted on driving the extra 15 minutes to take me right there, and wouldn't hear of taking any money. If anyone is in Bali I can recommend him as a guide!
https://www.instagram.com/balihilltop?igsh=MTk2emt0aXc3bGlsag==

I'm still debating which mountain in Indonesia I want to climb, but I don't think it's going to be the nearby one in the next couple of days. I'll try and do some research as I travel and will tackle one once I'm on Java.
If I make good progress and keep this momentum up, that could be tomorrow.

89.title: Day 96: Java
paragraphs: Saturday 2nd August

I had a small feeling of apprehension this morning towards starting to hitchhike. It can be hard rolling out of bed and standing beside the road, especially if it's one that's harder to get a lift from. All is instantly better upon getting in a lift, which I soon did.

I had great luck actually, and the first two lifts took me almost all the way across Bali, leaving me near to the ferry at around 1pm. I'd jumped out in the small beachfront town of Pemuteran, ditching my second lift early to do so. The town had a nice cafe and a beach to swim at, and I figured it would make a good place to have a break for lunch.

One of the nice things about the food being so cheap is that when a meal isn't quite filling enough, you can just try another main! My tacos were pretty small so I followed it up with a tofu Buddha bowl, and it made for a filling experience.

The beachfront was hidden behind resorts that rimmed it, hugging onto the prime real estate and as far as I could see, blocking public access. Luckily I look like a tourist so I walked into one of them, set up on their deck chairs, and took a swim at the beach and then a wash off in their pool. Resting on the shaded recliner afterwards, I could see how this type of holiday could be tempting.
Although I could have fallen asleep the road was calling to me, and I laced up and made my way dutifully back to the thoroughfare.

In 10 minutes, I had an amazing stroke of luck. Fikky was a driver who was heading over the ferry, deep into Java, all the way to Malang. This would be an almost 8 hour drive, and as it was already past 2, would go late into the night.
I decided I would go the full distance with him, but would go most of the way to Probolinggo. Probolinggo was close to Mt Bromo, and would be a good base for me to go and see it tomorrow.

After splitting the ferry between us and picking up another, pre organised, Indonesian hitchhiker, we were on Java and began our journey. It feels nice to be on Java, I now have only one more ferry within Indonesia to go, from Java to Sumatra.

We encountered a problem, as there had been an accident to the north and the road was completely backed up with traffic. Fikky whirled us around and started driving deep up into the mountains, while I practiced just having faith. Climbing higher and higher the sun set behind the fog, looking like cream lights from a distant stadium, and the road narrowed to a single file between jungle trees.

We made it to the top of Mt Ijen, where we took a break for dinner and saw the local tourists camping, and the gates to the walks beyond. It would have been great to have been here with time to spare and during the day.

The detour had added almost two hours, and our ETA at my hostel was 11pm, the check in closing time. Drifting in and out of sleep in the backseat, I woke up when we were close and we made it in the nick of time. Checked it, I took a shower and went straight to sleep, hoping to find some other backpackers to check out Bromo with tomorrow.

90.title: Day 97: Volcano
paragraphs: Sunday 3rd August

I'm currently camped at what may be the coolest location I've ever broken camp. It's completely silent and still, which wasn't what I was expecting at all when I started to make my way up the steep, sandy volcano in the late afternoon. From here I have a view over the top of Mt Bromo, spewing sulphurous fumes into the atmosphere, and the surrounding crater valley, an incredibly flat plain of volcanic black dust.

Unfortunately, the internet here is too spotty to upload any of my beautiful photos, so you'll just have to take my word for the fact I really am here. I'll either add them to this entry tomorrow, or put them in tomorrow's update, when I have a more robust connection.

I spent the late afternoon wandering around the valley, first summiting Mt Bromo for a peek into the acrid depths, and then spontaneously deciding to summit Mt Batok also to camp, rather than returning to the flat patch I'd spotted earlier near the crater rim.

It's a completely surreal and alien landscape here, like nothing I've ever seen before. The sand is so fine it's almost liquid, and the igneous rocks jut out of it at random. Contributing to my awestruck mood was the lord of the rings soundtrack I had in my ears.

The journey up the mountain was hard, and I had to charter a bus to make it up. I was disappointed to not be able to hitchhike the whole way, but these side trip offshoots are too far out of the way to have much traffic flowing towards them.

It's surprising I've made it this far having had such a slow morning, taking some time to have breakfast with some people from the hostel, and then a leisurely stroll in town to check out some of the Dutch colonial history. I only left the hostel just before 1, and a few short lifts later ended up paying my way up the hill. Honestly, I didn't enjoy the slow morning and felt I needed to keep moving. I was briefly toying with the idea of staying two nights Probolinggo, but couldn't stand the stagnation.
I'm too far gone with this whole rushing thing. Who knows maybe I'll have a breakdown at some point and render myself unable to hack it. That would make for some interesting blogs at the least.

I'm going to be up tomorrow to catch the dawn, and will have a better view of it than the flocks of tourists that will swarm the base of the valley. I just hope I retain the top of this volcano to myself for the morning.

91.title: Day 98: Streak breaker
paragraphs: Monday 4th August

I woke up at 5am to catch the sunrise from the top of the volcano. It was beautiful, and lit up the foggy valley, slowly dispelling the mist as it crested the distant peaks. While alone on my summit, I could hear the tourists on a distant ridge, cries echoing over the chasm to me.
Here are all the photos that I took yesterday and today from that region.

I descended the steep climb in 20 minutes, much faster than the slow ascent the evening before. At the bottom tourists were already trudging back from Bromo to their jeeps, parked in the sand like a scene from Burning Man.
After breakfast in the mountaintop town, I hitchhiked down the mountain with a couple of rides, arriving at an on ramp to the large toll road, the biggest road I've encountered so far.

I wasn't feeling it. On large highways hitchhiking is much harder, and there are only certain points you can stand at. A bus pulled up and I just jumped in, hoping to be taken to a smaller town on the way but instead going to the large city of Surabaya.

In Surabaya I was nearish to another on ramp to the toll road heading east, so I made my way there. Unfortunately it was too built up and had no lay-by to stand in, so I decided to stay on the non toll road. It sucked, and there was nowhere to pull over, and no one was stopping for me. I didn't enjoy it at all. When another bus pulled up and was going to Mojokerto for under a dollar, I decided to just jump in.

On the bus ride I was seriously evaluating my priorities. Should I have held out more before caving and getting a bus? How hard do I want to push the hitchhiking if it's hard? Would I have any luck at all on Java or not?

I came to a decision influenced by doing some reading on my phone. Firstly, one woman that had hitchhiked Sumatra and Java earlier this year had found it very difficult also, and had been stuck for a full 9 hours once. Here I was jumping in buses after a bit of trouble, and she was persevering through that! Secondly, the bus ride was boring. Sure, I could easily sit on buses and trains all the way to Germany, but it's just not interesting. There's no opportunity to talk to locals and loud buskers play on the bus and try to sell to you. If my trip was more goal based in terms of cities or sights, sure, getting buses between them is the expedient solution. I'm here for the journey itself though, and don't want to just bus my way to my destination.

It's a little more grey than that, and I think if I do side trips that are more easily accessible via paid transport, I'll just cop it, but try my best to maintain hitchhiking for the rest of the voyage, even if it's hard. At a minimum, I'm not going to let myself jump on another bus until I've waited at least three hours in one spot. That would be annoying enough for me to allow myself some re-evaluation of my position.

Reinvigorated, I jumped out at Mojokerto and dutifully proceeded to the roadside. It was tough, and I waited for about 45 minutes with some local spectators, but eventually a kind woman and her mother picked me up. She was a doctor and spoke great English, and they even took me to dinner, not letting me pay despite my protests. After, they dropped me at my hotel and told me to text if I had any questions or needed help. I'm very thankful to have met them at the end of a turbulent day.

92.title: Day 99: Tested
paragraphs: Tuesday 5th August
My hotel was right next to the road I was setting out on, so I gave myself a slower morning and got on the road at 9.
What followed was probably the slowest day of hitchhiking I've ever had, where every wait was at least half an hour, and each ride was short, some even going slightly perpendicular to my destination.
As I write this, I'm in Surakarta, only 2 hours drive from my starting point(to be fair, the slow non toll road route I took is over 4, which makes me feel better.)

I wanted to get to Prambanan temple today and tick that off, ready to push on tomorrow, but I just wasn't able to make it, despite a full day of trying. It was painful to stop close yet far from my destination, at about an hour's drive away, but the sun was setting and I was forced to tap out for the day and find a hotel.
Today also marks two weeks that I've been in Indonesia, and I still have a long way to go to leave the country.
As I write this I'm deciding to write off the temples and mountain hike to the southeast, and turn north instead directly towards Jakarta.

This isn't to say today was terrible, I had a few fun rides with a nice woman and her child, and a kind farmer who dropped me off at a perfect location by motorbike after a quick stop at his family home. He was a true friend, and when I translated that I wanted to hitchhike rather than get the bus, he understood instantly.
I decided to treat myself to a fancy dinner, costing a whole $12! I dined in a shmick restaurant and had the best gado gado I've tried so far.
I'm still feeling reflective about what I want this trip to be, as if the hitchhiking doesn't improve in the next week, I don't know how much I can force myself to be driven past in the sun.

I'm almost doing the opposite of most travel writing and making this sound as miserable as possible, but I've just had a tough couple days. Looking forward to pushing an early start tomorrow and seeing how far I make it! If I have a good day tomorrow, all will be forgiven. I could potentially be in Jakarta in a couple days with this new route.

93.title: Day 100: Shortcut
paragraphs: Wednesday 6th August

Wow, 100 days. My first instinct was to write the trite "I can't believe it's been that long" here, but honestly, I can. It feels like forever ago that I jumped on the boat, and the fact it was only 3 months ago feels too recent.

I think it's also why I've found the last bit of travelling a little harder; I'm not fresh into the adventure, as full of energy as I was on day 1, I've been on the road a while now. I wouldn't swap it for anything though, filling each day with unknown adventures and people is the best way to live for me.

In light of last night's decision to cut Yogyakarta and head north, I started earlier at 7:30 and proceeded out to one of the worst hitchhiking spots in the city of Surakarta. It was in a small layby on a busy city street, and I was excited to start a new day but apprehensive to work with this spot.

By a stroke of divine luck the nicest gentleman pulled over next to me, seeing me as he exited from a side street. My first destination was only 20 minutes away on the outskirts of town, where he agreed to take me. After dropping his kid off at daycare, he asked if I'd had breakfast and insisted we eat together when I hadn't. He was a businessman with great English, and we had a great talk. When he dropped me off at the turn-off North, I wished I was able to stay with them longer.

Again, I was fortunate and a young couple picked me up quite quickly, and were heading north for about an hour in the direction I wanted to go. They were in their early thirties and we're engaged to be married next year. They bought me some snacks and wouldn't take a cent when I offered to pitch in.

From where they dropped me at Ungaran I only had another short 15 minutes to go to the outskirts of Semaring, from where I could turn east toward Jakarta. I had to walk a little out of Ungaran until I found a workable layby, but after 15 minutes a young guy on a motorbike took me the distance. Luckily he had a second helmet on him. He wouldn't take any money but I was able to donate him the biscuits the previous couple had given me that I couldn't eat, and he was appreciative.

I was now in a good position, directly on the on ramp for the toll road that headed straight to Jakarta. Within a few minutes I had a funny situation, with a couple of an Indonesian woman and mid thirties, Dutch guy in the passenger seat pull up. She said they could take me a distance, but he was so obviously not into having me in the car at all. He couldn't even look at me and was uncomfortably smirking while she earnestly tried to figure out where would be the spot to take me, not picking up his hints at all. I read the room and declined the lift.
Immediately after a group of Indonesian real estate agents, from what I gathered, said they could take me about an hour to the next town, which I accepted.

I think this was a mistake, and it's one of the hard to call lines of hitchhiking that I'm not good at. As I was in such a favourable position, with a few offers in the minutes since my arrival, I certainly should have been more picky and waited for a lift further on, or to Jakarta itself. It's just too easy to accept any lift that goes in my direction, but maybe I could have avoided the adventure that followed.

It was 5 hours on the toll road to Jakarta from when I jumped in the car, and I was optimistic that I may be able to make it that day, as it was just after 1. On the non-toll road, it was well over 11 hours away, so I wanted to stay on the toll route.

Once I was dropped at Weleri, not very far from Semarang by the agents, I made my way to the on ramp there and started thumbing. Unluckily, the first four people that pulled over were all heading east back to Semarang, not to Jakarta in the west, four coin flips I devastatingly lost.

I was there for about an hour and a half, and at one point was moved on by the toll gate operators and had to move further back up the road, to a spot where I could see the far, far busier non toll road. While it was tempting, I knew that would slow my progress greatly.

Finally a trucker that had parked and left for lunch returned, and I went to talk to him. He was heading to Jakarta, but wouldn't arrive until tomorrow and didn't really want to take me, until I agreed to split petrol and toll costs. I jumped in and we started onto the road, but the truck was slow and averaged about 50 on the highway, cars flying past on our right.

We then exited the toll road for some reason, and crawled with the other traffic on the public road, swelling my potential ETA from 5 hours to 10 in one action. The hours crawled on and we stopped for a long tea break at a roadside stop for about an hour as the sun set. I asked if he was stopping there for the night and he said that if I wanted to go fast I could get the bus. Communication issues can lead to accidental rudeness, something I have to be aware of when language is an issue.

A few more hours later and it was around 9, and we stopped for dinner just near the toll road at a roadside restaurant. The tempe was good, and I thought we were stopping there for the night. I said I'd go and stay in a hotel nearby, but he informed me that this was just a dinner break and that we'd continue on. I should have called it and stayed near the toll road for the morning.

After dinner we drove another hour then pulled up in a truck lot. I set up my hammock using bars on the side of the truck and a nearby tree, and tried to sleep at around 10:30. Mosquitos were swarming me and I lathered myself in Bushman's repellent, as the humidity was high and prevented me from layering up. I started feeling sick again, and was forced to the bathroom around midnight, though luckily I didn't vomit this time, but it was a near thing.
I finally fell asleep properly around 2, after a fitful, sweaty, mosquito-plagued few hours of discomfort, where I was regretting my decision not to bail when I could have stayed in the hotel.

94.title: Day 101: Jakarta
paragraphs: Thursday 7th August.

I was scared awake at 4, after a whopping two hours of sleep, and informed we were back on the road. I was still feeling ill, tired and headachy, but knew I could get a hotel in Jakarta later that morning. Due to using the non toll road, we were still 5 hours drive away, roughly the same timeframe as when I was using the toll road over 12 hours ago. 🙃

I napped as best I could as we pressed on trying to patchwork together a nights sleep from hour sizes fragments. Sweat lived on my brow, and I felt dehydrated as I lost all my fluids out my skin. I just wanted to get to Jakarta.
That wasn't to be though, as one of our tyres popped on the highway, yippee! Cue over an hour of sitting in the shade at a repair shop, waiting for a patch fix that couldn't come fast enough.

The traffic near Jakarta on the public road is absolutely terrible, and we were bumper to bumper amongst trucks, barely moving at all. After a couple of hours of this, he reached where we needed to go and kicked me out at an intersection, where I crawled out into the heat in my miserable state. I crossed the road back to one heading to Jakarta, and was incredibly relieved when a pulled over Ute was heading into Jakarta. The driver was friendly, and I apologised to him that I wasn't more talkative, as I was feeling unwell. I'm sure I looked like shit too and he understood. It wasn't fast, but we crawled through the traffic to Jakarta, eventually arriving on the outskirts around 12. He said he could drop me at my hotel, but as it was still half an hour away I didn't let him, and said I could get a taxi. I didn't want him going further out of his way for me, and he thankfully agreed.

Cities don't count for me hitchhiking, it's an odious experience hitchhiking inside a city, so I had no qualms about getting into a taxi and gunning for the hostel. The driver was interesting and told me all about the embassies as we drove past them, and the economic situation in Indonesia. He said that due to the high population, unemployment is rife and wages are low, and many people come to Jakarta from the poorer countryside in hopes of making it. The result is the roads are constantly choked, and poverty is everywhere, sad circumstances.

At my hostel I booked a private room and collapsed into bed after a shower. Rewarding myself with some phone time, I did manage to get my laundry done, and eat for the first time that day in the late afternoon. I paid out the ass for a terrible burrito, but I just needed something western for my stomach. The food here is great but both times I've been ill I crave the familiarity of cuisines I'm more used to.

In the evening I watched an Indonesian movie with a Turk from the hostel, and I plan on going to where it was filmed in Jakarta tomorrow. I was thinking about taking two nights here to recover, but that is to be decided. It started to rain in the night so we'll see what the weather is doing in the morning and assess the situation from there. I'm keen to get over to Sumatra, back into the wilds where camping is free and the jungle is thick.

95.title: Day 102: Sumatra
paragraphs: Friday 8th August

I took the slow morning I needed this morning and got back up to date with my blogs, then went out to check the movie set I came through Jakarta to see. "The Raid: Redemption" is the greatest action movie of all time, and while I'm not normally into that genre, the choreography and tension is so good that I'm a huge fan.
