If you're not afraid of some incredible violence I'd recommend checking it out. It was filmed in Jakarta, and I'd purposefully booked a hostel close to the building so I could go check it out. I was quite disappointed that the security guards wouldn't let me upstairs to take a look around, but I recognised an area from a scene in the movie and snapped some photos there. Satisfied, I made my way back to the hostel to get ready for the noon checkout.

I had lunch at the Mexican place next door, and was on my way out of the city. I walked for a while then took a taxi to where I had sussed out that the toll road started. The toll road was actually much more approachable than I expected, as from the satellite image it looked like it was on an overpass, but a normal street flowed into it. I was preparing for a long wait, but quite quickly a truck pulled up and was heading in the same direction, so I hauled my pack up and jumped in.

It was a 35 year old guy from a nearby city who I had a nice conversation with. I found out he had a young child that he had to spend a lot of time away from driving, and he asked about my family too. While we didn't speak each other's languages, he wasn't hesitant at all to take full advantage of my translator.

We'd figured out that I would get out before he turned off, but then he started yelling to other drivers as we passed. The hero found one that was heading towards the coast further, and I made a mid traffic truck swap at the next stoppage. The traffic was quite thick at this point, a ubiquitous occurrence in Jakarta.

The next driver was nice too, and we talked a little as we drove. Somehow we pulled up and he spoke with another driver, Andre, that he knew was taking the ferry to Sumatra, who agreed to take me with him. He's actually going past an extra 100 kilometres in Sumatra in the direction I'm heading, to Bandar Lampung, which is amazing. While we were stopped the others had some coffee from an old woman who was selling packets by the side of the road. They beckoned that I buy something, but I didn't want anything. I could tell she was kind of disappointed so just gave her some money, but it was kind of awkward. I ended up saying it was for the coffees the others were drinking. That I have too much money and need to give it away is not the first impression I want to give to new people I'm riding with, so I probably shouldn't have. It's easier to offload cash onto people when I'm leaving them, rather than beginning a new social encounter, due to all the related baggage it brings. I said goodbye to my second driver and made another swap, three rides for the effort of one.
Andre is 21 and is looking out for me. We grabbed some dinner on the way to the harbour, and he told me to keep an eye on my phone and secure my valuables while on the ferry.
Once on board we came into a small room with mattress beds, and claimed two. I still haven't paid anyone, so assume my fee was included in the vehicle I was riding with.

In our room a masseuse grabbed my calf and beckoned, enquiring if I wanted a massage. I was startled and my immediate answer will always be no, but after watching him give someone else a good treatment I came around. It was my first massage of the trip and it was bloody good. My legs are sore and I smell of baby oil.

Where I'm staying tonight has not been decided yet, but it looks like I'll be getting into Bandar Lampung at 10pm at the earliest. Will I be able to find a hotel? Will Andre help me find somewhere to stay? Find out next time on travelling P.

96.title: Day 103: Snatching victory from the jaws of defeat
paragraphs: Saturday 9th August
Picking up from where I left off last night at 8, my night was far from over. We didn't end up making it to Bandar Lampung at 10, 11, or 12, but after 1am.

It was slow due to the ferry arriving later that I thought, the truck struggling to climb into the hilly Sumatra, the distance from the port to the town being further than I thought, and a few stops with the boys on the way.

It was a funny journey. At one point I about died laughing when Andre went through my Instagram, and earnestly asked if an old photo of me with long hair was my mum or friend, lmfao. I've put the photo on this page for reference.

I was pretty tired when we got into Bandar Lampung, and worried that I wouldn't be able to find a hotel with an open reception as it was after midnight. After a few stops to fill the fuel tank and give someone some money that seemed illicit, where I was akin to a clueless lab sitting in the passenger seat wondering what the others were up to when they left the car, I finally got my reprieve.

They'd earlier asked if I wanted to stay on an empty bed with their accommodation, which I had accepted on the drive there. I thought that was the plan but when they asked if I wanted a hotel close to 2am, I just said yes as I was so wrecked. They kindly dropped me to one and wouldn't accept any cash for fuel again, and as it was a fancier place the reception was still manned at the late hour.

I checked into my room around 2:30, and finally went to sleep about an hour later after a shower. This night riding was untenable, and I said to myself that I wanted to start beginning and finishing the days earlier, as travelling after dark is not ideal in terms of safety or rest.

At 8:30 I groggily woke up and started my slow morning routine. The hotel breakfast was nice and I enjoyed a rare hot shower before heading out to begin hitchhiking a little after 11. It was 5 hours to the next large city, Palembang, and I was naïvely hoping I could make it before dusk.

After a free lift to the outskirts of town, where the on ramp lead to the toll road, I was optimistic about my chances. Fortuna did not reciprocate, and every 15 or so minutes I would have someone stop for the next few hours, but always heading either back to Java or off east or west, no takers for my northern sell. At one point some toll officers came to say hi and took me back to the tollhouse with them to say hi to everyone. I thought I would be able to use the situation to my advantage by asking for rides at the toll gate, or them asking around for me, but that didn't pan out. They kind of just took me there, I had a chat with some of them, and the two that brought me just wandered off. I went to hitchhike at the toll gate and was told by the boss I couldn't, so I asked one of the other workers to drop me back up the road where I was before I had been brought there as a curio. In the same empty car of the absentees, no less.

My brief driver was nice and said he could help me find a lift. He was heading home but told me to wait half an hour or so and he'd be back. I said I'd try and hitchhike in the meantime but would probably be there when he got back, and if I was gone to assume I'd found a lift. While I was there nearby for another hour, I didn't see a trace of him unfortunately. He might have missed me due to me moving slightly, or came after I'd left.

It was after three and I'd still had no luck. A few vehicles stopped, but not for me which was disappointing, rather to drop someone off or have a smoke. I'd said to myself earlier I would go until 3:30, then just call it a day and retire to a hotel, and try again tomorrow. The sky darkened and drops of rain began to fall, so I decided to call it earlier at a quarter past.

As I was walking off my lay-by, I passed a truck that had been sitting there a while. One of the two guys in it had left earlier but just returned. They asked where I was headed and we were all going to Palembang, but they weren't super keen on taking me. I said I'd split fuel and won them over, and like that we were rolling. They thought they'd arrived in Palembang around 9.

We immediately pulled into the toll road heading back south back to Java, which I pointed out. They assured me I was wrong so I stayed quiet until we passed under a road sign. I felt extremely vindicated as we diverted off the total road just to do a u turn.

The vibes were a little off to start, but warmed up as we made our journey together. They warned me about Palembang and said it was dangerous, and not to talk to people on the street. This wasn't the first ill omen. Earlier in my travels I was warned about Sumatra, and last night I even saw karaoke joints, that were clearly illegal brothels in the early hours, for the first time (I am afraid of women). My yet again late arrival time had me slightly nervous.
The drive was uneventful, and I couldn't get any sleep despite probably needing it.

They dropped me near my hotel when I arrived and I gave them some cash as a thank you. While this area is poor, it didn't seem unsafe at all while I walked to my accom. I even saw a cute cat on the way, and if this was a zone with dangerous mobs nearby it wouldn't have been able to spawn.
The hotel was terrible and had an anti LGBT poster on the wall of the lobby. Just religious things.
Another late end to the day but I promise I'll try to call it earlier tomorrow. Try.

97.title: Day 104: Yippee.
paragraphs: Sunday 10th August.
Finally I'd had a reasonable night's sleep, even though I'd arrived at my accommodation later, and the new day was beckoning.
I'm in Palembang, and my final destination in Indonesia is the port of Dumai, from where I'll catch the ferry over to Malaysia, and be done with ocean crossings for the remainder of my trip!
It's roughly 20 hours of estimated driving to Dumai, broken down as such:
7 hours from Palembang to Jambi.
11 hours from Jambi to Pekanbaru.
3 hours from Pekanbaru to Dumai.
I'm not sure how I'll split the Jambi - Pekanbaru leg, as there don't seem to be too many big cities in between, but that's a problem for tomorrow, if I make it that far.
Today's plan would be to try and tackle the 7 hours to Jambi.
The shower was so gross in my hotel that I opted to skip it entirely, and was quickly on the road without breakfast or a wash at 7:30, the earlier start I'd been after.

I had a good feeling about the new day, and it proved to be a valid one. A quick lift in the back of a van brought me to the start of the road exiting town. While walking to a better position, I came across a large indoor breakfast buffet style restaurant, and loaded up with some delicious food. I then caught another short bike lift to where the two roads leaving town intersect, what I imagined would be the best place to hitchhike from.

After declining a few paid rides a young guy in a truck picked me up, who was very friendly and talkative! On the drive I saw some rubber farms, with the thick white gum from the trees dripping down into cups from cuts in the bark, waiting to be collected and refined.

Sumatra is more wild than java but primarily farmland unfortunately, and later in the day I saw hundreds of acres of oil palms, the infamous crop responsible for a huge amount of deforestation. It's quite interesting what the fruits look like that eventually get processed into palm oil, look it up.

He forked away from my path at a small town, and when I jumped out of the truck I was mobbed by old ladies in Indonesian dress demanding photos. Shortly after some kids repeated the process, also asking some questions and screaming in exulted chorus at each of my mundane answers.
"Where are you from?" "Australia" *screams*
"Where are you going?" "Jambi" *screams*

On the outskirts of town I was picked up again by three men. I thought they were a group but the driver was dropping the two customers at a ferry, then continuing on to his home. I suspect he pulled over to try and make some more cash, but still agreed when I said I was hitchhiking. I paid for his fuel as recompense.

He stopped for a very long, late lunch in the afternoon, only 2 hours from my destination I was excited to reach. I waited patiently for almost an hour, when he then informed me he would be taking a short break, and lit a cigarette. ???
I asked if it would be about an hour and he nodded, so I took my bag from the car and began hitching again. I wish I'd started this process an hour ago.
Luckily I was picked up by a lovely group that included a young Indonesian guy that had Chinese ancestry, spoke mandarin, and English too to a limited extent.

He had taught himself mandarin to assist him in getting a better job and learning more about his heritage, and came across as very driven. We had a great conversation about the differences between Indonesian and Australian culture, environmentalism, and why we both chose the paths we did.

They were heading all the way into Jambi but unfortunately it wasn't to be, and the car broke down right on the outskirts of town, due to issues with the bearings. Rain was threatening while the driver tried in vain to fix it, and when the others crammed into another small car that had arrived I offered to make my own way, as I didn't see my pack and myself fitting in.
I copped a taxi bike the last half an hour to my hotel, and just after I'd arrived the rain started to pour.
After the deluge and a chat with my beloved grandma and aunt back home, I ventured out for dinner before retiring to bed.

98.title: Day 105: Lost in the sauce
paragraphs: Monday 11th August

I allowed myself a later start after 9 this morning, due to my decision to break the 11 hours to Pekanbaru up into two shorter days. As the road out of town didn't really lead to any other major hubs, I figured getting a lift in that direction wouldn't be too hard, and that I could comfortably get the 5 or 6 hours done in daylight hours even with the later start.

It took just under an hour to get a couple of lifts to the road leading out of town, placing me there a touch after 10. I figured the first destination I should lead with should be Merlung, 2.5 hours along the way.

Almost immediately a smaller truck pulled up with two middle aged guys in it, and they agreed to take me without hesitation. The passenger scooted over next to the driver and I squeezed into his seat.

We stopped for lunch and I chucked my bag in the trailer, and was relegated to the centre seat, as the freeloading hitchhiker. The guys are friendly and told me a bit about their families, but we've mostly ridden in silence.

I asked where they were going and they're actually headed to Pekanbaru today. I couldn't resist and asked if I could come along, to which they agreed. In hindsight, I maybe should have considered breaking the day up anyway, as the journey has been rough.
It's almost 10pm now and we're still over 2 hours away from stopping. My back hurts as it's not comfortable, and I'm thinking I could have potentially been a bit choosier about my ride.

While the best day of travel yet, getting over 11 hours of driving done, it hasn't been enjoyable. I'm looking forward to checking into a hotel and collapsing, straightening my back for the first time in half a day. Hopefully it's not too far after midnight!

99.title: Day 106: A mostly chill one
paragraphs: Tuesday 12th August
So the night did not end as quickly as I would have hoped. The uncomfortable drive continued for hours longer, and the windy roads kept us at 40 km/h.

As we finally ticked down to one hour to go, the drivers swapped back for a final time. The one that was now driving had been sleeping intermittently on his rest shifts throughout the day, but it hadn't seemed to have helped at all.

I noticed we were driving slower, and assumed it was due to being late at night with poor visibility. When the driver jerked the wheel a couple of times in reaction to gentle turns, I realised he was straight up on the verge of falling asleep. I watched his eyelids lazily close out of the side of my eye and in the mirror, and he was scratching his head and neck constantly, obviously his personal equivalent to a bedtime glass of warm milk.

I asked him how he was going, and threw in a few exited interjections randomly that I knew he didn't understand to try and keep him awake, but it only mildly helped. After I'd verbally prod him he'd quickly start drifting again. I considered getting out, but given that would have stranded me on the outskirts of a large city surrounded by farmland and abandoned buildings, and that we were only doing like 30km/h, I decided to just bear it. Maybe a bad decision.

I don't think I've ever been further from rest at such a late hour, and was fully ready to grab the wheel if needed, for about 45 minutes. On the way into town, we turned away from the direct route and headed south around the centre, to my dismay. The minutes crawled by and we eventually came to a turn that would lead them further away from my intended hotel, so it was time for me to bail. Even though I was still a ride away from sleep in a new Sumatran city, I was extremely relieved to be out of the deathtrap.

I approached some guy standing in a cafe and explained my situation as best I could, and that I just needed a taxi. For some reason the guy was trying to tell me something almost quite aggressively, it was kind of intense. I'm glad this didn't happen on my first day, and I wasn't too bothered, as I think he was just a bit weird. Some others came over, and I repeated that I needed a taxi. One of them mentioned the word Grab, the taxi app for Indonesia that I haven't downloaded yet, so just said sure, stood slightly back and began downloading it on my phone. Next thing I'm is the weird guy agrees to take me and is gesturing me to get on the back of his bike. I jump on and direct, and we absolutely floor it down the midnight road to town. I'm talking 70, and I'm on the back with no helmet. I wasn't exactly falling asleep now, either.

We chat a bit on the bike and he even stops when I say I need to use an ATM and waits. We get to my hotel and I offer him 10 bucks, which he is hesitant to even accept, but I insist, and say he saved me. Luckily the hotel is 24 hour, and I'm quickly asleep, a bit after 2.

That was the end of Monday night, and it's Tuesday I wake up to begin the comparatively short 2.5 hours of driving to the port of Dumai, where I'll leave for Malaysia tomorrow. I give myself a slow morning, enjoying the complimentary breakfast, and only leave my hotel when I have to at 12. A few short lifts later and I'm on the road leading to Dumai out of town.

In about 5 minutes a family pulls up and invites me in. They're heading about halfway there on the toll road, and I'm glad to accept. Here's where I made a minor mistake, that I could see coming. As they're going to be turning off the highway at some point to a relatively minor town, I should have left them at the first, bigger entrance to it and secured a ride to Dumai all the way from there. What I thought might happen did, and I was dropped in a very awkward spot where a barely used entrance fed onto the motorway. I had to stand somewhat dangerously on the motorway and hitch from there. Equally annoyingly, the cars and trucks are already going too fast and it makes it hard to stop.

It was only 15 minutes before I did end up with a ride from a enthusiastic, somewhat slimy middle aged guy who tried too hard to be a friend before asking me to pay for some food for us, to which I agreed, and for some cigarette money, which I declined. At our roadside restaurant chosen by him, I was badly overcharged, paying over double what I should have. I looked to him for support but he offered none, so I just copped it rather than put up a fuss, but I was pissed off with him at this point, and didn't like the way he stared at my face the entire time I ate.

Back in the car he quickly started asking for pocket money, or at least that's what the translator spat out. I tried to clarify if he was asking for money, and he said no, so I was confused. He kept rephrasing it but he actually was, but was just trying to phrase it as weaselly as possible. I told him I'd already paid the amount for his lunch I had, and he did a big act about how it was too much and he didn't know, pointing back toward the vendor and shaking his head, lol. At least he dropped the money after that.
He dropped me on the outskirts of town and I had to jump on a motorbike to get me the final kilometres of my Indonesian leg, into Dumai.
Walking the 15 mins to my hotel, I absolutely cracked my head on a sign positioned over the path with no markings on the grey bar. My fault for being on my phone.

I splurged on a *gasp* $40 hotel that was nice and close to the port for my 9am ferry tomorrow, and didn't leave it at all after 6. I had two showers over the evening, enjoying the luxury of a hot, high pressure wash. They also had a rabbit garden, but it stank and while cute, the rabbits didn't seem super into it.
I booked my departure from the country at 10pm the night before like a genius, but all was well. I had to be at the port at 8, so tucked in with a 6:30 alarm.

100.title: Day 107: Malaysia
paragraphs: Wednesday 13th August
I've finally done it! Indonesia was beautiful but it was time to say goodbye and take my last ferry.
Check in went smoothly and I managed to bring my last minute breakfast cup of mi goreng through the entire process, gently cradling it like a babe.

I had to quickly book a hostel to be able to provide a Malaysian address, and chose one in Melaka, my first port of entry. The ferry was incredibly quick across the straight, dodging between the flotilla of container shops that pass through the east-west trade passage that is the Malacca Straight.

After a quick incoming interview, I was stamped and ushered into Malaysia. I didn't even have to pay a visa fee to get 90 days, unlike Indonesia. It was a short 15 minute walk to my hostel where I'd booked a private room, and I was in by 1:30. If I'd known I'd be there so quickly I probably would have just pushed on, but it was nice having the afternoon to relax.

I walked around the beautiful city, and the contrast between rural Sumatra and Malaysia couldn't be starker. Cars are everywhere here, amazing, and the buildings are of such fine quality! I visited the independence museum for a great quick run through of Melaka tumultuous history, being colonised first by the Portuguese in 1511, taken off them by the Dutch in 1642, and then traded to the English like a Pokémon card in 1824, before Japanese occupation in 1942.

I had a shave and then some Indian food, which I returned to again for dinner later. In the evening I had a single beer by the riverside, watching the tourists pass by in the cruises, while updating my diary and phrasebook with some Malay.
To cap off the night I walked to a nearby ATM from my hostel, only to realise I didn't even bring my card. Not bothered to go back, I postponed the task until morning and went to sleep.

101.title: Day 108: Kuala Lumpur
paragraphs: Thursday 14th August
I couldn't leave Melaka until the frisbee I was watching was finished, so after a delicious vegan breakfast at a Chinese restaurant, I finally jumped on the bus at around 11.

I was headed to a toll gate that fed into the main highway to Kuala Lumpur, a spot that I'd found on a hitchhiking Wikipedia website. I've never used it before, but it actually turned out to house some great advice. After two buses and a sketchy walk down the side of a thick road, I found the place and began hawking the prospect of taking me to passing drivers.

Within 10 minutes I was in a car that was heading most of the way, and the driver spoke quite good English and was knowledgeable about Australian sports. He dropped me at a rest stop halfway to KL where after a short break I quickly found my next ride, one that would take me the rest of the way.

He was in his early thirties and worked in tech management, from what I gathered for a company that was helping the Maldivian government in some capacity. He wasn't super talkative but was very  kind, and drove far out of his was to drop me right in the bustling centre of KL.

After the rural sprawl of Sumatra I almost felt overwhelmed, dropped off into the biggest mall I've seen in my life with a towering atrium above me and crowds of people from all over the world. I booked a hostel right in Bukit Bintang and lined up some drinks with other backpackers.

There were four of us. Myself, a Scott, a Dane, and a Dutchwoman. We stayed out until after midnight at a bar, learning in the process why you don't talk politics with random backpackers you've just met. The Scottish guy, Adam, was lovely and we shared an early morning falafel roll platter before saying our goodbyes, as he was leaving the following morning and I wouldn't see him. He'd just finished studying in Jakarta for 6 weeks and was very knowledgeable on the politics of the region, and I enjoyed talking to him.

While I'd considered staying only one night in KL, the other two backpackers and some others were headed to a temple in the morning, and I figured it'd be nice to hang out with some fellow travellers for a day.
Besides, it was around two when I went to sleep and I wasn't keen on getting up and moving that quickly.

102.title: Day 109: Standard backpacker stuff
paragraphs: Friday 15th August
I toyed with the idea of jetting off north immediately after we arrived  back from the temple this morning, but decided against it, so I extended my stay by another night in the morning.

Having gone to sleep at 2 and woken up before 8, I wasn't exactly well rested as I met some of the other backpackers and we piled into a taxi to the temple. There were 7 of us, 6 in the taxi plus Asgot, the Dane from last night, who'd wanted to come but had to make his own way on the train, poor guy.

The temple was beautiful, full of colours and Hindu sculptures and situated at a towering limestone outcropping, a common sight in Malaysia and southern Thailand. A rainbow set of stairs led up to the inside of the hill, a gaping cave with light trickling in from small holes in the ceiling. The light fell on the concreted floor and temple buildings that had been built inside it.

There were far more locals than tourists here, participating in ceremonies and tithing. The cave was astonishing, and felt like the entire inside of the limestone structure was hollow. I wonder how they form.
The only blight on the experience was the monkeys, bred into a pestilence by the good willed tourists feeding them bananas, they lined the bannisters and dashed around between us.

We took another taxi back into town and I went off by myself to visit a vegan cafe, before meeting back up with the others to head to the botanical gardens. We spent an hour or so wandering around them and chatting, before Asgot and I went into the massive open air aviary that the others were too cheap to spend the 30 bucks on.

Most of it was quite open and the birds seemed to be content, but some of them were alone in smaller cages, and made me regret buying a ticket. They were impressive though, with species of exotic birds I'd never seen wandering around as we made a lap of the place.

One nap that was more of a sleep later and I decided to take myself out for dinner. The vegan japanese I had was hands down the best meal I've had this trip, and made me want to stay in KL to try the whole menu.

I met the others and we saw the Petronas towers before having a couple of beers at a bar. The others retired early and taxied home, which Asgot and I walked it and had a late night meal again. The second night in a row I ended up dining after midnight with a friend in my hostel. I'm trying to pack on some weight for how little food I'm going to be able to eat in Kazakhstan.
I'd said goodbye as I'd be leaving in the morning, and wouldn't see any of them again.

It was nice having a day to relax and talk, but I was itching to get back on the road. The distance I'd travelled yesterday wasn't even far,  so combined with today I felt stagnant. I sussed out where I could go in the morning, and set my alarm for 8.

103.title: Day 110: Gito
paragraphs: Saturday 16th August
Getting out of KL turned out to be much harder than I anticipated.

I checked out of the hostel and made my way to the nearby metro station. I'd read on the hitchwiki that there was a good spot just on the northern side of KL. While the spot, a gas station on the freeway, was a very good spot for hitchhiking, it was very difficult to get to. It had said on the wiki that you could just walk down the highway to it, but as it was a fully separated highway, this was not something that was possible. The chain link fence blocking the area of even had "prohibited area" signs with a stick figure having a gun aimed at him, sweet.

Instead I had to walk a roundabout way for the better part of an hour to get close to the station, but I was still not on the freeway and it was. Eventually I could see it behind some apartment buildings, but the driveway to the rear was manned by attendants. Luckily, there was an empty lot next door with an opening in the fence, so I strolled through it, into the thick bushes at the back. In the bushes there was a fence separating the freeway, so I hauled myself over it and nonchalantly walked into the gas station, picking the plants from my boots as I did. I didn't even get shot.

Hitchhiking was easy and within 5 minutes a woman, her mother, and her young son picked me up. They were headed for about an hour in my direction, and dropped me perfectly at another gas station before they turned off.

From there it was more of the same, and that's where Gito found me 5 or so minutes later. He was a bar manager in his mid fifties, but looked much younger. As soon as I got in the car he was loudly asking about where I was going and talking about himself, one of those intense guys, friendly but without smiling much. He was very self assured and would constantly talk over me as I answered his questions, being more focused on getting his next thought out which was amusing.

After telling me a little about his work he launched into a love story about this woman he was trying to woo. They'd had a nice day together the other day at the temple, and she worked for him at the bar, an employee he'd brought with him from his previous role. They'd been friends for over twenty years but just six months ago her husband had passed away, and he was trying to assess whether she saw him as more than a friend too. He was quite intent on this, and told me he was going to ask her to marry him shortly after the one year morning period was over.

What did I think? He asked for my first reaction on the bare details, and I tried to give a balanced answer that it was pretty soon but if she was into it then go for it. I said I couldn't give a fair assessment having never met her, and he should tell from how she acts whether it's a good idea.

One funny detail was that he mentioned she had a couple of kids that were "old enough to look after themselves" and not of much concern to him. I asked him if the kids liked him and he said "like, don't like, I don't care. As long as they show respect."

A good hour into our ride he mentioned he actually had a daughter of his own, that had autism but was finishing a tertiary qualification and that he wanted to help open a cafe in Jakarta. He said he'd move her and his wife down there. Not the new, potential wife, his actual, current wife.

I was mildly shocked he had a wife, and by way of explanation he just said he would divorce her very soon. I asked him bluntly if he preferred the new woman more. He gave me a look and said it was complicated, not that simple, but I had a feeling it was.

He ended by showing me his most recent texts with the new woman, even explaining why he used the🫰, little love, emoji, where the fingers are crossed like a mini heart. He sure knew how to dive into the tea. Again, her text response could be interpreted either way but seemed mostly positive to me, so I related that to him.
He reminded me about the Thai immigration form and asked me to do his too. I was hesitant but said I would if I could, and he hit me with a very direct "why can't you??"

He was equally willful about my plans, and luckily he was driving much further than I'd asked for and even in the same direction tomorrow. He said he'd drop me at a hotel he knew and that there was a bar nearby that his friend owned where I could play darts. He was very nice but a little much, and I said that it would be great if I could come with him to the Thai border tomorrow, but I had family to call that night.

After swinging by his cosy little house he dropped me at the hotel and waited until I'd ensured that there was availability, and we agreed to meet in the morning. I went to dinner myself at a fantastic restaurant and was about to call a friend when he called me on WhatsApp. He was insisting we have dinner and go to the bar, which I declined, citing my dinner and call. He said he was there and asked for my room number, which I dodged and said I had to go but I'd see him in the morning at 10.
Funny guy.

As I went to bed I finished and paid for my Thai visa application, and as I thought to myself that it seemed a little expensive I properly checked the website. Fucking Ivisa.com, some bullshit virtual agent service that just charges you to to input all your details into their website instead while they forward it to they government after "checking over it". It's not a full blow scam but pretty much is, and I went to sleep angry that I'd probably wasted $130 bucks by not being thorough. I think most of that goes to a visa fee anyway but I haven't looked and don't plan on it, or I'll just be more annoyed if it didn't.

104.title: Day 111: Thailand
paragraphs: Sunday 17th August

Gito rang me nice and early and said he was 15 minutes away. I thought we were meeting at 10, and it was just past 8 so I was still in bed. I asked for half an hour to shower and get ready and he indulged me, after which he took me to a vegetarian breakfast buffet.

Malaysia has had the most amazing vegan food, and there were about 4 vegetarian restaurants in the vicinity of my hotel. The buffet was delicious, and my only regret is that I wasn't hungry enough to have a second helping.

On the road this time he told me the story of where he was going in Thailand. From what I gathered, he and his friend were involved in some sort of religious group, as mentors. They had met a guy trying to be a mentor on his own, and invited him to join them, providing him with contacts. The new guy had proceeded to scam ten thousand dollars of these contacts, and flee to Thailand, just over the border. Gito seemed surprisingly nonplussed about the whole situation, and was just heading there for an apology, to bring back to the people that had been scammed. It didn't seem like an apology would be enough to me, but again, different cultures.

He asked me to join him to meet this guy, which I declined but he pressured me and I caved. I consoled myself with the fact that maybe it would be an interesting experience, but I wasn't keen on the delay.

We zoomed to the Thai border, and were there around 12, gaining back an hour as we swapped timezone yet again. I've passed back and forth between two timezones multiple times, as you can see from my attached image.

I had to separate from Gito to go through customs, and we said we'd meet on the other side of the border. I passed through quickly and went to get a SIM card and some Thai cash, but couldn't see Gito at all, and hadn't heard from him. The road beckoned so I just made my way down the highway and started hitching. I didn't see Gito again, but I was thankful for the conversation and help he had given me.

What followed were the nicest four lifts I've had. I didn't wait long and had a some great chats with a soft spoken Thai taxi driver, a kind older man with stunning blue eyes, a young Thai driver who told me about his transgender sister working in Saudi Arabia that he missed 🥺, and a cute older couple that took me right to my hotel. The older couple were actually turning about 20 metres after where I was hitching from, but went out of their way by 20 minutes each way to take me to the next town where my hotel was. I protested when I learned that they lived right there, but they insisted on taking me and we're just the sweetest things.

Unfortunately I could not find any restaurants that could serve me nearby, but was saved by 7-11. In 2016 when I was here on my gap year I had so many meals from 7-11, and I foolishly presumed this time would be different. They have meals ready to go that they microwave for you, and the vegan fish burger actually slaps.
I sampled a collection of their vegan goods and took them back to my room for my microwave dinner  for one.
Finally I managed to have an earlier night, and read some of my history tome that I've been lugging around. I need to finish it, it'll be a load off my mind and back.

105.title: Day 112: I am become vagrant, avoider of hotels
paragraphs: Monday 18th August.

I arrived at the roadside at 10, having had to walk a decent way from my hotel down the highway to find a suitable spot to hitchhike from. The first ride to pull up 15 minutes later was the only one I needed for the day. A young guy in a truck that was full to the brim with his belongings, he was talkative and friendly, and immediately invited me to come with him further north than the place I'd asked for, when he realised that was where I was headed.
The afternoon passed mostly uneventfully. He bought me some water at a servo and wouldn't let me chip in for fuel, and I took a long nap at some point against my bag.

It was only as the evening approached that I started to think. I'd had too many days travelling beyond dark and didn't want to keep repeating that, even though we were headed in a good direction. I'd also been staying in cheap hotels so much and wanted to do some wild camping again, which is a lot of fun.

I checked my maps and eyed out a servo with some dense trees nearby it on the map, and figured if I stayed there I could set my tent in the trees, and get hitchhiking again from the good spot at the crack of down. When I told the driver I was getting out he looked almost sad and asked if I wasn't coming further with him. 😞
I'd made up my mind, however, and said that I would like to stay there.

I bought some dinner from the 7-11, and headed over to the trees as the sun began to set. It wasn't actually as dense as it had appeared from above, and was actually quite a sparse rubber farm. Additionally, the buildings that looked miles away on the map were visible through the trees, their lights peering into the thin forest. I waited until some bikes had passed me then ducked into the trees, and found the corner of the plantation that was the furthest away from the buildings.

Stealthily I erected my tent and cooked some noodles for dinner, all the while eyeing the treeline for movement like a paranoid schizophrenic. It felt wrong, and the lights from the nearby road would sometimes piece through the foliage at just the right angle and glance the side of my tent, sending a brief flash of light into my vision that made my heart rate jump.

I'm actually just too much of a coward for urban wild camping, and don't think I'll ever manage to get a good night's sleep doing it. The lights from the buildings seemed brighter on my tent from the inside than out, and I peered around a few times when I heard noises in the dark.
I was also sweating like a beast after my hot dinner, and my camping mattress was quickly moistened, leaving me feeling disgusting.

Eventually I fell asleep, only to wake up at 1 and 2 am to noises or flashes of light, my body on high alert and calling me back to consciousness at any wayward disturbance. If I haven't made it clear, it wasn't that fun, and I wished the trees had been thicker and further away from humanity.
Finally, I succumbed and fell into a deeper sleep, letting the noises of the night wash over me.

106.title: Day 113: A series of unfortunate events
paragraphs: Tuesday 19th August

My patchy sleep was interrupted again when I woke up for some reason and stared at the fly of the tent. I could see the lights from the nearby buildings on it, and hear a bit of noise in the distance. As I looked, I realised that the shadows of the grasses projected onto the tent were more defined than they had been before, and moving slightly? The noises also sounded like distant sticks breaking.
With how much I'd disturbed myself with my own fear throughout the night, I was sure it would be nothing as I peered out of the well tent in the middle of the night. Incorrect.

First I saw the lights, about 5 of them, combing the plantation horizontally about 50 metres away. There were roughly half a dozen people harvesting the dripping rubber, at 3:30 am in the morning. Fuck. While off to the side of the trees as far as I could go, I was still camped right next to one. Uh oh.

I mentally prepared my greeting and subsequent translation on my phone: "I'm sorry, I could not find anywhere to stay so I camped here, I will leave now." My heart was racing as I wondered how they would react. I knew it would probably be fine, but what if they were annoyed? The lights and voices grew stronger as the process drew them closer to my far end of the field, and I decided to start packing already. May as well be able to make as quick a getaway as possible.

I thought they'd hear my sleeping mat deflating they were so close, and must have been about 30 metres away. I hauled my bag outside my tent and started stuffing all my cooking equipment in it, followed by the misc goods lying on my tent floor. They still hadn't found me as the guy coming toward me was doing a loop to the end of the grove and back, so I continued to pack. As he came back he actually went past me into a smaller outcropping of trees to my right, and I could see a way from those that he could loop around once finished and come up behind me to finish off this corner.

While he was in that copse there were some bushes between us, and the other half a dozen or so workers had disappeared further afield at this point, so I had a moment alone. I realised I may actually be able to drop the tent, and head back the way they had came to give them the slip. With no tidiness I folded the skeleton of the tent, and stuffed the fly and floor into an external pocket on my back. Shoes on with shaking hands, and I was ready to go.

I whipped out my phone torch and figured I'd be safer using it as I'd look like a harvester from a distance, and not a creep stumbling around in the darkness. Clandestinely, I made my way around the only guy I could see back towards the road, and climbed the bank to relative safety. I'd done it.

At the entrance to the road the other workers were finished and waiting on bikes, so I waited for the last guy to join them and speed off, before I exited the farm. Watching him from the shadows, he had actually not gone to the 5 or so trees I was camped in, but done a larger loop through a swampy area back to the bikes! I had somehow picked an area for my tent that didn't get searched, and in all likelihood could have stayed there undetected, but how could I have known.

Now that the danger was gone I weighed the option of putting my tent up once more and sleeping for a couple more hours, but dismissed it. I went back to the servo, properly packed my back and brushed my teeth, and began waiting at the exit for the few cars that passed through. I'd wait here for the next 2 hours until dawn if necessary.

No one was interested in picking up a nighttime hitchhiker, that I well understood, so half an hour or so came and went. A group of young guys pulled up but their cars seemed full so I didn't bother asking them until one of them approached me. He asked what I was doing and to see my passport. I dodged by telling him it was Australian, and he asked to see it again. Using the translator, he said he would verify it with police? These guys were clearly not police so I declined.
I said I was hitching north to Bangkok and he said he'd take me for a fee. I countered that I wasn't paying but I'd chip in for petrol. He accepted and off we went.

As you'll see, I shouldn't have gone with these guys. They seemed like hustlers and after the passport red flag I should have politely declined.  I'm too blasé about safety and always am happy to take a ride and believe everything will be fine, which to be fair it almost always is. I'm hereby making a rule to myself: - Do not get in lifts if the driver has given you any reason not to
I'm going to bias myself towards using this rule over the next few days just to prove I will obey it.

In the passenger seat of the guy that had approached me, I quickly fell into a deep sleep that I hadn't achieved the previous night. At one point we stopped for a smoke break and I tried to make small talk that they weren't into.
The driver also worked in Phuket as a delivery person, but I suspect that was a lie. Phuket is the shitty party tourist hotspot.

I woke up feeling way better and the sun was above the horizon. The driver asked how much I'd chip in for fuel and I said twenty bucks. Oh, I can't take you to Bangkok for that price, he said, only to Phetchaburi, a few hours out. Not wanting to give this guy any more money, I accepted and said there would be fine. He'd taken me a few hours so I was happy enough, even though I was being ripped off a bit.

Before we got there he asked for the money, pulling up in town on the side of the highway. I asked if he was continuing to take me another 5 minutes to the petrol station, but he refused. Glad enough to be away we said our curt goodbyes.

I wandered for a bit to another intake ramp and the second car that passed pulled up, about 10 seconds of waiting for a lift, and contained an absolute hero. He was a member of the tourist police and had a decent grasp of English, and was glad to take me to Bangkok. Better yet, we quickly figured out he was actually heading north that day, and given that I didn't really want to see Bangkok again and that getting in and out of cities is a pain, I gladly accepted his offer to join him and head straight north, saving at least a full day.

We headed into the outskirts of Bangkok to pick up a friend of his that would be riding with us, and that's when the car started making some strange noises. This is the THIRD vehicle that's needed repairs while I'm in it, and I'm not sure if it's due to the poorer vehicle health here or I'm just some sort of cursed trinket for cars.

I found a nearby mechanic and we crawled there, where they tried to identify the problem and hoisted the car up. We were there for over three hours, my shortcut day quickly bleeding away, but I just wasted time on my phone and went to a restaurant.

Just before 4 they'd fixed the problem and we were out of there, sweeping up his friend and getting on the road north. They even went out of their way slightly to drop me right in Nakhon Sawan, the city at which our paths diverged, and I was only 5 minutes from my hotel.

Once I got there and went to pay, I realised that my money from my bag had been stolen. Annoyingly and stupidly, I'd left my large notes on an external pocket, a dumb error that I won't repeat. $150 bucks of Thai currency was taken, and while stinging about it for a minute I quickly got over it, it's just a day and a half a budget and I'm way under overall anyway.

It was almost certainly the shady guy from earlier. They must have stoked it while I was asleep or not looking at the cigarette stop, but the most annoying part is that he even took me for voluntary fuel money too, fucker. 😂
To be fair it could have been the mechanics as my bag was sitting in the car with them for 3 hours, but I doubt it.

Anyway, it's a cheap lesson overall and as I head into the late stages of this journey I'll be travelling through countries with far more thieves than SEA, and at least my card was left there thank god.
I had a great papaya salad for dinner and topped up with snacks afterwards, treats that I rightly deserved.

107.title: Day 114: Just up the road
paragraphs: Wednesday 20th August

It was a very slow morning this morning, and I only left the hotel just before checkout at noon. I'd had a later night and sleep- in, but with the distance I'd covered yesterday I was more than happy to have a half day of travel.

My first destination was a vegetarian restaurant on the north side of Nakhon Sawan, which was conveniently close to the road I'd be exiting town on. It was just under an hour's walk so I started along the road, but turned and waved at bikes every so often to try and speed the process up. Very quickly a Grab driver, the Uber Eats equivalent in SEA, pulled up and asked where I was going. His name was Tan and he was friendly and willing to take me there, but he just had a delivery he was in the middle of. I joined in for the delivery and cradled the box on the ride, and handed it to the surprised looking customer.

Tan knew the restaurant so we zoomed there, and as we were getting on well I asked him to join me for lunch, which he accepted. The food was phenomenal and cheap, so I bought four plates and ate more than my fill. Tan wanted to interview me so he set up a camera and asked me 3 questions about my time in Thailand:
What were my favourite things about Thailand?
What characteristic did I think the Thai people should hold onto?
Aaaand I've somehow forgotten the third.

We had a really great talk about the differences in culture, his religion and the tenets of Buddhism, and why I was vegetarian. The shop owners were also nice and had a long chat with Tan as we were leaving.

He went out of his way to drop me at a petrol station on the north of town, the perfect location. In two roughly hour long trips I was in Phitsanulok. I dropped the ball on my last trip and left a sweet older couple that I think may have been trying to take me to the temple in hindsight - an experience I missed out on due to not having good enough language skills.

I'm in a cheap mostly empty hostel and have spent the evening in. I'm going to be up early tomorrow to go to the temple, starting at 6, before hitting the road north. My goal for the day will be Chiang Rai in the far north, another 6 hour + day. I'll be pleased if I make it at all, but am aiming even higher to make it with some sunlight on the clock. Wish me luck!

108.title: Day 115: Chiang Rai
paragraphs: Thursday 21st August

I made it. The temple visit this morning paid off, not only because it was absolutely stunning and the best temple I've ever had the pleasure of visiting, but also because the offering I gave evidently worked and I was very lucky with my lifts today.

From the walk out of town where I was brought on the back of a bike, to the cosmetics saleswoman who took me the last hour, I only have one difficult experience finding a ride. Pretty good for the 8 lifts of varying lengths I used.
I also made it in daylight! The early start was hard but worth it, and I'm going to try to keep that routine.

Some of the highlights today were the motorbike side cart I rode in with some gas bottles, and the large melon I was gifted at the end of one of the rides. I don't have any photos of the melon but I'll take one with it tomorrow.

As I progressed north the mountains grew up out of the flats, and here in Chiang Rai there are plenty of waterfalls and hot springs to see in the surrounding area. I'm going to stay here two nights and tourist it up tomorrow, and have already lined up another backpacker to explore the area with.

109.title: Day 116: Temples and Hot Springs and Waterfalls oh my!
paragraphs: Friday 22nd August
Today felt like it was 2016 and I was back in Pai on my first solo travelling trip, but without the group that I explored the surroundings with back then.

Elsa was the only one to respond to my message yesterday seeing if anyone wanted to check out the temples, so we met up this morning and rode to a waterfall she'd been recommended by her hostel staff.

It was about a 40 minute ride each way through the scenic rice paddies nestled on terraces in the misty morning valleys. It took me a while to get used to having someone on the back of the bike, and every time she would lean around to talk it threw the weight off slightly which was interesting. We made it, only being chased by one barking dog and slipping slightly as I forced the bike up the muddy driveway to the start of the walk, which was a success to me.

A short scramble up a jungle path and we were at an impressively powerful waterfall, fuelled by the rain of the past few days. It was opaque and brown, but still quite a sight, and we wandered down a trail afterwards and saw some interesting bugs.
We then tried to stop in at a hot spring but the park was closed, so we went to a massive temple complex with three separate temple buildings.
The first was a circular temple with stairways ascending up 9 floors, each floor smaller than the last and  hosting a different intricately carved wooden statue.
The second was a white and silver temple hall, with beautiful relief sculptures on the wall that were slightly three dimensional, pushing outward into the air.

The third was a towering statue of Guanyin, a Buddhist bodhisattva, that stood 69 metres tall making it the 23rd tallest statue on the planet. We took the lift up into the inside of the head, where we had a great view of the surroundings and inside it was decorated with plaster dragons, gods, trees, and patterns.

Next, after a quick lunch, we found an open hot spring and I went for a dip in the mineral bath. I also had drank a mineral drink on the way there, so I was really double dipping on the mineralisation.

It was honestly just nice to have a proper long conversation, and we chatted about our travels, quitting our jobs, and life plans. While we both enjoy solo travel overall, we agreed that it was nice to have other people joining us on our trips. My cousin Gianluca for me, who I'm looking forward to seeing in Kyrgyzstan, and her boyfriend and brother for her, who she's meeting in Indonesia and Sri Lanka respectively, I think.

Our last stop was the blue temple, and blue it was. The colour themes of the temples are so well adhered to, most of which I've seen have primarily been red and gold, whereas the deep azures of this one, highlights of gold and white adoring the sculptures, was something very new.

I dropped her off and went back to my hostel for a deep nap, one I needed after a roommate this morning had set countless alarms from 5-7 am that he kept sleeping through. I'd actually asked him sternly to stop them at one point and he profusely apologised, but went back to sleep immediately, and one went off again just as I was doing the same. I took his phone but you can turn off iPhones when they're locked, annoyingly. I think if it happens again in the morning I'll give it to reception.

I met up with Elsa and two backpackers from her hostel for dinner at an outdoor market, and we shared the fruit I'd been gifted yesterday. The German guy knew what it was, a kind of milder grapefruit, and it was pretty tasty!

I'm back at the hostel now, getting a later night that I'd ideally like at 11, but I think the nap will count for something. Off I go in the morning hopefully I cross the border to Laos not too much after 2pm!

110.title: Day 117: Laos or: how I learned to stop worrying and love Lachie
paragraphs: Saturday 23rd August
Washing: picked up
Breakfast: eaten
Hotel: checked out
Yep.. it's hitchhiking time.

I made a relatively early start, but the gods were not smiling upon me this day. None of the lifts individually took too long to get, but none were too fast either. Combined with some walking to better spots here and there, and it took me over 4 hours to make it to the border with Laos.

The one stop I made during my itinerant morning was at a cat cafe I stumbled across. I wasn't in a city, but a sparse town, so the cafe felt very out of place. I suspect it was haunted, and that if I went back I'd just find an empty brick wall. The strange, inbred looking cats were pretty friendly and I stayed for 15 minutes petting them. Eventually the baleful state of the orange one with the sad, flat nose folded me and I left. The "green tea" I'd ordered had milk in it for some reason, which I can't have, but I was too ashamed to leave it I wandered down the street clutching it and looking for a place to get rid of it.

A small dog feigned interest but when I removed the lid and placed it on the ground, moved away aloofly. We repeated this charade once more before I continued on. Eventually I poured the contents into a bushy area and out the plastic in a bin, a cow milked for naught.
The road had fewer cars on it than I'd hoped, and the rides continued to be sparse, but I ended up arriving at the border around 2.

I gave the last of my Thai baht to my final driver as a thank you present, and walked to Thai immigration. My passport was stamped with an exit stamp and I was ushered on, immediately arriving at a desk where we had to buy bus tickets using aforementioned Thai baht; the bridge was closed to foot traffic.

I'd done everything in my power to avoid having to pay another godforsaken ten dollar ATM fee, an absolute rort wrought by the banking cabal, and I want a out to allow them to win the day. I turned instead to other, forbidden techniques of acquiring small change, and asked the gaggle of young English backpackers if they had 20 baht. While a dastardly act, it's only like a buck, and they kindly coughed up.

This turned out to be the least of my problems, as when I arrived at Laos, the ATM declined both my cards. This left me in limbo, unable to pay for my visa and enter Laos, with no way to get access to cash. After an hour in purgatory, I was presented with a generous, lifesaving offer: a taxi driver would pay my visa fee, then take me into town to an ATM, where I would get money out for him.

I was essentially a hostage as he had my passport, but I was glad to get out of no man's land and into the country. Four other tourists and I then visited 5 different ATMs, all of which blocked both my cards. I was unsure whether my cards had been locked, or they just weren't accepted here. It turned out to be the former.

It was quite stressful, as I had no way to pay back the driver. I also couldn't try to unlock my account, as I had no international credit, and I couldn't top up my credit due to having a locked account. A cute little catch-22.

Pierre, the German, helped me greatly. He paid the fare and offered to give me some cash if I could transfer money into his European account. I sat in his hostel lobby for another almost two hours trying, but couldn't get access to my accounts, and Australian contact desks for both my banks were closed.

To my rescue came my knight in shining armour, the one and only Gizmolad, Lachie. I contacted him in the most scam-like manner possible, explaining my situation and asking him to immediately transfer money to a foreign bank account. Luckily he knows I'm dumb enough to really end up in situations like this, so we sorted to transfer and Pierre passed on the cash.

I had a big dinner, and am looking forward to the joys of contacting my banks tomorrow and getting back in business. I also want to make it the rest of the way to Luang Namtha, which is a few hours drive.
Also, here's some more photos from yesterday at the bottom that Elsa sent me.

111.title: Day 118: Hitchhiking disallowed
paragraphs: Sunday 24th August

Nice slow start, only checked out of my hotel when I had to at 11. I'd had an earlier excursion for breakfast, a new sim, and to change some of the money Pierre had given me the previous night, so I was ready to hit the road straight away.

Getting across town, back to where the road dove into the heart of Laos toward Luang Namtha, proved to be hard. It was one of those awkward length distances, a ten minute drive or a 90 minute walk, and I ended up walking about half of it. I jumped on a bike for a portion, then someone called out from a garage, and offered to go out of his way to take me in his car the rest of the distance I needed. He even helped me with my Laotian phrasebook!

I think I was in the perfect spot to leave town properly for the 3.5 hour drive to Luang Namtha, but I can only theorise as I did not get picked up by anyone. The cars and trucks came and went, and no one stopped for over an hour. A minivan stopped at one point, but they were charging for rides and I didn't want to give up on hitchhiking just yet.

Luang Namtha was my target as it's a base for hikes, and I've been speeding north in anticipation of going on a hike in Laos. I had nothing booked as I didn't know which day I would arrive in the town, but assumed if I arrived there in the afternoon I could book a hike for the following day.

As it ticked past 1pm I was realising I needed to find a lift soon to retain any chance of starting a hike tomorrow, or I'd lose another day. When another minivan stopped and ushered me in, I accepted knowing I'd be paying when I arrived there.
The road quality here is surprisingly terrible, large potholes are scattered all over the only road between the two cities, and it was hard to relax as the van dodged around them.

The ride reminded me of why I'm primarily hitchhiking. It was boring. No conversation happened at all, and we rode in relative silence for almost four hours. It did get me there (here) in time though, and my first order of business after dumping my bag in a cheap hotel was to tour around the hiking companies and compare prices.

I took a bit of paper from the first company and wrote his offer on it, and compared with the other 4 or so tour guide shop fronts scattered around the main street. My main criteria was a company that already had a group going, as the price skyrockets when you're solo and hiring a guide yourself.

I settled on a 3 day hike, that has two others on it. We'll be camping one night and doing a village homestay the next. I'd prefer to hike alone, but it's not possible here. I think the chance of stepping on America UXO is too high.
I've also managed to unblock my card and withdraw some cash, thank the lord. I'll be more careful to let my banks know where I'm travelling in the future!
Also, it's been just over a month since I began in Kupang. I can't believe it's only been a month, as it feels like far more has happened than could fit in a single month!
Don't worry if you don't hear from me in the next two nights, I'll be camping off grid. Should be a big update when I'm back with plenty of trekking photos!

112.title: Day 119 - 121: Nam Ha National Park Trek
paragraphs: Monday 25th - Wednesday 27th August

I arrived down at the tour company before 9 with a lighter repacked bag, and one with everything I'd leave in the office for the duration of the hike. The guide, Keo, and tour company host, Itzik, greeted me, and Itzik proceeded to give me the 'good news':  both the other travellers on the 3 day hike had cancelled, I'd be doing it alone with the guide!

I was bitterly disappointed for 5 minutes, and contemplated going back to the other company I'd wanted to go with yesterday, but remembered Itzik's spiel about no refunds the night before. Although I'd said I'd prefer to do it alone, alone with a guide just didn't appeal to me at all. The whole time I was thinking about it Itzik was trying to talk to me and convince me how this was better, which was quite annoying. I'd been looking forward to meeting the German that had signed up and practicing my German with him, and having other people to share the experience with. I realised there was nothing to be done but make the best of it so off we went to the market to buy supplies for the trip.
Keo was nice, but didn't speak much English at all. He bought a bunch of veggies and sticky rice for meals, while I stocked up on sunscreen and toilet paper.

45 minutes or so in the tuk tuk later and we were at the start of the hike, a small sign next to it on a windy mountainous road. There was an open hut with two armed guards, and the entrance to the hike declared that no one could enter without a guide. It also said don't sleep with people from the village we would pass, which made me wonder if that's been a problem in the past.

Keo and I started up the hill into the jungle, accompanied by a local who I gathered was carrying some supplies for us. For most of the hike, I didn't know what was going  on in terms of the itinerary, timeframes, or route we were taking. It felt strange, as normally when hiking I have a good idea of how far we'd be going each day, but had just been told it'd be 6 hours of trekking each day.

After about 45 minutes of pretty steep climbing, and a couple of cigarette breaks for the two locals, which Keo called water breaks, we came to a small clearing. There Keo made a fire, at first having trouble with the damp wood, and then lighting one lighter on fire with another and using that as an accelerant. I shifted out of the acrid plastic smoke. He then proceeded to craft a bamboo cooking apparatus, and cook us a delicious meal of mushrooms, pumpkin, and greens, which we ate with sticky rice and a bamboo fry from the markets. He also made two bamboo spoons which were very impressive.

We hiked for another hour or so through the jungle before beginning a descent down to the river level, and tracked along the side of that for another halfa before coming to a hut where we would stay the night. I was drenched with sweat and washed off in the river, and had a poke about the area.

The jungle was extremely thick, and absolutely teeming with life. In Australia, I'm always surprised by how many insects you can find when you take the time to inspect a plant, but here it was something else. Every single leaf seemed to have a grasshopper/spider/ant/mantis/stick insect on it, and if you paused for a second you'd spy movement in the scrub as bugs clumsily manoeuvred their way through the greenery. The forested areas were also so thick, verdant tangles of vines and bamboo blocking every direction except for the path that had been cut away.

Down by the river some butterflies were feeding off the remains of some crabs that had been eaten, and large harvestmen skittered about on the logs and sand. I spied a tree snake on a dead branch by the water, a beautiful green and black striped specimen that I haven't had the time to ID yet.

I set up the inner tent inside the bamboo cabin, not keen on dealing with mosquitos all night. It was early when we arrived, around 3, so I spent the arvo reading and checking out the jungle. For dinner Keo made a tomato soup, flavoured with a salty spice packet but again delicious with sticky rice on the side. We had an early night, pretty much retiring soon after dinner when the sun had set.
Day 2

We were up at 6:30 but Keo said he'd make breakfast at 8, so until then I read. We had a nice mushroom soup and were on our way shortly after. Exiting the jungle proper we entered a paradise of rice paddies, and slowly made our way back into the outskirts of civilization. We stopped for a water break at a small house on stilts, where the larger family gathered with Leo to smoke and talk, while I watched their chickens and ducks meander around the property. It was a good glimpse into the countryside life of Laos, with all these people living under one roof and tending the crops.

The rest of the day was just walking along the unsealed country road as it rained on and off, and we paused for a very long lunch break at a traditional village, the one where Keo grew up. The clutch of houses stood on the bank of the river, and people cooked various meals and roasted harvested grains over fires. I walked around the village and took some photos of all the animals while Keo hung out with his friends. I joined them briefly and tried some of their food, a sweet tasty berry and an almost inedible bitter apple that was difficult to bite into. They also shared some "happy water" a local Laotian spirit of 20% brewed from barley, that tasted great.

We left in the early afternoon and just walked along the road in the rain for an hour before arriving at the village where we'd stay for the night. I was disappointed to have arrived so early, and Keo explains that we couldn't do the jungle route that day due to the rain. The village was picturesque, and had signs declaring it a model health village with some funding from Germany. Everyone was friendly but I couldn't actually communicate with anyone, so I played with some of the local kids kicking a ball around and racing, which we all enjoyed.

For dinner the hosts that we were staying with made me a pumpkin soup that I filled up on, and again went to bed shortly after dark. It was relaxing listening to the sounds of the village while lying there, children getting ready to sleep, music in the distance, and families talking all could be heard from the surrounding buildings. Not to get sentimental, but it reminded me of being a child and listening to family gatherings while falling asleep, and the sense of community I felt was touching. It's definitely something I didn't have while living as a single adult in a large city, and made me miss my siblings and family back home.

In the morning it was another slow start, and I had the feeling Keo was more keen to drink a beer with his friends than come hiking in the rain with me. He was great to me in the village and kept checking on me and showing me what was going on which was lovely, but he'd probably done the hike a million times, while I was keen to get muddy in the jungle. I turned down his offer for more spirits and beer before beginning the walk.
Breakfast was a feast of rattan, the young fibres of the plant mostly known for furniture can be cooked into a tasty rubbery food that reminded me of a mix of peas and coconut in flavour.

I'd been up since 7 and by 10 we still hadn't left, and Keo was sitting with his friends inviting me to join them. Having not done any proper hiking yesterday I was having none of it, and said I'd wait for him on the outskirts of the village. That got him moving and we finally started, pushing along the road in the rain.

We turned off the main road onto a smaller walkway then off that again into a barely visible path through the dense leaves we had to push through every step of the way. After passing a few more isolated paddies we climbed into the proper jungle, slipping our way up muddy slopes and bashing through the dense thick green leaves. It was great. We made quick progress and with a few short breaks were at the end of the jungle section in about an hour. It was unfortunately quicker than I would have liked but hikes like these cater to the slowest common denominator, while Keo and I were a crack team that breezed through most of it.

Ascending the final fields on the crown of the hill, we came to a viewpoint over Luang Namtha as grey clouds rolled in, quickly obscuring it after I'd snapped a few photos. I was still full from the breakfast but after Leo had eaten we made our way down the large hill. The rain had turned the muddy road into a waterslide, and at points each of us slipped over. At one steep section I accidentally picked up too much momentum and fell over forwards down the hill, covering myself in mud while Keo and I died with laughter. I took to trying to surf down the slippery sections with limited success.
It took about an hour to get to the bottom where our tuk tuk driver was waiting for us. Half an hour later we were back at the office before 2.

When I came to my hotel I asked to wash up before checking in, and the host pointed me to a tap out the back. While not hurting myself more than superficial scratches on the hike, I managed to slip on the slick algae covered concrete behind the hotel. I scraped my leg, and lifted up my thumbnail, shoving some dirt deep under the nail that I couldn't remove and had to painfully cut away. Excellent work.

Overall it was a great experience, and I'm glad I was able to take a break from the constant movement to dive a little deeper into one location. Trekking in the jungle is something I'd never done before, and would definitely like to do again in the future. The cultural aspect was also interesting, and the people were so lovely in welcoming foreign tourists to see how they live their lives. Keo was also a great guide and excellent cook, and I gave him a tip for his kindness in showing me around.

On the other hand, I wish there'd been more hiking! All the days were pretty short with lots of downtime, whereas when solo I like to push a lot more. I've taken for granted how nice well built and maintained hikes are in the countries I've hiked in, where one is able to guide themselves and go at their own pace. I wonder if one day the trails here will be well maintained enough for tourists to undertake them alone. Given the loss of revenue that would cause for the local economy, I'm sure there are enough forces pushing against that it wouldn't be for a long time.
Aiming for China tomorrow, and the border is only a few hours away driving so I'm confident I can make it!

113.title: Day 122: Buffoonery
paragraphs: Thursday 28th August

It's been a while since my last good travel day, since before Chiang Rai really. Between my slow days getting into and through Laos, and my three day hike, it was almost a week ago. It was an exciting prospect to arrive in China today.

Levering my hiking circadian rhythm into an early start, I was up at 6:30 and packed and ready to go about an hour later. I broke my fast at a little joint in town that overcharged me for a weird mushroom dish, and was walking to the north side of town, where I could take the road a few hours north to the border.

As I came to the road that pierced up through the valleys to Muang Sing, I worried a bit as there was very little traffic. It was a 15 hour walk or an hour and a half drive, and I tried to mentally resign myself to the fact maybe I'd be walking the whole way and arriving late tomorrow. I knew the chance of that happening was slim to none, but I find it's a good mental strategy to expect as little as possible, rather than risk hopes being dashed.

As I counted the few cars that did pass me doing so, it felt like I was going to be in for a bit of a walk, but eventually a van with a bed pulled up. I jumped in for 10 minutes until they turned off and leapt back down to the road.

Luckily, a bike that we'd passed on the road with two young guys on it has stopped with us, and ushered me on the back. It was the first time I've been on a bike with, and the engine complained under the extra strain of me and my pack. We rode this way for 45 mins, and it wasn't too bad. I was sitting on the metal that stuck out behind the seat, with no cushioning, but luckily my ass bones fit right in between the bars. We bumped around a lot and went slow up the hills, but powered through surprisingly well. A few muddy corners had me worried as we approached them at speed but we always came through alright.

I think they were going to take me all the way to Muang Sing, but we were halted by a pop in the rear tyre. I suspect my extra weight had something to do with it. After giving them some money to say thanks they actually turned around and started back the way we came on the flat, so I'm unsure if they were going out of their way to taxi me or what.

Rescue came quickly in the form of a father as his young son, who took  me the last half an hour into town. By all appearances it seemed clear I was hitchhiking, but upon arrival the cheeky bugger asked me for a full day's wage! I shook my head but gave him a quarter of it.

It was another 15 minutes to the border crossing from Muang Sing, and I jumped in the bed of a truck for 10 of it, capping my journey with a half hour walk. I'd arrived at the border just after 12, a commendable effort in my mind, and meant I'd be able to stop early satisfied with my progress.

At the border, there were a few people gathered in a small store with some bikes parked outside, and the gate seemed unattended. I sat with them for a couple of minutes, bought a soy milk and shared my rambutans, before heading forward. They tried to communicate something to me, but I wasn't sure what they were saying and strode toward China. There were no agents at the first boom gate, nor in the small toll booth looking second one, and someone called out to me 'no' from the hillside. Ah, lunch break probably, so back to the shack I went.

I sat there for a little longer and one of the men kept trying to tell me something. When he pointed at the time I told him I understood they were on lunch break, but he kept pointing to the gate, and then into the forest around it. I thought he was telling me to go in the forest around the border crossing, and I told him that I didn't really want to get shot, knowing he wouldn't understand.

They were all invested in communicating something to me and when I registered that they were saying "Boten" it clicked. He wasn't gesticulating to the forest, but to the other border crossing a few hundred Kms to the south, back on the other side of Luang Namtha, where I'd stayed this morning. That worried me so I pulled out my phone and did the research I should have done at the beginning of the day.
This border crossing was not an international one, only for Chinese and Laotians.
Oh, shit. Oh, frig.
A few minutes of frantic googling and it was confirmed. There was zero chance I'd be able to make it through here and would have to head back the entire distance I'd come this morning. Yippee.

I actually took it pretty well, and after a minute made ready to head back down the hill to town. I motioned that I was sad, and if anyone could take me back down the hill but got no takers. It was only as I began the walk that a guy jumped on his bike and picked me up.

As if the gods were laughing at me, the skies opened and a deluge came down upon us. I feebly held the umbrella in front of the drivers eyes while we both slowly sponged up the wayward droplets. One pause later to avoid the rain, followed by another short trip, and he motioned to the time, saying he had to head back to the border for crossing. I was incredibly thankful and gave him some cash even though he hadn't asked. He'd taken me two thirds of the way back to Muang Sing and I walked some of the way in the rain, before being picked up by a large family in a strange three wheeled tractor thing, riding with the kids in the back.

It was after 1pm and I'd changed my goal: just get back to Luang Namtha to try again tomorrow. I could handle losing a day, but beginning tomorrow up this detour and having to work to be even even again would be shit.

This was no given thing. The rain had seemingly scattered the traffic and the 90 minute road between Luang Namtha and Muang Sing was even more desolate than I'm the morning. I ended up walking to the far outskirts of town as 2pm came and went, and the traffic was very sparse, the vehicles that did come by not stopping at all.

It worsened the further down the road I went, and 20 minutes straight went by without a single car coming by. Things were looking grim. I talked with Josh on the phone while I walked. At one point was being tailed by two children on a motor scooter, the older of which was about 8, who silently watched seeing what I would do. A fantastic idea they implemented was to park ahead of me, and lay on the horn hoping to get my attention. I steadfastly ignored them. Any other day and it probably would have been more irritating, but with how terribly everything had already gone it wasn't wasn't my most pressing issue.
