Eventually I head a motor behind me and luckily they stopped. It was a passenger van that asked me for 7 bucks to go all the way. Seeing as I'd already hitchhiked this road in the other direction that day, I had no qualms about jumping in.
Another bumpy journey later and I was back at my hotel, patiently waiting to check back into the same room I'd vacated 9 hours ago. 😃
The kicker was when the guy asked me where I'd been that day. I had no desire to explain what had happened and told him I'd been to some villages. No, I hadn't got the bus.
He asked where I was headed tomorrow and I told him China. I'd completely forgotten that I'd said that to him this morning, and he said "China again?"
Yes, China again.

114.title: Day 123: China Again
paragraphs: Friday 29th August.

Bloody hell it's been four months. At least I've done distance to show for it now, and I think I can make Germany by the end of November. I'm quite settled into the rhythm of travel now, and will be sad to eventually end this nomadic journey.

When I started hitchhiking, every day weighed more heavily on me, and putting myself out there on the road to be rejected and stared at required effort and steeling myself. I don't even think about it much at this point. While I still get bored or question my location when an hour comes and goes, I'm much better at vying for attention and shamelessly waving at everyone to better my chances.

I've also learned not to try and mentally process the whole journey at once, it's just too much. In Indonesia I was overwhelming myself by doing so. I'd gawk at the daunting length of Sumatra, and think about how hard it would be to get across it, and then realise what a small portion of my trip even those 30 hours of driving would be.

I'm further along now but the same principle applies. I have so far to go, across China, Kazakhstan, and Turkey before I can feel like I'm on the home stretch. One foot in front of the other and one day at a time has been the headspace I'm doing my best to occupy. Of course each day will bring new challenges, but I'll be a new person on each, ready to tackle them as they come. There's no need to mentally grapple with that effort in there here and now. I think this is a revelation I'll try to hold onto in my "normal" life whatever they eventually looks like. Nope that bit is too cliché.

Anyway, today unsurprisingly started much the same yesterday, albeit my bag was already packed. I left around 9 and had to walk to the other side of town (perpendicular to yesterday 🙃) before starting to hitchhike.

To get to my first destination, an intersection of two roads that joined to head towards my destination, was about an hour's walk. It was a slow morning, and I only managed to hitchhike about a third of the distance, hiking along the road the rest of the way. I was in good spirits and it was a beautiful morning, sunlight piercing through the scattered clouds to highlight the fields in a green glow.

I used the last of my Laotian cash to buy some fruit and a bowl of Kao Soi. I was hoping I could make it the border without needing at more money, but it was a decision I regretted due to the peace of mind it would have given me to have more spare cash with me.
After turning down a few taxis a couple came to my aid and brought me to Nateuy. There a road fed out of the town northwards to Boten, the border town, while most of the traffic continued straight.
I was again lucky enough for a truck to stop quickly as begin bringing me northwards. He wasn't heading all the way to the border but every metre counted, an I jumped in.

The road quality on that stretch was surprisingly the worst road I've seen in my life. The roads in Laos are in disrepair in general, but I figured the one to the main Chinese border port would be an exception, whereas in reality it was the opposite. It was primarily composed of thick gravel, with large stones nestled in in places, though entirely uneven with large peaks and troughs. The rains had accumulated into huge brown mildly puddles that took up almost the entirety of the road in sections, and we bounced painfully up every ridge. The shocks of the truck were unsurprisingly in ruins, and I could hear them slamming together on every bounce. Eventually he stopped and I had to continue on foot, soiling my shoes with mud even I tried my best to dodge the mud amidst the traffic.

A smaller truck grabbed me after a while, taking me another 15 minutes. When he turned off and I left the truck on foot, I started to make my way up the road and reached for my phone in my pocket. It felt different, and when I pulled it out I realised it was his. No, I hadn't mistakenly swapped them, I still had mine too, I'd just accidentally stolen his in my rush to jump out as it was on the seat next to me. I raced back to where he'd dropped me and up the side road he'd turned off, and luckily he was coming back down it on a bike to find me. As I was seeking him he wasn't worried, and laughed as I mimed how I'd accidentally taken it and apologised.

Two more short walks and two lifts from Chinese nationals, an increasing presence in this proximity to the border and I was there. It was 2pm, not great, not terrible, and I'd be happy if I could successfully enter China.
It was daunting knowing that any mistake could massively realign my trip, but luckily the whole process went mostly smoothly. I didn't even have to pay the standard bribe while exiting Laos.

The most interesting part was when entering China. Two other backpackers I could see, a Chinese born Canadian citizen, and myself were pulled out of the line to a social area. The guard questioned us on where we were going, where we were staying, how long we'd be in China, etc.

It dragged on for a while, and then they decided to search through our bags. I was up first, and smiled watching as they dug through my dirty crap. They were very interested in my history book, flicking through the pages and translating the cover, asking me what it was about very suspiciously, which I found very amusing. They also were concerned about my sleeping bag cover that was loose in the pack, asking what the brand "western mountaineering" meant. I think they may have thought it was a flag.

Eventually I was deemed safe and waved on, and as I looked back the Belgian couple did not look amused in the slightest. They'd actually been before me but I'd been searched first for some reason. I hope they made it through ok.
I acquired my stamp and proceeded out the automatic doors to the People's Republic of China. I changed some cash and made my way down into the town, aiming to find a hotel and calibrate myself.

I'd come prepared with a VPN, a way to bypass the great firewall, but unfortunately the one I had selected did not work in China! Fantastic. Also, the Chinese SIM that I'd ordered in Australia did not provide any data, most likely having expired after 3 months without use.

With no internet, I was glad I'd brought the cash to change, and it will be something I'll continue to do in future. I forked out for a Chinese SIM, linked to my passport, and I was connected to some things on the internet. Most of Google was blocked, along with Facebook, the app store, Instagram, and the other search engine I used. I had no GPS, and no way of researching my predicament.
The kicker is that downloading a VPN is trivial, but that's outside of China. Now that I was in china, I pretty much needed a VPN to get a VPN, another fun Catch-22.

I went looking for some food and passed a small buffet. As I did, I noticed a guy in the restaurant having a good old stare, as I've grown very accustomed to being a foreigner in less traveled areas. To preserve my sanity and feel less like a zoo animal, I look back and smile. If they smile, great, normal interaction. If they don't, I'm in it to win it and stare back until they look away, which generally happens pretty fast.

Anyway, this guy smiled and gestured to the seat opposite him, so I loaded up with some tofu and noodles and sat with him. He spoke no English and I no mandarin, so we used the translator to communicate. He was working in construction in the area, on a new gate for the border. He offered to help me find a mid range hotel after we ate, which he did for me after we walked around a little searching. I downloaded WeChat and he validated my account using his, and we added each other. He invited me to come to a barbecue with him later, saying there would be meat free options, so I gladly accepted.
I cleaned up in the hotel and called Dad, my new data plan allowing WhatsApp connections, though they were blocked over the WiFi.
I had a few issues to sort out:
I tried in vain to get a VPN without the app store, installing an APK directly, but the downloads were blocked, or linked to the app store.

My new friend messaged saying he was outside, so I went down and he took me to a small barbecue restaurant, where you choose items on skewers that they cook up and bring to your table. We had a couple beers each and I enjoyed some lotus flowers and some absolutely delicious tofu, it's flavour belied by it's name "stinky tofu." We sat and talked in the wide alley, and I was thoroughly enjoying China already.

Afterwards we went on a short quest to find me an ice block, but I ended up settling for some watermelon juice. Along the way I found an ATM and allayed one of my concerns by withdrawing some more cash.
Back at the hotel after 11 I knew I wouldn't leave early tomorrow, as I wanted another crack at sorting this VPN first, so I could fare far better with a map.

115.title: Day 124: Song
paragraphs: Saturday 30th August
My first order of business was to try and sort out my VPN before leaving the border town, as boring as that is. After trying in vain for another hour in the morning, I came up with two ideas.
My first was to head back to the mobile shop where I had purchased my SIM card, and ask him to hotspot me, with his VPN on. I thought it might redirect traffic through his VPN, but it did not.

My second was to walk back up to the border gate where I entered China yesterday, and see if I could still reach the network towers in Laos using my Laotian SIM card. Painfully, it could juuuust see the towers with 0 bars of connection intermittently, not enough to send a message let alone download a program.

Foiled on both fronts I made do with the map from AllTrails that were not blocked, and started my way down the road after a quick lunch. It was a large 2 lane road at high speed, and there were no good spots for hitchhiking. I had to walk for over an hour to the toll gate, getting me there a little before 2 pm after my slow morning.
Hitchhiking is very difficult in China. It's not the done thing. A toll gate agent asked me what I was doing and told me to go to the station before eventually acquiescing and letting me stay.

I waited for 45 minutes with no one stopping, until the toll agent came back and was more insistent that I leave. As I was talking to her a truck stopped, so I engaged the driver who was asking what I was doing. He was mostly concerned, not pulling over to give me a lift, and I had to ask a few times whether he could take me to the next town before he thankfully agreed. I leapt in and we were through the toll gate onto the open road.

His name was Song and I'm incredibly lucky to have met him. Not only was he heading east on a route that would take him reasonably close to Kunming, but he was a talkative, caring person who gave me a great impression of Chinese culture.

He was 56 and had a family in the north of China that he was working to provide for. He explained how in China it was very important for the man to work hard to provide for his children, wife, and parents, and that's what he thought about on his brutal 18+ hour days of driving.
He was lonely, he shared, and missed being with his family but also knew he had to work hard for them and his country. He was full of Chinese pride and a real patriot.

A stereotype he shared was that in Indonesia the women work hard for the family, whereas in China it's the man. It does hold true with my experience of seeing many poor, hardworking women on the streets in indonesia, peddling their wares at traffic lights well past what would be retirement age in Australia.

He hated America. "Fuuck America" he said a few times in his thick accent, and didn't hold any positive feeling towards the UK either. I'm glad I'm from silly little Australia, without such a harsh international reputation.

He had learnt English in school 30 years ago, and had retained an incredible amount of it. We still struggled to communicate but I was very impressed, for some HST had been a trucker for over 30 years and not had many opportunities to practice.

He was very sweet, and worried about me and my trip. He said if his son was like me he wouldn't be able to sleep or eat. Better step it up mum and dad, if you're still eating and sleeping do you even really love me?
I was going to be dropped at Shiping the next morning to ostensibly take the bus, but I figured I'd be able to walk back to the highway after he dropped me off and resume hitchhiking.

When we stopped for food and drinks, he wouldn't let me pay for his or my own, and said that I was a child in his country. Upon finding out I was vegetarian he taught me some phrases, then kept worrying and wrote me a card to show people that explained in Chinese. He even wrote a second copy in case I lost the first, and wrapped them both in sticky tape as a form of lamination!

He warned me against hitchhiking any more in China, and said to get the trains for the remainder oF my journey. According to him while the people of Xinjiang province in the northwest where I'm headed are the friendliest in all of China, I could get left by the side of the road in the desert with no food or water! I question the motives of such a crime.

The scenery on the drive was stunning as we made our way north. The terrain is still very reminiscent of south-east Asia, with alternating hills and valleys dotted with farmland and rice paddies. The distinction was the infrastructure, with China building an incredible amount of bridges and tunnels to allow the smooth highway to penetrate through the jungles. For the lowish amount of traffic on this road, the building costs must have been astronomical.  I am very impressed. In Song's words "The American government gives money to the rich man, CCP to the poor man." I'm not informed enough to comment.

I didn't think it was that far to Kunming, around 8 hours, but we drove from 2-12 with a total of an hour's break and were still a few hours away. I think the truck was a bit slower than the average car.

We pulled into a truck stop for the night, 10 minutes away from the bus station at Shiping he was going to take me to in the morning. We washed up in the sink and he directed me to wash my hair and face with his shampoo and soap, even pouring the warm water over my head for me to help me rinse it. I think I was a stand in for his own sons that he missed.
Another point he made is that in China they don't speak to their love for family much no "I love you mummy I love you daddy" and more showing it through work and care.

I slept on the top bunk in his truck cabin, and fell asleep a bit after midnight. He said we'd be getting up at 6 the next morning to get me to the bus station in time, which I wasn't looking forward to.

116.title: Day 125: Kunming
paragraphs: Saturday 31st August
We woke up at 5, which was an hour earlier than we'd planned; Song was nervous I would miss the bus and wanted to make sure we made it on time.

We drove the ten minutes into a truck stop nearer town and then began walking to the bus station. Song was insistent he took me there, even though I said I could find it myself. My true motives were to make my way back to the highway once he left. I felt disingenuous letting him lead me there, but I didn't want to argue with him about not herding his advice, I think that would have been worse.
We walked for almost half an hour to arrive at the bus station a little before 6. It opened at 6:30, with the bus departing for Kunming an hour later.

Again, Song went above and beyond and waited the half an hour for it to open. I told him that I'd be fine, and that I could always go to the train station if I couldn't get a bus ticket for whatever reason, but he was having none of it. I also knew he was on a schedule, and needed to drive all the way to Shanghai over the next couple of days, and didn't want to put him behind.

When the counter opened he took my passport and bought me the ticket, not allowing me to give him money at all. At this point I knew I'd just be getting the bus, I wasn't about to throw the ticket in the bin and go back to the highway once he'd left.
We said our goodbyes and off he went, back to the truck to get behind the wheel for probably another 18 hour shift.
The bus was boring. Another reminder of why I'm hitchhiking. I caught up on some sleep and we arrived without hassle around 11 at a station to the south side of Kunming.

I bounced around asking a few people directions like a pinball in the bumpers, and ended up at the metro station ticket machines. Managing to decipher the ticket system and where I needed to go, I bought a ticket and jumped on one of the very frequent services.

I'd found a hostel on the west side of town, unfortunately quite far from the nearest metro station, so I walked for just over an hour to get there. I didn't mind it as walking in a new city is always interesting, especially the first big city in a country like China!

The amount of residential skyscrapers was staggering, but they weren't as packed as Sydney's CBD. Instead, they speckled the horizon and loomed over the mostly 3 storey buildings around them. Encrusted around their edges were market streets and restaurants, fruit vendors and retail stores that repeated as I journeyed through the city. Some areas were surprisingly suburban, older houses lined some streets with trees providing gentle shade, just a hundred metres from a more concreted downtown scene.

Buses hurried up and down the main streets but I dared not try to figure out where they were headed. When I arrived at my hostel, I checked in and found myself some lunch from the local market. My eyes were bigger than my stomach but it's hard not to overbuy when the stinky tofu is $2 for a generous helping.

After catching up on some more sleep I went for a walk into town as the sun set. There was a picturesque lake right in the centre of the city with walkways crossing between stone islands. Some of the resulting pools were full of lilly pads, others were clear. It reminded me of the German Christmas markets, but in the opposite season.

Back at the hostel I played some pool and talked with some fellow travellers. I decided to have a single beer and risked it all on a sweet wheat beer. It was disgusting and I had only two sips (the second one just to make sure).

117.title: Day 126: Rejection
paragraphs: Sunday 1st September
My early start was bled away by the difficulties of leaving Kunming.
Leaving large cities always brings challenges, as the roads are too developed and braided to provide one good spot for hitchhiking, and Kunming proved no exception.

I settled on an on-ramp to the highway that circled the city and split to head north, but it proved to be an incorrect choice. The journey there took me almost an hour, but I did successfully figure out which bus to take with the help of some locals which meant I didn't have to walk.

The ramp was fast and narrow, and I worried that standing by the side of it would have police telling me off. That didn't prove to be a problem, as several cop cars drove by me unphased. In the hour I was there, one person stopped and was just moving within the city, and I realised this was not the right place to be. Normally I'd be happy to stand in a place longer, but I could feel the ride wasn't coming.

I jumped in a taxi and moved across town to a carpark stop on the highway heading north. The highway was far too fast, so I could only wave at the seldom few cars that were exiting the lay-by. Eventually I decided to ask the next car to take me 5 minutes up the road to the toll gate, and I managed to wrangle one.

The toll gate was dauntingly large, with officials manning the weighting station upstream of me, and many more at the gate itself, with some police behind it. A staff member approached me as I was standing behind the guardrail after where the trucks were weighed, waving to them. I thought I'd be in trouble, but when I explained what I was up to he was chill and even asked if I wanted help finding a lift!

I resumed my work for another half an hour before he approached again, and said I may have better luck at the gate itself, and ask trucks while they're stopped. Locals have told me to be more aggressive before in Indonesia, and go up to stopped traffic asking, but I strongly dislike doing it that way. It's too intrusive and I find it better to let the good people come to you.

We were foiled however by one of the senior police officers that noticed me, and dismissed the other employee. I tried to explain by demonstrating that I was waving at the trucks, but he stopped me and said it was illegal to stop traffic on the highway. Oops.

I was then taken with him to the previously unseen small highway police station behind the booth, and seated in a metal row of chairs in the reception facing a wall. After about 15 minutes of not being sure whether I was detained or what was going on, I asked the officer at reception if I was waiting. He replied "You are going to Chengdu", which was promising at least.

A few minutes later the original officer and a bus driver entered, and the officer signalled for me to go with the bus driver. I cheerfully waved at him but he looked quite annoyed. I think what had happened is the police officer had stopped him and told him he was taking a random cheap foreigner for free, which he was unimpressed about.

The bus ride was boring, the only highlight being an adorable baby that states and smiled at me for a portion of it. As I'd joined the bus around 2, and it was a long way to Chengdu, I assumed we'd get there quite late in the night. What actually happened was that we didn't make it there at all, and the bus stopped in the city of Zhaotong, about halfway between the two.

It was 5pm and while the sun was still high in the sky, I knew it was unfortunately too late to try to go any further. I caught a taxi the 10 minutes into the proper town, and found a hotel for the evening. This day was pretty crap. Between the hours of waiting and no actual rides, I was feeling pretty down. It didn't bode well for the rest of my journey through China, and had me thinking about what Song had said.
Getting out of Zhaotong in the morning might also prove difficult, as it's a little way off the expressway.
I had dinner but didn't do much else with the evening, and turned in early.

118.title: Day 127: Redemption
paragraphs: Tuesday 2nd September.
It was an early start as I was keen to try and make it to Chengdu with some time to explore the city. A short pause for some noodles later and I was on my way.

My first stop was to make a cardboard sign for the first time this trip. I generally don't worry about using them but I thought between these large cities one could prove useful, and I just wanted to change something up after yesterday.
I'd purchased a marker when I arrived so this morning I went to a store where the attendant provided me with some cardboard and wrote "I want to go to ChengDu, can you give me a ride?"

The road out of town was large and had no walkway or lay-bys on the side, only fields behind a railing. I hopped over at a point where the outside lane was not supposed to have traffic, but it was sketchy as motorbikes were using it and I had to pull back my arm as they passed.

Just as I was gearing up for a long wait, a truck stopped! This is unusual, and I don't think I've had many lifts from trucks that have to stop from speed. It was a friendly young guy and he said he wasn't going all the way, but would take me to where he would turn, about halfway again. It felt great to be up in a truck again and though we didn't talk much, it was a good vibe. I was in my first lift by 9am. Trucks are a fair bit slower than the Google map estimates, but the increased distance is worth it.
When we stopped for lunch he wouldn't let me pay despite my protests, and I enjoyed some garlicky greens.

The scenery was changing as I pushed north, and it felt like we were leaving the tropics behind as the trees became more temperate. This is a first for this trip, really, as even where I started in Queensland was quite tropical.

When we at last came to the truck stop he'd leave me at, we said farewell and I began hitching again straight away. Not 10 minutes later another truck picked me up and was going all the way to Chengdu, locking me in for the day.
It also felt good as the service station attendants had been pointing at me and discussing the situation, so it was nice to show an example of success.

My new ride was extremely talkative, and we used the translator to its full extent to have a long conversation. We talked about work, culture, politics, and travel, and I really enjoyed getting another insight into Chinese culture. While still a great patriot, he talked a little about the online censorship and expressed interest in seeing what outsiders posted on TikTok, as he only had access to Douyin, the Chinese version.

The infrastructure has only grown larger as I've come north. At one point to get to a lower elevation the road did a large loop-de-loop that burrowed through a mountain and popped out onto a bridge to achieve this.

Arriving on the outskirts of Chengdu felt like I was seeing a real city for the first time. Skyscraper clusters densely dotted the landscape until the horizon, and some buildings were larger than I'd ever seen.

I was dropped near a metro station, so I made my way there and figured out where I needed to go to get to my hostel. The size of the metro system puts Sydney's to complete shame, and makes our slow efforts to build a couple of lines look absolutely amateurish.

For dinner I tried in vain to find a vegetarian restaurant I saw online, and settled for a touristy one that a worker invited me to. It was a mistake as while it was good the food was overpriced. As a marked tourist I also faced offerings from local peddlers while I ate, their efforts only encouraged and translated by the waitress.

I decided I'd stay another night in Chengdu, and use tomorrow to explore some of the sites the city had to offer. My second ride had given me several recommendations that I was interested in checking out.

119.title: Day 127: Dujiangyan
paragraphs: Wednesday 3rd September
A day off in Chengdu.

There were a few recommendations that I'd been given for Chengdu, and had a few on my list that I planned to check out. The first would be the Dujiangyan irrigation system to the west of the city, and after that I could make my way back, passing by some other sites on the way. The reality was that I spent so much time at the irrigation system that I didn't have time for the others.

It took me a while to get out of the city as leaving the hostel at 10, breakfasting, and catching the metro to the wrong station before arriving at the train station ate up the time. I then had to wait a while for the train to Dujiangyan, and struggle to get the metro there, so I only arrived at the attraction at 2.

I didn't know what to expect, and in my mind thought it was some sort of ancient water wheel, but it was much more than that. 1500  years ago, the Chengdu plain was the victim of frequent flooding that would destroy the harvest and lead to famine. The people attributed the waters to a dragon, believing its wrath caused their misfortune.

A great politician Li Bing managed to undertake an incredible building project to regulate the floodwaters, making the area far more productive. A building at the site is called dragon taming temple in his honour, and people worship him still.

I would recommend watching a video on the site if you're interested, I found it amazing wat was achieved so long ago. The area was also beautiful beyond belief, with temples nestled in the verdant hillside looking over the river. Climbing temples gave me a great view of the project and made me appreciate its scale.
I only saw a couple of other international tourists, while the place was filled to the brim with domestic tourists.

Time flew past as I meandered around the loop, and I only just made it back to return my audio guide in time. The woman was very displeased that I was not able to accept the deposit back via alipay, but finally gave me cash after the most pointed sighs I've ever heard 😂.

I knew I didn't have time to check out the mountain, but was happy with the day and made my way back to the train station. Some guys dashed to the station but I didn't follow, and when I arrived the next train back to Chengdu was two hours later, after 8. So much for an early night.

Across the road was a hotpot restaurant that I bumped into, so I sat down for the first hotpot of my life! The waitresses were fantastic and kind, and helped me do everything correctly as I had no idea what was going on. One pictured below filled my serving bowl with condiments for me, and slapped my hand away when I went to take food before it was cooked. They kept coming over and interacting with me through my meal, smiling and making sure I was enjoying it. They brought me emsp much for and took some photos with me too, having me say it was delicious in Chinese on video. Meiwei!
It was the highlight of my day and I'm so glad the train was late. The hotpot was also absolutely delicious, and though my first will not be my last!
Back at the hotel I was feeling restless, and messed around on my phone until 1. I wasn't looking forward to hitchhiking to Lanzhou, as the intercity hitchhiking was wearing me down.

120.title: Day 128: My side of the mountain
paragraphs: Thursday 4th September.
I woke up at almost 9 after my foolish night staying up late.

After evaluating my options I decided to make a sizeable change to my route. Rather than head north to Lanzhou, I'd head west over the mountains and into central China. From there I could curve north to meet back up with my originally planned route before heading to Urumqi.

I'd decided to make this change as I wasn't enjoying the intercity hitchhiking, and wanted to get out into the thinner middle of China. The route between Chengdu and Lanzhou also looked especially bad, and I knew I'd have to content with much of the traffic heading too far east to Xi'an. I'd planned on heading that way, but as I have to meet my cousin in Kazakhstan on the 20th, I wanted to gain some ground on that deadline.
Before I left the city, I wanted to see the temple that was right near my hostel. I'm glad I took the time, it was beautiful and the walk around the grounds was relaxing.

Next I was back at the train station to buy the same ticket I'd purchased yesterday, to Dujiangyan. It even managed to be the same 12:53 service. Annoyingly, the guards confiscated my cooking gas, but there was nothing I could do.

I was headed back to Dujiangyan as it lay on the west of Chengdu, alongside the road that pierced further into the mountains. Luckily the tram stopped right near a toll gate, and I arrived ready to begin my journey at 2. I bought some bananas and large green grapes off a street vendor, knowing it might be my dinner.

My luck turned for the better instantly and the third car to pass, within about 30 seconds, pulled over. It was a middle aged woman who called a friend that could speak English to translate. Unfortunately she was only heading 10 minutes up the road to a small town that lay off the highway, and there was nowhere to get off on the main highway before then. I think she was the millionth person that I've left slightly confused by jumping out at an odd spot I've deemed good for hitchhiking, but I thanked her and did so. While the main toll road was inaccessible to me, I decided to start on the windy old road north.

Again, within a couple of minutes a truck pulled up and I jumped in. He was friendly and I enjoyed riding with him, but I jumped out at a rest stop that intersected both the old and new highways. I walked through a guarded gate confidently and began the thumb at the exit to the rest stop back onto the quick, to sparse traffic.

Making calls about where to go is hard, and I'm sure I get it wrong sometimes. It also means my mind wanders to questioning my decisions, but another thing I've grown better at is just living with them. If I make a decision to go somewhere and it sucks, or wastes hours, I still did the best with the information I had at the time. All I can do is learn any lessons for next time.

I wasn't questioning myself for too long, as a lawyer in a shmick EV took me with him. He actually didn't seem too keen on even having me in the car, and had me sit in the back rather than in the front with him. We didn't talk much but I appreciated the ride a lot. In fact, I almost appreciate people more who don't really want you, as they're doing something they don't really want to do to help me out.

We stopped at a service station as the car was having some trouble, or that's what I gathered. He was fussing about under the back seat and tried to get another car to take me instead of having me wait, but they were going another direction so unluckily for him he couldn't get rid of me that easily.

It wasn't too long before we were back on the road, and it was breathtaking. I don't think I've ever experienced such a drastic biome change. From the dense forests of Dujiangyan, the road running through the mountains showcased all they had to offer. Pale green and grey slopes towered off to either side of the road, rising high into foggy peaks that power lines tracked along. The villages were small with out of place concrete buildings that looked like state issued soviet apartments. I couldn't stop taking photos and watching in awe as we passed through the thin river carved valleys.

It was getting on so I called it at a truck stop where the road turned to the north. I'd stay here the night and then head to the smaller road that I needed to take, unfortunately leaving the highway behind. After petting an adorable dog at the toll gate, I glanced left and right before plunging off the road up the side of the mountain. I'd seen some rainbow tents from the car as we'd driven, and I passed a dilapidated one on foot. It must have been from a festival or religious event, but was spooky with the bedraggled faded clothes hanging damply from the rib-like cables joining at a central point.
I didn't stay there as I think the resident ghosts probably would've devoured my soul in the night, and also it was too steep.

In the forest I made do with the flattest piece of ground I could find, and smoothed it as best I could. I erected my tent and ate my fruit for dinner, before tucking into my sleeping bag. The nighttime temperature has dropped so much since Laos, and I hadn't noticed as I hadn't been staying outdoors, and have covered the distance so quickly. I noticed it tonight though, and a sharp chill was in the air.

My sleeping bag is luckily very warm, and reminded me of why I like cold weather. Tucking myself in away from the cold took the snugness metre off the charts, and I had no problems sleeping knowing I was safe and alone.
I felt vindicated about my decision to head west.
I dreamed about being confused as to how I was going to cross the south pole on this trip.

121.title: Day 129: Tibetan hospitality
paragraphs: Friday 5th September
I woke up at 7 and allowed myself a relaxed morning. I was stoked with the progress I'd made in only the second half of yesterday and was optimistic about today.
It had rained in the night and was very grey, so I had to pack my tent away wet. I wasn't too fussed, as I planned on camping again tonight.

It feels early to say this, but I think this is a major turning point in my journey. I'd enjoyed my cozy camp so much, and wanted to find another tonight. The countryside is beautiful and easier to camp in, so I plan on utilising the opportunities to do so much more. I hope this will continue throughout central Asia.

During the morning I hadn't seen much traffic on the smaller road I was planning to take from my vantage point at camp, but when I arrived down there at 9, a few trucks passed and I just had a feeling I was in an excellent spot. I was correct. Not 2 minutes into my wait and I was picked up and by a driver heading four hours in my direction. He was even turning at a few intersections along the way in the same way I was going, so it was very lucky.

The mountains slimmed into rolling green hills as far as the eye could see, and again into the grassy plains like oceans between them. I cannot overstate how picturesque this part of the country is, and can only hope my photos capture some of the beauty.

Yaks grazed dangerously close to the road, and small towns came and went as we climbed and descended from saddle to trough. The driver kept looking at me funnily when I would wow at the scenery, I think it was pretty standard fare for him.
At Apa around 1 we parted ways, and I had two huge bowls of noodles for lunch. Not having had breakfast and knowing I might have a small packet dinner, I made sure to load up.

On the way out of town I saw a temple, and went to check it out. Running around the edge of the structure was a corridor full of cylindrical painted wooden objects, that people were walking along the row of and sending them spinning as they went past. I joined in and a local loved it, accompanying me and taking me into a room with a huge spinner we spun together, getting some pictures and videos in the process.

It was a long walk to the outskirts of town, but the harvest was well underway and provided a great spectacle. The traffic seemed to die away, and though I managed to find lifts quickly, they were very short. Around 4 I knew I'd have to get out of the town I was in soon to start looking for a camp, and I was picked up by a beautiful Tibetan family. While I'm not in Tibet, this area has a large Tibetan community and the temple I'd visited was a part of that.

In the car I spied where I'd gone wrong. There was a highway on the opposite side of the valley the trucks were using, and I'd managed to turn away from it. It was going to be difficult to get back onto it as it was quite separated, and as we drove I didn't see any way to.
I said I'd probably just camp and deal with it tomorrow, and they instantly invited me to stay with them. My first proper homestay this trip, I likewise instantly accepted.

I'm currently tucked in under 3 blankets on a makeshift bed at their house, and I've had the sweetest evening. They are the most hospitable hosts and fed me, and helped me with my language skills. Their house is small, made of mud brick and by the old highway. It's situated in a long narrow valley, with just the two highways running through it. 50 metres away on the opposite side of the wide gravel layby they live in is the father's brother, in a smaller building. As a guest I was given pride of place by the hearth, a warm cozy spot where I watched the family operate. I showed the young kid how to make a cat fishing rod for their kitty, just like I did in my childhood.

After dinner they informed me that starting tomorrow is a Tibetan festival to celebrate the commencing harvest, and invited me to go with them. Of course I accepted, so will stay here again tomorrow night.

I was using a translator between English and Chinese for most of our communications, but when they told me about their heritage I switched it to Tibetan. The father was excited, the only one that could read it as well as speak it, and wanted to download it on his phone. Unfortunately he couldn't due to internet restrictions.
It was a great evening, and I'm really looking forward to the festival tomorrow.

122.title: Day 130: The festival
paragraphs: Saturday 6th September
I woke up earlier than the family, which was surprising. I think it may be due to the fact the sun rises and sets relatively late in this part of the timezone.

After breakfast we piled in the car and headed into town for the festival. They said we might be staying at another place in town that night, as it would be easier for me to leave from, so I packed my bag and brought it.
On the way in we passed by a large temple that I'd seen yesterday, and I accepted their offer to take a look around.

It was a Tibetan temple with a religious ceremony underway. Peering into the depths of a huge dark hall, hundreds of monks were sitting on the ground while others poured a liquid into bowls they were holding. An older monk in the central corridor wore a large headpiece and held a staff, periodically tapping it into the ground. Myself and a crowd of domestic tourists looked on.
Photography was prohibited, so I don't have any photos of the inside of the temples.

Behind this building were the monks quarters, and an even larger temple structure 8 stories tall. Inside was a huge hall, with massive Buddhas at each end and in the middle. The walls were intricately painted with religious scenes, and everything was trimmed with gold. On higher floors I could see rows of cabinets with small wrapped parcels in them, but I'm not sure what they contained. Draped around were the beautiful Tibetan fabrics that I'd seen before, with vibrant colour palettes and angular patterns.

It was close to 12, when the temple would close, but a monk took us upstairs to view a small gallery. There were traditional outfits and saddles, carved shells and chunks of coral, and small golden containers of all sizes. We had to wear covers around our shoes to not dirty the pristine wooden floor.

In town we eventually found parking for the festival, and wanted down the main strip of stalls. The events would happen at night, so during the day it was just food and a variety of tents selling trinkets, clothes and toys.
Next we went back into town and I bought a new gas canister and some pens. It'll be nice being able to cook a hot meal for myself next time I'm camping.

For somewhere to rest until the festival, we parked in a field and set up a large hanging cloth shade to protect us from the light train that had started to fall. I pet done horses that were nearby, and played with a crowd of children that had a basketball they were kicking around. They were very impressed by my mediocre juggling skills.
It grew later and we went for dinner at a local restaurant, as they said the festival wouldn't have much I could eat. Mapo tofu did me well.

Over dinner they said we would just head back after, and I expressed disappointment we hadn't seen the festival event. Most of the day, I hadn't known what the plan was and had just been following along, which was bigger by me.

They changed the plan and we headed back to the festival grounds where the stage was pumping music. We made our way inside and stood with the thick crowd watching on a screen back from the main stage. Many musicians came and went, each playing a song or two before cycling out. The music was fun and the visuals were cool, but the crowd was incredibly still. No one was dancing at all, only staring, with some people waving light sticks. When the camera panned to the VIP seats right in front of the stage, half of the people weren't even watching the act but on their phones, and the monks looked stunned at the stared at the colourful performance.
At the end there were some fireworks and I put the older daughter on my shoulders so she could see, which was fun.
I'm still unsure of the family dynamic, as I've thought it would be rude to ask, especially if someone had passed. There are two children, probably 2 and 4, and their mother is in her early 20s.
Her father, the kids grandfather, only looks to be in his thirties or forties, and is a great father figure to them all. I'm unsure of where the children's father is, or of the grandfather's wife.
When the show ended the crowd dangerously squeezed out the small entrance, and we made it back out onto the street. It was late, so we went straight home to bed.
It was a perfect day, and I feel honoured to have been treated as a family member for a day. They are all lovely, and I had to fight to pay for the restaurant dinner.

Back at the house, the father fussed over my bedding, even finding an extension cord so I could charge my phone in bed. I'm planning on heading out tomorrow morning after breakfast, and seeing how far I make it.

123.title: Day 131: Ticket to ride
paragraphs: Sunday 7th September

A bleak, grey blanket was draped over the valley this morning. At breakfast a gentle, sad rain started to come down to match. There was no anger or wind in it, just the constant background static of the drum on the tin roof.

The family said I'd have to wait until the rain abated to depart, but I had waterproof gear and was champing to get moving again. We said our goodbyes and I gave them the gift of incense I'd purchased from the monastery. They, in return, fussed over me and tried to make me take far more food than I was willing to. I accepted some rice, spices, and tsampa, a tasty barley drink that they'd shared with me on my initial arrival.

Our last photos taken I was in the car with the father, as I'd asked to be dropped at a layby on the highway 5 minutes up the road. When we arrived, we found that not only was it unfinished, but the entrances and exits to it were blocked by makeshift barricades. I wouldn't have much luck here.

I said I'd just wait on the old highway, as there was the occasional car, but he tutted and insisted on driving me a little further. When we passed under bridges, I pointed and said I'd get out here away from the rain, but he indicated there was a spot further up where the roads met. 15 minutes later we came to it, and I pointed to a spot where I knew I'd be able to find a lift.
He was worried about me and didn't want to leave me in the rain, but I said I'd be fine in my waterproof gear. He eventually turned, we exchanged waves, and was off.

I was at a point where the old highway split, one road making its way down the hill to the new, faster highway, and another just continuing along the old. I could differentiate where the oncoming traffic was heading from my position, so I just waved at all the first few cars that approached.

In about a minute a car stopped going along the old highway, so I went over and jumped in. They were a couple of boys headed north to a small town where the roads met once again, which I figured would be an equally good spot to get on the main highway.

I was dropped in the centre of the town and made my way to the toll gate. It wasn't far, but the rain was cold and my fingers were freezing. Incredible to think that under two weeks ago I was camping in tropical Laos.

The toll gate was bleak, and for the first 5 minutes I saw only one van drive past me. The second small truck did stop a few minutes later, to my relief. The guy didn't seem super friendly or keen to take me. I asked to be taken just to the first lay-by on the actual highway. He asked for money, and I countered with the fact it would be under 10 minutes, to which he agreed. A few minutes later and I was on a tiny lay-by on the highway, just 100m of extra lane that trucks were permitted to park in. I don't think pedestrians were allowed to be there.

The FIRST truck that came by came to a quick halt at the end of the rest area when he saw me. I approached and opened the high door, and tried to explain where I was going. Google maps doesn't display the town names in this area so I just had the name of the prefecture up ahead Golog and my eventual destination Urumqi to give him. He immediately said he was going to Korla in Xinjiang and that I could come along. That's almost 2000kms from where I was, and would take us a few days to cover.

His name is Jiao and he's a fun, cheerful guy. He has the best setup in his truck that I've seen so far, with a pressure cooker, nice decorations, and a custom speaker system. The scenery as we slowly descended from the mountains was again, incredible. The valleys broadened and flattened, and I saw snowcapped mountains for the first time this trip!

We drove until 11 when I pulled out my tent and set it up on the edge of the tarmac on the outside of the truck. The ground was marshy so I was forced to put my tent there, though I was paranoid about a wayward stone popping my mat.
I heard some rustling in the bushes during the night but otherwise had a good night's sleep.

124.title: Day 132: Police checks
paragraphs: Monday 8th September
The police checks were the most notable thing that happened today, hence the title, but that isn't saying much.

We started early and I quickly packed my tent away, having had a surprisingly solid sleep despite the fact I was on highway tarmac. I napped for the first couple hours of driving anyway as the sun rose and the scenery changed.

We left the green hillsides and mountains behind completely, and the surroundings slowly morphed into desert as the sun ascended. The mountains were now rocky and bare, some with large sand banks lying against them.

We followed the road northwest, with the bare desert on our right and the range on our left for most of the day. I enjoyed watching out the window, though the constant driving has grown tiring. I think we should arrive at Korla tomorrow, but it'll be later in the day.
I started an audiobook today, but it's terrible. I already spent 8 bucks on it though so I'm going to see through the 11 hours. I can't just waste money and not time on this thing 🤡

The police here are annoying. At two checkpoints today I've been taken into the office and asked a bunch of questions about my trip, itinerary, entry point, and route. I've answered all these questions a bunch of times, but every officer wants to hear them again. They even make poor Jiao come in and show his licence and barrack for me, but he's been chill with it. I do feel bad for them, the first cop looked about 20 and daunted by the large paper form he had to fill out about me, surely thinking his ass would be on the line if a crucial field was empty.
We also stopped for a proper dinner, and Jiao recorded me and put me on Douyin, Chinese TikTok. Maybe this is my shot at making it big.
I'm now in my tent at our layby for the night. It's a pretty good one, it even has a raised sidewalk. Move over Ritz.

125.title: Day 133: Roadblock
paragraphs: Tuesday 9th September
What it says on the tin. After a bog standard morning we arrived at an unfortunate roadblock; the road was being repaired.

It was about 10, and we were in an ugly, halfway town built to support the trucks pouring through this intersection. Jiao told me that they said it'd reopen at 9 pm, and we'd be driving through the night to make it to Korla tomorrow morning. Delightful.

I didn't want to completely waste the day so I went for a smaller than anticipated stroll around the direct surroundings. The town had no redeeming qualities. The heat has risen in the desert, and pushed down on my skin as I peered around. Everyone seemed half awake, myself included, just avoiding the heat and waiting for the road to open as best as possible.
I finished my audiobook, and it got a little better in the end.

The hours trickled by. I snatched some sleep in the passenger seat but it wasn't very restful. The internet connection on my phone has slowed to a crawl, so I couldn't even scroll most of the day away, how awful!

Finally around 5 Jiao pointed at the roadblock, it was gone! We started immediately down the clear passage with a massive line of trucks like fuzzy caterpillars making their way in a procession across the pavement.
The desert is beautiful, and more treed than I thought it'd be. It's a shame we only had a few hours of driving through it before sunset.
We stopped for dinner at a roadside restaurant and Jiao loved the fact I ordered 2 tofu dishes.

After midnight we stopped at another truck stop, and I pitched the tent in the dry dirt next to the truck. We'll be leaving at 6 so I've set an alarm. My GPS has stopped working since I entered Xinjiang, which is fun. I therefore don't know when we'll arrive tomorrow, and it's going to make hitchhiking the remaining hours interesting for sure.
Keen to check into a hotel early tomorrow, and spend one or two nights in Korla.

126.title: Day 134: Korla
paragraphs: Wednesday 10th September

Well before 6 I was up, doing my best to pack my tent while avoiding the swarm of mosquitoes. Never had I seen such an aggressive species, and they'd careen into my arms and legs without hesitation, grabbing on and instantly biting.
20 minutes later and I was in the cab itching my legs as Jiao hoisted himself into the driver's seat. We were on the road at 5:50.

It was only a couple of hours to Korla, and we had breakfast together on the outskirts, which Jiao insisted on paying for, before he dropped me near to town. Despite the fact we'd travelled together for 3 days it was a relatively short goodbye. We shook hands and I pulled him into an embrace  he deflected into a side hug, and we were on our separate ways.

I needed to use the facilities badly, and the nearest hotels were 20 minutes walk away, so I hurried there. No time to be picky, I chose the first upmarket hotel I saw. I'd decided today would be an actual full rest day, catching up on sleep and buying a few necessities in town would be my only orders of business. It was still before 9, so I hoped they'd let me check in quite early.
The receptionist spoke no English, so we struggled to communicate through the whole check in process. The amount of detail they wanted from me was ridiculous. The needed:
I didn't show my exacerbation as I understood they just needed the details, but it still wasn't fun. She apologised to me as we went through the list, which was nice.

Eventually we had it sorted and I was given the room key. She'd forgotten to give me back my passport which I pointed to on the desk, and she was embarrassed again, apologising and quickly relayed what she'd done to her coworker.

I slept for a few hours and took a long overdue shower and changed out of my clothes, their overtime shift finally over. At 2 I went exploring for some food and some things I needed to buy, and checkout out the town.

Korla is not the most beautiful city, a place that I take it is focused on industry rather than tourism. While a large city, there was no proper centre, with small shops scattered throughout encrusted around the feet of the large scattered skyscrapers. I called a friend and managed to get my shopping done.
When I arrived back at the hotel I didn't leave it again. I enjoyed having another hot shower and listened to the great audiobook I'm now onto for a few hours.
I needed this day of rest.
I just checked my camera roll, and didn't take a single photo.

128.title: Day 136: Urumqi
paragraphs: Friday 12th September

I dragged out my departure from my riverbed for as long as possible. It was a beautiful spot and I was loathe to leave it, but when the sun crested over the crest of the embankment I was scoured out by the heat.
I'm so far west into China's massive timezone that the sun only rises at a quarter to 8. Waking up at 9 felt late, but in truth was in accordance with nature.

Interestingly, when I cross the border into Kazakhstan in a few days, I'll be crossing a 3 hour timezone border, gaining 3 hours in the day. This differential is only bested by the tiny mountainous border between China and Afghanistan at 3:30 as the largest in the world. I so far have no plans for my upcoming mega-day, so I'm open to suggestions.
But I digress. I listened to the final moments of my audiobook from a ridge as I said goodbye to my camp, just after 12. The time to Urumqi was only a few hours.

At the truck stop I was beleaguered by the police, asking me what I was doing and stopping me from hitchhiking, trying to put me on a bus. Luckily the three of them were placated and I snagged a lift within a minute of walking away from them, not looking back as I sped off with 3 adults, heading all the way to the city.

The initial driver swapped and sat in the back with me, and was interesting conversation. While the majority of people in China have extolled its virtues which I love to hear about, some take a different tack. No one is openly critical, and I don't feel like they are harbouring those feelings and trying to surreptitiously share them, but some people try to gauge my thoughts and share views on aspects of China they disagree with.

He was one that sat in this camp, and talked about how many of the natural sights in the area were now fenced off and no access was allowed. When I said that that also transpires in Australia, he countered that in Australia or the west it may be done for environmentalism, but in China it was done "for no reason." I think the situation was landowners, be that I don't fully agree, but it was interesting to hear his perspective.
They dropped me in town and I made my way to a hostel. It was almost 5 when I was checked in, so I only left to get dinner at the foot of the tower. It's on the 23rd floor.
I decided to stay another night and check out the heavenly lake near the city tomorrow, which should be nice.

127.title: Day 135: Mars
paragraphs: Thursday 11th September

Despite my full day of rest yesterday, I still had a slow morning and only left the hotel at 11. It didn't matter, as after my 3 days of full travel I'm well ahead of schedule. I can take it slow for the next week to Almaty, which is a welcome change.
My junk packed I found a restaurant and had a nice breakfast, noodles and some leek pastry things. The staff smiled at me and brought me a free drink, while most of the other patrons stared.

I'd sussed out where I wanted to go, to the east of town along the smaller, old highway. From there I could take the road north through the mountains, and camp in them for the night. There were two roads to Urumqi from Korla, the faster one that followed the plains to the east, and the windy mountain route that I was interested in.

I walked all the way out of town to my goal, and it was an interesting walk. From the side of one highway I went through some bushes to find a pedestrian bridge to the other side. When I descended the bridge a small, defunct looking amusement park was nestled between the two lanes of the highway!

I had to backtrack at one point when the footpath ended, but eventually I was in a pretty good spot on the road, with plenty of traffic. It wasn't long, as I knew it wouldn't be, until I found a ride.

He luckily but unfortunately informed me that the mountain road was blocked, and wouldn't reopen until next month. Dropped off on the side of the road leading into a small town along the eastern route, I assessed my options.

I could walk the couple of Ks through some fields to the actual highway, where there was a rest station, and start along the main route from there. My other option was to just start hitchhiking along this road, and maybe meet back up with the highway, which I opted to do. I figured that hitchhiking was so easy here I'd probably be back on the highway faster than walking directly to it.
Some almost Caucasian guys that were speaking what I think was Arabic picked me up. They were friendly and said they were from Xinjiang, I should look into the ethnic mix here.

They didn't understand or ignored what I was saying about hitchhiking, and took me straight to the train station. When we arrived, I realised I'd lost my sunnies, which I'd had for almost 2 years. They were a nice pair that I'd bought in NZ, pretty scratched at this point but I still searched the car for them. No dice.

I confused them by walking away from the train station back to the main street, and when one came by I jumped in a cab for 10 minutes straight back to where I had jumped in the previous lift. I fruitlessly searched for the sunnies, and the cabbie joined in, but again couldn't find them.

I had the cab drive through the cornfields to the outside of the highway, along some bumpy dirt roads for 5 minutes. The fare was 16.60, and I gave him a 20. He exclaimed and gave me 5 back, which would have given me a discount. I tried to refuse but he insisted, so I gave him the only 1 I had in addition, paying 16 yuan.
The sense of pride has been strong all the way through China, no one wanting to accept handouts of any kind, be it tips, round ups, or food for the most part. It's very interesting and I respect it.
The barbed wire fence shielding the highway appeared like it had to scramble through a small crack, but luckily had an unlocked gate.

At the service station I bought a coconut milk coffee. While I was looking in the fridge I looked around at the counter, and the girl had her phone up filming me which she quickly lowered. I'm mostly understanding of cultural differences in regards to privacy but that felt a bit off, especially the way she tried to hide it.

I found a lift quickly again. I haven't waited more than about 10 minutes for a week! Three fun eastern Chinese guys that were here for work were heading all the way to Urumqi, and were willing to take me the whole way if I wanted.
I actually didn't want to go the whole way, and as we passed through the rocky foothills of the mountain range as we skirted it, I jumped out and said goodbye.

The terrain outside of Korla is insane. It's like Mars. There is barely any plant life in this rocky desert, with jagged ochre stones jutting out of the ground like teeth. The foothills had very steep slopes on either side of the road, and I wandered out into them for 20 minutes to find a secluded spot.

I also walked for a while as just behind the truck stop is littered with dry human excrement, which has been a mainstay of the whole desert leg. There's not many toilets or people, so truckers just drop trou wherever they stop. It's pretty chat.

This has been one of my favourite campsites though, in a dry creekbed nestled away from the road I can barely hear. I terraformed, flattening the dusty stony earth to make a place for my tent. On either side of me rise chossy ridges that I had to scramble up and down. They are interestingly easier to climb than descend, and at a few points I had to be quite careful. I wouldn't want to break my leg out here alone.
I cooked in one of the parched tributary arms, shielded from the wind. My dinner of rice, mixed nuts, and pickled cabbage all blended together went down a treat.
Camping out here makes me happy, and I'm excited to spend as much of central Asia as I can in my tent, safely away from the road.

129.title: Day 137: Tianchi Lake
paragraphs: Saturday 13th September

I'd decided against paying for the hostel's overpriced private tour to Tianchi Lake, and that I'd figure out how the locals did it. To that end, I was very lucky as the gentleman in the bed beneath me was heading to the lake today, via the public transportation, and offered to take me with him.

Xing, another person from the hostel and I had breakfast together early and then caught a taxi to the bus station. There we bought bus tickets to the stop near the lake, and jumped aboard when it departed. It was an hour's journey there.

Once we arrived I was in a pickle, as there was an extra charge for the shuttle bus to the lake that I hadn't anticipated, and not brought the cash for. I spoke with the teller multiple times, but was finally bailed out by a friend from home that was able to pay for me. Phew.

The amount of domestic tourists was staggering. Busloads of us were dropped off to mob at the shuttle station, where huge queues waited despite the frequent services. This is a highly rated tourist attraction and it was shown by the sheer volume of visitors.

When I finally made it up to the lake it was very pretty. It was unfortunately an overcast day until the late afternoon but the views over the clear water were still lovely. I used my hours there to follow the perimeter of the lake all the way around, probably about a 10 km walk. Not many others walked around the lake, so it was still and quiet as I listened to the Frankenstein audiobook.

Xing was hurrying me via text during the afternoon which I didn't appreciate. Apparently the bus situation was terrible on the way back, and he was anxious to get there early while I didn't really care if I missed it and would have paid for a taxi. He was trying to look out for me but wouldn't leave until I was back, which was done nobly but was actually worse for both of us.

We arrived back at the hotel after 8 pm, it had been a full day affair. I had dinner downstairs and retired, getting some washing done too. I'm glad I managed to see the lake and get a standard tourist day in, but as always was keen to get moving tomorrow.

130.title: Day 138: Sayram Lake
paragraphs: Sunday 14th September
It was raining heavily in the morning, but I had a goal and so left amongst it. Xing and I had a quick breakfast before saying goodbye and I made my way into the shopping district near the hostel.
I had to pick up some essentials: lollies, bananas, 2 minute noodles, and tea, which I found with ease.

Despite the abundance of taxis I had a little trouble flagging down an empty one, but eventually did and was dropped on the outward highway at a rest stop. I'd wandered around town for a while earlier, so I had an early lunch of Mapo tofu, a staple of my diet.

Once I commenced my efforts my streak of quick rides stayed strong. A young Uighur couple actually backed their truck up to collect me after initially declining. They were very sweet and shared food with me, and we made great use of the translator to converse. They were from Kashgar in the west, which was on my original route.

They brought me a few hours west, from where I'd planned to head down through the beginnings of the Tien Shan mountain range into the Ili valley. Luckily, while on the phone to a friend I was beckoned to a car with two guys. They were curious about where I was headed and informed me that the road was closed due to snowfall, as it often was at this time of year.

I was disappointed as the valley beyond looked like a great place to camp, but appreciated that I'd found out before proceeding much further towards the dead end. They tried to take me to the bus station but dropped me off instead at the toll gate at my insistence. They warned that it would be hard to hitchhike here, but before they could even pull away another car stopped and picked me up!

These two new guys in their early 20s worked in the cotton industry that is prolific in the area, and we're driving 400ks west to Ili. Perfect. I rode with them along the plains at the feet of the mountains to Sayram lake, where I decided I'd stay. Again, they were very kind and wouldn't accept any money for fuel or tolls, and wished me the best. The warning this time was about the cold, wolves, and bears.

It's honestly hard to know who to take seriously about warnings, as I have complete alarm fatigue relating to this journey. The amount of locals warning me about random stuff, hard hitchhiking, criminals, and the like makes it impossible to know what to actually pay attention to. I suffered from the same before I left, many people warning me fearfully about things that just realistically don't happen. I have to date not seen a single, even mildly dangerous situation.

I correctly wrote off their animal warnings but it was bloody cold. The mountains overlooking the blue lake are steep, and the few flat places offered little protection from the wind. I had to rug up in all my layers during the night, and will invest in some mittens and a beanie the next time I can. Maybe some warm pants too but I don't want anything too bulky.

The campsite itself is beautiful. I walked up a steep derelict staircase on a hillside overlooking the water, and while it may be private land it seems seldom used. I can just see the far side of the water, and to it's right the valley southward that the road proceeds down. I made a small fire mostly just to prove i could, and stupidly built it too close to my tent and had to sit in-between the two to block wayward embers.
I cooked some noodles for dinner with veggies and tofu added, and watched the landscape grow dark.

I'm only a bit over an hour from the Kazakhstan border, and will decide tomorrow where I want to head with my free time. I essentially halved the distance to the meeting point of Almaty today from Urumqi, so I have a few days to play with if I arrive on the 19th.

131.title: Day 139: One small step
paragraphs: Monday 15th September
My hilltop campsite was cold during the night. I had to pitch in a semi open area, as all the sheltering pines only seemed to grow on the slopes, meaning I couldn't nestle amongst them.

During the night the frigid wind found its way under the lip of my tent and over my sleeping form. At one point I had to rouse and put more layers on to get back to sleep. I don't think this means I need to buy warmer gear yet, just that this camp was a particularly chill one.

I also felt the first tickles of sickness in my throat and body, and I know exactly where I've contracted it from. On the crowded tourist bus to Tianchi two days ago, the old lady sitting next to me was coughing and spluttering straight into the air in front of us. No mask or covering attempted at all. It's actually very irritating and selfish when people do this, now I have to deal with a sickness for days all because she couldn't wear a mask or stay home.

The view from my camp was beautiful once the sun rose and thawed me, and I stayed for hours sitting in the sun or shade as I desired. I debated staying another night but decided I'd move a little way down the valley around 2pm, just to change things up.

I made my way back down the stairs and to the road, and was quickly picked up by two women that worked in the area. They were on a little tourist drive and agreed to take me 20 minutes down the road. On the way we stopped at a viewpoint overlooking the valley behind the lake, and the spectacularly large bridge that spanned it.

I left them at a layby on the windy valley road, where some farmhouses sat by a dry riverbed that jutted away from the road perpendicularly. I spied a somewhat flat area far up the valley, and began making my way there when I passed one of the farmers. He was a Kazakh, with light blue eyes and led two horses in tow. He invited me into his house where we shared some bread and tsampa and I rested for 15 minutes.

He left and so I continued up the valley, past many sheep up the rocky riverbed that would annually flow when the snowmelt ran down, but was dry for the autumn. It was difficult to find flat ground on the sides of the narrow valley, but I found a dry tributary cascade that was covered in grass, and used a level section. My tent barely fit in the small trough, and warped from corner to corner at an awkward angle, but just worked.
While it was around 4 the sun was still high in the sky, and I decided to get a small fire going. I was bored and figured it would make relighting it easier later that evening.

This proved to be a mistake as the farmer found me and informed me I shouldn't have fires during the day, lest someone see the smoke and report a wildfire. I felt bad and apologised, and we both covered my coals with dirt. I didn't risk relighting it even after it did fall dark.
I went to bed early, as I was feeling pretty wrecked. I was only getting sicker, and knew I was in for a poor night's sleep.

132.title: Day 140: Kazakhstan
paragraphs: Tuesday 16th September
I didn't dawdle in the morning, and was packed and down on the road around 10. The farmer was nowhere to be seen, just sheep that eyed me warily as I proceeded back down the stony way.
I wasn't sure what my destination was for the day. Camping was off the table as I needed to rest in a hotel after my poor night's sleep, but I wasn't sure which town that would be in.

A truck pulled up pretty quickly with two Uighur guys in it, heading to Horgos on the Kazakh border. I accepted the lift and thus set my destination. It was a chill ride, they were friendly and we translated a few messages while the hour passed. The drive took me from the valley down into the plains, with a view out to the north to the mountains in the distance.

I arrived in Horgos and decided I wouldn't stay there, but get across the border. I'd been dropped on the outskirts of town, and it was over 10 ks into the centre. It was before noon and I had nothing better to do, so I began the walk.

After a stop for lunch at a roadside restaurant, I bumped into an interesting character. He was white, probably mid forties and a backpacker like myself. He had a large leather sack on his back and a smaller one on hi front, that didn't look comfortable at all. Atop his pack sat an old fashioned sleeping mat, and on his head a large cowboy hat.

He said he was from Kazakhstan but held a different passport (probably Russian) and was travelling around China for the next 3 weeks. His name was "Cowboy" due to his love of country music, such as kid rock.

He lamented his need for a VPN just as I had on my arrival, so I tried to point him in the right direction. Luckily, he was able to tell me that I'd gone too far past the border, and should turn around and head west. I turned and walked with him back that way, until we parted ways and he headed for the train station.

As I approached the megalith gate building that denoted the border area, I couldn't seem to find a way through it. I found a stream of people trickling in from Kazakhstan out a gate, but it was one way. One of the guards directed me to a large building back the other way I'd come, saying it was the bus station, where I'd have to get a bus from as walking through the border was not allowed.

When I arrived at the large building, I was on the south side of it and it looked like an office block. I figure that the guard had just been pointing in this direction, not to this specific building. I searched on my phone for the bus station and it was over an hour's walk away in the centre of town.

I jumped in a ride there, knowing he'd want money but wanting to just get over the border. When I went to that location, the locals there informed me that it was the wrong address, and that I should take a taxi to the bus station. They hailed a taxi for me and I jumped in, the driver having received instructions from the locals.
He brought me straight back to the large office building I'd been at half an hour ago, and it was the bus station from the other side. 🙃

From there purchasing a ticket was easy and I was shortly on the way to Kazakhstan. The bus waited at the border building while all of the passengers proceeded through the Chinese emigration and then the Kazakhstan immigration. Again, I received more questions leaving China than I did entering Kazakhstan. I wondered what would happen if I refused to answer, would China not allow me to leave? I didn't care to find out, but having to go through the rigmarole again on my departure was annoying.
Then we were through! I'm sad to be leaving the delicious food, beautiful landscape, and friendly people of China. I know I'll come back one day to see more of the eastern side.

On the bus ride into the first town across the border, Zharkent, I met Mel. He was a Uighur that had been living in the US for most of his adult life, but had been back in Xinjiang for the last year. He was currently doing a border run to refresh his 60 day stay, and would be getting the bus straight back after we arrived.

He was very friendly, and told me about his life, divorce, and future goals. When we arrived in Zharkent we had a meal together, and he helped me to get a great exchange rate from the locals that he knew.
When he jumped back on the next bus I made my way to an inn for the night.

On the way I stopped at a supermarket and that's where the realisation of the cultural divide id just crossed hit me. I'd expected to feel like I was arriving in Europe later in the trip, but it has happened already. The supermarket had rows of pasta, jars of sauce, and a lack of Asian vegetable pickles that I'd come to rely on.
I was also confronted with a huge table of vodka, which checked out.

The street is also much more European, with road signs I recognise and houses that are more Western than Eastern. Kazakhstan seems more Western, rather than the mix of both east and west, or individual identity that I thought it would have.
The friendly housekeeper was a lovely old woman called Katarina, and she was all smiles as she showed me to my room.

I probably should have stayed put today, and I was only moved by external forces really as I went with the flow of the day. I wasn't feeling any better and needed to rest, so had a quiet dinner downstairs at the restaurant and went to bed early.
It was another bad night's sleep, and my throat stung whenever I swallowed. I decided to see how I felt tomorrow, and maybe take a whole day to rest.

133.title: Day 141: Fully Sick
paragraphs: Wednesday 17th September
Well, this is going to be a quick one.

I had a bad night's sleep and knew I needed to take a day to rest rather than head to Almaty. Emergences from my room once in the morning to pay for another night and once in the evening to get dinner from the supermarket were my only forays into the world outside my room.
I scrolled the day away on my phone, coughing in bed and pitying myself for the pain in my throat. Sometimes, I mixed things up by taking yet another hot shower.
It did work, and I felt better when I went to bed. Not a fun nor memorable day, but it had to be done. Oh, I didn't take any pictures either.

134.title: Day 142: Almaty
paragraphs: Thursday 18th September
I'd somewhat recovered when I woke up, and packed my bags quickly in eagerness to leave.
The dreary weather let down a light rain throughout the morning, but the omnipresent grey cloud showed no signs of letting up, so I pushed out into it.

Standing in the muddy gravel beside my gradually dampening pack wasn't the best first impression of Kazakhstan, but it wasn't too long before a kind soul stopped. He was a Uighur man in his forties or fifties, and was heading down the road in my direction.
After a few minutes he said he was actually heading to Almaty but not directly, and if I wasn't in a rush I would be welcome to travel with him. I accepted.

The sky was grey but that didn't dampen our spirits. The journey through the rocky plains and by the distant ridges was pretty. We even drove off the road to stop atop a small ridge line and take some photos. We talked about travel and family, and he was given great pause by the fact I had and wanted no children. He also started to extol the benefits of his favourite book, the Qur'an at one point.
I slept more towards the end of the leg and eventually we were near the city of Almaty. In the distance snowcapped mountains loomed over the plains.

We parted ways at a layby and I had no trouble finding a new ride for the remaining kilometres. It was fortunate for both me and my hosts, Sars and Asel, as they were two soldiers my age that were nervous about their English language exam on Monday.
