They needed a passing grade to be able to work for the UN, and get deployed as peacekeeping troops. I paid for my passage by speaking with them in English, and answering their questions about the upcoming exam and how they should answer. They were built, soldiers through and through, and showed great kindness by insisting I take a few dollars of money that I was disallowed from rejecting and dropping me right at my hostel in town. I promised they could call me to talk over the next few days to speak in English if they desired.

My hostel was mediocre but it was good to get there. The last leg of the journey had been mired by thick traffic and slow, and I was still tired from my sickness. I went for dinner at an Indian restaurant, as Kazakh food is essentially off limits for me, and had a few mains with some naan.

I overheard a man speaking English with an English accent, and introduced myself to him when I'd finished eating. His name was Callum and he was travelling solo in Kazakhstan, having taken a terrible overnight train to the city from Astana a few days previously. He was also in IT, and this was his first real solo travel trip.
I invited him to come to the museum with me the next day, which he accepted.
At the hostel I had no problems falling asleep quickly, looking forward to having one day to spend in Almaty before Gianluca arrived on Saturday morning.

135.title: Day 143: About Town
paragraphs: Friday 19th September
I didn't have anywhere to be today. All I had to do was while away the day until Gianluca arrived tomorrow, and maybe check out the museum.

My first objective was to feed myself, and to that end there was a vegan patisserie on the south side of town. I figured out the sole metro line, taking that and walking the rest of the way only to find it had moved addresses.
I then downloaded and signed up for the local taxi app, and taxied over to their new location, per their Instagram. Closed, even though it was during business hours!

My next mode of transport was the bus, which I rode further out of tow to another vegan breakfast cafe. The bus didn't take cash but no one questioned me as I stole a ride on it. The cafe was incredibly hard to find, and ended up being in a hotel as part of a wellness centre. It was a tiny room with a single table, but the food ended up being pretty good.

I then figured out the bus app, rode a bus as a paying customer back into town, and then had a crack at the electric rental scooters everyone was using. They were very fun, and I immediately knew I'd be riding them around town as much as possible.

After a short rest at the hostel, I had to move to a hotel. It was an immense screw around as my booking was cancelled from one place and I couldn't locate another. I ended up sitting in the rain while a ginger cat came and curled up on my lap while I searched for accommodation. The hotels are surprisingly expensive here, and it was difficult to find one for under 100 aud per night, but I ended up finding an apartment.

Once checked in I headed to the history museum. It was a wide building full of small rooms with information about the history of the region and city. It wasn't as in depth as I would have liked, but the artifacts in the display cases were interesting to see.

In the evening I walked around the main street of town, which was popping off. People of all ages were walking up and down the strip, with stalls open and music blaring. I found my way to a quiet underground bar with a retro vibe and gallery from a local artist in the back where I spent over an hour writing some postcards.

The city is very Western, far more so than even the smaller town of Zharkent that surprised me with its Russian influences. It's the young people especially, dressing and acting the same as in Sydney, and it made me wonder if the internet has contributed to a homogenisation of fashion between cultures.

It's going to get more expensive from here on out, so all the more reason to camp and speed up the journey. Restaurants aren't that much cheaper than Sydney so I may eat out less too, which would be a devastating turn of events.

I felt better and excited for Gianluca to arrive tomorrow. I'd figure out the metro, taxis, bus, and scooters, and had an apartment booked for two nights. It took me a while to get to sleep, fretting over his 4am arrival time and worrying he'd have no internet, but eventually sleep took me.

136.title: Day 144: The Cousin
paragraphs: Saturday 20th September

This day felt longer than almost any other in my life. That's not a bad thing as it was a fantastic day, just so filled with events that by the evening, the morning felt like it had happened 2 days ago.

I awoke to my alarm at 4, but it wasn't for another hour that Gianluca disembarked the plane and jumped in a taxi, and another hour until he actually arrived. I dressed in a shirt and shorts and ventured out into the chill morning air to meet him at his cab.
It was great to see him, and I'm really looking forward to the next week of travel together.
Back at the hotel we were both too wired to get back to sleep, and chatted for almost two hours before deciding to start the day.

Our first outing was to the Green Bazaar markets where Gianluca bought some souvenirs, and I some jeans for the upcoming ride. Notably, we also both bought some traditional Kazakh clothing, a small vest for him and a longer open coat style one for myself. I hesitated on the purchase but I love the look.

To get there we'd rented the small electric scooters that populate the city, and are used widely. They're incredibly fun, and zip one along the pavement at 20 kmh. We used solely them for the entire day, not jumping in an unnecessary cab, bus or metro due to the noble scooter steeds that bore us around town.

After dropping our loot back off at the apartment, we then hunted for some camping gear for Gian. We plan on mostly camping during our ride in Kyrgyzstan, so he decided he'd buy gear once he arrived. He needed a sleeping mat and a sleeping bag, and potentially a tent if mine turns out to be too small to share.

After checking out a subpar sports goods store, we were nearby to a gondola so decided to take it up to a hill overlooking town. It turned out to be a small, strange amusement park on the top of a narrow ridge, with mostly local families taking their children up. We bought the combined ticket of gondola, Ferris wheel, and "Fast Coaster", a sitting roller coaster that you controlled the speed of as it raced down a track.

In addition to the rides, we went on another small rollercoaster that sped around a tiny track before coming to a crunching stop. Gian also played a shooting game, and I a throwing game, which I won a fridge magnet for my performance in.

The ridge had a commanding view of the city, and we could see the lower city centre area surrounded by clusters of residential towers. Interestingly, each cluster of towers seemed to consist of four or so identical buildings, giving the skyline a patchwork appearance.

Down to street level once again we decided to cross town to a decathlon, and rode the scooters for 45 minutes through a combination of backstreets and canal walkways. It was such a nice way to see the town, and the residential areas varied from green leafy suburbs to soviet apartment blocks cloned along crusty streets. The decathlon proved fruitless, and we decided to return to the previous store tomorrow.
Next we found a shopping centre, and finally Gian bought a sleeping bag that will hopefully keep him alive against the cold night winds in Kyrgyzstan, but I have my doubts.

Swinging back by the apartment to drop it off, we kitted up in our fresh new Kazakh drip and hit the town for dinner. We felt silly in our outfits and Gianluca was worried we'd get glassed for causing offense, but we were only stared at a bit. Dinner was great and we finished the night at a bar called "Queen of Darkness" with live music and a friendly Czech bartender.

I haven't documented all the small occurrences that happened throughout the day, but it truly didn't stop from 6am until 10pm. We were constantly joking that we couldn't believe the morning was the same day, and it really felt like he'd been here a couple of days already. We both had made it through despite poor sleep, and Gianluca had barely slept on the plane so I don't know how he did it. Needless to say we collapsed into bed and instantly fell asleep.

It seems to me to be a phenomenon that when you have a massive day you can actually wake up feeling better the following day due to the high quality sleep that you get, and it happened for me this night with over 9 hours of uninterrupted respite.

137.title: Day 145: Big Almaty Lake
paragraphs: Sunday 21st September
I was brought up to speed with the newfangled happening of society by trying a matcha latte with Gian in the morning. Wild what the kids are up to these days. It was alright.

I was also told it was simply not possible to omit yoghurt from a granola bowl and put coconut milk in instead. Couldn't be done. Gianluca had the excellent suggestion of ordering a bowl with no yoghurt and a glass of coconut milk, which successfully circumvented the block and allowed me to enjoy breakfast.

We pissed away a bit more time at the hotel and only called a taxi to take us to the lake in the mountains just after 12. It was about an hour's drive away, but seeing as the taxi cost under 20 bucks we decided to just cop that rather than do any research into the bus or tours.

The driver that collected us, Aska, was very engaged and blasted some Tupac a bit too loud for our enjoyment. We asked if we could commandeer him for the day but he was hesitant about the idea, and said we'd just get up there first.

An hour later we arrived at a locked gate on the road to the lake that cars could not pass. We had to either walk TWO AND HALF HOURS each way, or rent motorbikes. The resident motorbike hawkers all approached us, and the one we talked to told us the price was 35,000 tenge for two hours. That's over $100 PER BIKE. A truly ridiculous cost for this country, and an absolute tourist scam. The price was non flexible.
Even Aska wasn't impressed, and told us that this was just Kazakhstan. It was annoying, as we really wanted to go up but just didn't have the time to walk up as down as it was just before 2.

We had Aska take us back down the road a bit in search of a cheaper rental. The best we could do was find some E bikes for 25000 each, and haggle the price down and time up a bit. We were being rorted, but there was nothing to be done, we'd come this far.
Aska had been excited to see the lake with us for the first time, but this price barrier nipped that in the bud sadly. We paid him a holding fee to wait for us while we ventured on.

While I was salty about the price, it actually turned out to be awesome. The E bikes had way more power than I thought and carried us briskly up the steep mountain roads. The views into the valley behind us were only surpassed by those of the lake itself, a soft teal that almost matched that of the Kazakh flag. At a lookout over the lake we stopped and soaked up the view of the soft, still lake.
We could see people walking along a side track to the lake's edge, and while the rental clock was ticking down on us made a quick excursion there to see it up close.

If I thought the ride up was fun, speeding down the mountain blew it out of the water, and I almost had a couple of accidents as I was carried away in seeing how fast I could descend. We stopped once to take some photos with a horse, but otherwise sped back to the start.

Aska was waiting for us and gave us some local commentary as we wove through the backstreets into town. We ended up getting along well with him, and took some photos once we arrived. He had looked out for us well.
We stopped twice for dinner, at both Chinese and Georgian restaurants, while zipping around on yet more scooters.

The night wrapped up at the same artsy bar that I'd had a drink in a few nights ago, and we played a couple of games of chess. I just want to emphasize how cultured and dignified we looked, battling away at the erudite game while sipping our cocktails.

We'd be heading up to the mountains tomorrow to camp, a trial run for the gear that we'd be using for the bike trip. If we need to, we'll buy Gianluca a tent or some warmer gear, but hopefully what we have is enough as the panniers are going to be packed enough already.

138.title: Day 146: Shymbulak
paragraphs: Monday 22nd September

We spent the morning packing, which proved quite the challenge for both of us. While I did need some jeans and I like my new robe, my pack is only growing in size and I'm not sure this rate of gear acquisition is sustainable. Including the food I bought yesterday was difficult and the weight is getting silly. Hopefully the panniers on the bikes are large, and we can eat our way through the bulk of the extra weight.
It wasn't any less of a challenge for Gian, whose new sleeping bag and mat barely compress. We're each now bearing an extra carry bag in addition to our backpacks.
Once we checked out at 12 I made a beeline to a nearby vego restaurant as I hadn't eaten. While I feasted Gianluca hobomaxxed on the bench outside with our assorted bags.
We then bought the two most important goods, water and bread, and jumped on a bus up the mountains to the south of the city.

The public transport app is terrible, and said the bus ride would take 90 minutes. I probably should have clocked that as a lie based on the distance, but believed it until we'd just passed our stop. Our stop was only two from the end of the line where the bus turned around, so we waited on board as it did. The bus driver questioned us so I explained that we'd just missed our stop and were going two stops back to it. He made me buy new tickets.

The campground was only 15 minutes from the stop and we walked up the side of the valley to it. It wasn't quite as secluded as I would have hoped, and we passed a few houses and hotels on the way to it.

The campground itself was well maintained, and had two wooden shelters to camp inside of, one of which was free. There was also a giant wooden swing that Gianluca and I slowly built up the momentum of until it swung dangerously high.

We erected the tent and stashed our bags in the corner of the shelter, and then made our way back to the road. At the end of the mountain road was a sports complex, where a gondola offered rides further up the mountain. It was late in the day so we didn't have time to dawdle, but bought tickets and jumped in one of the carriages.
In the carriage with us was Madi, a local Kazakh that told us a bit about Kazakhstan and asked us about Australia.

During a wide section between support towers, where the cable dipped in a large arc as we were overhanging a particularly high drop to the valley floor, the gondola line quickly came to a stop. The momentum of the carriages led to us swinging up and down as the parabola wobbled, and the carriages on the other cable swung from 10 metres beneath us to 10 metres above us. We couldn't feel the swinging just see the other carriages flying up and down, and Madi mistakenly tried to reassure us that it was an illusion.
Once we started moving again and made it past the next tower the wobbling abated.

We had to change to the next line up at a midway station and before long were also at the top of that. The final line to the top of the ski slope was closed, but the views from there were more than enough. Above us towered the peak of Shymbulak and below the valley disappeared into a sea of clouds. I wanted to scramble up the slope to some wayward snow I could see, but an announcement boomed that we had to head straight back down.

At the bottom we grabbed a bite to eat before heading back to the camp, where luckily our belongings hadn't been pillaged. I cooked one of the dry couscous based meals I'd bought, and it was pretty mediocre. I invested heavily in these meals so I hope some of the other lentil variants I bought actually taste good, but I will consume them either way.
It's pretty tight with two grown adults in my one man tent, but we made it work. We'll see if we can find a 1 man for Gian in Bishkek but won't stress if we can't.

During the night some drunk locals parked themselves in the camping area and talked loudly while blasting music. When they first arrived I valiantly told Gianluca I'd go and tell them to quieten down if necessary, but pussied out immediately when he asked me to do just that in the middle of the night. I just gave him my earplugs instead. Sorry dude.

139.title: Day 147: Kyrgyzstan
paragraphs: Tuesday 23rd September

When we awoke the local drinkers were gone. There was also no sign of them and we disagreed on the direction the noise was coming from, so maybe they were modern fae attempting to lure us off into the night.
We made good time getting down to the bus stop, as we didn't have breakfast and just packed and left. There was a light rain but it wasn't bad enough to bother kitting up.
We were going to arrive in the city around 9:30, which solidified our earlier idea to get the 12 pm bus to Bishkek, rather than the 4 pm one.

Our approach to the morning was far too leisurely. We bought some more food at a supermarket, and then made our way in the intensifying rain to a cathedral that I wanted to check out. It sat in a park, so Gianluca sat in a cafe nearby while I went inside. It was 10:45, and we had plenty of time.

The cathedral was beautiful both outside and in, like you dear reader, and the inside was decorated with a majestic array of stained glass windows, murals, paintings, display cases, and hanging chalices. When I returned to the cafe I encouraged Gian to check it out, and copied him in ordering food.
He returned and went to the bathroom, and when we came out I looked at booking a taxi. It was 11:30, and the bus station was half an hour away. Shit.

We rushed out to meet our taxi, or "YandexGo" as the kids here call it, and nervously watched our ETA tick up from 12:01 to 12:04 over the course of the ride. I was mentally preparing to miss it, and had accepted that we'd probably spend a few hours in a pub sheltering from the rain and time.
When we arrived at the bus station we stormed the building, managed to find the entrance, and made it onto the bus just before it left.

The journey to Kyrgyzstan was mostly uneventful. My window was completely fogged on the outside, so I could barely see the scenery and mostly dozed for the few hours of driving. At the border we shuffled out and through the checkpoint without issue, receiving a cool orange stamp in our passports. If more countries used colours other than red for their stamps the world would be a better place.

In the new country there was no sign of our bus, and some of the other passengers decided to jump in a taxi. Gian and I did the same with a young kiwi bloke we'd just met, and covered the last hour to town.
The journey had taken far longer than we'd thought, and we'd also lost an hour to the timezone difference. All up, we arrived at our hotel at 6:30.

Instead of getting any downtime we then spent two hours trying and failing to get SIM cards and locating an ATM. The woman at the corner store tried to help us activate our new sims for over an hour with no luck. We did eventually locate an ATM right near our hotel we'd somehow walked past and missed.

We withdrew over 2000 USD in local currency to pay for the motorbikes we are renting for the week and the deposit. It is truly a ridiculous amount of currency, and we felt like dealers as we counted and rubber banded the 50k bundles.
We gave up just before 9 and headed to a restaurant we'd had our eyes on since we'd left the hotel. It closed at 9 and turned us away.
I was ready to eat some cup noodles and call it a night, but we found a middle eastern restaurant with suitable offerings. I helped myself to two bowls of lentil soup.
It ended up being a later night with none of the rest period that we'd hoped for before jumping on the bikes tomorrow. Oh well.

140.title: Day 148: Into the mountains
paragraphs: Wednesday 24th September

The first notable event of the day happened when I misplaced my travel card. I slowly grew more anxious like a pot on the boil until the burner was turned off when I found it in my folder. My main and backup cards look very similar from one side and I'd mistakenly swapped them.
The second was to withdraw the remaining cash we needed from the ATM, which brought us to carrying even more ridiculous amounts of cash on our persons.
A quick Yandex later and we met Sergey, the Russian that Gianluca had organised the bikes through and had been in communication with.

Sergey was pretty gruff and matter of fact, which wasn't aided by his rightful worry about my level of motorbike experience. When he asked me directly if I had a licence with a motorbike category Gianluca and I both blurted out yes, not exactly selling the lie, but he didn't question it.

The motorbikes seem to be in pretty good nick, but the accessories we've rented to go with them are not. The saddle bags are on their last legs and dangle off the sides of the bike dangerously. Gianluca is in an oversized jacket while I'm in a ladies one that shows my midriff. There was nothing in between. We make quite the duo. The gloves, pants, and boots are functioning as intended.

It was difficult fitting our gear into the bags, but we managed to get most of it in. Sergey said there was no way we'd want to camp as it would be too cold, but we're in too deep at this point. Gianluca had even bought camping equipment solely for this trip so I'll be damned if we aren't using it.

We counted out the cash for Sergey and everyone was happy. I asked him if the stacked E-Girl on his calendar was his wife. He replied that she was but that he was getting a divorce soon, flipping the page to reveal the lady for next month.
I once again fueled Sergey's doubts about me at the final minute by needing him to remind me to hold the clutch in as I started the bike, but somehow made it away without stalling.

On the road! Our first stop was nearby for Gian to give me some more instructions on the bike, but before long we left the complex and headed onto the road. At one point I had a car waiting, very patiently I might add, behind me while I repeatedly stalled on the uphill start.

We stopped for a brief lunch and then hit the road proper. The city fell away to the north of us and we climbed into the brown fields in the southeast, veering east after a while. On our right to the south rose a huge mountain range, the snowcapped peaks seeming to be out of a different season entirely to the dead grasses surrounding us.
To the north was a smaller line of peaks, and the road we followed wound through the flat valley between them.

The riding was great fun, and there isn't too much traffic to get in our way. Even though this is my first time on a motorbike I've ridden a lot of bikes and driven a lot of cars, which have motors, so I pretty much have it down already.

After an hour and a half of riding we arrived at Burana Tower, a 10 century minaret in a field that was an ancient town. The minaret has had its exterior reconstructed, but is still mostly the original brickwork. Amazingly, the minaret is open to the general public and we ascended the cramped, dark, winding, steep staircase inside. Only two narrow windows provide light, until one emerges onto the roof. The omnipresent mountains provided a picturesque background for the scene. I thoroughly enjoyed imagining the call to prayer ringing out over 1000 years ago from where I stood, and what the surrounding town would have looked like.

Back on the road we headed towards a valley nestled between some of the southern peaks, the promise of a lake that I had been recommended to visit calling. The day was growing late so rather than heading to the lake today, we found accommodation in a single chamber wooden hut.

There was charcoal provided that I spent an hour alighting fully in the hearth, it finally reaching a self perpetuating temperature at which I could feed it. I cleaned and filled the huge pot that sat on top with water, the massive volume taking over an hour again to reach boiling point. I nestled my pot of simmering cous cous next to the pot, and it cooked to perfection at the gentle boil.

The fire warmed the chamber almost too well, and by the time I was heading to bed it was swelteringly hot. I had to relax to cope with the heat, as I was repulsed by the idea of opening the door to let out even a little excess of the warmth I had put so much effort into breeding.

Gianluca fell asleep before 8 with a headache, and ended up sleeping for over 12 hours. I stayed up a little later, but when I did fall asleep on my mattress tucked under the blankets, barely stirred until morning.

141.title: Day 149: Kol Tor
paragraphs: Thursday 25th September

Gianluca and I slept like the dead, rising at 8 to slowly thaw from our sleep into the warm sunny morning. It was 8 when we rolled out of our beds, and we had some oaty gruel slop for breakfast. It needed flavour of some kind.

We were on the porch when some hikers passed our cabin, heading up the path to Kol Tor that we planned on leaving up soon. To our surprise they informed us that the hike was actually two and half hours each way! Far longer than the hour or so that we assumed it would take. This threw our day's plan in the air as we wanted to check this lake out then head further east, but five hours hiking was a full day of effort.

I was very keen to see the lake as we were staying so close anyway, and pushed for us to steam ahead. We tried to start the hike on the bike, but quickly realised that it was far too steep for that. We walked for almost an hour before Gianluca decided to head back into town to get some shopping we needed. He isn't as keen on hiking so it worked out fine.

I pushed for the lake and made it up there about two hours after we'd left. It became very steep, and eventually the treeline ended while small patches of snow began to appear. The patches grew until they eventually carpeted the ground, and as I neared the goal a chill wind bit me in the alpine terrain. I passed the hikers we'd talked to in the morning.

The final stretch to the lake was a steep muddy, snowy incline, beneath which horses grazed on areas of exposed grass. I almost slipped ascending the final steps, and ended up wrapping my scarf around my head like a tusken raider.

It was all worth it when I reached the water. The bright blue gives the water an enchanted feel, as if drinking from it would restore my weary limbs, though I decided against succumbing to the idea. The lake, Kol Tor, sat in a shallow depression in the mountainside that provided welcome respite from the wind. I rested a while and snapped some photos with Gianluca film camera.
The dutch women I'd overtaken caught up and gave me an energy bar, pitying my empty pockets.

I left the lake about a quarter to one, and as I began to descend almost immediately slipped and fell into the mud. Not only had I dirtied myself, but it was also freezing cold and I couldn't wash my soiled hands off in the snow with more than a handful at a time.
I passed a large group of hikers climbing, some sort of tour group, but otherwise my descent was brisk. I listened to more of "Mrs. Dalloway" on the way down.

The hut was empty when I returned, and I made myself lunch and took a very brief swim in a rocky pool set up in the cold stream. When Gian returned from town after 3, with supplies and fuel for my thirsty bike, we decided to push on rather than stay another night. I was also just looking forward to doing some riding today.

We rode an hour into a town and found a dorm style room that we rented two of the four beds in, but had it to ourselves. Dinner was had at a cafe nearby, where I reached the end of my rope with misunderstandings about food. I swear to god I asked the waitress if the soup had meat in it and she said no, but both that and the EGGPLANT SALAD, marked as such on the menu, both arrived with meat. Thank heavens the enoki mushroom salad was there to save the day, my hero. 🥹

142.title: Day 150: Konorchek Canyon
paragraphs: Friday 26th September
Lotta riding today.
We made an early start at 8 as we had a fair amount of ground to cover. It was a grey day, and quite cold on the bikes as we exited town onto the highway.

After stopping for fuel, both for the bikes and us, we were cruising at about 100 along the flat plain. The road quality is quite sufficient here, and even travelling quickly feels safe. The bike is quite intuitive and I haven't had any real problems with it yet.

There was one dicey situation, where a bloody plastic roll of some sort came loose from a truck, which Gian missed by a few metres. I also didn't see it until it had passed him, so if it had been in either of our paths we would have hit it. We both honked at the moron as we passed him stopped on the road further up, but in a foreign country we have no real recourse.

It was an hour's ride until we arrived at the Canyon, the one stop I wanted to make for the day. The final section of riding was down a winding valley, with sweeping downhill curves that were enjoyable to lean the bike around.

We pulled up next to a train line with a couple of other parked cars, and began the hike perpendicular to the highway. It started out in a wide riverbed, currently dry that would probably only flood during heavy rains and spring, but narrowed as we rose into the red hills.

A variety of shrubs with muted colours populated the sides of the stream, with the sparse rocky canyon walls rising steeply above them. As the path narrowed and steepened further, there were some tall ledges in the path with frayed ropes dangles to assist in the scramble.

After an hour the canyon quickly opened up into a bowl shaped valley, with beautiful earth formations in the centre and far side. Columns resembling huge conjoined termite mounds rimmed the canyon, and layers of heavily compared earth formed ridges along the base of the centre. Tiny worming cavities carved from snowmelt streams snaked down their carved paths, coalescing into bigger streams as they reached the ground, and made their way to the riverbed we had entered from.
There was a further hike up onto the plateau, but we didn't really have time to check it out, and I think the view of the formation would be better than from it.
We were back at the bikes at about 12:30, and had 3 hours of riding ahead of us to the hotel with hot springs that Gianluca was keen on.
My bike has only a 200km range, and left me wondering if I'd be stuck by the side of the road as the gauge quickly ticked down during a desert of service stations, but finally one came into view.

Three hours of riding is a lot, and motorbikes don't allow for passive driving as do cars. It's much more engaging, both in fun and tiring ways. The last couple of hours of riding were along the northern side of Issyk-Kul, a huge lake that I couldn't make out the far shore of. In fact I could barely look at the lake as any tilt in my helmet at the speeds we were travelling would catch the wind and pull my head to the side roughly.

We were both relieved to stop when we finally arrived at the hotel, only to find the small heated pool was drained outside of the tourist season! Another hotel nearby backed onto a hot pool though, so we moved over to it to stay.

The "Hot Spring", an overused term to describe heated pools that needs to be regulated, was a great relief and the perfect treatment after a long day. We played around swapping between the warm and icy pools.

We have more long days ahead of us, and have to cover over 4 hours of riding for the next two. Breaking the days up with lunch should make them more enjoyable, but while the biking is fun, the danger and effort of it isn't inclining me to pursue further riding in the future.

143.title: Day 151: Off piste
paragraphs: Saturday 27th September

When I woke up this morning, any inclination I had to make good on my promise to visit the pool again was dispelled. Instead, I waited for breakfast at the hotel to open and ate an obscene amount of bread and raspberry jam.

We had four plus hours of riding ahead of us and were aiming for a yurt camp on the south side of Issyk Kul. The mornings ride was much like the previous day's: busy one lane highway interspersed with rodeworks that retarded our progress.

During one of these unsealed sectimy phone managed to wriggle free of the clasp mount on the bike, and threw itself into the mud. I instantly parked and started running back to grab it, about 50m back up the road. Horrifyingly, a driver too intent on staring at me to look at the road drove right over it in front of me, followed by another vehicle. I picked up the smashed remains of my phone and verified it had passed on to the cloud above.

I was so angry, more than I had any right to be. Initially, I was annoyed at the driver, but he probably wouldn't have seen it in the sodden dirt even if he was paying attention, I was just looking for something to be annoyed at. I snapped the broken phone in half in my anger, but like many hasty actions fueled by emotion, I immediately regretted it as the punctured battery began to smoke and flame as I was putting it in my pocket. I threw the piece of smouldering rubbish away in a rush and walked back to the bike.

Gianluca looked bored with me, and it's something I well remember from being in his position: when a grown adult gets pissy, it's pretty unimpressive. He reminded me to get my SIM, so I trudged back down the highway to the melted plastic metal mess and broke it open to retrieve the card directly from the inside like an autopsy. I put the rest of it that I could in my pocket, not to litter. I had to take a breather before getting back on the bike, to concentrate better on the road.

In hindsight, I'm not actually sure why I became so irate, as I'd bought a budget phone for exactly this reason. I haven't been angry like that in a long time. It just felt like a stupid waste, and watching it be destroyed before my eyes was vent to all the frustration I had in me at the time. I'll remember how stupid I felt after my mantrum next time I'm incensed.

I toyed with the idea of waiting until the motorbike trip ended and I was back in Bishkek to buy a new phone,  but Gian talked me out of it. Instead, we used the time we were going to spend checking out a church and mosque to get lunch and a new phone for me. I couldn't bring myself to put it in the phone clamp.

The afternoon's ride was beautiful, and exactly what I'd wanted from the ride along the lake. The road trailed right along the lakeshore for sections, and we stopped for a fun photoshoot, lying and standing on our bikes like teenagers with new whips. The water was surprisingly quite tepid, as I thought it would be icy.

We stopped to check out a lively festival that was happening by the roadside and peering into some open yurts saw large feats of fruits and breads set on circular tables with opulent golden tableware surrounded by rings of adults in traditional dress. Each yurt in the long arc seemed to contain an identical set-up. However interesting we found their culture, they seemed to find us equally novel, and we found ourselves taking photos with a few groups of people as we left to get on our bikes.

In the later afternoon, we turned away from the highway to head up a back road to a panoramic lookout I'd seen on the map. The road was unsealed and quite rocky in places, the first real riding of the sort that I'd done. We climbed up a gentle valley and passed through a gate before a turn that opened the roof of the world. Suddenly, we were in a flat, deep plain with peaks on either side of us. The grassy plains slowly curved upwards, an encrusting of trees shrouding the upper half of the slopes under the apexes. A few scattered brick buildings populated the fields, while here and there some cattle and horses watched us pass.

Riding on the unsealed road was intimidating at first, but I quickly realised I wasn't going to immediately lose traction on any slight turn. Nevertheless, I played it quite safe and cornered much slower than I probably needed to.

A few more photos ops later and we were at the entrance to the view, just after both of us took a corner a little hot and drove through some mud. (That was the only time that happened.) There were some cabins and buildings at the start of the short walk, and we were immediately offered tea upon our arrival. The sun was beginning to set so I said we'd join when we returned, and we hurried to the lookout.

I didn't realise how far we'd climbed, and the view of the lake's shore was phenomenal. From our vista, we could see hundreds of tiny canyonridges, some redder, and others a more dusty green, sprawling away to the foggy horizon. The angled light cast hard shadows on the jagged lines, emphasising their contours all the more. I hope the photos do it justice.
We decided to stay for the night and booked a small cabin. There was no dinner, so we cooked some of the grain sachets we'd bought and gave them some much needed extra flavouring too.

144.title: Day 152: Song Kul
paragraphs: Sunday 28th September
I'd fallen asleep before 9, so I was feeling pretty well slept by our alarm at 7. There was no sign of our host when we jumped on the bikes and hit the road at 8.

The day began with winding descent down to lake level, with the dusty sweeping corners in succession lowering us gradually to the water. Downhill is much harder than uphill, and I had trouble keeping up with Gian. Once we reached the lake, the road was again sealed and even improved in quality from yesterday. I was able to take the bike up to the max speed that the little 250cc could manage, and the wide corners were simple to follow. We said goodbye to Issyk Kul and turned south at the lake's southwest corner, where a single lane road passed into a dry valley. Rocky mountains rimmed our entire horizon, and we joined back up with another sealed highway that fed directly to Kochkor.

It had been about two hours since we'd left in the morning, and for once, we were making good time. We also met some English hitch-hikers in the town that asked us for a ride but had gone by the time we finished lunch.

We faced a problem: my bikes fuel capacity. A sport bike unsuited for road trips, my bike has about a 200km range on the tank and had constantly surprised and stressed me with how quickly it managed to chew through its compact tank. The upcoming journey through Song Kul, a remote mountain lake, posed a challenge as there were no petrol stations for hundreds of kilometres.

Searching through town for a jerry can, the best we could do was an empty plastic engine oil container that a mechanic sold me for a dollar and filled it with extra fuel. We spun a web of ratchet strap around it on the back and latched it on, hoping it wouldn't leak gasoline onto the exhaust below. It didn't, and Gianluca survives to this day.

At one light in town, Gianluca and I were honked at by a waiting car for seemingly no reason, then again as we took off and they passed. Gianluca gave them the finger as they passed, and they instantly braked in front of him and began driving aggressively next to him, pushing him to the side. My heart started to race as I could see them exchanging words, and I thought I'd have to do my best to diffuse an angry Kyrgyz from trying to fight Gian. Thank the heavens above they sped off after yelling things he couldn't understand at him. Afterwards, I stressed that we were in a foreign country and had essentially no recourse for anything that happened and to let any poor behaviour slide while here.

On the road out of Kochkor, we passed around ten herds of animals heading back towards the city. Herders on horseback ushered their flocks down the highway, unworriedly stopping traffic as their animals bleated their way along the asphalt. The groups were of cows, horses, goats, or sheep, some hundreds in size. It was fortunate that we were moving against the tide, as even when brought to a standstill, the movement of the animals would shift us out of the back of the herd, and on our merry way. Vehicles heading in the opposite direction were worked against, and I saw frustrated truckers losing progress against the swarm as goats rushed around and their crawling vehicles. It seemed like they would be stuck forever.

After the better part of an hour, we turned off the main highway towards the lake. Not a kilometre along the dirt road, the ground fell away into a majestic valley in front of us, where the distant road snaked into invisibility out of sight. I stopped to take photos and, for the first time, dropped my bike. It suddenly tipped in the soft surface beneath me, falling onto its side. I felt a fool and rushed to lift it from blocking the road, hastily heaving and hurting my back slightly.

The valley floor had one concentrated village centre, with natural pasture surrounding the road otherwise. A few herds of goats blocked the road here and there, but nothing like the highway. The road wound up and zig-zagged to the left-hand ridge, cresting it triumphantly with a view of the distant lake, our destination. I was too excited and tried to take the bike off-road onto the grassy slope, but hesitated at the last second and hit the bump on the roadside at an awkward angle, going for a spill. I was doing under 10ks, and both the bike and I were fine.

The road down to and along the lake was solid compacted dirt, and I learned to trust it at high speeds. As we approached the yurt camp, though, we both hit an unexpected, slightly obscured bump doing around 80. Our asses firmly in the saddles at impact, we each had a bit of a fright as we were launched up but landed our unintended stunts intact. The lakeshore was all grassy fields, and in one, we went for an offroad joyride, taking some videos and pictures as we cruised around the scene.  It was flat in all directions, and I felt like I'd been transported to a three-dimensional treadmill of grass, my movements only changing the horizon ever so slightly.

We'd stayed in a few huts, but this was our first proper yurt! The inside was colourful and our beds warm, with a mini hearth for warmth. There were two plastic bags of coal next to the hearth, and the inside was full of wood, so I lit a fire. There weren't any tongs or spatula to feed the coal on, so I had the hands of a chimneysweep when I'd finished delicately placing some large chunks on the burning wood, but it worked well and I had the coals going before long.

When we returned from dinner, we found our remaining coal bags missing, having only used half of one. I checked the fire and discovered that they had been lobbed onto the fire, plastic bags, and all. I quickly shut the latch again when the awful smell of burning plastic spilled out, and it explained the awful smell outside our yurt. Thankfully, the hearth was mostly self-contained, and only a minor, but still irritating, amount of the plastic odour escaped into our shelter. Plastic burning has been surprisingly common throughout my whole trip, from my first day off the boat in Indonesia, where roadside fires filled the air with their acrid scent.  It's a cheap and convenient way to dispose of rubbish, so I understand why it's done, but it doesn't make it any less malodorous.
The yurt was warm when we fell asleep but became chilly during the night when the fire died. We were both glad to have the excessively thick blankets Gianluca had complained about initially.

145.title: Day 153: Today's journey: Small, cold, and nice, but broken up [6]
paragraphs: Monday 29th September.
It was quite chilly in the yurt when we woke up. The fire had long smouldered out, and air had crept in through the small gaps in the fabric. It's never easy to leave a cosy bed on a cold morning.
Breakfast was on a schedule, though, and we were ready for it when it arrived at 8. I was relegated to the bread tray by the daried, and gianluca did his best with the pancakes and porridge.

The morning ride saw us say farewell to the lake and climb the hills as they grew up into mountains around us. Gianluca's front brake gave up, roping in his confidence and bringing him closer back down to my speed. As we crested the minor mountain pass, we could see a huge mine on the opposite valley wall below, the tiers of excavation reminding me of the rice paddies earlier in my journey, but on a grand scale.

We could see the rode that we were to take passing through the scene before us and meandered down the steep winding mountainside to it. Riding downhill isn't as ennoyable as up, as the decline reduces traction instead of adding to it, and rather than giving throttle, I found myself sitting on the brake. In the mine, we overtook a few large coal trucks, and it felt like a virtual track as we moved between piles of large rocky clods and mounds of earth. What looked like a village from a distance turned out to be a huge truck parking lot, with the soviet era blocky vehicles splashing the land with their bright colours.

It was slow going, with trucks billowing clouds of dirt in their wake that obscured all vision. When it did open up again, I relaxed too readily and came around a sharp corner too fast, almost bumping the truck in the other lane. Neither of us was going very fast, and it wouldn't have been too bad, but I dialled it in after that.

We exited the mine through an almost vertical valley that widened as it spat us back out onto a huge expanse. In front of us in the distance was another mountain range, and it felt like we weren't moving at all as we rode toward it. Just before arriving back on the east west highway, Gianluca's front brake issue grew worse. Rather than simply not working, the calliper had now come loose and was rubbing against the disc, as a bolt had rattled loose god knows where along the journey. After much fruitless mucking about trying to find another non critical bolt on one of the brakes that we could substitute for the awol one, we gave up and simpley removed the entire thing, storing it on his handlebars.

Back on the highway, we had lunch in a town with a large Lenin statue, or rather a medium-sized Lenin statue on an extremely tall pedestal. The town I had picked to stay the night that was halfway between Song Kul and Bishkek didn't show any accommodation options on the map. Instead, we decided to stay in another town before then and shift some of today's riding to the next day. That left us with under an hours ride left, so we were in no rush.
On the way out of town, we dodged both a scared calf and a vacant man who found themselves on the highway.

We parted with the sealed road back into another valley, and it gave us some of the most scenic views we've had yet. Huge ochre rock formations rose to the east of the road, with horses grazing in the foreground. Further on, a wide turn was rimmed by a steep slope of sand hundred of metres high on the other side of the river, at such an angle I couldn't believe it didn't slide down into the water. We stopped for half an hour in the shade of some trees, while some Belgian kayakers left the water and ended their trip.

It was only another 15 to the town we were staying at, Kyzyl-Oi, and when we arrived, we checked into our room early. The walls were bright pink, and the red bedding and decorations matched the theme. Gian reckoned it looked like a brothel.

We had hours to kill, so I rested in my hammock by the river for a few hours. There was an adorable, friendly dog just down the rode with incredibly stubby legs, looking like a corgi in a normal dog costume.
Soup for dinner was provided by our hosts, and we slept well with a long but final day of riding ahead of us.

146.title: Day 154: The final ride
paragraphs: Tuesday 30th September

We'd said 8 for breakfast to our host, so relaxed back in bed until 9 after we'd eaten. I say eaten, but I'd had bread while Gian had gone hungry. We'd been served two fried eggs each, but me being vegan and Gian not liking fried eggs, they went uneaten.

We would never commit such an offence as to leave the plates untouched, so we stashed the eggs in a plastic bag when the host left, to feed to the cute dog down the road. Gian suggested mashing one up with a fork on our plates to really sell the lie that we had indeed eaten them, but I thought that would be overkill, and they'd do better fed to the pup. They did.

Back in the saddle for the last time, I had mixed feelings about arriving back in the city. While it would be sad to end this journey with Gian, I was also looking forward to giving the keys back and escaping from the possibility of crashing on the bike. I don't think my health insurance would cover any injury, given I don't have a bike licence in the first place. It would also be a relief to resume my journey toward my eventual destination.

The road escaped the valley that the town sat in after half an hour or so into a wide plain. We came through the town we had originally planned on staying in last night and found three interesting sights at a stop that I will list in order of noteability.

First, there was a beautiful Muslim cemetery, with a crypt on top of a hill and smaller gravesites behind it on the slope. We've seen many of these throughout our ride, and they always sit apart from the town on a rise. Metal crescents that resemble unmoving wind vanes decorate the stone buildings, and silence fills the air. The buildings seem to date from the early 20th century, with unmarked mounds that lie between them that I would guess are older.

Secondly, there was an awesome monument of an atlas like figure carrying a stone on his back. It was marked "100" at the top, with the figure made from concrete and rebar and the rock real. It was super cool, made even better by the mountain backdrop behind it. Gianluca had me take some film photos of him in front of it.

I will not keep you waiting. I saw a sheep with the fattest goddamn ass I've seen on any animal. Seriously, check the photo out because whatever you're currently imagining won't do justice to the wagon this thing was draggin'. Naturally, I spotted it from a mile away, and when we approached the few men standing at the back of a truck I was suddenly asked to help lift it inside. I tried my best with a back leg, but they did most of the work. On the ride out of town we saw a few more flocks of the BBLs (big booty lambs), and I decided against taking more photos.

We met back up with the sealed highway that would pass over the formidable range to our north to make it back to Bishkek. Riding up the road as it snaked back and forth in hairpins bends up the steep slope was some of the best riding I've done. I can finally say I'm alright at cornering and was leaning low on each turn as we reached the apex. The climb brought us to a lengthy dark tunnel that descended at a steady angle before we popped out in a gorge that was lightly sprinkled with snow. Another snaking descent ensued, taking what felt like forever before we reached ground level.

We turned east to head back to Bishkek, the end of our journey.  On a tributary stretch of road, we stopped at a crusty looking convenience store. We each gambled on a snack, and Gianluca lost with some sweet tube things he didn't like. Some young children were passing us on the way from school, so I encouraged him to try and palm the pack off before chucking it in the bin. The boy didn't react as he approached, but the little girl screamed and ran back from him, giving him a wide margin even as he retreated in shame. I was bent over laughing while I'm sure he felt like a right creature.

Our maps were massively overestimating the time it would take to journey back, saying it would take an hour and a half to travel 50 ks. I speculated it was due to the abnormally low nominal speed limits in the suburbs, 30 kph signs being normal while traffic could be moving at up to 80. Maybe the maps couldn't say one can move faster than the official limit.

Riding into the city was tragic compared to the open roads of the last week. I'm glad I'd had a week's practice shifting gears before we hit the traffic lights every hundred metres. It only worsened as we arrived in town, and we were forced to detour by roadworks through a back alley chocked still with cars that even we couldn't squeeze past, only an agonising few kilometres from our destination.

After a late lunch, we checked into the hotel and lay down. Originally, we had planned to return the bikes in the morning, as Sergey wasn't going to be back until 7pm, but we decided to just get it done. The ride there was 45 minutes of thick, peak our traffic. Both Almaty and Bishkek have had awful traffic jams, and I wonder what makes these central Asian capitals so especially susceptible to clogged roads.

Hilariously, Gian's directions sent us through a children's play area. I'm not being technical here. Are the end of a cul-de-sac, the route veered left to another road we could see, through some bollards and between the metal play equipment of a playground. We manoeuvred around the bollards and dodged the girl on the swing, I squeezed through by timing my passage as she moved back for more clearance.

We had timed it perfectly and arrived at sergeys just as he returned from his own trip. He was visibly surprised nothing was damaged and returned our deposit without issue. He huffed about a tear in a saddle bag, but those things were so shit and annoying the whole trip, I hoped it would make him replace them for the next person. We'd paid extra for them, and half the buckles had already been ripped off.

A taxi ride back and the biking was done. Keys returned. I'm stoked at how well I performed, but don't worry, I'm not going to buy a bike. I could feel the risks at the high speeds of receiving an injury for someone else's error, and wouldn't want to roll the dice any more than I had. We'd also never been stopped by police the whole week, which could have led to issues due to my licenceless (not licentious!) state.
We ordered takeaway to the hotel on our way back and collapsed into our beds after showers. It had been a fantastic week.

147.title: Day 155: I walk a lonely road
paragraphs: Wednesday 1st October

Gianluca's flight wasn't until the evening, so we didn't brave the cold rain that flittered down in the morning. He did have to make a dash out to buy a new charger, which he deeply regretted not taking his jacket for, but apart from that, we only left the hotel at 12.

I've been forced to make an unfortunate decision. I will be flying over the Caspian from Aktau to Baku. In the last few weeks I thought I had a chance to secure passage on a boat across the sea, but from further readings it seems the chance of procuring and exemption to Azerbaijan's border policy is slim to none. I spent last night and this morning seeing if I could apply for a russian visa while jn Bishkek, but the earliest appointment I could make with the embassy is a month away, and I shalln't be waiting around for that. So I haven't changed course, but I now have more realistic expectations of what will happen in Aktau. It's a shame to have not been able to make it from Australia to Germany completely overland, but what am I gonna do.

We did some shopping and exchanged some money when we left the hotel, and the bazaar we visited was very beautiful. It was in a huge hall, with rows of racks of spices, grains, nuts, fruits, flowers, rocks, and fireworks. I refilled the seasoning containers that I travel with.

We walked to the hostel I'd booked and shortly said our goodbyes as Gianlucas taxi arrived. It had been a great adventure we'd both enjoyed, and maybe one day we'll hit the road together again. I felt more alone when he left than I did before he arrived, my solitude accentuated by the void he'd left with his departure.

It was a freezing day in Bishkek, and it even started to snow in the early afternoon. It's the first I've seen on this trip. I spent the afternoon curled up in the common area and didn't end up heading to the museum. I dined at an Indian restaurant and meditated over my next steps. It's 40 hours of driving to get from Bishkek to Aktau, and I hope I arrive there in about a week. I'm looking forward to camping in the vast spaces that Kazakhstan has to offer.

148.title: Day 156: Back to Kazakhstan
paragraphs: Thursday 2nd October
The night reminded me of how bad hostels can be. Some people were constantly walking in, out, and around the room at night, and it was incredibly irritating.

I left the hostel just before ten and walked west out of bishkek for over two hours. The walk was relaxing, and the roadwork on my side of the road provided a good excuse to just walk and not worry about hitch-hiking. I bought some breakfast along the way.

Just after 12, the roadwork ended, so I found a suitable spot, plopped by bag down, and stuck my thumb out. Not a minute later, I had a lift from a local in military uniform who asked about my trip in Kyrgyzstan. He showed me a video of Kok-Boru, a national sport of the country. Riders on horseback competed to lob a decapitated and limbless sheep carcass into a goal, with opposing riders trying to snatch it off them. It seemed extremely dangerous as riders fell off horses, collided with others at high speeds, and launched themselves into the goal with the cadaver to ensure it scored. He showed me the 2016 match against Kazakhstanan, one where Kyrgyzstan won in a landslide victory. I wasnt a huge fan, but the horsemanship on display was quite impressive.
At the end of our ride, he ripped off the Velcro patch of the Kyrgyzstan flag he had on his sleeve and gave it to me. It attaches well to my jumper, and I'm proud to own it.

Another short wait later and I was in the car of Shams, a middle-aged construction worker. He drove an ancient Lada, the steering wheel held almost upside down to keep the car straight, and the engine complaining loudly when taken near 80.

He was very knowledgeable about the different influences on Kyrgyzstan, USSR, European, Middle Eastern, and Chinese, and would point out the different building types as we drove past them. He also demonstrated his prowess as identifying people heritage, and would say Russian, Kyrgyz, Kazakh, or Uzbek as we passed people, pointing at them.

He insisted we take a detour to his workplace, a section of a korean language school that was being heavily renovated. I was curious as to why he was taking me through and pointing out all the work. We toured his small town, and he pointed out the USSR weapons facility, the local park, and what used to be apparently the largest sugar mill in the area.

He insisted on buying me some drinks and wouldn't take any money. When he dropped me off, he asked to help him if there was any construction work in Australia, as he wanted to move there for work. A few people throughout my trip have mistakenly believed I have much more sway than I do in being able to help them move to Australia. I said I would if I heard about an opportunity, but that I wasn't in a position to really help.

I was at the border and was able to quickly walk through past the line of waiting vehicles, as I was on foot. The Kazakhstan immigration posed no problems, and I was quickly in the other country. It was after 3, and I wanted to travel a little before finding somewhere to camp, so I made my way to th3 next town with a short lift. After having some noodles, I walked another 90 minutes to a gas station that I knew would be good for finding a truck in the morning.

I almost decided to squat in some derelict buildings in the middle of the highway intersection, but I couldn't bring myself to do it even for the content and with the forecast of rain. Instead, I found a cosy gap in some trees a little way off the road and set my tent up just as the sun set. The place is secluded, and while I can see the traffic, there's no danger anyone sees me.
I cooked a rice dinner for myself and tucked in, battening down my tent against the incoming showers.

149.title: Day 157: Didar & Aibek
paragraphs: Friday 3rd October

My little grotto behind the trucks top was very secluded, so I spent the morning relaxing while the fly of my tent dried from the overnight rain. I took a slow pace, cooked myself a hearty breakfast in my stove, and all said and done didn't leave until 12.

No one noticed when I emerged from the copse of trees behind the service station and made my way to the exit ramp. There were no trucks parked, unfortunately, but there was plenty of traffic on the highway. Not 5 minutes into thumbing, I hear a car behind me and turn to see a new SUV reversing quickly up the roadside. They're definitely coming for me the way they steer towards me across the gravel, and I go to the window.

Inside are Didar, Aibek, and Didar's son, who is about 8. Didar and Aibek are Kazakh brothers, Didar the older at 38, and Aibek 28, the same age as I am. I begin my standard memorised greeting in russian, but we switch to English that they both speak fluently. They'd driven all the way from Almaty, about 4 hours away, and were continuing on to Shymkent, a similar distance down the road. They offer to take me the full way, and I accept.

On the road we talk about my trip, their monthly visit to their parents in Shymkent, and my plans for the next days. Didar offers to host me in Shymkent, which I also accept. I would have liked to continue further, but as it will be around 4 when we arrive there, I'm content to call it a day. I'll have to just start earlier in future. The drive is pretty, with the road stretching over flats that erupt into huge snowcapped mountains around 10km to the south.

As we approach Shymkent, Didar tells me about the city of his upbringing. They call it "Texas" due to the farm warmer climate, its southern position, and the friendly attitude of the people. It's a very spread out city, the largest in Kazakhstan by area, and wedding venues line the road as we make our way into the suburbs.

We arrive at a hotel, and Didar informs me he has booked me a night. He says he would have been happy to host me at his parents' home, but wanted to make sure I was comfortable. I am surprised and just offer to pay for it myself, but he refuses, citing the importance of the traveller in Kazakh culture, and throughout the evening steadfastly refuses to let me spend a cent.

After dropping my bag off we head to his parents' home, a large house very close to where im staying. His gentle parents invite me in and suddenly have prepared a meal they are serving! I was under the impression that we would be heading to a restaurant together, and had neglected to inform them in was vegan up until now! This is the hardest part of my dietary requirement while travelling. I'm very used to not eating for a while or subsisting on breads or whatever I can that is available, thst doesn't bother me. What is difficult is causing offence through not eating food thst people have prepared.

In this instance, I think I was quite lucky. There was a delicious eggplant salad, potato dumplings, vegetable platter, soup with homemade noodles, and bread that I was able to fill up on. His mother was disappointed I wouldn't eat the lamb and horse meat, but I tried to amend this by eating as much as I could of the other foods, which wasn't difficult. Didar didn't seem too worried.

The brothers walked me back to my hotel and said that we'd meet in a few hours to go to dinner. I washed the sweat of camping off me and lay in the huge bed. We met back up and jumped in a taxi to the city, where their cousin Aska joined us. At a busy little restaurant more food was ordered, even though I still felt stuffed from eating only a few hours previously. Along with the food, I had a half litre of Kazakh beer, and a bottle of vodka was ordered. As we ate, we drank vodka to toasts to Aska and his new house, my trip, and the brothers hospitality.

After my fourth shot in about half an hour, I was starting to feel pretty rocked. I then noticed all their shot glasses weren't empty; they hadn't been draining them each time but drinking about half and refilling from there. Goddamn it. I'm glad my stomach was full and I started drinking way less of the subsequent shots, saving me. I have barely drank in these last 5 months of travel, so I'm glad I didn't push my luck against my little tolerance. When I offered to throw in some money Didar did the full horse lips scoff that I don't know if there's a specific name for, blowing and rolling his lips. I laughed and smiled at the fact he thought a guest paying was so preposterous. They were good people.

Didar and I tipsily rambled about the importance of hosting and how it's been lost in city culture. As Kazakhs would have to travel long distances, and Muslims also traditionally travelled for learning or pilgrimages, hosting is a sacred part of the culture here. I want to absorb that and hopefully open up a spare room when I settle for travellers needing to rest. I'd like to show the hospitality that's been shown to me on this journey.

I was very tired so we went back to the hotel, rather than rest, we ordered more drinks at the bar at the base of the building. I had a beer rather than more vodka, despite their protests. After a good chat and arguing over whether the flowers on the table had a scent or not, I excused myself and went to bed. It had been a great fun night, and whil3 not the rest in originally planned on, I'm very glad to have met Didar and Aibek.

150.title: Day 158: Turkistan
paragraphs: Saturday 4th October

Naturally, I had quite the sleep in after the late night last night, and only met Didar at 11:30. It was nice to have a tea with him, and talk about our plans. I truly hope some day he or Aibek visits Australia so I can show them the same hospitality.

Didar insisted on paying for a taxi for me to the next city, Turkistan. I'd stupidly forgotten about the hotel breakfast, but I just planned on waiting until I was in Turkistan. When he asked if I'd eaten and found out I hadn't, we rushed to a small supermarket and bought some hot food just as the taxi arrived. We hugged goodbye and wished each other all the best. I would have liked to have stayed in Shymkent and met more of his friends that night, but winter is coming.

I'm not sure if I've written about this, but I am on a schedule now. My german visa having already started is one thing, and the oncoming colder weather is another. While those are both important points, the main thing is I'm just mentally ready to arrive in Germany, sooner rather than later. I'm looking forward to beginning a life there and seeing what I make of it, and as I'm beyond halfway now, I feel as if I'm closing in. This isn't to say I'm going to rush the rest too much, or I am not enjoying the trip. I don't want to arrive after the end of next month, which I believe is possible.

The taxi ride to Turkistan was intense. The driver was doing 140 while looking at his phone, and I was swaying around in the back seat as he dut across lanes to take corners. I was relieved to arrive in the new city around 2.

Didar had recommended that I take at least a few hours to explore Turkistan, which was a golden piece of advice. The city surrounds a sort of historical park, an open walking area filled with ruins and excavated sites from the ancient city. The highlight is the "Mausoleum of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi," a huge 14th century mausoleum that towers over the surrounds. I spent almost three hours wandering around and did a self guided audio tour, which enhanced the experience.

It was after 4 by the time I was done, so I abandoned any idea of pushing onto the next city a few hours away. I found a hostel with some friendly stray cats out the front, went out to dinner, and had an early, restful night to consolidate for tomorrow .

151.title: Day 159: Aral
paragraphs: Sunday 5th October

While I started early, the long walk out of town to a suitable spot ate up a couple of hours. The highlight was breakfast, where I bought 4 of these large baked bread wraps with potato inside. Most of these that I've seen only contain meat, so it was a treat to be able to try them, and they were fantastic with the provided sauce. The woman was friendly, smiling, which showed her front few gold teeth. She even threw in a juice for me.

I made a couple of calls back home on the walk, which was nice, and I eventually ended up at a service station that seemed suitable. I was shortly picked up by two older middle-aged guys. The driver had a pretty intense manner and was wearing circular glasses with yellow lenses, giving him quite the look. The passenger barely spoke a word, and I wasn't sure of their relationship, but it seemed more business than friendship.

The driver asked about what I was doing, and when I explained that I was headed to Aktau to fly to Baku in Azerbaijan, he said he could take me the whole way there! I was stoked and said that would be fantastic, to which he nodded. It was over a 2000km drive, and getting it done in a couple of days would be great. He then started asking about my flight, and I said I was going to book it once I arrived, as I didn't know how long it would take me to get there. He strongly suggested I fly from Atryau instead, a city earlier along our path but far further north.

When I say he communicated this stuff, it was all pretty interpretive. I was trying to use the translator, but he kept forgetting about it and talking in Kazakh at me. He said he had a friend working at the airport and could help me book a flight and started pulling up flight lists. I did not want to fly from Atyrau, nor have this guy involved in my flight booking process. Many people have helped me on this trip, but when strong suggestions move into strongarm territory, I push back. I kept saying I wanted to go to Aktau, and he would yell back at me: "No Aktau, Atyrau!" He showed me it was further to Aktau, which I knew, and seemed irate when I didn't start agreeing with him due to that fact. I was never scared during this conversation, more just confused and immediately resolving not to fly from his suggested destination, which I had been mulling over, when he started getting full on. Eventually, he stopped talking about it, and I later developed a theory as to why he was so passionate about this.

We drove past Kyzylorda, a large city, and pushed on towards Aral. It had been around four hours. We stopped for dinner which I paid for as a gesture of my appreciation. I thought I'd finally communicated that I was going to leave him at Aral and head west on a desert shortcut to Aktau, but he seemed to think I was maybe staying at the roadside dinner venue. I said I was coming to Aral and he understood. It was only a few more hours.

About an hour away from Aral we pulled into a small lay by with a toilet and nothing else. He said he was going to sleep here for two hours and then continue. It seemed like a weird place to stop, while we were so close to where I presumed he'd stop for the night. They lay their seats back while I lay uncomfortably across the back seats behind them. Both of them instantly fell asleep while I couldn't. Two hours came and went, it was dark and cold, and I didn't know what the fuck was going on, but I was tired and wanted to be in bed hours ago. It was almost 10pm.

I resolved to just grab my pack from the back, walk off the highway, and camp. I was over it. The boot was locked so I had to open the driver's door to find the lever for it, which semi awoke him and he pulled it. I grabbed my pack, donned my head torch, and started making ready to leave while the silent passenger curiously watched from his seat. As I started walking away I heard to engine rev, and the passenger beckoned me back over. Back in the boot went the pack, and into the back seat I returned. It was quite chilly, so I was glad that this meant I would probably be indoors tonight instead.

An hour later and we were at Aral. We didn't turn into the town immediately but were continuing along the highway parallel to the town, and there were multiple entry points. We stopped for fuel and I sussed a roadside hotel a couple of minutes up the road. I didn't know what these guys were doing but I was going to stay there. As we came up, I made it clear that I would like to get out there with gesticulations and basic english words. When I jumped out and shook their hands goodbye, the driver stuck out his hand for money. "Taxi" he said. This was no taxi, and id clearly stated I was hitchhiking when I was invited in. No price was discussed, nor was this raised when I'd paid for all our dinners. Ass. I tried to communicate that I didn't know this was a taxi, and after a bit, he said goodbye and left. If he'd been in the right, he definitely wouldn't have given up that easily. I figured out why he wanted me to go to Atyrau: he was hoping if I'd covered thousands of kms with him and paid, he'd get some good money. A shame of a way to end the ride.

I walked over to the hotel and up to reception, while people lounged around awake in booths, even though it was midnight. I asked the receptionist for the price, and he said it was the last room, and quoted me 75 bucks aud. I'd seen online that the price was 15. I stared at him blankly after he pulled the calculator, a common medium for communicating numbers using its screen, back. He immediately lowered the price to 60, but that wasn't going to cut it for me. While it was certainly worth it, I am a stubborn bastard if anything and hate paying prices that are inflated because I'm a tourist. I should have countered with 30, the max I would have paid just to see what he said, but to instead turned and walked out into the cold, immediately regretting not having that final swing as the icy air hit me.

I wasn't actually in too bad of a mood after the last few hours. I hyped myself as I quickly walked over the highway and into the dimly lit desert. "Cmon, cmon" was my mantra as I found a spot probably too close to the highway but good enough for me then. The lights from the buildings illuminated my spot enough for me to not need my headtorch, but I was still a few hundred metres away.

The tent probably went up in my average time; my haste in assembling the tent was balanced out by my awkward, chill fingers. I was in the sleeping bag, but it was still a while before I slept as my body warmed up. It was only well after 1am I finally found true sleep. Even inside the bag, it was cold.

152.title: Day 160: The sunbleached ships of the lost sea
paragraphs: Monday 6th October

There were no cars to be seen leaving towars the minor village of Zhalanash from Aral, and I'd been warned that there wouldn't be traffic. The sun shining straight down was a relief due to the wind, keeping me somewhat warm, bundled as I was in my meagre layers. The beanie I'd bought on my way through town earlier was already pulling its weight.

It was around 11, as I'd spent two hours walking from my highway camp into town, and continuing to the other side to where I was now. The morning had been mostly uneventful except for the footsteps that approached my tent, a curious camel herder who continued to lead his pack in two columns from his bike after I greeted him.

I was on a detour. I didn't need to go to Zhalanash; the city was the dead end of an unsealed road from Aral, one I would also have to find a ride back up. I was heading there hoping to see something I'd wanted to for years, since reading about Tim Cope and Jamie Maslin's travels through this area.

The Aral Sea was a huge inland Saltwater sea, with an area of 68,000 km2 historically. In the second half of the 20th century, its two main tributary rivers, the Syr Darya and the Oxus, were dammed and diverted for irrigation by the USSR, mostly for cotton. When the water stopped reaching the sea, it began to dry up, and by the mid 00s, was at 10% of its former area. It's maybe the worst localised environmental disaster in history, discounting global phenomena. Fishing villages once lined the shoes, but as they receded back into the desert, the industry was decimated. To me, it showcases how devastating the effects we can have on our environments can be.

It almost feels like the shallow plot of a kids' TV show: evil government diverts water, destroying the local fishing industry and decimating biodiversity in the region, but that's exactly what happened. Can you imagine being an xth generation fisherman in the village and watching the waters ease further back each year, reducing hour catches and sealing the fate of your town? What are you going to do, complain to the USSR?

The sea is still a long way away and is prohibitively far from Aral now. While there has actually been some progress towards refilling the small northern Aral Sea, this is quite localised. Once the water is given to farmers, it's hard to take it away from them. Is another industry to injured also with the fixing of this issue? Even with the collapse of one state, it's not likely.

Zhalanash is only an hour away though, and it is, or was, one of those very fishing villages. Apparently, there you can find dessicated ships lying in the desert, and I was very interested in seeing the relics of the disaster first hand. Providence's hand seems to always provide when I ask, and within 20 minutes a car was approaching from town. It seemed to take forever to arrive at my position on the long straight road. When it did, the two foremen invited me in, heading to Zhalanash to see a jobsite. Perfect.

It was quite bumpy along the unsealed road and I was glad to not be the one driving. We communicated what we could, but there was no internet as soon as we entered the desert, and my voice translator only works with connection.

We arrived at the job site in Zhalanash and I greeted some of the workers for them. As has awkwardly happened a few times, I was filmed and waved at, not knowing what I was supposed to do or say so just waving a bit to the camera. I asked a couple of the guys where I could see the ships and he told me they weren't there, but 20km out in th3 desert. Hmmmm. I decided to take a walk around anyway. It was worrying, as I didn't have internet and couldn't verify his claim, but I hoped that wasn't true. As I walked to the other side of town some kids started to follow me so I said hello and also asked them, they also said they didn't know. Some young guys briefly joined us and they agreed, saying they didn't exist.

Zhalanash was a tiny sandy town in the desert, with maybe 5 streets by 5 streets all filled with sandy tracks, and barely any people to be seen walking around. It felt like a ghost town. I decided to do a lap of the outside of the town and see if I could see anything off in the desert, and then make my way back to the road. I was preparing myself to be pretty disappointed. Out in the desert perimeter to the south-east a bored camel watched me, and I spied a corsac fox slinking into the dunes, but no boats.

I began to head back through town and thought that I'd have to go to Uzbekistan one day, where the best spot to find old metal ships lying in the sand is when I saw some. There were some derelict old wooden boats in an alley forming a fence, and when I explored the area I found some metal rusting shells too.
