They weren't quite the large ships I'd seen photos of camels resting under, but I was excited to have found them. I photographed all that I could find and wondered when the last time they'd floated was. Cpearly not for a while.

Happy with my visit, I made my way back to the road and prepared for a long wait. I hadn't seen a single car enter or leave, and went to photograph a beautiful little religious building nearby. On the way back to my back, a car was approaching, and it looked familiar. I waved it down but it wasn't stopping, and as it came past me the passenger had his hands covering his face, pretending not to see me. The hands lowered and revealed a playfully smiling face as the car stopped, it was the same guys! They laughed and beckoned me in, and we hit the road. What timing.

I wasn't going to head all the way back to Aral with them. My next destination was Saksaulskiy, a city that was actually accessed by a road further up the main highway. To get there via road, I would have had to go back to Aral, get back to the highway, and then hitch a short lift up the highway to reach the road to Saksaulskiy. Looking at the map, the road that I was on and the road I wanted to get to actually weren't that far away from each other, running parallel but not joining. The shortest distance between them was about 8kms through the desert, which I had already decided to walk. I have included a map at the bottom of the post to help explain. I had my compass on me, the route was pretty much north, and gps luckily worked. I just needed to get out as the road turned south back to Aral.

The drive was uneventful until we suddenly slammed into a huge pothole, bucked over the road, and were brought to a stop. The undercarriage had connected with the ground hard, and we were leaking oil. Christ. We weren't going anywhere. I'd already explained where I was getting off to them, and accordingly, my guardian angel had delayed the accident until we were only 1km away. They even pointed up the road and we said our goodbyes. I offered a little money for fuel and toward the accident but was declined. We shook hands with a smile and I trudged into the desert.

The two hour walk through the desert was magnificent, past horses, camels, a small lizard, and a frantic dash across the train tracks. I never lost sight of telegraph poles in the distance, and I knew I could always head east to meet the highway. The cold wind helped to stave off some of the sweat that was accumulating on my back. It didn't feel like two hours before I was at the road the left the main highway and diverted to Saksaulskiy, and I'd aimed right at the serve where the roads met. I stood a little way down the road and began to wave at the sparse trickle of vehicles.

I was headed to Saksaulskiy and away from the sealed highway to try and attempt something questionable. I'll explain with diagrams tomorrow, but essentially I wanted to cut across the desert on an unsealed road towards Aktau, which would cut over a thousand kilometres off my route west and potentially save me days. Today's goal was to make it to Saksaulskiy to set me up to begin the shortcut tomorrow.

It wasn't long until an ancient soviet truck stopped and manoeuvred my legs to squash into the passenger seat. The guy was a little older than me, running oil out to Saksaulskiy every day from Aral. He dodged the potholes expertly with the poor suspension and laughed when I imitated him doing it with his eyes closed. He saw me staring at some camels next to the road and stopped the truck, and led me over to them. They weren't his camels but apparently they're way more chill than horses, and it stood there as he handed me its rope. I didn't even need to hold it as the beast sniffed at me while I patted its soft fur. It was huge, and I was a little nervous as I don't know how to read these animals at all, but it was domestic and completely ambivalent to my presence.

When I was dropped in town I had a fun little bonus walk searching for a hotel that didn't exist, and made sure i got my steps in for the day by wandering around until I found maybe the only one in the small town. I had dinner and fell asleep early, spent after a full day of movement.

153.title: Day 161: The Desert
paragraphs: Tuesday 7th October

Today would be an interesting day as I began my shortcut across the desert. Didar, my gracious ride and host from Shymkent, had informed me about it, and I'd done some reading since. It cut directly across the desert from near Aral(Saksaulskiy) to Beyneu, passing through only one small town along the way, and would be about ten hours of driving. Who knew how long of hitchhiking.

The sealed highway that leads to Aktau, my final destination in Kazakhstan, does connect the east and west also, but it passes incredibly far north through Aktobe, near the russian border. It adds over 1000kms of distance in its inverted U shape that I hoped to avoid. The first pictures at the bottom help to illustrate this.

This shortcut was not without risks, however, as it was a rarely used road that I may have trouble finding lifts on, and I would be in the desert while waiting. The risk reward ratio fell slightly to the green side of the tipping point in my mind, so they were dice I was willing to roll.

I swung by a supermarket on the way out of town to top up on extra water - bringing me to a total of around 5 litres - and some extra fruit and nuts. I honestly had no idea how long i would be in the desert as I waited for rides, but I was hoping it wouldn't be more than two nights. The drive was probably around ten hours, but as I approached the end of town, I saw zero traffic. Even the road into Saksaulskiy was not thoroughly driven, so I already knew the continuing dusty road in the quiet south-eastern corner of town that peeled away into the flat expanse would have just a fraction of that.

It was just after 9 as I arrived at the corner, but I was already cursing myself for not arriving earlier. There may only be a few drivers entering the desert each day, and they would probably make an early start. I should have been here after dawn to ensure I didn't miss a lift, but there was no point worrying about that now.

A young guy approached me as I was walking and started a conversation, asking about what I was doing and for a photo. I was a little curt and tried not to engage too much as I was desperate to not miss a potential ride. He pulled up in his car and handed me a lighter with the Kazakhstan flag on it that I really liked, making me feel bad for not talking to him more, but he obviously hadn't noticed. He even followed me further and was questioning me when I continued walking, arriving at the exit.

I was trying to communicate that I would just wait for as long as it took to find a ride, when suddenly two old guys pulled up. I explained where I was heading and didn't know where their destination was, but it apparently was in the same direction, so I jumped in. To be in a ride this quick was great, and I settled in for a long drive. Unfortunately, that wasn't to be as around 20 minutes later we stopped near a factory in the desert, where a gravel road peeled away into the distance, the one I would follow. They were apparently working from what I gathered, but didn't seem to do much but sit in their car nearby while I was on the gravel road 100m away.

The wind whistled through my thin layers and I could feel its keen touch, so I positioned my pack standing and sat on the edge of the road behind it, shielding myself from the cold somewhat. There was no traffic. It was before 10 and I considered my options.

I could always head back to the main highway and go the very long way around, and it was a strong possibility that that would be the best course of action. If traffic was this sparse here, who knew what it would be like further down the road. I was better off only accepting a ride that would take me most of the way through the desert rather than one that would leave me stranded. I said to myself I'd wait most of the day and leave for the walk back to Saksaulskiy so I could get there before dark. We'd driven 17 kms in those 20 minutes, so it would be at three and a half hour walk back. If I left at three, I could stay at the same hotel and get back to the main highway tomorrow morning. It wouldn't be ideal to lose a day, given I'd already had a side trip today and not made many kms of progress, but it would be better than sunk costing my way into wasting too much time trying to shortcut across the desert. I was content with my plan.

I heard the car start and thought the two that brought me here were leaving, but they just readjusted the position. The passenger beckoned me over with my pack and communicated that I should sit inside out of the cold while waiting, and we could watch the road from the window, which I happily took him up on. It was around half an hour before a vehicle came by, and he joined me when I intercepted them. It was a truck with three people in the cab, and they were only heading to the nearby village of Akespe. When they left I looked at the map and decided I wouldn't accept a lift there anyway, even if one did come past. It was further or nothing. The two places in my mind were Beyneu, my destination ten hours away back on the highway on the other side of the desert, and Bozoy, a small town about 2/5ths of the way across. I mulled over if I would accept a lift only to Bozoy and decided that I would. Some portion of my mind was telling me not to, as any ride crossing the whole way would have to pass here anyway, but I ignored it as my "full send or no send" voice was louder.

A few more rides came past in the next half hour, more than I was expecting. They were all heading to Akespe, even the cop car I hopefully flagged down. Gotta be in it to win it, right? A little after these failures, two large Russian trucks bumped up the road. Come oooooon. The driver was friendly and they were heading to Bozoy, I was invited! My doubts about the destination dissipated with the excitement of finding a lift. I was in the middle of the cab with Andre on my left, who drove and spoke no English, and Misha on my right. Misha had studied earth science and worked in the oil industry, and spoke some English. During the ride, he showed me some travel videos he had made, compilations of his travels around Russia, Kazakhstan, and Belarus synced up to music. In  one of the videos, a tank labelled with a 'Z' rolled by. We talked but not extensively, and Misha and I fell asleep at different points on the journey. The road was very badly corrugated in places and violently vibrated the cabin at our slow speeds. I wanted to recommend the driver speed up before I realised I was a complete layman and he drove the truck for a living.

We stopped a couple of times for brief breaks and each time the driver of the other truck came to speak with me. His name was Nurdaulet, and he was a Kazakh working with the Russians. He was also the one I had initially spoken with when I hailed them, who had said I could travel with them. At our second stop, he commented that I may have difficulty finding a ride heading west from Bozoy, which resurfaced my worries.

Hours passed and we arrived in Bozoy at around 2. The town rose out of the desert, contained in a compact area with a few dense streets. The buildings were colourful, and there were a few cars rolling around the streets, but very few people. Some ramshackle wooden houses were clustered on the eastern side of the town and dried animal droppings littered the sand. I could feel the radiant heat of the UV simultaneously with the cold air. The photos of the bright sand and sunny day will make it appear warm, but it wasn't. On a rise on the southern side of town rested one of the large cemeteries. Identical stone building sat in rows, with a few larger crypts in the centre. Most of the ones I'd seen previously had far fewer buildings, instead having some smaller structures, so it was surprising to find the most built-up one out here in the desert.

Nurdaulet was keen to help me out when we arrived and walked a couple of minutes into the main street after I said goodbye to Andre and Misha. He said he would help me ask around to see if anyone was heading west, and if not help me book a taxi to a town back on the highway waaaaaaay in the north-east, which I declined. He flagged down a couple of cars that passed and asked them to no avail. He then invited me back to the accommodation with the Russians, thinking the matter settled, but it was far from it in my mind.

I said I would head to the highway until sunset to see if any cars passed, and we shared contact info. He said I could come back later, but I informed him I'd probably camp. I am in love with my home away from home and have begun to feel far more comfortable alone in my tent, camp dinner in my stomach, than I do in the cheap hotels I stay in.

He redirected me when I started to head west from town to the southern road, as my maps provided woefully little information. I corroborated this information with a few locals as I left town, and it was correct. If people would head west, first they would go south to the road we had entered on. I walked the half hour back to the T-junction south of town, taking some up close photos of the cemetery as I passed.

When I arrived there it was desolate. I hadn't seen a single vehicle pass, and I was somewhat worried. I set my back down and scouted out a camping spot on the lee side of a dune that would provide some shielding during the night and called a friend back home. Luckily, I had reception.

I assessed the situation and relayed it to Nina, an old schoolmate, and it was grim. The road west from here wasn't even gravel but dirt for hundred of kilometres. I had covered four hours but probably had six to go to get out of the desert, six hours that may not see traffic for extended periods. Nina laughed with me at my predicament, and my mind wandered to what my out could be. My contingency would have to be to catch a ride on the slightly more driven road back to Bozoy and continue from there, as gruesome a prospect that seemed. Given the days I would lose doing that, I did not want to take that option unless I had to.

I decided I would keep up my efforts at this spot for all of the few remaining hours today, all of tomorrow, and head back the day after that if I remained on the vine, as it were. My little foray into the desert would then have cost me 3 days, and I'd still need to get around it. I thought back to Tim Cope, who copped having his epic journey be delayed by 5 weeks due to beauracratic problems, and felt better.

It's funny how quickly after beginning to hitchhike I've needed to come up with my escape plan both times. I've also done it on other occasions, setting myself an hour limit before trying another plan. It's a great relief to know how long I have to wait somewhere and takes the weight of an endless task off my mind.
The sun was hanging low when a car and a truck crossed the ridge into view, the car diverting into Bozoy and the truck parking in my view. Neither continued along the road.

A shining teal SUV crested into view and came to a stop as I waved. It was a beautiful sight in the desert, not only because of the prospect of vindication that it offered. An SUV is a majestic sight in its natural environment as its suspension cruised over the terrible road, contrasting sharply to how much I loathe seeing them in the city (get your fucking oversized american masculinity aid out of my Inner West.) I told Nina to wish me luck as I put her on hold.

They were well-known Kazakh travel bloggers, as I later found out, with over half a million followers on insta. More importantly, they agreed to take me! My photo was taken with a gigantic telescopic lense as I did my best to smile into the setting sun. Although it was hard to show it as I battled against the squinting instinct, I was absolutely beaming inside. I was going to make it out of the desert, and the thought of having to backtrack evaporated into a passing fantasy. They dissolved with glee.

A second vehicle was following, which I jumped in. It was a couple, and the interior was lined with expensive looking jackets, photography equipment, and a drone. While we drove, they swapped places, and the guy flew the drone alongside the truck at a distance to capture some beautiful golden hour footage. Their english wasn't great and we had a limited conversation. We stopped again to capture some photos of a fox and the other vehicle. At one point, they had a bit of a spat that was quite awkward for me, but I don't think that made it to the feed. It's all fake, folks. I am the only reliable source of truth in this rogues den of an internet.

Dark covered the night, and while we could travel far, far faster than the previous russian truck, we were hours away from Beyneu. I wasn't sure if they were planning on stopping for the night, or even had camping equipment with them. I asked the driver if we were stopping and he confirmed that we would be going all the way to Beyneu tonight. Oh boy. Pros and cons.

There wasn't too much to say about the rest of the journey, I was tired and fell asleep after 11, and at one point we hit a lump in the road at such speed it even slammed into the high frame of the SUV. Both vehicles stop and the three guys took a look at it, but we continued at the same speed afterwards.

We closed in on Beyneu just after midnight, and I weighed my options. I could jump out wherever and camp, but it was only a few degrees above 0 and the prospect of a warm hotel was extremely appealing. I stuck with them to see where we'd end up. They chucked the hazards on and started driving at 40, the other vehicle escorting us. The driver said we'd go to a mechanic and then a hotel, so I stuck by them.

It seemed we had received some damage from the impact, and what are the chances that two vehicles had required attention on consecutive days? I'll have to make a list of how many times this has happened on this trip, but I'm starting to feel like quite the ill omen for the unsuspecting driver that picks me up. Surely, this can't continue at this rate?

The car was driven into a garage bay over the pit, and a couple of mechanics greeted us. The men all swarmed the front of the car while I waited in the cold. It bit through my sweater. 1am came and went, and after half an hour of waiting, I was ready to make my own way, very tired. I didn't rate my chances of finding a hotel in this small city highly, so called a taxi to the edge of town where I could again race to set up my tent in the cold and dive into my bag. The requested ride was never accepted, which made sense. It was late and not a large city.

Instead, I said farewell and ventured into the city centre. A few hotels showed on the google maps the listing of which I have learned to view with extreme scepticism, even for me, in this country. It was also the shortest way to the desert, about an hour away, that I would unhappily be forced to accept at this hour if I couldn't find a bed.

I must be leeching the luck from my gracious hosts along my travel, and surely you agree with the sheer number of times I've been incredibly lucky juxtaposing sharply against the wounds the vehicles that bear me receive. The first hotel I tried was open, and when I knocked, a tired but sweet woman checked me in and gave me a room. She didn't even try and overcharge me. Another draught of luck drained directly to my cause.

It was a long while before I slept around 4, as the brief sleep I had taken in the ride and exciting finish to the night had thoroughly reinvigorated me. I spoke with Riley back home for a while. This day had delivered more than I had dared ask of it, as I had accounted for spending days in the desert. I was ecstatic, and the high of this magnificent day will be a long while in dimming. This is one of the ones you remember forever. I fell asleep feeling warm and fuzzy, and I'm sure I smiled as I did. I messaged the influencers, informing them that this hotel was an oasis in a sleeping city before I joined it.

154.title: Day 162: Aktau
paragraphs: Wednesday 8th October

I had fallen asleep late last night, so I left my hotel at 12, treating myself to a much needed rest after the streak of tiring days. I had lunch at a restaurant on the way out of town and was at the highway that headed west out of Beyneu around 1. Aktau was my final destination in Kazakhstan, a city resting on the eastern coastline of the Caspian Sea, and was only 5 hours drive away.

I was unsure of if I'd be able to make it there today as I was starting so late, but within minutes a car pulled up that was heading directly there, and the driver agreed to take me without hesitation. He was an older man who spoke a little English and had a professional demeanour. Previously, he had worked as an engineer, lecturing at the university and working in the oilfields. We made some use of the translator to converse. He seemed unimpressed by my trip, saying, "Why waste time?" And something about needing to work to invent things that didn't translate well. He seemed mollified by the fact I had worked for a few years, lol.

The drive brought us from the desert down into a rocky basin, and it provided some scenic views as we descended a gentle valley between some white cliffs that transitioned from vertical faces to the horizontal ground with curves like frozen waves.

After a couple of hours we turned off the main highway down a still sealed but single lane road into the countryside. I checked my map and it seemed to reconnect to a different highway that would lead to Aktau, like we were travelling from one corner of a square to another and had picked the other two sides instead.

We gradually approached a shining golden monument on a hill, and I think this was the reason we came this way. He drove us to the carpark at the base of the path but declined to come with when I started to walk. Instead, he rolled out a large mat from his trunk and lay in the gentle lowering sun.

The brief walk to the monument was very rewarding. The main part of the monument was a large white tower capped with a golden dome that blazed in the setting sun. Connected to it at the front sides were two smaller towers, with similar but smaller caps. Nearby was an imposing wolf statue on a pedestal and an elevstdd fire brazier that would impressive when lit. Atop the hill, the gusty wind rushed my absorption of the sight.

Next, we pulled over for another camel, and he captured a great photo of it sniffing into my neck. It was so chill with me petting it, I really hope I find some in a field while camping somewhere so I can interact with them more. They have beautiful thick curly fur like if Edge and prehensile lips they reach out with. A small natural spring with a sign dedicated to some sort of folk hero or something provided a nice refreshing splash.

Just as we made it back to a highway that swung straight toward Aktau, the spectre curled a third bony finger. Not 100m onto the road, we heard a  flapping sound after mounting up onto the asphalt from the gravel. A tyre had deflated. He had a spare but no jack, and it was a little while before we flagged someone down with one. Once we had it, it was easy work replacing it and we were back on our way shotly albeit at a slower pace on the narrow, janky looking spare. Three vehicular problems in three days.
It was night when we arrived on the outskirts of Aktau and passed through the fields of pumpjacks gently nodding in the darkness like fent zombies.

As we returned into reception and could use the translator, we had an insightful conversation. It started by him asking me if I had a wife, a common question. I answered saying no, I probably wouldn't be allowed to be hitchhiking through Kazakhstan if it did, which generally gets a laugh. He didn't go for the joke and responded that in Kazakhstan, women don't control their men, but the opposite and that the man led. I explained that in Australia, partnerships were equal, and he said that women could never occupy the role of a man. When I said that women are just as capable as men, he said that even though his late wife was also a professor, she deferred to him as the head of the household. I didn't want to continue the discussion, thinking that more disagreement on my part could be perceived as a slight against his marriage, and just said that our cultures were very different. At one point during the discussions, which was slightly longer than the summarisation above, he said that women were taught to be submissive and listen to men, an absolutely terrible statement. Feminism is needed the world over, and I hope the following generations reject these sexist ideals bit by bit.

When he dropped me in town he was proud to showcase the large buildings of Aktau, a city wealthy from oil and trade. He rejected my offer of money for fuel also, and I wished him and his sons the best.

I had some packet ramen at a korean shop where they cook your chosen packet and toppings for you, and then headed to a hostel. It's an army barracks style sleeping arrangement, two rows of beds with heads against the walls and feet inward, rather than the typical bunk in the wall. I had some chips from the supermarket for dinner and went to bed. I booked only one night so I could change to a hotel if there was a snorer.

155.title: Day 163: Recuperation
paragraphs: Thursday 9th October
Today I did barely anything.

In the morning I booked my flight to Baku and paid for my Azerbaijan Visa, and I'll be flying on Sunday. Having these three days of forced idleness in Aktau is what I need before landing in the Caucasus.

I had a great sleep in, did my washing, stitched some tears on my clothes, and only went for an excusion out for dinner. I met a fellow Aussie and then a Canadian that I really liked. He had an early morning flight, so we stayed up talking politics for a couple of hours. I might catch up to him in Georgia, but who knows. The Aussie also wanted to try hitchhiking, so I offered to show him the roles if I see him over the Caspian. It was nice to have some normal conversations in English, and I suspect ill be having way more from here on out as I head into Europe.
It was a long while before I fell asleep for some reason, not sure why. I couldn't stop thinking about what arriving in Germany would be like.

156.title: Day 164: A stroll
paragraphs: Friday 10th October
Another day idled away, waiting for my flight to Baku on Sunday.

At lunch, I went for a stroll for a couple of hours, following the shoreline of the Caspian into town. It is a sea, but I was still surprised at how ocean like it is, the sandstone shoreline looking like it could be from the Australian coast. People were even swimming, but it was a bit chilly for me.

I'd planned on visiting the museum but decided to put it off until tomorrow, when I'd come into town and get a few more things done. Those plans were nixed at the hostel later when I met a German guy who was doing a one day tour to the National Park a few hours away. I'd been recommended it before, so an English guy and I decided to join him, and signed up in the evening for tomorrow.
The tour will go from 7am until 11pm, but coveres 5 different sights throughout the day. I'll just have to buy the new shoelaces I need another day.

157.title: Day 165: Ustyurt National Reserve
paragraphs: Saturday 11th October
The day started early, with Felix, Paul and I getting up to our 6 am alarms.  I'll let you figure out who was german and who was english.

We were heading out on a full day tour of the National Park, which started at 7 and ended at 11. Pm. We took a taxi to meet the bus, and waited in the cold for it to arrive. I had only fallen asleep around midnight so was pretty keen to get on the bus and fall back asleep. The bus arrives, we pile on, and in the back row I rest my head as best I can on my sweater. To our absolute delight, within 15 minutes of beginning our voyage we had left the city onto some of the worst unpaved roads I had seen <3 sitting in the very rear of the bus also provided the most powerful cantilevering action to launch us off our seats at every bump, sweet! No sleep was had.

An hour and a half later, we arrived at the first site. It was a narrow canyon, around ten metres deep, that we were dropped off above. Some tourists walked so close to the edge I could barely watch. We walked down to the entrance and inside, and the sandstone was eroded into organic porous looking patterns, reminding me of the reticulum of a ruminant or the gills of a mushroom. The whole area was shrouded in a thick mist, lending an ethereal, purgatory like atmosphere. The dampened voiced of the other tourists penetrated to us from the obscured shades.

We then visited an underground mosque that's now unesco listed and had lunch, with over an hour of driving in between each. The afternoon until sunset was spent mostly driving, with three half hour stops at canyon viewpoints. To round out the day, we drove around 3 more hours back to Aktau, arriving at 11pm without dinner.

There was a guy from China, Dengyi, on the tour who was also staying in our hostel, so the four of us went out for dinner. It was a fun end to the day, with us trying and failing to order food correctly, as none of us spoke Kazakh or Russian.
I was glad to get out and see the national park, but I would probably reconsider doing this tour given the amount of driving.

158.title: Day 166: Combo breaker!
paragraphs: Sunday 12th October
Azerbaijan! The Caucasus!
My flight today brougut me from Aktau in Kazakhstan to Baku in Azerbaijan. With this leap, my overland track record that had taken me from Australia to Aktau was broken, a most unwelcome development.

But there's no use crying over spilt soymilk, so off to the airport I went. My flight was at 4 so I managed to fit in a lunch with Paul beforehand, and we had a good laugh about the night before, and discussed our travel plans.

The airport experience was quite smooth, and I gave my remaining Kazakh 5 bucks to another traveller who was eyeing up the kiosk. The flight was an hour long, cancelled out by the hour time zone difference, meaning I arrived at 4 pm also.

Once I was through customs to the other side in Baku, I was waiting in line for the airport bus that would take me into the city. When it arrived it turned out they didn't accept card nor cash, and some other travellers and I missed it as we had to deal with an annoying ticket machine instead. One of the others was the woman I'd given the spare cash to, and I found out she was Italian and had been hitchhiking in central Asia.

She told me about her experiences in Afghanistan, and how she'd never wished she was a man more due to the limited freedoms she was afforded. At every checkpoint she'd had to argue about not having a guide, and even when staying with families they worried over her simply walking to the corner store alone. The talks she'd had with the women sounded fascinating, with the younger girls not understanding the magnitude of how much freedom they'd lost in recent years, while women our age went from living relatively normal lives to relegation to the house. Incredibly sad.

I jumped off at a train station and made my way to a hostel, which wasn't much to write home about. Baku is a stunning city, and well-dressed people filled the streets of downtown late into the Sunday night. I found a sim card for my phone, and had dinner at a vegan restaurant, the first one I've found since Malaysia.

I sat on a bench with a cat on my lap for a while, practising my german language skills. I'd talked with Felix and was struck by how much I'd stuttered attempting to speak in german, and it shocked me into resolving to practice daily to ease my oncoming arrival in the country.
The only other person in my room was a large, older man who  snored like a chainsaw throughout the night, the sound rumbling straight through my earplugs. I resolved to get a hotel tomorrow night.

159.title: Day 167: Baku
paragraphs: Monday 13th October

I couldn't leave Baku after one measly night so I decided to stay another, giving me a full day to explore the city. In the morning I went for a nice breakfast at a cafe, and returned to the hostel before 12 to check out. The hotel I was staying at luckily allowed me to check in early, so I dropped my bag off there and went for an unencumbered dag, a special rarity for me, as my pack has become quite the shell on my back.

Looking back across the Caspian to the east, I imagined Kazakhstan on the far side, so close yet so annoying sectioned off. It's hard to grasp while standing on the foreshore that it's not the actual ocean, as the salty breeze blows in over the piers and gulls line the bannisters.

The old town is nestled right behind the foreshore, adjacent to the more modern district where my accommodation lay. The old wall protects a tight squeeze of stone building and narrow alleys, populated with cats and tourists. It reminded me of italy, cars seeming to pull their shoulders in as they squirm through the tight corridors.

Baku, in my opinion, is a charming city. The central streets are full of people and life, but this does thin out quickly when moving towards the suburbs. If I had stayed further days here, they would not have been in vain.

I used the afternoon to tick off a few items from my to-do list: namely buying some jeans, gas, and re lacing my degloved shoelaces. While I completed these successfully, I have one chore that I have yet been unable to tackle: dealing with my reeking shoes. I've been wearing them daily for months, and my sweaty feet have endowed them with quite the odour. What they need is a proper wash and dry, but I need them daily and can not allow them the two days of leave they need, I'm simply too short staffed. I shall have to continue lacing them tightly to sequester the foul emenance as robustly as possible.

The evening came and went, and I decided on my plan for the next two days. I wanted to spent two days getting to Georgia, where I could then do a three day hike that lies just over the border. It wasn't too far the border, and there wasn't too much I needed to see along the way, so I thought that an apt goal.

Finally, I must apologise to you, dear reader. I'm sure you've worriedly noticed the absence of my posts this last week, and I feel that I owe it to you to explain myself. I'm sure the wily amongst you will have noticed that I don't always write these on the day they are titled, but sometimes in the next few days. In this case, this week of entries will be written around a week after the fact. I will not change the tense to reflect this, as I'd prefer them to read neatly together. Essentially, I've been writing these blogs for 6 months now and the chore is weighing on me heavily. I've had a busy week and have not found the time to sit down and catch back up to the constantly growing list of days behind that I am. I will do my best to alleviate this.

160.title: Day 168: A real hole in the wall joint
paragraphs: Tuesday 14th September

As I only had around 6 hours of ground to cover to get to the Georgian border, just on the far side of which was the hike, I thought I could take it at quite a relaxed pace. The pace ended up being slightly too relaxed.

I checked out around 11 and found myself some lunch while catching up with some friends on the phone. I then had to figure out the Baku bus system to get to the edge of town, which was another hour and a half, leaving me finally at an acceptable spot around 1:30. Cities and sleep ins cost me much time.

Hitchhiking is common here, but with the expectation that you'll pay. Many locals are happy to turn their car into a taxi whenever someone is waiting by the side of the road. I, however, am hitchhiking as you well know, and this leaves me turning down constant paid lifts. At least people are stopping though, and it feels more like making progress towards finding a ride than standing there ignored.

Not too long into my wait a couple of guys grab me and are heading through the town I want to stop in. They're chill and we use the translator to talk a little about the country. I jumped out at Gobustan, where I wanted to see the caves on the south side of the town. There was a mausoleum on the north side of the town that led to some confusion as they thought I wanted to go there and was getting out at the wrong spot. I reassured them I wanted to get out, though internally I was worried I was wrong as google maps isn't as reliable here as back home.

I dashed across the highway after some encouragement from locals that it was the only way to cross, and made my way up a hill to the outskirts of town overlooking a valley. Geese complained about my passing and some local children stared.

Just as I found the path leading to the caves I was joined by a local who had heard me from his house backing onto the street. We did not share a language but he instantly gestured for me to follow and 'guided' me down the path I was already walking down. I could see where this was going. The caves were man-made, scraped out of the loose layered rock in the hillside into a few rooms connected by tunnels, with large open faces in the cliff and fire and rubbish holes in their floors. One of the tunnels was incredibly low and dark, and I had to frog walk along on my knees to get through.

I haven't been able to find out how old they are, but they were very impressive, and I would have stayed in them the night had it been later and I unaccompanied. It would have been a far more enjoyable excursion had it not been for this local. He was constantly waving me around the place unnecessarily, getting in the way of my photos, and staring at me chain smoking while waiting for me to continue at each stop. I wish I was able to enjoy things the same with him annoyingly waiting on me, but I disliked feeling his concentration on me.

When he wanted to go back to the other side, trying to usher me through the experience as quickly as possible so he could collect some money and go home, I stubbornly sat down. Had I been alone, I probably would have sat for half an hour or so on the side of the picturesque valley, and I tried my best to relax and enjoy it anyway, but I honestly couldn't with him standing there watching me. I checkout out some caves to the north too and he followed me there, despite me trying to communicate he could leave.
On the south side there were more caves, and I have to say they were very interesting. I tried to examine how they had been carved out but there weren't obvious tool markings in the walls.

I debated not giving him any money as he'd detracted from the experience, but what would even be the point of that. I gave him 5 Manat, about 4.50, and he thanked me then immediately asked me for more. I showed him that I only had two more Manat in my pocket and he left it. Urgh.

Back on the road I was in a other car before long, two guys that seemed aeound 30. They were super friendly and I had a fun time with them as we drove. I hadn't come as far as I wanted and was forced to stop in Shamakhi, only a couple hours from Baku. We had dinner there and I booked a hotel, the town too crowded around for me to camp. When they left I asked for a picture, and in return they asked me to repeat something after them in Azerbaijani on video. They giggled like schoolgirls and there's now a video out there of me saying something silly in Azerbaijani but I didnt mind, they had been fun.
I haggled the hotel down from 60 to 50 at it looked cheap from the outside, but the room turned out to be large and schmick.

161.title: Day 169: Qakh
paragraphs: Wednesday 15th October

Again, I thought I could eeeeeasily make it to the Georgian border today, even though it hadn't made much progress yesterday. I ordered two lentil soups at the restaurant, and they mistakenly set the table with two sets of tableware, unaware that I would be dining alone.

On the road, a cabbie took it quite personally that I didn't want to pay and was hitchhiking, and I could see him talking smack with some other drivers. A few more paid offers later, and a red minivan pulled up with a nice older man who was willing to take me a fair way down the road.

I was dropped at an interesting spot. The road ran along the broad crest of a hill, with only a smattering of deciduous trees sitting atop a carpet of their discarded golden leaves. This clearing extended back from the road for about 100m on each side, beyond which a thicker tangle of greenery overtook. Amongst the trees sat unused seating arrangements, not abandoned but not having been cleared of debris either. One open indoor restaurant on the opposite side of the road had customers inside, and I suspect this area was only used in warmer weather. I wish I had been able to dine or camp here, it was a warm embrace of a scene.

The next driver acquiesced after I declined playing him, but tried again when I was in the car, asking for a hefty amount. I didn't laugh at him but played his request off and he left it. By the end of the ride we were having a fun time and talking, but I still made sure not to withdraw the money I needed from the ATM right in front of where he dropped me.

The walk to the southern end of town was roughly an hour, and when I arrived it was already 3pm. These towns were now lining the southern side of the Greater Caucasus, so to the north the first of the smaller snowcapped peeks watch from beneath the clouds. Some young guys grabbed me, dropped me off a little way down the road, and then grabbed me again when they resumed their journey down the road. One more vehicle change later and I was in Qakh, a  town an hour and change from the border.

At this point I had realised that I wasn't going to be making it to the border today, and that I'd have to leave in the morning. Theoretically, if I left early and crossed quickly, I could start the first day of the hike tomorrow regardless. Theoretically.

The sun setting forced me to stop for the day, and I found some accommodation in a hotel that was inside a sport complex. Wheelchair basketballers were eating dinner at the adjoining cafe while I tracked down someone to check me in. It didn't seem like they received many guests. I only had a 100 Manat bill, which the custodian didn't have change for, so I just told him to keep it. He was ADAMANT that that would not happen, and reassured me he would hunt down change, which he did and returned to me shortly.

I couldn't find anywhere to eat so cooked my lentils on my camping stove indoors on the single bench in the room. They were not that great, as camping food is only passable when it gets the synergy bonus from being camping. There was qlsk a router but no wifi password anywhere, so I reset it using the button. It didn't reset to the one on the back, whoops.
Oh, and I petted a bunch of animals today, which was pretty rad.

162.title: Day 170: The Devil went down to Georgia 😈
paragraphs: Thursday 16th October

My first impression of Georgia was the frogs. Just beyond the border checkpoint, a culvert ran along the side of the road with a delicate stream in the bottom, and as I walked alongside it frogs wojld flush from the sides and launch themselves into the water. They were blchunky frogs, too, large green and brown flashes that I only caught thrusting into the shadows and mud at the bottom of the water.

I didn't end up making it to Lagodekhi, the first Georgian town across the border, in time to start the hike today. Instead, I had earlier decided to skip the hike, as my tardiness in arriving and poor weather tomorrow left the prospect unappealing. The morning had been relatively uneventful, and one gentleman brought me all the way from Qakh to the row of trucks queued at the border.

After skipping past the row of trucks to the pedestrian entrance (figuratively), and also skipping the busloads of tourists at the pedestrian entrance for some reason, I was through Azerbaijan and into Georgia. The passage closed behind me, as it were, as overland travellers may leave the country of Azerbaijan, but not enter, hence my flight. I had no desire to cross back over the border, just as I hadn't for any of the previous border I. This trip, but I still felt the option leave my arsenal in this instance.

Given I wasn't going to be doing the hike today, I decided just to head to Tbilisi, the Georgian capital. It was already after 12, but I warned Alex that I may potentially be arriving two days earlier than anticipated. Alex is an old friend of mine from my time in Constance, Germany. He's English, and is studying in Tbilisi for 6 months for his PhD, and offered me his couch. I was very excited to see him, as it had been around 6 years since I'd seen him last in 2019.

I was walking the hour or so to Lagodekhi from the border, but still absently flagging cars as they passed, to no success. I hadn't eaten yet today, and my Azerbaijani sims reception was fading out as I distanced myself from the border, two issues I would have to sort out, probably in that order. To my surprise, a truck actually stopped when I waved, driven by a Uzbek named Yusuf. He was heading quite close to Tbilisi and agreed to take me there.

I had no internet or food on the 3 hour drive, so was relegated to gazing out the window at the unbelievably picturesque scenery of the Georgian countryside. It's harvesting season for the grapes, destined to become renowned georgian wine, and Kamaз trucks rolled past, piled with steep cones of grapes in their beds. I was amazed more weren't falling out.

At one point I started to drift off and daydreamed about the lentil soup from the day before. I've never had this happen, but I actually tried to bite into the food I was picturing in front of my face, coming too confused and salivating, smiling as I realised what had just happened. It's too easy to miss meals while on the road, and I've never felt hunger very strongly anyway. I'll work on putting back on the 5 kilos I've lost when I get to Germany.

One short conjoining ride brought me from where Yusuf dropped me to the city, and after acquiring a SIM, I made my way to Alex's apartment. Traffic in these ex soviet cities is absolutely terrible, so while the bus services are frequent, they move inch by inch. I just made it to Alex in time before he had to jet off for some classes. He'd also of course said I was welcome to arrive today when I'd contacted him earlier in the day, but that there was a party on tonight that I'd have to come to.

I showered and had a delicious authentic georgian dinner of flat bean filled bread, and potato and mushroom dumplings. When Alex finished his georgian class, I met him and some fellow students, bought a bottle of wine, and went to the house party. We stayed a few hours and I had some nice chats, talking to people in a social setting like that was a novelty, and I was even able to get some german practice in.

Back at Alex's apartment, we demolished my dinner leftovers and passed out. I was stoked to be there, and had had a great day. I couldn't believe I'd been hundreds of ks away in Azerbaijan that morning.

163.title: Day 171: Tbilisi
paragraphs: Friday 17th October

Alex and I had gone to bed around 2 or so last night after the party, so had a slow morning before heading into town. There were a few things on the agenda, and we began by heading to a vegan lunch place that I'd found online. This wasn't one of the main attractions on offer in Tbilisi, but I was hungry and desperate for a restaurant I could order freely at. The food was great, and we walked from there into town refilled.

As we were walking down the street into town, I was telling Alex about the Italian woman that I'd met and her travels in Afghanistan.  Not 5 minutes later, we bumped right into her, and I barely needed to introduce her. It was wild, as if I'd summoned her by mentioning her name like Voldemort. I asked if she wrote about her travels anywhere that I could read, and she frankly responded, "No, but there are other women who write about their experiences in Afghanistan which you can read." Fair play.

The first real stop was a beautiful golden cathedral in the centre of town. The exterior was white and gold, its square layered shape giving me a cake like impression. Inside, there was a cluster of people gathered around a priest as he flung holy water over them and chanted, with relics ans paintings attached to the walls and columns. Interestingly, the only landing I could see on the interior walls that had a balcony was only about 1 floor above us. This meant that the walls all the way up to the ceiling far, far above us were smooth, only windows populating their sheer faces. I wondered if there was some way to access the higher portion of the church, but some high scaffolding against a wall suggested otherwise. I felt a sensation of vertigo as I gawked up at the gulf between me and the ceiling.

Next up we jumped in a taxi across the city and then a gondola up to a hillside adjacent to the city centre. Here stands the old soviet TV tower, still in use but asking for a new paint job. We strolled around atop the hill, looking down into the cityscape beneath us at the different landmarks. There is always a strange amusement park at locations like this, very similar to the one Gian and I had visited in Almaty. It felt like a jump back to the 00s with the wacky cartoon characters begging you not to smoke in the children's area.

From the gondola Alex identified a russian orthodox church beneath us from the architectural style and we made our way there on foot, but it was unfortunately closed. We then walked to the uni where Alex had some classes, and I went and had dinner and picked up our coats from the apartment. I dared think I might have time for a power nap before meeting Alex when his class ended at 9, but had to leave as soon as I got back due to the thick traffic.

I met up with Alex and we headed to a bar to meet with some others. We ended up at a strange cowboy themed American bar with a group of students, before heading on a long walk to a club. I had a blast at the first club, dancing and losing a game of table tennis badly on the table they had.

Alex was wrecked and went home around 2, while I continued to have a great time. I was all ears when another english lad James suggested we go to the most famous club in Tbilisi, established in an old soviet era Olympic pool. At this point I was pretty drunk, and I only have a vague recollection of the photo of me and the random street dog I forced to pose for the camera by pointing its muzzle forward, taken at 5:30. The dog was happy for the attention.

The club was insanely cool, the main dance floor a huge wide drained swimming pool floor, DJs at the front. The cloak room, bar, qnd another dance floor had been retrofitted into the adjoining passageways which I almost became lost in each time I had to traverse them, and smooe machines gave the whole establishment an eerie feel, as the vacuous spaces were filled with cloud. The downside was the music, and I know everyone that dislikes EDM uses this same line, but it also sounds exactly the same. I could not tell the difference from one song to the next in the slightest, and people barely danced along.

I left the club at 7:30, and fielded a call from Alex, who was worried when he'd woken up and I wasn't home. Seeing the sun rising is an awful feeling, and I knew I wouldn't be seeing much of this particular day. I fell asleep instantly in the taxi, but managed to get upstairs and drink some water. Luckily I hadn't drank much since the first club so had sobered up a lot by the time I fell asleep, the tiredness taking up every inch of my consciousness that was given up by my receding intoxication.
The last photo of James and I was taken when we left the club, and he pointed out other people that were still ARRIVING from other venues, to party on deeper into the new day. Christ.

164.title: Day 172: Write off
paragraphs: Saturday 18th October
Well, if you've read yesterday's entry, I'm sure you can imagine that this will be a short one.
I first rose around 1 and went to the nearby bakery for some potato bread things that I shared in the park with a cute husky. Back the apartment, I resumed my slumber until 4.

When Alex finished uni at, I met with him in town, and we had dinner at a nice restaurant he'd spotted on the walk to the abandoned russian orthodox church. It was like a perfect little date, sitting in the courtyard of a cosy restaurant under a fruiting grape vineyard canopy while a cat sat on a chair at the next table. A grumpy georgian waiter served us, and then spoiled the atmosphere by watching YouTube shorts on speakerphone nearby. All part of the experience. I was leaving the next morning, so it was the last time we'd see each other until maybe Christmas if I head to the UK.

A traveller that I'd met in Aktau was in town and invited me to go out, which I initially accepted, but decided last minute that it would be too much. It was hard to sleep, going back to bed around 6 hours after I had woken up, but I managed.

165.title: Day 173: Didgori Battle Memorial
paragraphs: Sunday 19th October
I walked from Alex's to the eastern edge of Tbilisi. Luckily, he lives on that side so it was only about an hour. Adding in my stop for lunch, I was on the road just before 12.

I quickly found a great lift that brought me to the turn of that led to the memorial I was headed to. The driver was a potato farmer, and we got on well. I thanked him for his service in growing the delicious spuds I enjoyed so much while in Tbilisi. If there's anything after life, I hope it includes a brief highlight reel of coincidences, because wouldn't it be amazing if I'd actually eaten potatoes that he'd grown. It scares me to think that coincidences like that happen, and we never get the joy of finding out about them. Like, what if Hamish and I met as toddlers in some play park, and we just never knew?
He was cool, so I asked him his opinion on Russia, interested to hear what a georgian thought. His balanced answer is below.

There wasn't much traffic travelling from the turn off up to the memorial, but after 20 minutes of so, two women from Lithuania and Russia picked me up. As soon as I was in the car, we were all jumpscared by a dog dashing out in front of the car, the driver swerving violently. The memorial wasn't far, and they travelled onward while I stayed to admire it.

The Didgori Battle Memorial is a tribute to a battle the proto georgian state won in 1121, against the odds as they faced a powerful Turkish-Seljuk army. Years ago, I saw a photo of the monument online and added it to my travel list, so finally being there was a great achievement. The monument consists of a towering metal T shape, surrounded by a variety of giant swords sticking out of the ground. The weapons differ slightly in the sizes and hilt styles, but are similar enough to present a united appearance. There were also some faceless humanoid sculptures bearing arms, reminiscent of cave art, albeit 3 dimensional.

I didn't have to wait long before some germans conveyed me back to the main road, and from there a couple more lifts left me at Tsalka as the day waned. The final ride was a sweet georgian family, the mother cradling an infant in the passenger seat, and both the babe and I fell asleep during the ride.

They dropped me right at the "Diamond Bridge" near town, a glass structure that spans across a scenic valley. I balked at the ludicrous entry fee and decided to wander to the north and view the canyon from the side. It was sufficient.

The sun was slinking off so I walked over to a pine forest we'd driven past on the way. I cooked my dinner at a bench, and this particular packet of lentils was terribly flavoured. Rather than follow up my first serving by cooking the second half of the packet, as is tradition, I fell back to trusty packet noodles for the second course. I then disappeared into the thin forest, hoping no one would come by. I wasn't that sheltered, but hadn't seen many people in the area. Through the trees I could juuuust see the road, and occasionally a distant headlight glanced off my fly, but I was undisturbed.
During the night I repeatedly awoke to a cacophony of barking coming from the town. There must have been 30-50 feral dogs running around the town, all barking to each other constantly.

166.title: Day 174: A long day of nothing
paragraphs: Monday 20th October

I'm still unsure where this day disappeared off to, but it somehow slipped away from me before I could wring much proper progress out of it. It wasn't too slow of a start by any means, and I left camp a little after 9 to make my way into town.

The town I was camped near was Tsalka, and while it wasn't a large one, it was stretched out east to west along a thin, dusty main road. Unfortunately, I was camped on the eastern side and needed to head West, the direction I am almost always heading. I probably could have tried to hitch a ride through the town and saved an hour, but I talked with a friend while i walked. I also bought a massive twist of bread along the way and clogged my digestive system by eating almost all of it over the morning.

I came to a suitable hitchhiking spot under a bridge at around 10:45, fed a stray the remnants of the bread, and started waiting for a ride. A lovely old man picked me up, taking me all the way to Ninotsminda, where we arrived at about 12:30. He was heading south while I was veering North, so I said farewell, snapped a photo, and headed on my way. I had a short break for lunch, and visited a memorial to the Armenian genocide.

I ended up waiting on the northern side of Ninotsminda for a long while, finally finding a lift for it to turn out to be only to 5 minutes down the road. From there, another wait ensued until a lively pair of van drivers picked ke up. They agreed to take me to Akhalkalaki (9 of the 11 letters are A,  K, or L) but were actually heading further toward my destination. They dropped of a quick delivery in the town, and we resumed our journey.

Where they left me was the turn-off from the main road to Vardzia, which you'll have to wait until tomorrow to hear more about. The road we had been travelling on had been following a valley, which split at the turn-off accordingly. The road i would be following headed south down the new gap in that direction. In the middle of this triple point, atop a ridge that descended from between two of the exits was the mostly intact ruin of a phenomenal 15th-century castle. We stopped on the side of the road and I snapped some photos.

I was quickly picked up by a russian couple heading down the road to Vardzia, but they were only going about 500m to the base of the castle. They were interesting and had been living in Georgia for a while, and had travelled extensively before that. We took some photos together and I began walking south alone.

It was now after 3, and while the drive to Vardzia was only 20 minutes, there was an absence of traffic. A few cars were coming back after spending the afternoon at the attraction, but the few that were heading there didn't stop. I resigned myself to undertake the walk there, but was picked up by an old Georgian guest house owner. He had no English but spoke a little german, a relic of his time in East Germany with the USSR army in 85', which was an astonishing thing to hear.

He stopped 2/3rds of the way there and I resumed my walk. I'd hoped to be able to visit the attraction today and get back to the main road, but I realised that wasn't going to happen. A few drops of rain started landing around me and I looked at accommodation options for the night. It seemed that there was a guest house around an hour's walk down the road, so I started walking. As I walked some kids picked me up, expediting the journey greatly.

The timing was awkward, as I'd arrived at the accommodation a little after 4 and maybe could have pressed on, but the grey sky shifted the balance of my decision into the staying side. I had a minor worry ar the guest house as they didn't accept card and I'd stupidly run out of Lari. Luckily, they accepted Euros which I still had thanks to Dr Pierre in Laos.
It was a cute older couple running the guest house, and they prepared me a fantastic meal that I dined on alone. I barely had a few glasses from the massive wine jug they set the table with.
I was only a 20 minute walk from Vardzia, and breakfast at 9 meant I could easily be there for when it opened at 10.

167.title: Day 175: Vardzia
paragraphs: Tuesday 21st October
My first view of Vardzia was from a carpark on the southern side of the valley, looking up to it on the steeper northern side opposite.

Vardzia is a 12th century town/place of worship astonishingly built into the cliff face itself. The construction has many intertwined levels, each building joining to the next via walkways and staircases, the uneven and chaotic crowding of the dwellings giving the whole site an organic appearance. King Tamar, a great figure in Georgian history, and her father Giorgi III worked to build the site.

Unfortunately, an earthquake devastated the from of Vardzia two centuries after its construction, the weakened pockmarked and tunnelled limestone collapsing in many sections, leaving only the rear sections of most of the building to last until this day. It was also sacked in the 16th century by the Persians, but some paintings and artefacts remained.

I fed the eggs and cheese that I had been served at breakfast to an old semi blind dog, and made my way down to the bridge to cross the valley and approach the site. My arrival was just about perfectly on 10. I purchased an audio tour and made my way up the hill.

Vardzia is now the scenic highlight of the trip. Walking between the different levels and viewing the carved homes was incredibly special. Each home had multiple small chambers adjoining the main area, with places of worship dotted throughout. Something about being able to walk directly on the ancient sandstone steps, and seeing the view of the neighbouring cliffside buildings from each protruding building took me breath away. If I had a time machine and could travel to anywhere in history, I think I would now go to Vardzia, while populated and before the earthquake. I couldn't stop imagining the shades of people living their lives in the place, carrying bundles up and down the winding staircases.

There is a church in Vardzia that has survived fully intact, and the inside is still closed off for services. Behind it deeper into the rock is a tunnel leading to a well, and narrow, low escape passages that curve in a huge arc to come out above and to the right of the church. One splits off and heads back to a deep drop that overlooks the entrance to itself, allowing invaders to be attacked from above while they tried to breach the blocked entrance.

I spent two hours there and could have stayed longer had the road not called. The audio tour was great also, describing what many of the rooms were used for and providing interesting information. I hope you enjoy the photos.

An Austrian couple dropped me back at the main road, and from there a few shorter lifts brought me to the town of Akhaltsikhe. I had a decision before me, as the road split. I could head south a short distance to the Turkish border and from there make my way north to the coast. I'd heard the east of Turkey was incredibly beautiful, so was interested to see it. I could also head straight west to Batumi on the Georgian coast on the black sea, and then cross the coastal border to Turkey probably tomorrow. The coastal route was a little faster, but they were pretty close.

I decided to let the universe decide as I was hitchhiking before the turn. I would just jump in the first car going either way and see that course through. The decision was made for me, and I began heading to the Georgian coast.

The road began climbing as I swapped between a couple of cars, and the towns became less distinct as farmhouses lined the road perpetually, with settlements in between them. At one stop I made the mistake of petting an excited young dog that relentlessly jumped at me from then on, even while I tried to flag cars. I shoved it away with my knee and it calmed down somewhat.

I was picked up from that spot by Jo, a Swiss that spoke French, English, and German, so we spoke in the latter. He had worked in intelligence in Africa for almost a decade, and we talked throughout th drive. A friend of his had been travelling in Georgia for a bit with him, but he had a few extra days alone that he was heading to the coast with. The road we were on, I hadn't  realised, was not the main one to the coast. It was horrifically windy and unsealed in parts, heading up through a high pass in the Lesser Caucasus. Snow began to cover the ground less that a kilometre away from the road at the peak, taking over from the thick brown green grass. Jo navigated the winding turns in the rental with a speed and agility he attributed to his Swiss experience. It's interesting how quickly you can tell if a driver is in control of a vehicle or not, and Jo had it down pat. We swerved past other slow cars and made what I'm sure was record time through the pass.

As we dropped down from the high altitude, we came into breathtaking scenery. The valley sides were still steep, evenly covered with houses, pastures, and forested slopes. I imagined living a quiet village life here, knowing that it is not my lot. At the bottom of the valley ran a broad shallow river over an oversized riverbed; the snowmelt would cause the river to fill in the spring.

The air was still cold and the sun began to set. The question arose of what I would do. Jo would drive for another hour or so before finding accommodation, but I was keen to camp as I'd stayed indoors last night. We kept a look out for suitable spots but the steep slopes and poor vantage from the road meant we didn't spot much. I was starting to resign myself to the idea of booking a room wherever he stayed, but that's when I saw the thin strip of clearing.

We pulled off the winding highway and unfortunately the road led to an active factory. There was a thin driveway turn off back up the valley though, so I jumped out and quickly ran along it scouting. I spied the perfect spot. Down a steep embankment there was a disused mossy green drive right at the riverbank. I grabbed my pack, said goodbye to Jo and scrambled down to it. It had originally been an access road but I could see that it had been a very long time since a vehicle had traversed it.
The ground was soft and mossy, and it was one of my favourite spots to camp. I ate my leftovers from lunch and listened to the stream flow behind me as darkness enveloped.

168.title: Day 176: Turkey 🇹🇷
paragraphs: Wednesday 22nd October

When I was leaving Tbilisi I believed I could have been in Turkey in two days, so two days ago now. It was fine that it had taken longer than I thought, but I was pretty keen to ensure that I arrived today.
I said goodbye to my beautiful little camp, and snapped a photo that I'm quite proud of of it in the first rays of sun that were cresting over the distant ridge.

On the road, it was a little while before I snagged my first lift but they picked up from there. The journey out of the narrow valley and down to the black sea lasted a few hours, and I drank in the sights as we snaked our way along. At one village, I could see a ruined castle on a hill on the opposite side. Above it flew a Georgian flag, and there were no houses or paths visible on that side of the river here. I would have loved to get out and scramble up the steep forest to it, but decided against it.

I came to Batumi on the coast before 12, but it was difficult to find a ride the short 10kms south from there, taking over an hour. My first step of this annoying leg was a bearded lumberjack of man in a new SUV. He didn't speak English much but bought me a Georgian coffee along the way. I have had almost 0 coffee in these last 6 months, and I could feel my heart beating in my chest, my face clammy. I hoped the border guards wouldn't mistake it for nerves at my crossing and gun me down.

And just like that I was finally at the black sea. The coast was stunning here in the sunlight, but I could already see the jellyfish in the water that I'd been warned about. I have strong feelings about jellyfish. The temperature had risen over 20 degrees from the mountain pass yesterday with the regulating effect of the sea, and I was sweating in my jeans as I walked.
The border crossing was uneventful, but with more dogs in no man's land that I expected. I mean, I guess it doesn't include them.

A turkish man fiercely protected the two scared women accompanying him from a curious stray that made its way through the waiting line. An elderly lady slowly pushed her way past me as I waited to gain one precious space. Dogs were flopped down throughout like they'd been died attempting illegal crossings.

Turkey! I'm finally mentally allowing myself to consider this the home stretch. While Turkey is wide, it's nothing compared to some of the previous distances. Once I'm in Bulgaria, I'm practically on Germany's doorstep. I'd like to make it to Bulgaria by the end of the month, then spend around three weeks making it to Hamburg, as I have a few friends to visit along the way.

When I arrived at the first reasonably large town across the border, I set out to find a SIM card. The first shop had prices of around 5-10 aud for their various plans, fantastic. On my turn at the front of the line, I was instead presented with a laminated "tourist SIM" prices paper, beginning at $50 for 5 gigs. Hmmmm. I said I'd think about it and went to have lunch.

I tried another electronics store that didn't stock sims and he directed me to another store. He spoke fluent English so I asked him if the prices would be the same there as I'd seen previously. He looked apologetic and said that they would, that that was the arbitrary price the big fish had set for tourists sims. It is an easy market to fleece.

I was pretty fucked off about that, especially since the regular local sim card ads were plastered all over the walls of the shops, with prices about a tenth of what I would be forced to pay. My phone is not Esim compatible.

Was it worth it to pay that much to have data for the week I'd be in Turkey? Absolutely. A couple of hours pay to stay connected to maps, booking apps, and everything I relied on would for sure see me get my money's worth.

Was I going to fork it out? Absolutely not. I'm nothing if not stubborn, and as soon I viewed paying for it as letting the companies win, my mind was made up. I used the restaurant wifi to download some offline maps and made my way back to the road for the beginning of a more interesting week. If my posting is less frequent this week, it's not because I'm not writing, but because I have no internet. I'll probably be able to get connected once a day or so in a restaurant or something. We'll, see.

I walked west out of town, admiring the black sea coastline to the north. Some fishermen were scattered around the shore, and I spied one brave soul swimming. A stretched, separated lay-by was the best I could find, but the entrance was unfortunately blocked by a broken down minibus and attending repair truck. No traffic was enticed by my waving at the lay-by's exit.

Three old Iranian women approached me from the bus, and one of them spoke fluent English. She offered me money to take a taxi to the next town that I refused. She said I looked her sons age. Sweetheart.

When the minibus started rolling, it pulled up next to me and the driver asked where I was going. I said Trabzon, and he waved me in. When I jumped in, I was greeted by an emphatic "G'day!" I was just as surprised as he that the other was australian, and his thick initial accent definitely waned. He was from Canberra, a building inspector that had taken a few weeks of leave to explore turkey. It was nice to speak to a fellow aussie, and we chatted for the whole journey to Trabzon. The ladies behind us gave us some water and snacks too.

When we arrived I jumped out with him and we walked around the town for a little while I found a hotel. I'd wanted to camp again, but it was too late and I was in a city. We said goodbye and I had dinner then found the hotel.

Tomorrow, I wanted to make it to Sinop, right near the northernmost point of Turkey. That would put me in a good position to make it to Istanbul two days after, and at only 6 hours away, it was doable if I started early.

169.title: Day 177: The Trial of Trabzon
paragraphs: Thursday 23rd October

I ate some breaded potato things for breakfast and then made my way to the road. Along the way, I bought some more socks, as my now four crusty pairs desperately needed some relief at the fore from their gruelling two day shifts. It was a long walk to a suitable layby, the better part of an hour, and I only started to hail traffic at 10:45.

Similarly to yesterday, the lay-by here was not well suited to getting a ride. The entrance to the separated layby was too narrow, and pulled off from the road quickly at a sharp angle. Even if anyone wanted to stop for me, it would too late by the time they'd seen me on the fast road. Traffic was stopping, but barely anything, maybe one car every 5 minutes on average. I tried my luck by approaching the cars already parked, but had none.

After a while I approached a friendly driver. He wasn't heading further down the highway but wanted to help. He said this was a bad spot, and I agreed, and suggested a service station down the road. I asked if he could drop me there, and he agreed.

When he left me at the service station, it was only marginally better than the spot I was already in. There were few cars, but more importantly, it was on a city road that was only a tributary of the highway. I asked two cars, both of which were heading into town, before I knew I had to move.

To his credit, at least I had been moved forward and was now closer to a different lay-by, which could potentially be better. I walked there and it wasn't, but after failing to get a ride in one spot for a while I always itched for a change of scenery. I immediately realised the spot was bad and looked for a solution. There were a few cars sitting in the lay-by, their patrons sipping tea in an outdoor restaurant. I approached a group of three guys in their thirties, shooting with the two phrases I could say properly: "merhaba" (hello) "Giresun'a otostop çekiyorum" (I am hitchhiking to Giresun.) They smiled and motioned for me to sit, agreeing that they could take me! Hurrah!

They ordered me a tea and declined my offer of paying for our teas. We made some small talk with their limited English, exchanged names, and some pleasantries. The tea was nice. Then, they stood up to leave, and said goodbye! It was all a misunderstanding, and they weren't actually heading to Giresun, but back into town. Welp.

That blow was softened by the fact I flagged a car down not too long after, but that guy was only heading 10 minutes up the road. I went with him just so I could look out the window for a better spot. I saw a petrol station on top of a rise that would slow traffic, and with a broad entryway, and leapt at the opportunity. There was a steady flow of traffic, and plenty of place to stop, surely someone would pick me up soon?

I waited for over an hour, with not a single car stopping. A few times cars pulled into the servo slowly, giving me false hope, and I was honked at a bit, but no takers. What was going on? I'd heard that the north coast of Turkey was a great spot for hitchhiking, but it didn't seem to be the case for me.

I was slowly worn down and decided to take a half hour break at 1pm. I walked up a small rise near the station and sat on the grass. Further down the lot, a farmer worked near some goats, and a happy cat jumped around in the field. Then the farmer saw me, stared for a while and didn't wave back when I waved at him. He went and got someone else who came and nicely told me I couldn't be there.

I went to the petrol station cafe with with the new guy, Cuncur, and he bought me some tea. We had a nice chat and he told me about a hitchiking trip he'd done all around Turkey for 40 days. He said that Trabzon was a particularly difficult spot and that it would get easier from here, which was reassuring. I went back to the road around 1:45. It did not get easier. At 3, over another hour of smiling into traffic later, I was feeling flat. Why was this so hard?

I knew the most logical course of action would be to just persist in my current location, but I need to stretch my legs. I honestly dont know how I did it in Indonesia at the start of this trip when the going was regularly this rough. Central asia has spoilt me, and I wouldn't be able to do that again. My pack back on, I started to walk down the path. 3pm, and I'd come a few ks from where I'd woken up. So much for the great 6-hour leap I wanted to take today.

As I reached the bottom of the gentle slope down from the servo, a minute or two into my walk, a car pulled up. The driver was grinning up at me, and I did a double take after initially looking away. He was still smiling at me. He rolled down the window and said hello, gesturing for me to get in. I approached and said my lines, but to a town further along than Giresun, Ordu. He nodded and waved me in!

This was Ogzhn, the saviour of my day. He was such a nice guy, and had actually done a lap and circled back around to get me after passing me the first time. He said the deciding factor was that he only saw my pack at the last minute. Many drivers will pick up someone with a pack (a backpacker) but not someone without one (a hobo.) He told me about his family and showed me some pictures of his kids and wife. His mood instantly lifted my spirits, along with the fact I had instantly recouped a portion of the day I'd all but written off.

We used the translator liberally, but it wasn't as good as mine. There was a hilarious misinterpretation of me saying "I like hitchhiking, it is a good way to meet people" that you can see at the bottom. Ogzhn laughed and said "No, no, no" shaking his hands at the equivalent translation it read aloud to him before I could stop it.

Two hours passed, and I jumped out at a caravan park I'd found during the drive. Ogzhn confirmed I could camp there, and we snapped a pic before he jetted off. I thanked him profusely, he'd completely saved my day from being a complete failure.

A caravan guest at the park had a small poodle cross dog that I gave a pat. I cooked dinner, and an extremely friendly cat joined me, followed by an attempt by the dog to also join that the cat sternly repelled. It's nice to be fought over.

The campground was right next to the world's second airport build on water, a madmade protrusion from the land supporting the runway, so I had to listen to a few flights come and go. It made me feel right back at home in the inner west.

As I went to bed, it started to lightly rain. No biggie, as I'd seen some scattered showers on the forecast. You can imagine my groggy surprise then, when an absolute downpour abruptly hit my tent at 2:30, waking me up. It was the quickest I'd ever heard a shower start, but I guess that can happen.
