Then, as quickly as it started, it ended completely. I looked up at the big thick water droplets sitting on my fly, shining in the light of the nearby streetlamps. Wtf?

Then, another brief torrent hit the tent and I could hear voices nearby. Were some kids spraying my tent with super soakers, what the fuck was going on? My super soaker hypothesis lasted until the rhythmic sprays came again, with the same gap between them. God. Damn. Sprinklers.

I crawled out of my tent and looked at he jets wave back and forth, spraying my tent again. I shoved my bag further under the fly, one of the arms already soaked. This was untenable. I investigated the spinning sprinklers that had popped up from the ground like diglett and was just thankful that I wasnt camped on one. The voices were from a new nearby canvas tent that had been set up after midnight, but they did not emerge.

I was pretty proud of my solution, where I hunted down some cinderblocks, and placed them a few centimetres away from the sprinkler, the wedge shielded from the spray including my tent. After verifying that they weren't knocked over, and adjusting them slightly, I went back to sleep.

170.title: Day 178: The Great Leap Forward
paragraphs: Friday 24th October

The good thing about not entering a town is being able to jump straight back on the road in the morning. The sky was grey, so I couldn't use the justification of drying my tent to stick around any longer, and quickly packed and left the campground. My wet tent would have to be sorted out tonight.

I strolled down the road a little way and found a wide entrance to a side-street. Again, I wasn't having much luck and was beginning to fear I'd had a repeat of yesterday. After half an hour of a few fake outs, a car pulled up. The driver said he could take me to Samsum.

He was nice but we didn't talk much. Not having internet means I can't use the voice transcription element of my translator, and I can't exactly hand him the phone to read while driving. He said he was going to Istanbul today, and I could see on his phone directions that it was about 10 hours away.

I mulled over asking to go with him, skipping a sizeable portion of Turkey if I did. Eventually I did ask, as I didn't want to be stuck again like yesterday, and while it would be a shame to miss some of Turkey, I know I'll come back. He said yes no problem, and that was that.

The day thus passed quite uneventfully, sitting in the passenger seat and looking out the window. We only stopped a couple of times for tea and food, his quick driving ploughing through the miles. I had multiple naps during the journey.

Day turned to evening and I was dropped on the outskirts of the massive city at a petrol station, wondering how I'd get further in. It was almost too dark to continue hitchhiking but I resolved to use the last of the light, and stood at the exit. A young man parked nearby asked where I was headed within minutes, and offered to take me to the metro station at the university!

The drive through istanbul was terrible, the traffic unbelievably thick and slow. It was over an hour just to cover the 20ks or so to the station. Once there, I jumped on a metro a few minutes into town.

It was buuuustling in the city centre. Old cobbled streets choked with people, taxis bullying their way through the crowds on the hunt for quarry. Cats were everywhere, true to the reputation of the city. As much as I like cats, seeing multiple cats digging into pot plants to use as toilets, and smelling their smells in every street was too much. Discarded cat biscuits and meat lie in piles everywhere, attracting slugs and rot. Having a huge stray population is not a good thing, but the cats themselves are pretty cute.
At the hostel there was a pub crawl starting, but I decided against going. I hung my tent out in the claustrophobic luggage room as best I could and went to sleep, after hunting down some dinner.

171.title: Day 179: Istanbul (not Constantinople)
paragraphs: Saturday 25th October

I spent the day wandering around Istanbul, ticking off some of the main sights. It's a beautiful city, if not overcrowded with locals and tourists, and the mosques are a sight to behold. After breakfast, my first stop was the Galata tower, a stone tower on the northern peninsula above the old city.

While I walked, I listened to a podcast episode on the fall of Constantinople in 1453 to the Ottoman Empire. I was actually standing on the headland over which the ships had been beached and rolled using logs to avoid a chain blocking their entry into the golden horn on the north of the old city.
My next stop was Suleymaniye Mosque, a huge structure with a cavernous open entry hall. Outside lay the tomb of Suleiman the Magnificant.

Inside, I'd never seen such spanning stained glass windows, and as it's slightly further out from the city centre, there's no queue. On the ceiling rings of arabic form kaleidescopic patterned circles, while over the floor hung broad concentric circles of lights a few metres of the ground. I'd love to see what the place looked like at night with them on.

The Istanbul Archaeological museum was on my wanted list before I departed on this trip. It was the highlight of my day. I'd never seen so many roman and Greek artefacts in one place, bar maybe the British museum, and the exhibition was laid out very well. The large hall followed a historical timeline of the region as one walked through it, supplying commentary on the broad strokes of history with each information panel. The marble statues of the Roman and Greek gods and historical figures blew me away with their detail. There were areas dedicated to Roman history, Greek history, the timeline of Troy(which is in modern-day Turkey), pottery styles, coinage, and sarcophagus from the early first millenium.

I spent almost four hours there, and would have done another lap if I could spare the time. The only disappointment, that was quite bitter, was that the item I had come here specifically to see was in a hall under construction. It was a section of the Treaty of Kadesh, the earliest peace treaty that survives to this day, but it gives me an excuse to go back another time!

The afternoon was pressing on at this point, so I moved quickly through my next few destinations. First was the Topkapi palace museum, residence of the Ottoman Sultans, but they were asking over 80 dollars for entry!

I saw that the guard was barely checking tickets and waved my museum ticked to sneak past him. Unfortunately, he was only a preliminary check, ans there was a full gate ticket scanning system manned with security. On the left was an employee entrance gate, so I timed my entry and squeezed my knees through the side of it as the guard was looking away. An old lady shrugged at me. I was sooooo close guys and thought I'd made it, but the guard saw me walking away and made me leave when he saw I didn't have a ticket. I was glad the Ottoman empire was over, as I'd have probably been impaled on a spike for attempting to sneak into the palace otherwise.

I only observed the Hagia Sofia and Blue Mosque from the outsides. The queus were ridiculous, and I'd heard that while beautiful, it wasn't worth it. The outside of the Hagia Sofia was encrusted with other buildings, like a crab that has been slowly covered with barnacles and anemones over its extended life. A testament to the history of the building.

I went for dinner at a vegan turkish restaurant that meant I could finally have a pide! I had to move hostels as the one I'd stayed in last night was fully booked tonight, which was annoying. The new hostel was weird, and the guy that checked me in was tipsy, making me promise to come back down from my room to awkwardly celebrate someone's birthday with other patrons in the same situation.

In my room was the most annoying American I've ever met. I love most of them but this guy was all the negative stereotypes incarnate, bragging about being able to work part time, the countries he'd been to, and giving me unsolicited advice to move my career into tech sales. 🤢 🤮  I was planning on joining the pub crawl that night, but the strange crew there saw me retiring to bed early instead, for the better.

172.title: Day 180: Edirne
paragraphs: Sunday 26th October
I left the hostel in the morning and began the quadruped bus route that would take me to just the outskirts of Istanbul. It's an extremely large city.

This was no trivial task as I had no internet connection and needed to screenshot each individual step so I could string them together. It went well, overall, though I couldn't get a live update on the final step, so I opted to skip it entirely by walking.

The final challenge was finding my way from the rear side of a small town to a service station on the massive outbound highway. My exploration route saw me through empty lots, a construction area, and over a small muddy creek. I managed to completely cover my boots in mud in this process, but found a fortuitous old carpet that I used to give them a good polishing. Having to keep my boots clean is something I'm still learning. On a hike, I enjoy walking through mud and letting it eventually scrape off; I can't do this when I'm about to get into some poor persons car.

I had a hasty lunch at the servo and started flagging down cars. Given I was standing right near some cardboard, I opted to make myself a sign to Edirne, and I was picked up shortly after I finished colouring the final letter.

The ride was two brothers, a tattoo artist a year older than me, and a younger that was studying computer science. The younger brother had better English, but the older still managed to stress that he was not a fan of Erdogan.
They had been travelling all the way to Edirne, so it worked well. I felt bad as I declined staying in the hotel next to them, looking like a cheap bastard when I left to search for a hostel.

It was after four when I checked in, so I chilled for a bit, then walked around the town, seeing the mosque and securing some dinner. Today hadn't been too eventful, but I'd covered the ground that I wanted to, and was looking forward to entering entering the EU tomorrow.

173.title: Day 181: Bulgaria
paragraphs: Monday 27th October
The rain poured down in front of me as I stood in the empty garage, waiting for it to pass. I hoped the owners wouldn't arrive home while I was there.
I hadn't even taken a single lift yet, as the walk out of Edirne was quite long. The race had been on as soon as I'd started walking and felt the chill breeze and seen the approaching grey clouds.

When the downpour subsided somewhat, I made my way to the road and began my wait. Normally, a bit of rain can turn up the pity factor and expedite the process of finding a car, but that didn't seem to hold water. Maybe the amount of water I was visually holding deterred people from inviting me along.

It was only 3.5 hours to Sofia, Bulgaria, from my starting point in Edirne that morning. The border crossing lay only a half hour into that distance, so I was keen to get that out of the way and tackle the remaining distance with the rest of the day.

A car pulled up eventually, after about half an hour of waiting. Surprisingly, the driver was from Türkmenistan, studying here in Turkey. He wasn't crossing the border but brought me to a walkable distance away, and I made it there around 12.

Walking through the border was an interesting experience, as it has no pedestrian passage. When leaving Turkey and entering Bulgaria, I had to walk through a vehicle gate and present my passport, drive-through style. This must happen fairly often, as the guards were unphased. The crossing into the EU was quick and painless, and just like that, I was even closer to my destination.

While waiting on the far side of the border, the rain returned, and it was another half hour before I managed to find a ride. That lift ended and a nice Greek gentleman picked me up quickly afterwards, but they were both pretty short. I ended up at a petrol station on the highway a few hours from Sofia, maybe a third of the way to my destination, at around 2. After sharing a coffee with the Greek man, it was 2:30 when I started to hitchhike.

I thought this would be an easy ride into the capital. I was mistaken. Three hours later and I'd only had a couple of people stop, both of whom were heading in a different direction to me. The Balkans are going to be hard to get through, I can already feel it.

Unbelievably, I was saved by an absolute miracle worker. The sun was setting and it was time to find a camp, so I slung my pack over my shoulder and started to walk to the fence. There was no obvious camp-site candidate, so I'd be tracking along the edge of a sown field for a while. On my last glance over my shoulder I saw a car, and decided I'd try this final vehicle. He stopped, was heading to Sofia,  and could take me the whole way!

This was Nikolai, a local in his forties who made my stay in Sofia so much better. Not only did he provide a great political chat on the way to the city. Not only did he order us dinner from his restaurant, which had delicious vegan options. Not only did he let me take a warm shower at his office building. Not only did he provide me with accommodation in an apartment he owned undergoing renovations. Yeah, no, that was all, but how good! He was such a nice host and dropped me off at the spare apartment, which was in a bit of a state, but had a couch for me to sleep on.
I was, as I am most days, dead tired after the day of travel and had no problems quickly falling asleep on the apartment couch, ready to spend a full day exploring the new city tomorrow.

174.title: Day 182: Sofia
paragraphs: Tuesday 28th October

Sofia, Bulgaria. I didn't know what to expect from the city, so I was pleasantly surprised by the old city centre. There were no skyscrapers to be seen in the old town, the wide streets lined by old stone buildings, mostly three stories high. Grand churches dotted the city, so I meandered around between them, taking in the sights.

I'd secured a SIM card that morning, putting me back in touch with the outside world when I didn't have wifi. Accordingly, a sizeable portion of the day was spent chatting with friends in a sunlit city park.

I've lined up a hike with Liam in about a week in Slovenia, and I'm immensely looking forward to seeing him. He's been living in Europe for a year already, and I haven't seen him since he left Australia. More on that when it happens.

I spent an hour or so in the archaeological museum, admiring the bulgar weaponry from the first half of the last millennium, and the great collection of Palaeolithic artefacts. The museum was almost unnecessary; there was a Roman wall built during the reign of Marcus Aurelius in a pedestrian tunnel under the road.

As the day handed over to the evening, the temperature dropped rapidly. I'd also placed my Kazakh beanie down somewhere while talking on the phone, and couldn't find it again when I retraced my steps. A larger coat would be heavy and greedily occupy much of the space in my pack, but I couldn't delay buying one any longer. My black sweater has done incredibly well to get me this far on its own, but the gelid European wind was biting straight through it. Time for a charity shop run.

I enjoy thrifting and was stoked to find a cute scarf and a thick, well-made coat, both for under 15€. The coat is one size too small for me, but the price means I'll have no qualms about swapping it out if I need to. When I re-emerged into the chill night, my palms began to immediately sweat in my pockets. I'll have to find a happy middle ground somehow.
It was a nice day. I'll have to come back to Sofia, as there is so much more to see here. A shame to pass through with so much unseen, but that's the journey I chose.

175.title: Day 183: Back to the forest
paragraphs: Wednesday 29th October

It's Wednesday, and I'm planning on being in Ljubljana on Monday night to meet Edge when he arrives on Tuesday morning. My plan is to spend two nights in Belgrade, Serbia, and two nights in Zagreb, Croatia. These countries are in between, and given there's 5 nights between now and Monday, it allows me one day of wiggle room if I don't manage to cover the distance in a day.
If it comes to it, I could even cut out one of my nights in either of the capitals, but I'd like a full day of checking the city out for each. Surely it won't come to that, right?

To be fair to the tale of woe I'm about to spin you, I did have a very slow start. I met up with Nikolai to say bye and give him the keys back, and then went into town for lunch before actually leaving. The metro line went quite far noth but I walked for a bit to get to the start of the road leading north. All said and done, I was there around 1.

The first and last ride of the day came quite quickly! It was only half an hour to the border, but he was only going half that distance. It was better than nothing, and he dropped me at a layby right on the highway heading north from Sofia to the border. There was a reasonable flow of traffic, so I started trying to hitch.

Nothing. No one even stopped for me for over two hours. Those that did pull into the lay-by did so by mistake, thinking it was the right hand turn a ways up ahead. It briefly excited me every time, only to be disappointed when they drove straight through. I was sweating in the sun and decided to call it at 4. The sun started to set quite early in this time zone, at 5:30, and I wanted to be able to find a camp before dark. I lugged my pack over my shoulders and started walking in the gutter of the highway up to a forested hill, where a road passed close by to the treeline, and I could dash into the natural cover.

As I walked up the road to the forest, a car passed me on the unsealed road. He was blasting music and stared at me with an impassive frown as he passed. I didn't like the look of him. The car stopped behind me just before the next turn, and I wondered if he was debating turning around and investigating what I was doing. After a minute or so, he drove off. I walked perpendicularly away from the road up to the trees, and as soon as I did, I heard his music coming back up the road. Goddamnit. I made it to the treeline, but he would know I left the road there. I knew it probably wouldn't matter, but avoiding people is the number one rule of stealth camping. Hopefully, he wasn't the curious type.

Due to the encounter, I followed the ridgeline for a while before picking a campsite. There was an overgrown path that I tried to find a campsite away from, but I couldn't. The sides of the ridge fell away into slopes too steep to camp on, so I had to camp next to the path.
Adjacent to the path were some ruins, a deep trench with stone walls running in an interesting half circle shape, with a deep pit at each end. I had no idea what era they could be from.

It was a beautiful spot. My tent peeked under the canopy of the pine forest that lined the side of the hill, and the sunset lit the scene well. I made some lentils for dinner and had an early night, undisturbed by the surrounding forest.

176.title: Day 184: Serbia
paragraphs: Thursday 30th October

I made breakfast at the campsite this morning, something I don't usually do. The oats were pretty mediocre, even with a couple of the vegan chocolate balls that Nikolai had given me mixed in. The dregs went in the bush. Hopefully a forest critter found them more appealing than I did.

The nice thing about camping next to the road is that when I get up, I can get straight back to hitchhiking, saving me the painful hour of getting to the road from proper accommodation. That's the theory anyway.

To get to my campsite yesterday, I'd walked a little south to get into the forest, and then north again once I was in the forest. This meant I'd walked a U shape, and the quickest way back to back to the layby would be to cut straight down the side of the hill to the road. I regretted taking this 'shortcut' immensely, as the bushes were incredibly dense in this part of the forest, and i had to crash my way through woody, spiked bushed that poked my hands and head as I did so. I ended up with a bloody scratch on my right hand to match the one on my left I'd received in Istanbul while trying to pet a grumpy cat.

Nevertheless, I made it through and arrived down on the layby, ready to begin the day, at about 10:30. Resuming hitchhiking at the same place I'd failed the previous day didn't feel great. Rather than breaking into a new day, I felt like a dog returning to its vomit. My luck did not improve, and the midday came and went with no ride. I began to doubt I would make it to Belgrade today, either.

At half past 12, I finally found a ride. Vlado was a Serb in his thirties, and a cheerful guy overall. He told me about how he'd finally bought the cabin in a village he'd talked about for a decade last year, and was enjoying his new lifestyle. Good on him.

He wasn't going all the way to the border, but halfway there. It was only 20 minutes away, and became 10. This initial 20 minute drive to the border I'd wanted to get done quickly in the morning, but it was turning out to be quite the effort. When Vlado left, he said he would come back if I was still stuck there when he finished work and drive me out of his way to the border. We exchanged information, and I greatly appreciate the backup plan. He turned my day around.

I had an overpriced lunch at the petrol station I'd been dropped at, and continued the woefully slow process of finding a lift. It was almost another hour before a truck driver I approached agreed to take me. It was a small truck, and he was dropping off goods at service stations along the way. He apologised for the delay, but I emphasised that I'd been waiting so long this ride was a godsend.

It was 2:30 when I crossed the border to Serbia. It had been four hours since I began today's journey, and I had travelled a 20-minute car ride over my two lifts. The chance to make it to Belgrade today had slipped away from me in the intervening time.

I crossed back out of the EU in Serbia without issue and found a good spot past the border. There were a million cars heading to germany, driven by turkish people who were heading there, but none of them stopped.

Finally, a Serbian chef stopped and was heading an hour or so up the highway, and brought me with him. He was originally from Serbia but lived in Bulgaria, and was headed home to see family. At one point, he patted his large belly and said, "I just love food too much." I enjoyed his company.

He was cluey and dropped me at a large gas station, where there was a hotel and amenities. Serbia is in the central EU timezone, even though it is quite far east. This is exacerbated by the approaching winter, meaning that the sun sets here at 4:30! I evaluated my options and decided not to stay in the hotel; some trees on the opposite side of the highway looked like they'd provide ample cover.
I found a cosy, secluded spot on some soft grass and again settled in after a tasty camp-stove dinner. My bedtime had crept earlier to 8pm, and I slept well despite the noise from the traffic.

Again, I hadn't made it to Belgrade. This meant I'd have to arrive there tomorrow and leave the day after, foregoing a full day of relative relaxation in the city. It was only two hours' drive away, so I hoped I could make it there before noon and spend the afternoon in the historical city.

177.title: Day 185: Balked at
paragraphs: Friday 31st October 👻

Due to yesterday's timezone shift and my 8pm bedtime, I woke up at 6am rather than 7am today. I made good on the early start and was back at the petrol station shortly after 7am. The sun was shining, the birds chirping, and there was a steady flow of traffic refuelling before continuing their journey north, towards Belgrade. It was ~2 hours to the city, and I was confident that I could be there before noon.

The hours came and went. 8am, 9am, nothing. The sun grew hotter as I squinted into it; sunglasses are not conducive to presenting a friendly appearance. A homeless lady came and stood 10 metres in front of me, and I felt like like my turf had been infringed upon. What was this? No one would stop for me with her scoring them off. I moved further upstream and hoped she'd find a ride soon.
I had to take a break around 10 to eat and sit down, but I couldn't bring myself to rest long. What if a ride came and went while I sat around?

I'm not the most stoic individual, and as 11 came and went I was pretty over it. This journey is great and all, but at that point I was missing seeing a beautoful city to stand on the side of the road in the sun while getting stared at like I was in the stockade.

After what felt like an eternity, a truck pulled up a little after 12. He was heading past Belgrade and could drop me nearby. Thank the Lord above, I was away. The driver was a middle-aged Serbian guy who spoke middling English. He was excited to be on his way home to his family after a two week stint of driving, and accentuated the point by honking the horn and hollowing when he said it, probably confusing the surrounding cars. It was his sons birthday, and I re-gifted him and his son the two chocolate bars I'd been given by the trucker yesterday. He shared some crispy peanut snacks in return.

Our ETA to Belgrade was around 3. I knew it would take me even longer to get into the city, probably getting there around 4. The sunset was at 4:30, so I'd barely be able to see the city in the light before needing to continue in the morning. I knew what needed to be done.

As badly as I needed a shower, desired a meal that wasn't cooked on my stove, and would regret not seeing Belgrade, I had to skip it. The route we were taking was around to the west of the city, which was the direction of Zagreb, my next destination.

I jumped out on the western ring road, not quite on the road heading west, but close to the turn-off onto it.  The sun was dropping low, and I couldn't see anywhere nearby to camp. The closest safe bet on my map was half an hour away, a forested lot I was confident I could find space in. I'd give myself the half an hour until 4 to try and find a ride, then call it and hustle to campsite for sunset.

Even though most of the traffic was heading straight north, not turning west, I actually found a ride in a reasonable time. A young Muslim Serbian guy helpfully transported me to the western road. We talked about personal philosophies and anime.

This service centre looked like it was near some trees on the map, but they were inside a fenced off field. I could have jumped the fence, but the fields were being tilled, and the actual bush looked too thick to stay in. I ended up having to pitch my tent on the service station lot, in the furthest corner from the road, but with nothing to shelter me from it.

I didn't like the spot at alm and waited until the last minute before dark to pitch the tent. To my relief, on my return from the building, my tent was practically invisible, and I thanked myself for buying a dark green tent. When the last rays of light disappeared and I sequestered myself inside, I was happy enough that no one would disturb me.

My last ride had said that was one of the things he loves about Serbia. No one disturbs you, and people are relaxed. He said he could grill on the side of the road, and no one would care. This proved true for me, and I slept undisturbed bar the traffic noise.

178.title: Day 186: Croatia
paragraphs: Saturday 1st November

While the darkness had shrouded my home for the night well, the first predawn light felt like a spotlight on my sorry excuse for an abode. There is no sleeping in under such conditions, as I worry too much about being approached.
That was fine, I'd camped for three nights now and was excited to tackle the few hours to Zagreb. I was already on the road facing Croatia, at a restaurant stop, and approached the new day with vim.

I began my efforts at 6:20! Awakening before 6 and not dallying with trifles such as breakfast makes for a hasty vacation. The hours, as they have tended to do here in the Balkans, whiled away in a fruitless slide. The cars come and go, talking of Michaelangelo.

By the time 10 had dragged its way to me, my heavy coat shed and the sun beating on my face, I was ready to take a short break. I needed to use the bathroom and eat after standing there for four hours, mustering all the positivity I could from the dregs of my soul and whipping it into position on my face. Try as I might, I just couldn't bring myself to leave my post. What if my ride came now? To my delight, at about a quarter past 10, it did.

Lilya pulled up and was really wanted to help me, but was unfortunately planning on turning left at the next intersection and heading to Bosnia. It was unfortunate as she was the first to stop in a while, but I thanked her for stopping and said I'd continue my efforts. She told me to wait while she checked if she could go a different route, confirmed she could, and ushered me in!

Lilya ended up driving not only to the Croatian border, but through it and deep into Croatia before turning south towards Bosnia. She drove through a country she wasn't planning on heading through just to help me! I couldn't thank her enough.

On top of that, we had a great time talking. She told me about Belgrade that I'd unfortunately missed, gave me some literature and sightseeing recommendations, and told me about her life. She was a very interesting person, born originally in  Yugoslavia in modern day Bosnia, but currently lived in Belgrade. She'd opened an art gallery at one point, but was now happily retired. She had a couple of kids older than I living in Graz, Austria, one of whom was recently married.
It was a great ride, and she made sure to leave me at a service station on the highway before she had to turn south towards her hometown.

I feared the wait at the servo but a young Russian couple came to my aid before long. They had a cute cocker spaniel in the back, but I didn't get to pet it much unfortunately, as the woman swapped into the back-seat to leave me the front. I offered to take the back seat, presenting it as a kindness when I really just wanted to sit with the dog, but she said it was fine. I wasn't in a position to reveal my real motives to sit with their dog, and accepted the front seat graciously.
They were cool too and had been living in Belgrade for a few years, and the guy told me about his time in China during lockdown, when his company offered the opportunity to work there for a while.
I alighted the ride right near my hostel, as they were staying in Zagreb nearby.
I'd made it.

I checked in to the party hostel, planning on joining the pub crawl that night in celebration of getting back to a city. These plans were extinguished when I arrived back at the hostel after dinner. When I had excitedly booked the party hostel at 3pm, I had not accounted for the fact that my bedtime the last two night had been 8pm. The pub crawl started at 9:30.

I ceded the day to the crushing wave of fatigue that hit me, and collapsed into bed after a rejuvenating shower. One of the hostel staff had said they were going to watch Twilight when the pub crawl left, and invited me. It sounded great and I wanted to join, but I didn't make it down the stairs.
Sweet, sweet bedsheets.

179.title: Day 187: Zagreb
paragraphs: Sunday 2nd November
Ah, finally a full day I can spend wandering around a city, and not mentally decomposing as I stand beside the road for hours on end. I'm ready to wrap this endeavour up.

Zagrab makes me feel like I'm finally in Western Europe. Trams shuffle down the cobbled streets, and tourists gape around the main square, but not an overwhelming number. I've been to Zagreb before in 2016, and was looking forward to visiting the city again. The museum of naive art, which is the main attraction I am excited to see again, is unfortunately only open tomorrow.

I had quite a relaxed day. I spend most of it sitting, be that in a cafe, restaurant, or park, enjoying watching the sights. The time sitting I used to catch back up on these entries. A park I sat in was carpeted with discarded leaves, littering the floor in a sharp gradient from the clear open spaces to the covered bases of the trees.
In the late afternoon, I strolled around the higher side of town and looped back to the hostel, taking some photos as the sun set. I dined at a restaurant and called it a night.
I didn't really speak to anyone bar the new French arrival in my hostel room, who I had a nice talk about life, meaning, and travel with before bed.
Today was a day I needed to relax after the last few epics, and I felt ready for tomorrow's small journey to Ljubljana when I hit the sack.

180.title: Day 188: Whoops
paragraphs: Monday 3rd November

The first fun surprise of the day was when I made my way up to the naive art museum, and it was closed for two weeks! I've had art from the museum on my wall for years and was excited to see the originals, but I'll just have to come back another time.

I returned to the hostel to pick up my bag and went for an early lunch, then made my way out of town to start hitchiking. It's under two hours' drive from Zagreb to Ljubljana, and I was confident I could track swiftly along the main highway. The journey out of town involved a tram and a bus, but after a little over an hour, I finally found myself near the road leaving town. It was around 12:30.

The spot I was in didn't seem great. There wasn't a nice spot for cars to pull into, just an entry ramp for a servo, nor was the traffic all leaving the country. Most of it seemed to just be heading to the west of Croatia. After 1 came and went, I decided to try my luck on the exit ramp for the service station. Even though there would be a hundredth the traffic, I think being one on one with cars and having a suitable place for them to stop does increase the odds of a pick up by over a hundred fold.

This seemed to work, and after only a few cars drove past me, a woman stopped and picked me up. She was only driving 10 minutes up the road, but importantly it was past an intersection that I knew was diverting much of the traffic away from my destination, and it would be beneficial to continue from the far side of. She was a psychologist and said she was thus able to tell I wasn't a threatening guy when she saw me.

When she dropped me at a service station at around 1:30, I received a message from Romain, the French guy I'd had a nice conversation with last night. He told me that the hostel had asked him if he knew me, as apparently I'd left some important stuff in the room locker, namely my passport and cash. Fuuuuuuck.

I had, in fact, left my passport and money at the hostel. Normally, I never used the hostel lockers, but I had figured yesterday that it was a party hostel and that I'd be out for a few hours, so I should put my valuables inside. When leaving this morning, I'd completely forgotten about them, even though I went as far to check under my bed otherwise.

I needed to make it to Ljubljana today. Liam was arriving in the morning, and I had to be there for that. There was no time to delay or hitchhike back to the hostel and back, so after cursing my stupidity for a minute, I dialed it in and called a taxi back. It was expensive, but I didn't have an alternative.

I spent the next hour and a half making my way back into the city with the cab, picking up my valuables from reception, and then heading back out of the city the same way. The driver told me we'd just been fast enough to avoid the incoming peak hour that would have slowed us down greatly.

On the way back to the service station I realised that the actual border was only another 5 minutes down the road, so had the taxi take me there instead. I jumped out in front of a toll gate and stood in between two lanes where they split to pass through the gate. As I turned to face the music and stuck my thumb out, a car waved me in immediately.

This driver was a middle aged woman from Ljubljana, and agreed to take me all the way there, finishing my day. It was a beautiful drive along the well developed motorway in the flatter southern half of Slovenia, and we spoke about the hiking options in the area. She gave me some delicious mandarins from her mum's garden, and before I knew it we were coming through the outskirts of the small capital to the central train station.

I checked into a nearby hostel and spent the evening walking along the river after dinner. The cobbled riverside boulevard was populated with outdoor seating areas and hanging lights, and I had a beer at one of the cozy tables.
In about 12 hours, I'd get to see Liam, marking a clear step toward the very final stages of my trip.

181.title: Day 189 - 191: Hiking in Slovenia.
paragraphs: Tuesday 4th - Thursday 6th November

I waited excitedly for Liam in the hostel lobby, and ran out to greet him when he made his way down the street at 8:30. It had been over a year since I'd seen him in person, but we'd stayed in great contact online with frequent chats so it strangely felt like it hadn't been that long.

We quickly caught up over breakfast and then started planning the hike. Unfortunately we weren't able to explore the mountains in the north of the country, due to the low temperatures and Liam's knee injury, but picked a section of forest very close to the capital that would most likely make for some easy hiking. We planned a rough route and the campsite we picked for the first day was actually only four hours walk from our current location in the inner city, so that's where we began.

We made our way outward from the inner city, stopping to pick up some food on way, and soon the large buildings fell away behind us. They were replaced by residential housing, which itself was soon interspersed with plots of farmland. We found it surprising that even on the very outskirts of the city, there was no sign of poverty, or even cheaper housing, at all. From my Australian perspective land prices are much lower when in areas that also contain farmland, but that didn't seem to be the case here.

We wound over a highway and then turned into a valley to the west, following the road deeper as it tracked along the flat valley bottom. There was unfortunately no pavement on the side of the road, and while the scenery was beautiful, we were looking forward to getting into the forest.

After an hour and change of walking, we diverted perpendicularly away from the road and began ascending into the orange leaf covered hills. At one point we had to backtrack for 15 minutes into reception to submit our diplomacy orders.

The trail we follow split and branched as we pursued it to higher elevations, passing through some farmland on the lower slopes before disappearing into the woods as we approached the ridgeline. For such a thick forest, the species count of the trees was surprisingly low, with spaced beech trees covering most of the land we crossed. At their feet were some sparse bushes, but mostly lay covered with the thick blanket of their lost leaves, smothering the forest floor with a dense carpet.
The one point of diversity we were pleased to witness was the periodic sighting of mushrooms. They poked out of the ground here and there, various shapes of mostly whitish colours.

The campsite we could see on our map had little information concerning it, but it was nevertheless our goal for the day. A steep descent down a disused pathway finally expelled us onto a worn path, only a few hundred metres from the camp. We were mentally preparing for a cold night, and arrived at our destination after 4.

As we approached, we saw the flat of the campground and a middle aged man chopping some firewood near a car. He smiled upon seeing us and came over to greet us. His name was Janko and he was very cheerful and friendly, and asked where we had come from and where we were headed. We filled him in on our trip and he was delighted to have us, and invited us to warm up in his guest cabin nearby. He had built everything himself, and we were amazed by the site.

He shared some whiskey with us and started the fire for us, saying that we could sleep inside if we wished. I was stoked to have some indoor sleeping away from the frosty oncoming night, and asked him how much we should pay for the accommodation.
"Oh, it's ok" he said, "The season is over so no cost."
What a hero! We insisted on giving him some money after he even said we could have any beers from the cupboard we wanted.
He didn't stay too long but said he would take us out for coffee tomorrow morning in his nearby village. We accepted his offer and organised to meet again at 9.
Liam and I cooked on the stove above the fire and inflated our mats on the floor of the cabin.

The next morning our slow start kept Janko waiting for five minutes while we hurriedly packed our belongings. We jumped in his car and he drove through his village to a cafe in the cozy town centre. As we passed through his village he pointed to where he and his relatives lived in the white, two story houses, and I imagined what a life like that would be like. Living with friends and family around while being less than half an hours drive from the capital seems like a beautiful dream.

We drank a coffee together and then were dropped at the local supermarket. Normally, Liam and I consume copious amount of hummus while hiking, but this time we angled for a 1kg bucket of sauerkraut instead. I will not repeatedly detail the attacks on the sauerkraut over the next day, but I have to say it was a fantastic hiking snack with the bread rolls and baguette we had bought. I don't quite think it is a strong enough contender to dethrone the reigning position hummus holds over my hiking diets, but I'll definitely be buying more in future.

From the village of Polhov Gradec we climbed the hills to the north, once again hitting the ridgeline above the valleys. It came to a head when we reached a peak, rising above the path and with a great view over the surrounding valleys. While we stood under a clear sky, we could see that low-lying Ljubljana in the distance was still covered under a thick carpet of fog. In the middle distance, a break in a ridgeline acted as a spout in slow motion, and we could see where the clouds were slowly spilling through and dissolving into the transparent air.

We ascended to the highest point in our vicinity, and ate lunch while gazing towards some distant peaks. The forested region we were in wasn't massive, and we could see roads and farmland 15-20 kilometres before us. We decided to not push the distance, to give us something to do tomorrow, and just walk another 5 or so km before settling in for the night on a small ridge next to the path.

The campsite was quite an interesting one, positioned on the narrow ridge with steep but scrambleable slopes on either side. We patted down the soft leaves and pitched the tent as chill air started to crest the ridge and force us indoors.

The final day of walking brought us back into civilisation. We exited the forest into a beautiful hillside village, with bee boxes and paddocks cutting into the thick trees. We sat on a bench and pet a large friendly black cat that was sniffing about for food, while other day trippers took similar breaks from their walking and mountain biking nearby. From the village we rose again to find a white church perched on the peak of a hill, similar to many we'd seen in the distance over the last few days.

The church marked the last ascent of the hike as we clambered steeply down a slope towards the roads of society proper. An hour or so later and we were back to a town, saying goodbye again for the next couple of days. Liam jumped on a bus back to Ljubljana, where he would take a train back to Zürich, while I made my way to the road to resume hitchhiking. My next major destination was also Zürich, but my self imposed trip rules prevented me from jumping on the train too.
It was around 3, and I ambitiously hoped to make to Zürich late the next day. It was 8 hours of driving from where I was, which made it an achievable goal, but I would need luck on my side.
I replenished my energy with a light meal, then went right to it at the road. The day was starting to get on, but I was excited to be on the "home" stretch. In about half an hour, I had a ride.

The young guy that picked me up was an absolute legend. His name was Jan, and he was a video editor/animator trying to move into the voice acting space. He spoke English with a strong American accent, where I initially thought he was from. He explained that a career in voice acting would not be possible with a Slovenian accent, so he had worked hard to improve it. Apparently he was still unsatisfied with it as Americans were still able to tell, but I was impressed.

Unfortunately he wasn't heading very far in my direction, but was more than willing to drop me on the highway heading north. We missed the first turn onto it and had to do a big loop around to pass it again, but it didn't matter as we had a great conversation along the way.

The rest stop I had elected to jump out at was perfect. It was headed north on the main highway out of Slovenia into central Europe, and had a gentle exit ramp I could use to snag my last ride. The only problem was time, as the sun was starting to set and unfortunately my fears of not finding a ride before sunset came true.

That was OK. I was still clinging onto the hope I'd be able to make it to Zürich tomorrow, but knew the chance was slipping away. At least I'd definitely be able to make it to Austria tomorrow, where I would finally be in a German speaking country, a huge milestone.

On the northern side of the rest area there was a cluster of pine trees, the spacing between them harbouring deep shadows, a few benches, and most importantly, flat ground. I picked a spot in darkness, mostly free from the thick knurled roots that wound through the topsoil, and pitched my tent.
I'd somehow lost my spoon that day, but luckily had bought a tongue scraper a few days previously. Luckily it's shaped almost exactly like a spoon, bar the gigantic hole in the centre. :)
It had been a great couple of days doing a normal hike, and the thought of hanging out in Zürich for a few days was exciting.

182.title: Day 192: Austria
paragraphs: Friday 7th November

I packed my tent and was at the exit of the rest stop by about 8. I didn't want to miss too many of the trucks parked there that would be taking off for the day, but I'd unfortunately already heard a few depart.

The spot was up there with the best of them. There wasn't too much traffic, but I was clearly visible and in a great stop for drivers to spot. Surprisingly, it still took an hour to find a lift, but I couldn't complain too much.

The truck I was traveling with brought me to within striking distance of the Austrian border, a journey of about an hour. Another hour long wait passed at another truck stop, before I was picked up by a longer ride.

It was a stressed out cook that grabbed me, and he was desperate to make it to his job in a hotel in the alps before his shift started in a few hours. He'd been down in Serbia visiting his family over the last few days, and had stayed an additional unplanned night the previous night. He'd been on the road since 5 or so, and while he had a bit of time to spare, he was still worried.

We had an interesting conversation, and he told me about how he'd left his job in Germany as he'd seen too much about terror attacks on the news to feel safe there. I think he was a little highly strung.

Luckily he was heading quite deep into Austria, a bit rural but along the route I had intended it take. It bypassed Villach and also turned off the highway that lead up to Germany, both of which would have been difficult obstacles to get around on my own.

He dropped me at Zell am See, a small town in the Austrian countryside, incredibly beautiful but without much traffic. Unfortunately the highways linking the east to the west of Austria aren't as large as those heading in the other directions. This meant that between the highway I was on before, and Innsbruck in the west, was an awkward stretch of intertwined country roads that I would have to find my way through. I figured that the reduced speed would be compensated for by the reduced wait times.

I was wrong. I snagged a few very short lifts in the next few hours, but nothing substantial. The afternoon crept on and I'd only made it about 40km from where I'd been dropped. There wasn't much traffic, and the traffic that was present was mostly local. I started to keep an eye out for somewhere to camp the night, but Austria is quite developed and I couldn't see much flat ground in the rugged terrain beyond the paddocks.

I persisted with my hitching and found one more short ride that brought me to the sight of a beautiful resort town and the Krimmler Waterfall. It wasn't tourist season so everything was closed, and the accommodation I could find was well beyond my budget.

The sky began to quickly darken and I scouted for campsites, but all was either open walking paths or steep, dense forested mountainside with plenty of "no camping" signage. The night was also coming on cold, and I knew I would have a terrible time sleeping in it.

I'd been chilly in my setup previously at under 5 degrees, but tonight would be a few degrees below 0 at this altitude. I wasn't in mortal danger, but I may have had to do some crunches in my bag throughout the night to stay warm. Not a prospect I was loving in the slightest, but resigned myself to anyway.

I waved at a few more cars without success and then made my way up the road towards the east. It exited the town and doubled back for a view over the distant waterfall, where there was a lookout platform. I wasn't sure what was there, but the satellite image seemed to reveal that there was at least a clearing that I could probably stay in.
A few cars passed me as I tried to stay off the road as best I could, walking in the gutter on the right hand side against the cliff.

As I arrived into the viewing platform, a father and son jumped out of a car and approached me. The father, Jochen, greeted me with a grin and inquired as to what I was doing. He'd passed me as I was walking up the road but couldn't stop.

I explained my situation and trip, and he immediately invited me to ride with them if I needed. We had a quick look out at the waterfall together, then I jumped in the back and we were on our way. They were a friendly pair and we had a great conversation as we drove further east into the dense forest. They told me all about their "boys trip" that they were enjoying, with a mother and sister back home, and how the last few days had been spent with fun activities together. It sounded like a blast.

I still didn't have my accommodation figured out, but the drive would take me through more residential area where I was able to find something on the cheaper side to book. It was a little out of the way for the pair and I was prepared to walk, but they gladly dropped me off at the place I had found. We said goodbye but exchanged numbers to stay in touch.

The accommodation I had picked ended up being a bit of a nightmare, with plenty of rules and regulations to keep it self maintaining for the distant owner in Germany. I wont bore you with my complaints.

The highlight of my evening was having a swim in the caravan park pool, before eating and heading to bed. I was stoked to be in a warm bed rather than freezing my toes off in a tent in the Austrian winter.

Fortuna clearly still wanted to even the scales a little though, as I'd clearly turned my fate too much for the better. During the night I used the caravan park bathroom, and slipped badly during my return on the frosted caravan porch wood floor. I scraped my shin and smacked my knee painfully in my half asleep state, and crawled back into bed wincing after wiping some blood off my leg.
I still have the scar on my shin.

183.title: Day 193: Zürich
paragraphs: Saturday 8th November

The night had been frosty, and I counted my lucky stars that I didn't have to sleep outside in it. The valley was filled with a thick mist, that drained the warmth out of me as it rolled across my path.

After ensuring that the caravan would pass the cleaning check and I would get my deposit back, I made my way out onto the road. It was still early, and I hoped I would find a ride that would take me back to the main highway.

While I waited for the first lift, the cold crept through me. It was -2 or so, and I had to periodically pump out a few squats to keep warm. I did eventually get a ride, which allowed me to warm up my hands and face, but it was only for a few minutes up the road, and actually brought me to a worse spot for hitchhiking.

Over the next hour or so I managed to snag a few more rides, and finally make it up to the main highway leading east to Innsbruck, and eventually Switzerland. In the intervening time the fog dispersed and the sun came out, showcasing the beautiful valleys of western Austria.

Getting onto the actual highway proved another challenge. I'd just jumped out of a dangerously old man's car, who'd almost ran over my foot as I was getting my back out, and assessed how I could approach it. I was on the older country road that ran parallel to the highway, but needed to swap to it if I was going to make quicker progress. The ramp leading toward it exited a roundabout and immediately turned onto a bridge with no footpath, meaning there was nowhere for me to really stand to catch the isolated traffic.

I braved it anyway and stood on the side of the widest stretch of road, hoping that a car would be brave enough to stop while still slightly blocking traffic. I copped a few looks in my strange position but within 10 minutes a young guy pulled up and was heading east to my delight.

He was a huge fan of trip I was doing, but was turning South soon to head to Italy so couldn't take me very far. I was very thankful for the ride as he was cheerful and put me in a great mood, and also dropped me at a service centre on the main highway. Potentially making it to Zürich today was back on the cards.
I gladly soaked up some warm rays of sun while waiting at the exit to the petrol station, and before long had another ride, and this one was for a couple of hours!

It was a cheerful woman who's name I've since forgotten who brought me all the way west in Austria to the Swiss border. We talked about travel and the beautiful Austrian mountainsides as we zipped along the motorway westward through the various tunnels and valleys. One of the tunnels we passed through, the Arlberg Road Tunnel, is almost 14km long, piercing straight through the mountainous terrain.

She was kind enough to briefly pull off the highway to find a spot to drop me off, and we hugged goodbye before she resumed her journey north into Germany. I was under an hour's drive from Zürich, and getting more excited by the minute to reach my penultimate destination.

I walked across the border into Switzerland past some cows and chickens grazing in some fields, and stopped at the first petrol station across the border. It was quite residential, but I figured the traffic coming internationally may be heading further west.

I was right, and within 15 minutes an expensive sports car pulled up, with a young driver beckoning for me to jump in. He was a charismatic sports TV presenter for an Austrian channel, and while he wasn't heading into Zürich, he spared no effort in ensuring I copped a subsequent ride. We first sought a layby in St Gallen, but when that proved fruitless he drove me further along the highway to the next rest stop. Not done there, he walked around the parking lot and asked everyone if they could take me further while I waited behind like a child, and found someone heading all the way to Zürich!

I was amazed, and so excited to have locked in one of my last rides. I thanked him profusely and was on my way. The last ride of the day couldn't have been better, and the young German that was heading to Zürich was even heading along the main road right near Liam's house. It felt great to be using my German again consistently.
The rest was history, and I secured some wifi at a café to liaise with Liam, and shortly after I was at his place.
A final step had been done, and now I had three nights to relax and hanging out with some friends. I would be back on the road on Tuesday for my final stretch to Germany...

184.title: Day 194 - 195: Just hanging around
paragraphs: Sunday 9th - Monday 10th November
So I checked my camera roll for the two days I spent in Zürich with Liam and Laura, and I had taken 0 photos, which pretty much checks out.

The only times we left the house were to eat or go shopping, with one short bike ride being our only proper activity. I'd already been to Zürich a couple of times, so was more excited to hang out and play video games with Liam, which is exactly what we did.
We did cook a couple of nice meals, but that's pretty much it.
I loved every second of it.

185.title: Day 196: Done and Dusted
paragraphs: Tuesday 11th November
It was to be the last day of the trip.

I said goodbye to Liam in the mid morning, and made my way to the train station to get to the outskirts of Zürich, where I would find my way to the highway. After not being able to initially understand the train schedules and having to phone Liam for help, I managed to make it to a smaller suburb on the north side of the city.
I was looking forward to sharing with whichever driver I found that they were the last right of some random epic voyage they wouldn't care about, which I thought would be fun.

I'd already decided to end my hitchhiking journey when I crossed the border into Germany. I now had a schedule to stick to with friends to visit, and didn't want to put them out by being delayed. The adventurous part of the journey was also over, and I knew I would have an extended period or residence in Germany to experience the culture here; I didn't need to hitchhike to meet people anymore, nor did I have anywhere to be.

I'd told an old friend Andy that I'd be meeting him in Constance that night, where I would be staying with him. Constance is well known to me, as it is the town that I'd spent almost a year in while on exchange here in Germany in 2018-19. It borders Switzerland, so I was going to be able to enter Germany directly into it and the accompanying flood of old memories. It was a location that marked the end of this trip, memories of a previous life, and the new beginnings of my future life here.

I wandered outward from the train station into some picturesque rolling fields under a wallpaper sky. There was a layby in the highway bordering this small parkland, and I figured I would enter that directly from the rear side.

The park walk was pretty to walk through, and before long I came to the side of the rest area. There in my path sat a nice tall fence, but I managed to hurl my park and self over it without too much trouble. Someone saw me emerge covered in leaves from behind the toilet block, but didn't say anything.

I posted up at the exit and began to wait. A few people stopped over the next couple of hours, but unfortunately none of them were heading to Constance. I did see a few German number plates beginning with "KN", for "Konstanz, but all unfortunately passed me by.

While Constance was only an hour or so away, it was unfortunately not the primary destination of most of the traffic on this outgoing road. The lions share of the traffic was heading back east to St Gallen, or further into Austria. That that was heading to Germany would be mostly turning north-west through Neuhausen. Attached is a handy diagram detailing the predicament I faced.

I'd left it late in the day to start, it already being past 1 when I arrived at the rest area anticipating a quick final leg. This was obviously a mistake, and as the hours passed by I became more dejected that I wouldn't find a lift, and regretful of my lackadaisical attitude that morning.

Finally, a wonderful truck driver stopped and scooped me up. he was heading to Germany, but north west through Neuhausen. He even crunched the numbers and calculated if he could afford to divert through Constance for me, but it was just too far out of the way. He offered to take me as far as we shared a road, which was about 10 minutes. Still, it was a first step.
It also turned out to be my last.

Sunset was early, at around 4:30 at this late in the year, and I used up every minute of the daylight waiting for a lift that didn't come. A heartbreaking amount of "KN" cars passed me by, that I knew would be heading to the destination I hoped for. I had a few more drivers stop too, but all were heading east to St Gallen.
The sun set to my left as I pushed it all the way into the darkness to hope to find a final ride. Nothing came.
I had to assess my options and give up on the hitchhiking; it was too dark, and I couldn't stand around at the lonely gas station indefinitely.

The choice before me was to either creep into some bushes and camp the night, resuming in the morning, or walk just under an hour to the nearest train station and jump aboard for the home stretch. It was a difficult decision, and as much as I didn't want to break my oath properly on the final stretch of the trip, I wanted to sleep in the park even less.
I'm not going to lie, it was a shit end to the trip. I was really looking forward to the finality of a last ride, and ended up essentially breaking my avowed goal in the very final stretch.

At the same time, it was kind of funny that the most proper break in my hitchhiking would happen right here at the end, my crumbling will sending me crawling back to the tried and true methods of public transportation.

My real mistake was fleshing out my timeline before my trip had ended. If I didn't just have one night planned to spend with Andy that I would have had to miss, I definitely would have slept in that park.
The train was, well, pretty standard, compared to the adventure of hitchhiking over the last 3.5 months. As a final gesture I got off on the Swiss side of the border, and walked into Germany on foot.
I thought of the streets ahead of me, the friends waiting, and the journey behind, and walked passed the German flags into a new kind of adventure.
